Five official family flagships / 正式中英文研究題名 F046 | Magnetic Motion Control for Acupuncture Microrobots at the Limit / 磁控針灸微機器人運動控制極限 F047 | Magnetic-Gradient Microrobot Localization at the Limit / 磁場梯度與微機器人定位極限 F048 | Magnetic Microrobot Navigation in Tissue Phantoms at the Limit / 磁控微機器人組織模型導航極限 F049 | Multi-Body Interference in Magnetic Acupuncture Microrobots at the Limit / 磁控針灸微機器人多體干擾極限 F050 | Safety Envelopes for Magnetic Acupuncture Microrobots at the Limit / 磁控微機器人針灸安全包絡極限 The family integration and five distinct microphysical research objects F046 — Dipole-force steering and motion residuals Three-coupling: calibrated magnetic moment × field-gradient actuation × independently witnessed low-Reynolds trajectory. The admissible nonclinical bench is sealed nonliving magnetic-fluid phantoms with independently logged coil current, field map and optical fiducials. The observable endpoint is independent cross-track path deviation [um]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is calibrated deterministic magnetic-field controller with identical coils, tracking, time and electrical energy. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is fluid advection, remanence or field-gradient map bias rather than improved robot steering. This family retains independent contracts for magnetic force and rotation, magnetic-gradient inverse localization, three-dimensional hydrogel routing, particle-resolved interactions and hardware witnessed cutoff. Neither one global accuracy score nor a synthetic optimum can substitute for their native physical units. Withdraw or narrow the claim if field calibration is invalid, coil cutoff fails, measured heating exceeds preregistered bench limits, or control extends beyond sealed inert phantoms. The acupuncture image of measured action inspires precise restraint; it supplies no evidence for an anatomical meridian magnetic mechanism. F047 — Gradient map identifiability and external location truth Three-coupling: 3D gradient-field inverse problem × magnetic-source ambiguity × independently calibrated fiducial localization. The admissible nonclinical bench is sealed transparent nonliving phantom with triaxial field probes, physical calibration grid and optically tracked position truth. The observable endpoint is 95 percent held-out position error [um]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is classical fiducial-calibrated position estimator with fixed field-map interpolation and identical sensor resource budgets. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is magnetization ambiguity, axis misalignment and a shared field-reference calibration artifact. This family retains independent contracts for magnetic force and rotation, magnetic-gradient inverse localization, three-dimensional hydrogel routing, particle-resolved interactions and hardware witnessed cutoff. Neither one global accuracy score nor a synthetic optimum can substitute for their native physical units. Withdraw or narrow the claim if position uncertainty exceeds the frozen bound, field inversion becomes nonidentifiable, or an uncalibrated source is interpreted as a precise location. The philosophical limits of naming become a disciplined willingness to mark location as unknown when observability is lost. F048 — Porous-gel navigation under geometry and drag uncertainty Three-coupling: hydrogel pore geometry × viscosity-dependent magnetic transport × independent depth and obstacle witness. The admissible nonclinical bench is sealed nonliving hydrogel microchannels with matched pore-size phantoms, calibrated viscosity and no living-cell exposure. The observable endpoint is obstacle-adjusted route deviation [um]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is fixed magnetic steering schedule and passive tracer comparison in matched porous phantoms. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is gel swelling, wall slip, phantom channel shortcut or passive convective transport. This family retains independent contracts for magnetic force and rotation, magnetic-gradient inverse localization, three-dimensional hydrogel routing, particle-resolved interactions and hardware witnessed cutoff. Neither one global accuracy score nor a synthetic optimum can substitute for their native physical units. Withdraw or narrow the claim if phantom tear or trapped particle is unaccounted, path error breaches the route envelope, or biologic tissue performance is inferred from an inert gel. A route through an inert model is not the acupuncture meridian; the distinction keeps analogy from overruling measured anatomy. F049 — Dipole–dipole coupling, agglomeration and identity conservation Three-coupling: pairwise magnetic interaction × hydrodynamic collective coupling × independently resolved particle identity. The admissible nonclinical bench is sealed transparent nonliving suspension with known particle count, adjustable spacing and a separately measured magnetic-field schedule. The observable endpoint is nearest-neighbor trajectory divergence [um]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is noninteracting independent-particle model and fixed-spacing passive-bead control under equal field and imaging budgets. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is particle collision, reversible chains, optical overlap or concentration-induced fluid dynamics rather than controlled coordination. This family retains independent contracts for magnetic force and rotation, magnetic-gradient inverse localization, three-dimensional hydrogel routing, particle-resolved interactions and hardware witnessed cutoff. Neither one global accuracy score nor a synthetic optimum can substitute for their native physical units. Withdraw or narrow the claim if agglomeration breaches the count ledger, identities cannot be resolved, unintended chain growth occurs, or a cluster is counted as a single controlled object. Harmony is a philosophical question about coexistence, but the scientific test is an interaction tensor and complete particle inventory. F050 — Hardwired stop and worst-tail magnetic energy control Three-coupling: magnetic energy and heating envelope × independent stop authority × physical containment and material inventory. The admissible nonclinical bench is interlocked sealed hydrogel and magnetic-fluid phantom with electrical shunt, temperature sensor, independent relay and complete tool-count ledger. The observable endpoint is post-veto unintended displacement [um]. Its strongest plausible benchmark is hardwired field cutoff and low-complexity deterministic controller evaluated against identical extreme tests. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is inductive energy discharge, stale position estimates, hidden field hot spots or uncounted tool remnants. This family retains independent contracts for magnetic force and rotation, magnetic-gradient inverse localization, three-dimensional hydrogel routing, particle-resolved interactions and hardware witnessed cutoff. Neither one global accuracy score nor a synthetic optimum can substitute for their native physical units. Withdraw or narrow the claim if any field remains without authorization, measured thermal limit is exceeded, lost particle is unaccounted, or veto does not physically disable actuation. 有底氣的溫暖 becomes an engineering demand: reversible action, independently effective boundaries and a witnessed stop, not a therapeutic assertion.

The observable endpoint is independent cross-track path deviation [um]. The central mistaken-mechanism alternative is fluid advection, remanence or field-gradient map bias rather than improved robot steering. Neither one global accuracy score nor a synthetic optimum can substitute for their native physical units. summary: This version (v3.1.0-2021-2024) contains reproducibility materials for the 2021-2024 National Immunization Survey-Teen analysis of parent-reported clinician recommendation, preventive-care access, and insurance gaps in U.S. adolescent HPV vaccination. The provider-phase sample comprises 66,938 adolescents aged 13-17 years, and multivariable complete-case models comprise 60,338 adolescents. Relative to v3.0.0-2021-2024 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22796335), every statistical analysis script (01, 02, 04, 07, 08) and all 35 aggregate statistical and diagnostic tables are preserved byte-for-byte without refitting any models. This update upgrades script 06_ahp_figures.R, the PDF/SVG vector exports for Figures 1-3 and Supplementary Figure S1, and their companion aggregate figure source-data CSVs to match journal artwork conventions (adding the annual recommendation-stratified up-to-date panel to Figure 1, expanding Figure 2 to display both primary overall and insurance-stratified adjusted probabilities and differences, and adding private-insurance benchmark reference lines to Figure 3). The package includes six scientific R scripts, an optional public CDC downloader, a dependency checker, aggregate analysis and diagnostic tables (including 999 Rao-Wu stratified bootstrap replicates for two-stage inverse-probability complete-case weighting and complete six-category reason reporting), source data and PDF/SVG exports for three main figures and one supplementary figure, software session records, execution-verification files, and SHA-256 checksums. Primary adjusted recommendation-associated differences are 21.7 and 22.5 percentage points for initiation and up-to-date vaccination; IPCW sensitivity differences are 21.2 and 22.1 points. Script 01 reads source files for 2018-2024; script 04 restricts the analysis to 2021-2024 and uses annual provider weights divided by four. Run scripts in the order documented in the README: dependency check, 01, 04 with --skip-ipcw, 07 final 999 8, 08, and 06. Script 02 supplies analysis functions and should not be run as a standalone seven-year analysis. Raw CDC public-use files and individual-level processed extracts are not redistributed. Obtain public-use files and documentation from the CDC NIS-Teen data and documentation page . The package contains code and aggregate outputs only.
title: Reproducibility package for NIS-Teen HPV vaccination analysis, 2021-2024

Research link for F191: the controlled domain is a hard-gated risk taxonomy integrating material exposure, reversibility, field energy, traceability and permitted use. Its main independent observations are false-permission rate [1], hazard-class recall [1], stop response [ms], contrasted with prespecified hazard classification table plus independent FMEA review under the same case and assessor budget. A predeclared antagonist is a favorable mean score hiding a rare severe or irreversible event; the blinded intervention is to plant a concealed high-severity case among low-risk nominal cases and blind-score both gate decision and audit trail. This flagship-specific design keeps the title from being an empty keyword bundle and ensures that future discoverability points readers to an actual falsifiable method. 02 | Five-Flagship Coupling from Risk Classification to Genuine Withdrawal Evidence F191 asks what may enter an authorized test. F192 asks who can revoke permission and whether output actually stops. F193 asks if a safe-looking microtool stays safe after aging. F194 asks whether a safety decision survives a second platform. F195 asks what remains without mechanical help. Together they form a sequence of noncompensatory evidence gates. Every equation receives unique physical interpretation and unit assumptions, its own three-dimensional observable sensitivity question, and a predeclared competitor with a stopping threshold. Its main independent observations are schema field fidelity [%], missed-veto fraction [1], replay disagreement [1], contrasted with versioned open-schema adapter with independent human semantic inspection and matched classical computation. A predeclared antagonist is an incompatible platform silently dropping stop conditions while preserving favorable prediction scores; the blinded intervention is to withhold a schema-version mutation that changes one hard refusal field and replay identical cases on isolated stacks. This flagship-specific design keeps the title from being an empty keyword bundle and ensures that future discoverability points readers to an actual falsifiable method. 05 | A Five-Layer Nonclinical Evidence System with Hard Refusal First constrain identity and approved use. Second calibrate independent hazard, force and material witnesses. Third conduct fair cost-matched benchmark experiments. Fourth conceal severe exceptions, aged lots and broken schema fields. Fifth let an independent laboratory reconstruct both an allowed event and a refusal from a frozen audit archive. Its main independent observations are unassisted proxy task score [1], residual actuator force [N], cutoff delay [ms], contrasted with assistance-matched passive dummy controller, blinded independent task assessment and wired cutoff. summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FAIR-bioHeaders Specification

summary: SideCow-VSS is a side-view dairy cow video semantic segmentation dataset developed to support computer vision research in precision livestock farming. The original study describes 921 five-second video clips with dense pixel-level annotations, sampled at 10 frames per second under real dairy farm conditions. The annotations were generated using a semi-automated pipeline involving YOLOv11, SAM2, and manual verification. This version (v1.0.0) provides the currently available JPEG frames and PNG segmentation annotation files, organized into the original training, validation, and testing splits. The release contains 46,024 JPEG files and 46,024 PNG files, distributed as follows: Training: 32,177 JPEG files and 32,177 PNG files. Validation: 6,897 JPEG files and 6,897 PNG files. Testing: 6,950 JPEG files and 6,950 PNG files. The dataset supports semantic segmentation of dairy cows and background regions. The original data partitions and available files are preserved without reconstructing missing frames. For details of dataset construction, annotation methodology, and benchmarking, please refer to the associated publication: Yao, L., Liu, J., Hong, W., Kong, F., Fan, Z., Lei, L., & Li, X. (2025). SideCow-VSS: A Video Semantic Segmentation Dataset and Benchmark for Intelligent Monitoring of Dairy Cows Health in Smart Ranch Environments. Veterinary Sciences , 12(11), 1104. DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/vetsci12111104
title: SideCow-VSS: A Side-View Dairy Cow Video Semantic Segmentation Dataset

summary: Configuration-driven Python pipeline (code and locked analysis plan) for the study 'Survey-design-calibrated independence tests reduce adjustment-set validity in PC-based causal discovery'. It implements design-corrected conditional-independence tests (Rao-Scott, design t test), PC-stable with temporal tiers, seven confounder-selection strategies, cross-fitted AIPW with design-based standard errors, and a simulation benchmark mimicking the 2017 Indonesia Demographic and Health Survey. IDHS microdata are not included and must be requested from The DHS Program. Release v1.1 added the deviation log (CATATAN_DEVIASI.md) and the verification scripts and reports in verifikasi/. Release v1.2 adds the exploratory strategy M7 (optimal adjustment set estimated from the M3 graph): bench_v4_m7.py and its per-replication output naskah/data/benchmark_v4/per_rep_m7.csv (4,800 replications; data and graphs identical to M0-M6), documented as a deviation in CATATAN_DEVIASI.md section 7. Release v1.3 adds the verification material for the reproducibility manuscript (verifikasi/naskah3/revisi5/): an AST-based configuration-import checker run over the git history, controlled fault injection, a BLAS thread test, bootstrap seeding schemes, a 2x2 code x configuration benchmark design with Monte Carlo intervals, and OpenTimestamps proofs for two analysis-plan manifests. The application modules causal.py, baseline.py and sol_dag.py now seed the random stream per analysis (deviation log section 8). Release v1.4 adds verification material requested in the review of the reproducibility manuscript (verifikasi/naskah3/revisi6/): detection limits of the import checker on 11 stale-import variants compared with Import Linter and a runtime guard, fault injection derived from an external configuration-error taxonomy (Yin et al., SOSP 2011), Holm correction for the 2x2 design, ULP-based floating-point differences, and an independent check of the OpenTimestamps block attestations. Import Linter is listed separately in requirements-verifikasi.txt so that the locked analysis environment is unchanged.
title: Kausal IDHS: design-based causal graph discovery and confounder selection for complex survey data

summary: Large language model research agents can connect literature retrieval, analysis code, and manuscript preparation, but coherent output does not establish scientific validity. We developed Plato-Bio, a biology-routed extension of the open Plato/Denario architecture that couples explicit workflow states with provenance records, citation checks, claim-to-evidence links, scoped file writes, and publication gates. A source audit identified and repaired three defects that could distort evaluation: loss of task domain in the default factory, omission of declared method signals from scoring, and evidence sidecars that lacked the drafted-claim denominator. On the current clean revision, the full Python suite completed with 931 passes, six skips, and no failures or errors; targeted biology, genomics, evidence/citation, and adversarial-safety suites likewise completed without failure. We evaluated two narrow use cases. In a frozen historical rediscovery task, independent pre-1986 literature bridges ranked the later-studied relation between fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon first; TF-IDF ranked it second and corpus frequency third. This single curated task measures retrospective ranking, not prospective discovery. In a separate comparison of AlphaFold models with experimental structures for 15 human proteins, 11 targets had high-confidence-core C-alpha RMSD below 1 Angstrom (median 0.501 Angstrom). Four targets exceeded 2 Angstrom, and confidence masking reduced the SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Angstrom over 74 residues. The workflow emitted 27 traceable discrepancy regions, all retained as unvalidated hypotheses. Plato-Bio therefore provides reproducible software contracts and auditable screening baselines; broader claims of agent efficacy or biological novelty require preregistered evaluation, independent review, and prospective validation.
title: Plato-Bio: verification-first biological novelty screening with temporal rediscovery and structural benchmarks

summary: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). The stability term was lower at the savanna site (0.39) than at the zoo (0.65-0.67), showing that it penalises the natural diel cycle of bird activity. Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation provide a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.
title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo

summary: The study examines the physiological adaptation of boxers to mid-altitude conditions (1,800‒2,200 m above sea level) and substantiates the need to individualize training loads based on functional markers: blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), heart rate (HR), lactate levels, and maximum oxygen consumption (VO2). The article presents the results of a pedagogical experiment involving 24 qualified boxers (CMS and MS), divided into control and experimental groups. The experimental methodology included real-time monitoring of functional markers and real-time adjustment of the weekly microcycle. Following a 4-week high-altitude training camp, the experimental group demonstrated a significant increase in VO2 by 6.8%, hemoglobin concentration by 4.3%, and an improvement in the heart rate recovery index by 34.4% compared to the control group (p<0.05). The obtained data demonstrate the high efficiency of an individualized approach to load planning in midaltitude areas and are recommended for use in the training of highly qualified athletes.
title: Individualization of Boxing Training Loads in Middle-Altitude Conditions Based on Functional Adaptation Markers.

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: This paper presents our submission to the ACMMM25 - Grand Challenge on Multimedia Verification. We developed a multi-agent verification system that combines Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with specialized verification tools to detect multimedia misinformation. Our system operates through six stages: raw data processing, planning, information extraction, deep research, evidence collection, and report generation. The core Deep Researcher Agent employs four tools: reverse image search, metadata analysis, fact-checking databases, and verified news processing that extracts spatial, temporal, attribution, and motivational context. We demonstrate our approach on a challenge dataset sample involving complex multimedia content. Our system successfully verified content authenticity, extracted precise geolocation and timing information, and traced source attribution across multiple platforms, effectively addressing real-world multimedia verification scenarios.
title: Multimedia Verification Through Multi-Agent Deep Research Multimodal Large Language Models

summary: This version extends the previously archived replication package for within-project and cross-project just-in-time software defect prediction. The package includes four additional experimental components: C4: Controlled training-set size and class-distribution matching across 13 Apache projects, four machine learning algorithms, and 20 model refits. C5: Sensitivity analyses examining SHAP evaluation sample size and background selection. C6: A descriptive simulation of defect-oriented commit review prioritization. C7: External validation using six historical Kamei projects, comprising 960 model records and corresponding global SHAP feature-importance vectors. The C7 source-provenance audit confirmed that SHA-256 fingerprints, input summaries, and temporal training/test splits matched the archived experimental records for all six projects. All 36 crosschecks passed. This verification does not constitute independent retraining of all models. The findings concern the sensitivity of global SHAP feature rankings to training conditions. They do not establish causal effects, explanation correctness, or demonstrated benefits to software developers. The archive contains experimental outputs, analysis scripts, figures, and reproducibility documentation. Original third-party ApacheJIT and Kamei datasets are not redistributed. Previous version: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23301636
title: Replication Package for Training-Source Sensitivity of Global SHAP Explanations in Just-in-Time Defect Prediction: Matched-Class Refits and Kamei External Validation

summary: Supporting code and data for the exploratory ETV4 case study “Sequence and family context shape ETV4 representations in protein language models”. The deposit contains 711 biological/control activation arrays from ESM-2 650M, ESM-2 3B and ProFam, 71 numerical-qualification arrays with receipts, and a versioned repository snapshot containing processed results, input sequences and prompts, fixed readout masks and configurations, analysis and figure-generation code, provenance and supplementary information. A portable NumPy analysis verifies array identities and recomputes both canonical summaries without rerunning the protein models. All saved fields, including 107,102 numerical values, matched in local verification. The study examines dependence of protein representations on sequence and family context; it does not establish regulatory specificity or an allosteric mechanism. Original code is licensed under MIT; original derived data and written materials are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials retain their own terms. The code snapshot filename identifies its Git commit. Development repository: https://github.com/amoyag/etv4-context-representations .
tags: ETV4; protein language models; ESM-2; ProFam; intrinsically disordered regions; protein representations; reproducibility.
title: Code and data for "Sequence and family context shape ETV4 representations in protein language models"

summary: We present the first mechanised formalisation of Romanov's Triplet Logic (TLS) in the Rocq proof assistant. TLS is a combinatorial framework originally motivated by Boolean satisfiability, based on triplet structures and a filter that we call Simple Vertex Intersection (SVI). We formalise the core of TLS, including its translation from 3-CNF, the clearing procedure, and the SVI algorithm. For the well-formed sliding-window fragment, we prove explicit polynomial-time bounds for the filter stages and verify the translation and intersection operations. Our main contribution is a precise correctness boundary: for general formulas, SVI non-emptiness is necessary but not sufficient for satisfiability; for aligned structures, we prove a full bi-implication, extended to systems of structures. We also formalise the grouped-window translation and provide a formal counterexample to its completeness. We introduce VFR (Verified Filter for Romanov's triplet logic), an extracted OCaml prototype that implements a verified decision procedure for the sliding-window fragment and a sound filter for general 3-CNF, with a Python runtime and Docker packaging. Benchmarks corroborate the predicted behaviour, and the complete toolchain is available as a curated Zenodo artifact. The Rocq development comprises over 23,000 lines of code, with 424 proved lemmas and no unproved assumptions.
title: Formal Verification of Romanov's Triplet Logic: A Verified Filter for Sliding-window 3-CNF with Application to Structured Formulas

summary: Reusable robot skills are becoming the basic units through which embodied agents turn open-ended instructions into long-horizon physical behavior. We argue that, while foundation models have collapsed the cost of creating these skills, the cost of trusting them has not. Existing skill-evolution loops refine skills through execution feedback, unit tests, environment reward, or LLM self-critique, but these signals provide only trace-level evidence: they show that a skill worked on sampled executions, not that skill-induced plans satisfy temporal safety contracts under untested conditions. We introduce VASO, a framework for verification-guided self-evolution of LLM-generated robot skill contracts. In VASO, each skill is represented as a semantic contract with two coupled interfaces: a formal interface that aligns robot states, observations, and control commands with logical propositions for model checking, and a planner-facing interface that guides executable behavior generation. A model checker first filters logically inconsistent skill contracts, then verifies plans induced by the skill against global and local temporal specifications. When verification fails, VASO translates the counterexample trace into a textual gradient that updates the reusable skill contract while keeping foundation-model weights frozen. On Clearpath Jackal and PX4 quadcopter tasks, VASO reaches 97.2% formal-specification compliance using fewer than 100 optimization samples, outperforming execution-feedback, prompt-optimization, and fine-tuning baselines. To our knowledge, VASO is the first framework that closes the loop between formal verification and self-evolving LLM-generated skills for physical AI agents: formal counterexamples become optimization feedback for reusable robot skill contracts, rather than merely verifying one-off plans, tuning planner prompts, or fine-tuning model weights.
title: VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents

summary: Mathematical reasoning demands two critical, complementary skills: constructing rigorous proofs for true statements and discovering counterexamples that disprove false ones. However, current AI efforts in mathematics focus almost exclusively on proof construction, often neglecting the equally important task of finding counterexamples. In this paper, we address this gap by fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to reason about and generate counterexamples. We formalize this task as formal counterexample generation, which requires LLMs not only to propose candidate counterexamples but also to produce formal proofs that can be automatically verified in the Lean 4 theorem prover. To enable effective learning, we introduce a symbolic mutation strategy that constructs candidate counterexample-generation tasks by systematically extracting theorems and removing selected hypotheses. Together with curated datasets, this strategy enables a multi-reward expert iteration framework that substantially enhances both the effectiveness and efficiency of training LLMs for counterexample generation and theorem proving. Experiments on three newly collected benchmarks validate the advantages of our approach, showing that the mutation strategy and training framework yield substantial performance gains.
title: Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with Large Language Models

summary: Hydrogen threatens the structural integrity of metals and thus predicting hydrogen-material interactions is key to unlocking the role of hydrogen in the energy transition. Quantifying the interplay between material deformation and hydrogen diffusion ahead of cracks and other stress concentrators is key to the prediction and prevention of hydrogen-assisted failures. In this work, a generalised theoretical and computational framework is presented that for the first time encompasses: (i) stress-assisted diffusion, (ii) hydrogen trapping due to multiple trap types, rigorously accounting for the rate of creation of dislocation trap sites, (iii) hydrogen transport through dislocations, (iv) equilibrium (Oriani) and non-equilibrium (McNabb-Foster) trapping kinetics, (v) hydrogen-induced softening, and (vi) hydrogen uptake, considering the role of hydrostatic stresses and local electrochemistry. Particular emphasis is placed on the numerical implementation in COMSOL Multiphysics, releasing the relevant models and discussing stability, discretisation and solver details. Each of the elements of the framework is independently benchmarked against results from the literature and implications for the prediction of hydrogen-assisted fractures are discussed. The second part of this work (Part II) shows how these crack tip predictions can be combined with crack growth simulations.
title: A COMSOL framework for predicting hydrogen embrittlement -- Part I: coupled hydrogen transport

summary: We introduce an automated, formal, counterexample-based approach to synthesise Barrier Certificates (BC) for the safety verification of continuous and hybrid dynamical models. The approach is underpinned by an inductive framework: this is structured as a sequential loop between a learner, which manipulates a candidate BC structured as a neural network, and a sound verifier, which either certifies the candidate's validity or generates counter-examples to further guide the learner. We compare the approach against state-of-the-art techniques, over polynomial and non-polynomial dynamical models: the outcomes show that we can synthesise sound BCs up to two orders of magnitude faster, with in particular a stark speedup on the verification engine (up to five orders less), whilst needing a far smaller data set (up to three orders less) for the learning part. Beyond improvements over the state of the art, we further challenge the new approach on a hybrid dynamical model and on larger-dimensional models, and showcase the numerical robustness of our algorithms and codebase.
title: Automated and Formal Synthesis of Neural Barrier Certificates for Dynamical Models

summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 42 examines why enterprise artificial intelligence strategy is moving beyond the assumption that one general-purpose model should serve every workload. The paper argues that model selection is increasingly an intelligence-allocation decision involving capability, cost, latency, governance, data restrictions, decision authority and measurable business outcomes. As enterprise AI expands across routine classification, specialised extraction, complex reasoning, multimodal production and consequential decisions, different categories of work require different execution approaches. The paper distinguishes model selection, inference tiering, model routing, policy-controlled routing and outcome verification. It proposes that enterprises should first determine whether generative inference is required, define the minimum capability needed, apply mandatory eligibility constraints, select an appropriate execution route, establish escalation conditions and verify whether the completed outcome meets a predetermined business acceptance standard. Six author-developed frameworks structure this operating model. The AI Workload Classification framework divides work into deterministic, routine language, specialised, complex reasoning and consequential-decision categories. The Model Routing Matrix separates mandatory policy constraints from economic and performance preferences. The Capability-Cost Frontier evaluates eligible models against verified acceptance and complete delivery cost. The Model Escalation Ladder defines structured movement from deterministic execution through compact, specialised and frontier intelligence to human authority. Minimum Sufficient Intelligence identifies the least expensive eligible intelligence capable of satisfying the complete business requirement. Cost per Accepted Outcome, or CPAO, measures total attributable workflow delivery cost against completed business outcomes that satisfy defined acceptance standards. The analysis also challenges the assumption that sophisticated routing automatically produces superior economics. Evidence from LLMRouterBench shows strong model complementarity while demonstrating that several routing approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines. The paper therefore argues that routing complexity requires evidence of incremental value rather than being treated as an architectural objective in itself. Commercial case studies examine three different intelligence-allocation mechanisms. Sword Health illustrates central gateway control, provider portability, policy enforcement and cost attribution. Forethought demonstrates how specialised deployment, multi-model endpoints and serverless inference affect AI infrastructure economics. gimmefy illustrates multimodel execution across different marketing modalities and provider capabilities. The cases are treated separately because their reported outcomes rely on different commercial baselines and measurement approaches. The paper proposes a 90-day evaluation path based on workload classification, baseline measurement, shadow testing, controlled deployment and an explicit investment decision. summary: Herrero García, José Luis. “La reivindicación marroquí y la soberanía española sobre Ceuta y Melilla.” Boletín CODESEL , vol. 2, no. 11, Oct. 2026, pp. 1–15. ISSN 3045-7750 LEGAL REVIEW The territorial claims advanced by the Kingdom of Morocco concerning Ceuta, Melilla and the remaining Spanish territories in North Africa constitute a particularly complex controversy at the intersection of international public law, historical sovereignty, territorial integrity, decolonisation and European security. Although these claims are frequently presented through the political vocabulary of colonial restitution and national reunification, their historical and legal foundations require examination beyond the geographical proximity of the disputed territories or the nationalist narratives surrounding Morocco's independence. In this extensive historical and juridical study, José Luis Herrero García undertakes a systematic examination of Moroccan territorial revisionism and the legal continuity of Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. His principal argument challenges the doctrine of Greater Morocco by distinguishing premodern religious allegiances, dynastic dominion and military expansion from the legal characteristics of territorial sovereignty under contemporary international law. Through the combined analysis of medieval political formations, historical treaties, constitutional provisions, international judicial reasoning and European institutional practice, the article develops a comprehensive interpretation of the historical and legal circumstances supporting Spain's position. The significance of the study extends beyond the bilateral dispute, raising fundamental questions concerning the construction of historical territorial titles, the stability of international borders and the limitations imposed by international law upon irredentist claims. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 43 examines the governance and evidence requirements that arise when artificial intelligence influences consequential business decisions. The paper defines a decision chain of custody as a controlled, verifiable record connecting the information used, systems involved, applicable policies, delegated authority, approvals, execution and preserved evidence behind an AI-influenced decision. Its central operating test is independent reconstruction: an authorised reviewer should be able to determine what happened, which authority permitted the action and how the resulting business state was verified without relying on the original operator's memory. The analysis distinguishes decision custody from related concepts including accuracy, explainability, data lineage, observability and content provenance. It argues that these controls answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable forms of transparency. Content provenance might identify the history of a digital asset, for example, while providing no evidence that a user held authority to approve a payment or that the resulting transaction was correctly executed. The paper proposes eight linked evidence domains for consequential AI-influenced decisions: information received, intelligence used, rules applied, tools invoked, state changed, authority held, outcome approved and evidence preserved. These domains connect through a shared decision identifier and are intended to preserve relationships between initial inputs, policy evaluation, delegated authority, approval, execution and verified outcome. Particular attention is given to the moment of commitment, when an AI-generated recommendation becomes an external or financial business action. The paper argues that approvals must remain linked to the material terms ultimately executed. Changes to amount, recipient, purpose or other material conditions require a defined re-evaluation path rather than reliance on an earlier approval. The paper also addresses delegation across multiple agents and systems, retry behaviour, transaction reconciliation, evidence integrity, retention, human oversight and supplier evidence obligations. It distinguishes reconstruction from reproduction and outcome verification, noting that exact reproduction of stochastic model output is neither always possible nor necessary for reconstructing observable system behaviour. Three cases illustrate different dimensions of the argument. IBM provides company-reported evidence of reduced data-clearance processing time within an integrated governance programme. HSBC demonstrates large-scale financial-crime detection alongside explainable and auditable investigative outputs. AstraZeneca provides published evidence concerning the organisational scope and challenges of ethics-based AI auditing. None of these cases is presented as proof of a complete decision-custody architecture. The paper proposes consequence-based evidence requirements, independent reconstruction tests, explicit stop conditions for missing authority or mandatory evidence, supplier acceptance tests and measurable indicators including reconstruction pass rate, authority coverage, approval match, outcome reconciliation and preservation verification. The chapter concludes that auditability after an AI-influenced decision is becoming as important as intelligence before the decision. Enterprises expanding autonomous authority should first demonstrate that completed consequential decisions can be independently reconstructed from preserved evidence with clear ownership, valid authority and verified outcomes. The eight-domain decision record, consequence-based evidence model, reconstruction tests and associated management controls are author-developed conceptual frameworks informed by established provenance, AI governance, legal and assurance sources. They are not externally validated standards or universal legal requirements.
title: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 43: Every AI Decision Needs a Chain of Custody

summary: A negative and methodological result on Edward Elgar's Dorabella cipher (87 arc symbols, 14 July 1897). Thirty decipherment hypotheses were each tested against shuffled-symbol nulls and enciphered-English controls; all were ruled out or disfavoured. About 10% drawing slips reduce a standard substitution solver from 97% to about 57% accuracy on 87-letter controls, so earlier "not English" verdicts do not cover a carelessly drawn cipher; a slip-tolerant solver places Dorabella above all shuffles but below all English controls. Neighbouring arcs that are 180° flips of each other are strongly over-represented (27 of 86 against 12.6 expected, p ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵). The cipher is not solved. AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) was used in transcription, decipherment, checking and drafting, under the author's direction; it is disclosed in the text. No archival images are reproduced.
title: Elgar's Dorabella cipher (14 July 1897): thirty hypothesis tests with shuffled and enciphered controls, a slip-tolerance loophole, and an excess of opposed neighbouring arcs

summary: RSE-AS: Research Code, Trained SAC Models, and Evaluation Results for Renewable Microgrid Energy Management This repository accompanies the research study entitled “Causality-Aware Economic Action Selection for Battery-Constrained Microgrid Energy Management: A Computational Trade-off Between Soft Actor-Critic and Model Predictive Control.” It provides the original research code, five pretrained Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) models, experimental evaluation results, and additional numerical verification artifacts for Causality-Aware Risk-Sensitive Economic Action Selection (RSE-AS) . RSE-AS is a post-policy economic action-selection mechanism that evaluates battery-feasible candidate actions using chronologically available forecasts, economic scoring, and uncertainty-dependent regularization without retraining the underlying SAC policies. Repository Contents Original research archive (Version 1) Research notebooks: Two Google Colab notebooks documenting the research workflow and dataset preparation. Pretrained SAC models: Five saved policies corresponding to random seeds 42, 43, 44, 45, and 46, each trained for 100,000 environment interactions. Chronological evaluation: Results for validation in 2021, full-year testing in 2022, and the available 8,753 hourly observations from 2023. Distribution-shift evaluation: Results under increased electricity demand (+20%), reduced photovoltaic (PV) generation (−30%), increased electricity tariffs (+50%), and combined perturbations. Ablation analysis: Comparisons among RSE-AS, Economic-Only, Fixed attenuation, Adaptive attenuation, and unmodified SAC actions. Statistical analysis: Seed-level results, paired cost differences, nominal confidence intervals, and exact two-sided sign tests. Documentation: README, software requirements, reproducibility notes, data-source attribution, and licensing information. Additional verification archive (Version 2) reproduce_rse_2023.py — Python source code for the numerical replay audit. RSE_AS_2023_hourly_all_seeds.csv — Hourly replay trajectories for five frozen SAC policies. replay_vs_original.csv — Comparison of replayed and previously recorded results. verification_report.csv — Results of the 16 implemented verification checks. verification_metadata.json — Evaluation configuration, numerical discrepancies, and software environment information. README_VERIFICATION.md — Documentation of the additional audit and its limitations. The Version 2 verification materials are included in RSE_AS_2023_Verification_Update.zip , alongside the retained original research archive. Experimental Configuration The investigated grid-connected microgrid includes a battery energy storage system with the following parameters: Nominal battery capacity: 200 kWh . Maximum charging/discharging power: 50 kW . State-of-charge (SOC) limits: 20%–90% . Charging and discharging efficiencies: 95% . Nominal initial SOC: 50% . Dispatch interval: 1 hour . SAC observation dimension: 12 . SAC action dimension: 1 . The SAC policies were trained using the 2017–2020 dataset, with 2021 reserved for validation and controller development. The complete 2022 period was used for primary chronological testing, while the available 2023 observations provided an additional evaluation period. The 2023 data were examined during research development and are not presented as a previously untouched holdout. Under four controlled distribution-shift scenarios, cost savings relative to Fixed attenuation ranged from 1.46% to 1.76% . summary: The rapid growth of blockchain networks has raised concerns about their environmental sustainability, yet existing assessments are fragmented and often rely on problematic metrics or unverifiable self-reported data. This article addresses these gaps by combining quantitative measures of annual energy consumption and carbon emissions with a qualitative assessment of sustainability initiatives. Using data from the Crypto Carbon Ratings Institute (CCRI) and corporate sustainability reports, we evaluate Bitcoin, Ethereum, Binance Chain, XRP, Cardano, Solana, Dogecoin, Polygon, and Polkadot, and benchmark their operational footprints against those of Visa and Mastercard as representatives of traditional payment systems. Results show wide variation in sustainability performance: Proof-of-Stake networks exhibit substantially lower energy use and carbon intensity than Proof-of-Work systems, while transparency and reporting practices differ significantly across projects. This research contributes to the sustainability discourse by providing one of the first systematic comparisons between blockchain networks and incumbent payment systems, identifying methodological challenges in sustainability accounting, and advancing policy recommendations for standardized reporting, third-party verification, and energy-efficient design. This is the published version of: Mabrouk, H., Paul, L., & Wild, D. (2026). Sustainability Metrics and Disclosure Alignment in Blockchain Networks. Blockchain and Cryptocurrency, 4(1), 1–9. IFSA Publishing, S. L. Originally published on 23 March 2026. summary: Data and code that reproduce every number, table and figure in the manuscript "What Do Indonesian Artificial Intelligence Courses Teach That Industry Asks For? A Multi-University Curriculum Audit That Accounts for Lecturer Disagreement" (submitted to Computer Applications in Engineering Education). The study compares 953 course learning outcomes from 71 AI-related courses at 19 Indonesian universities with 840 requirement sentences from 51 AI job postings. A multilingual sentence-embedding model (paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2) finds the closest match in both directions, and similarity is converted into the probability that a lecturer would accept the match, using judgements from four faculty validators and a lead researcher, under six judgement standards and three calibration curve shapes. Curriculum relevance, demand coverage and their harmonic mean (alignment) are reported for the corpus, universities, Bloom levels, AI-relevance tiers, courses and skills, with cluster-bootstrap intervals, size controls, cross-validation of the calibration curves and a verb-swap check. Contents: paper4_replication.zip holds the anonymised data (universities coded U01 to U19, courses C01 to C71), the expert labels (cosine similarity, labels and job-statement group only; the texts of the judged pairs are not included), one Google Colab script (code/paper4_replication.py) and a README that maps each output file to the table or figure it produces. paper4_results.zip holds the outputs of the published run, and similarity_matrix.npy the 953 x 840 cosine similarity matrix. Raw validator forms contain personal data and are not released.
title: Replication package for: What Do Indonesian Artificial Intelligence Courses Teach That Industry Asks For? A Multi-University Curriculum Audit That Accounts for Lecturer Disagreement

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: for every preorder that contains no “crown”, the support polynomial of its preorder polytope is the h-polynomial of a flag simplicial sphere, which settles the flag form of a 2026 conjecture of Athanasiadis and Chapoton for that class. The release also identifies the gamma-coefficients as counts of matchable pairs (found at the same time, independently, by Y. Zhong) and proves two Ehrhart conjectures from the same paper. The objects. A preorder is a way of ranking things in which ties are allowed. Athanasiadis and Chapoton (arXiv:2605.26916) attached to each preorder τ on n elements a lattice polytope Q τ : its integer points are the ways of putting nonnegative whole-number loads on the elements so that no downward-closed group carries more than its own size. Counting these points by how many loads are nonzero gives a polynomial H τ (t). For the chain 1 < 2 < 3 the counts are 1, 6, 6, 1, and 1 + 6t + 6t 2 + t 3 = (1+t) 3 + 3t(1+t); the 3 counts the three ways to pick one element and one strictly above it. The conjectures. Athanasiadis and Chapoton conjectured that H τ always looks like the h-polynomial of a sphere: palindromic, unimodal, gamma-positive (a nonnegative combination of t j (1+t) n−2j ) and realised by a simplicial, even a flag simplicial, polytope. They also conjectured several Ehrhart identities. Gal conjectured that flag spheres always have gamma-positive h-polynomials, so families that are both gamma-positive and realised by flag spheres are natural test cases. Results. (1) The gamma-coefficient γ j counts ordered pairs of disjoint j-element sets that can be matched upwards in τ; this proves gamma-positivity (their Conjecture 5.2). Y. Zhong (arXiv:2611.16858, 12 November 2026) obtained the same formula independently and concurrently, by the same route. (2) New here: if τ contains no crown (2k ≥ 6 elements joined in a closed zig-zag), then H τ is the h-polynomial of the boundary of an n-dimensional flag simplicial polytope (Conjecture 5.1(d) for this class). The class includes all arbors (Chapoton’s original setting), compositions, width-two posets, series–parallel and interval orders, and every preorder with at most five blocks. The proof builds a quadratic Gröbner basis for a root polytope, adapting Ohsugi–Hibi and Ohsugi–Tsuchiya; the new step is to pull a special simplex first. For preorders with a crown, the two polytopes used here have no flag regular unimodular triangulation, and the six-element crown is the smallest open case. (3) Matrix Ehrhart–zeta duality (Conjecture 4.2) and double Ehrhart reciprocity (Conjecture 7.2) hold for every preorder; the descent formula (Conjecture 4.4) and the zeta value Z(P τ , −1) = (−1) n #max(P τ ) follow. Also: a simplicial-polytope realisation for every preorder (Conjecture 5.1(c)), an explicit reflexive polytope with Ehrhart numerator H τ , and a table of the status of every conjecture in the originating paper (Conjecture 5.4 was proved by Dai et al., Conjecture 6.3 by Luo, and Conjecture 5.3 is false by Patel’s example). Limits. The flag result covers crown-free preorders only. Several of the Ehrhart proofs are short applications of standard tools (Postnikov’s lattice-point formula, Ehrhart–Macdonald reciprocity, Athanasiadis’s special-simplex theorem). Magic positivity, Conjectures 6.2, 8.1 and 8.2 and the q-form of Conjecture 4.9 remain open. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); exact Python checks with a runner that compares every output byte for byte in normal and python -O mode (all 355 labelled four-element preorders and smaller ones, 24 seeded preorders at each size 5–8, 689 small bipartite graphs, 560 matrix-duality cases, 390 preorders for the corollaries); flag-sphere checks on 570 crown-free preorders and Macaulay2 Gröbner-basis certificates for 461

title: Preorder polytopes: matching endpoint pairs, flag spheres and the Athanasiadis–Chapoton conjectures

summary: This record contains two complementary reproducibility packages supporting the manuscript "Mean Squared Error of 3 x 3 Median Filtering for Two-Dimensional Ising Images: Local Determinant Representation and Denoising Improvement Boundaries" by Jun Tsuzurugi. The filtering-examples package contains one reproducibly generated 256 x 256 free-boundary Ising image at K = 0.40, independent pixel-flip noise at p = 0.10 and 0.30, a single simultaneous 3 x 3 median-filtering pass, saved arrays, measured sample mean squared errors, thermalization diagnostics, and plotting code. These images are illustrative single-sample results, not estimates of infinite-lattice expected risk. The near-critical finite-size package contains deterministic central-pixel mean squared errors for free-boundary square lattices of side length 15, 31, and 63 at K = Kc +/- 0.005 and flip probabilities 0.10 and 0.20, compared with infinite-lattice references. It includes code, numerical tables, figures, convergence checks, validation records, and provenance. Numerical checks are empirical and do not constitute rigorous error bounds or a critical-exponent analysis. These additional materials supplement the original computational reproducibility archive at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22987387. Both uploaded ZIPs preserve their original contents and provenance. Historical manuscript references remain unchanged: the filtering package includes original-submission and R1_4 records; the near-critical package includes R1_6 records and manuscript text extracted for source checking. This deposit does not claim a fresh verification against a later manuscript revision. No scientific calculations were rerun during deposit preparation. summary: Experimental data from tests on timber–concrete composite beam–floor slab joints, carried out at PEMADE (Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Lugo Campus) with the project's own test procedure within the FrameTCC project. Three specimens were tested (J1–J3), each representing the intersection of two floor slab sections on a beam. Each test comprised two load cycles, loading to failure and unloading. The first cycle of J2 is not discussed in the related manuscript. For each record (the unloading of J1 is in a separate record, so there are ten), the dataset provides the time series of applied load, actuator stroke, the vertical displacement at mid-length measured by two transducers and the slip between the flanges of the floor slabs and the flange of the beam measured by four transducers, sampled at intervals of about 0.28 s, as CSV files (10 files). It also includes the processing workbook of each record, the maximum load of each record, the mass and failure mode of each specimen and 15 selected photographs with descriptions, five per specimen. It also contains nine digital image correlation (DIC) projects (created with GOM Software 2017), described in dic.csv together with the free software that can open them, and the calibration report of the DIC system. The results are discussed in the manuscript «Continuity effect over beams of timber-concrete composite floor slabs» (under review; doi:10.5281/zenodo.24142933).

summary: Experimental data from axial compression tests on supports, carried out at CITEEC (Universidade da Coruña) with the project's own test procedure, within the FrameTCC project. Twenty-three supports were tested in two series. Series 1 (1.35 m long): reinforced concrete reference supports RC-1 and RC-2, and timber–concrete composite supports TCC-N-1 to TCC-N-4. Series 2 (1.45 m long): timber box-section supports of birch plywood PLY-P, PLY-N and PLY-S (three each), and timber–concrete composite supports TCC-P and TCC-S (four each). The suffix of the timber and composite supports gives the connection type: P plain, S slots and N notches. All channels were recorded at 5 Hz. RC-1, RC-2 and TCC-N-1 were instrumented with the pressure of two hydraulic jacks, four displacement transducers (LVDT) and four strain gauges; the other supports, with the force and displacement of the press and four strain gauges. The strain gauges measure the shortening of the timber boards and, internally, of the steel bars. The dataset includes 24 CSV files: one per support, plus a short record of TCC-N-3 taken after failure. The results are discussed in the manuscript «Axially loaded timber-concrete composite supports» (under review; doi:10.5281/zenodo.24143983). The package follows the FrameTCC data standard v7: a README, metadata files (test, specimens, channels, publications, SHA-256 manifest and changelog), the converted test data as CSV files and the other files described above. Time is given relative to the start of each acquisition; no calendar dates are included. Original acquisition files are kept unmodified by the project and are not published.

summary: Experimental data from four-point bending tests on cross-laminated timber–concrete composite floors, carried out at PEMADE (Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Lugo Campus) following EN 408 within the FrameTCC project. Three floor elements were tested (F1–F3), 6.10 m long with a span of 6.00 m. F1 and F2 were loaded to failure; F3 was loaded twice up to 60 kN without failure (F3a and F3b) and was then used in the long-term test of dataset 2.4, so there are four records. For each record, the dataset provides the time series of applied load, actuator stroke, mid-span deflection, local deflection over 1500 mm and the slip between concrete and timber at both ends, sampled at intervals of about 0.28 s, as CSV files (4 files). It also includes the processing workbook of each record, the values obtained (maximum load, loads and readings at two load levels, and local and global bending stiffness), the failure mode of F1 and F2 and 15 selected photographs with descriptions, at least four per floor. It also contains the digital image correlation (DIC) projects of F1, F2 and F3a (created with GOM Software 2017; the second cycle of F3 was not recorded with DIC), described in dic.csv together with the free software that can open them, and the calibration report of the DIC system. The results are discussed in Martín-Gutiérrez, Suárez-Riestra and Otero-Chans (2026), Structures 88, 111857 (doi:10.1016/j.istruc.2026.111857). The package follows the FrameTCC data standard v7: a README, metadata files (test, specimens, channels, publications, SHA-256 manifest and changelog), the converted test data as CSV files and the other files described above. Time is given relative to the start of each acquisition; no calendar dates are included. Original acquisition files are kept unmodified by the project and are not published.

summary: Analysis panel of 32 Indonesian provinces over 2020-2025, assembled from six editions of Statistik Indonesia (BPS) and from Indeks Pembangunan Manusia 2025, together with the extraction scripts, the 15 data-verification checks, the estimation code for the five specifications and the province-trend extensions, and the executed notebooks. The deposit contains no source PDFs: data/SOURCES.md records the SHA-256 of each BPS publication so that a re-download can be verified before the panel is rebuilt. Every number in the paper is reproduced from the included analysis panel by scripts/rev_ee_checks.py and scripts/legacy_panel_checks.py, and scripts/verify_bies_numbers.py asserts that each constant in the manuscript matches the computed output. summary: theorem A316626 : conjectureA316626 (unconditional, universal in k, standard axioms only): for every k >= 1, the occurrence count of k in OEIS A316626 equals its occurrence count in the sister sequence A081832 plus exactly one when k is a power of 2 - the on-entry conjecture of N. Fox and A. Alkan (2018), i.e. the first stated (2,1) case of Conjecture 5.1 of Erickson-Isgur-Jackson-Ruskey-Tanny (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 26(1) (2012) 206-238, DOI 10.1137/100795425, arXiv:1509.02613), published open and found unproved in a prior-art audit covering 8 registries (2026-11-08). The proof formalizes the two well-founded meta-Fibonacci recurrences in the positive subtype (termination via simultaneous value+bound induction), proves uniqueness of the solutions, then identifies both sequences with explicit closed forms via cumulative block sums S(m) = 4m - s2(m) and S_b(m) = 4m - s2(m) - floor(log2 m) - 1: the inverse functions c, d satisfy the nested recurrences by a block-position case analysis, giving exact frequencies occ_A(k) = 3 + v2(k) and occ_B(k) = 3 + v2(k) - [k a power of 2], whence the conjecture by subtraction. Also proved: kernel anchors a(1..31) and b(1..30) matching the entry data, exact fibers of 1, and the k = 1 case. NOT claimed: the companion on-entry conjectures (slow increments {0,1}, density 1/4 - elementary corollaries of a = c but not kernel-exported), the remaining 179 recurrences of Conjecture 5.1, the 'the only' enumeration direction, and the informal slowness proof of A081832 by A. Alkan (2018, cited for context, not used). Trust base: Lean kernel only, axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], zero sorryAx, zero native_decide; build replayed green on continuous integration; leanexport-serialized re-exports re-checked with zero errors by three independent Lean kernel re-implementations (nanoda_bin with strict axiom whitelist, con-leche, con-ron) ship in the companion archive A316626-seal-exports.tar.zst. Six modules: A316626, Spec_A316626, Check_Spec_A316626, Check_AntiVacuite_A316626, AxiomsReport_A316626, plus the root harness Scratch_A316626_proof.lean. Package: A316626-paper.pdf (6 pp.) + A316626-ancillary.tar.gz (37 members: Lean sources with pinned toolchain, spec/check modules, verification scripts and outputs, OEIS snapshots, SEAL replay material) + A316626-seal-exports.tar.zst (four leanexport-serialized transitive closures re-checked by three independent Lean kernel re-implementations: nanoda_bin with strict axiom whitelist [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] as hard error, con-leche, con-ron; zero errors on all four exports; replay via VERIFICATIONS/SEAL/replay_seal.sh). summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-six entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963), converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters, gives the absorbance template of a visual pigment of Govardovskii et al. (2000) for a peak wavelength and chromophore the caller states, and gives the distance between two colours in units of receptor noise by the model of Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), for a noise the caller states. Without a water type, it gives Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001) or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013), the remote sensing reflectance from a and bb (Gordon et al. 1988; Lee et al. 2002), and the Secchi depth from Kd and that reflectance (Lee et al. 2015), and inverts the reflectance to the absorption and backscattering coefficients by the quasi-analytical algorithm, in the version of IOCCG Report 5 (2006), checked against that report's published statistics, and as QAA_v6, checked against its author's spreadsheet. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-six entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963), converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters, gives the absorbance template of a visual pigment of Govardovskii et al. (2000) for a peak wavelength and chromophore the caller states, and gives the distance between two colours in units of receptor noise by the model of Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), for a noise the caller states. Without a water type, it gives Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001) or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013), the remote sensing reflectance from a and bb (Gordon et al. 1988; Lee et al. 2002), and the Secchi depth from Kd and that reflectance (Lee et al. 2015), and inverts the reflectance to the absorption and backscattering coefficients by the quasi-analytical algorithm, in the version of IOCCG Report 5 (2006), checked against that report's published statistics, and as QAA_v6, checked against its author's spreadsheet. It carries four published spectra of the absorption of pure water, Pope & Fry (1997), Smith & Baker (1981), Mason, Cone & Fry (2016) and Lee et al. (2015), for the caller to choose from, and
