summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: for 1 < p < 2 this paper finds the exact Schatten-norm constant for sums of matrix moduli when there are at least as many matrices as the matrix size, gives a new general upper bound ((1+√m)/2) 1−1/p , and certifies in exact arithmetic that rank-one matrices do not give the answer to Lee’s two-matrix problem. The question. For numbers, |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b|. A matrix A has a natural absolute value |A| = (A*A) 1/2 , but for matrices the size of a sum can exceed the size of the sum of the absolute values. Measuring size by the Schatten p-norm (p = 1 is the trace norm, p = 2 the Frobenius norm), one asks for the smallest constant c with ‖A 1 +…+A m ‖ p ≤ c ‖|A 1 |+…+|A m |‖ p . What was known. Eun-Young Lee (2010, 2012) asked for the best constant for two matrices. Lin and Zhang (2022) settled p = 2; Tang and Zhang extended the question to m matrices and conjectured a formula; Qiu (2026) proved it for p ≥ 2; below p = 2 the formula fails, by counterexamples of Zeng, Liu and Ratnavelu, of Pang and of Qiu, all built from rank-one matrices. The survey of Bourin and Zhang (2026) lists the range 1 < p < 2 as open. Results (1 < p < 2, n-by-n matrices). (1) When m ≥ n the best constant is an explicit one-variable maximum D p,n ; it depends only on the rank of the sum of the moduli, every equality case is classified, and for m < n the constant is strictly smaller. Consequently the best constant for rank-one summands is D p,min(m,n) in every dimension. (2) The best constant is log-convex in 1/p, so interpolating between p = 1 and p = 2 gives the dimension-free bound ((1+√m)/2) 1−1/p , better than the previous m (p−1)/(2p) for every m ≥ 2 (for two matrices at p = 3/2: 1.0648 instead of 1.1225, while the true value is at least 1.0364). (3) For two 3-by-3 matrices a computer-assisted proof in exact rational and interval arithmetic shows that the best rank-one value is beaten at nine exponents between 11/10 and 17/10. How. The sum is written as a product of two block matrices and Hölder’s inequality is applied; the problem reduces to comparing two Rényi entropies of the spectrum, whose extremal shape is one large eigenvalue and the rest equal. This extends T. Zhang’s Frobenius-norm argument; the matching examples are Pang’s, with a re-tuned parameter. Limits. The exact constant for two matrices of arbitrary size (Lee’s problem) for 1 < p < 2 remains open, as does the case m < n; the interpolation bound is not sharp; the certified excess over the rank-one value is tiny (about 10 −5 to 10 −7 ) and covers nine specific exponents, not an interval. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF) with Figure 1; the certificate script certify_rank_gap.py with its exact rational witnesses; verify_schatten.py (128 numerical checks of the scalar constant, equality families, adversarial searches, the bounds table and asymptotics, with negative controls); the figure script; recorded outputs; the bibliography from registry records; a machine-readable index; a research-gate record; a rating-free review summary; a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Assurance. Written proofs, except one computer-assisted proof in exact arithmetic (Proposition 2.5). Internal AI-assisted review only (five reviewer roles, an adversarial review and audit by a second AI model, a clean replay, a re-review and a proof audit): not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Sharp constants for sums of matrix moduli when 1<p<2

summary: A law $F$ with mean $\mu$ is $n$-completely mixable if there are $n$ random variables with law $F$ whose sum is almost surely $n\mu$. Wang proved that such a law satisfies a family of inequalities between the norms of the positive and negative parts of $X-t$ and $X-s$, where $X\sim F$ and $s=(n\mu-t)/(n-1)$, for every threshold $t$ and every law-determined norm, and asked when these inequalities are also sufficient (Open Problem 4 in his 2015 survey). We show that for bounded $F$ the whole family is equivalent to the single convex-order condition $X-\mu\cx-(n-1)(X-\mu)$, and that the same holds for integrable $F$ if the norms are required to have the Fatou property. The inequalities do not imply $n$-complete mixability: for $n=3$ the analytic density $\frac1{10}+\frac{27}{10}(2x-1)^2$ on $[0,1]$ satisfies all of them and is not $3$-completely mixable, and for $n=3$ and $n=4$ there are counterexamples with densities bounded away from zero on $[0,1]$ and with $C^\infty$ densities, the one for $n=4$ not symmetric. A Bernoulli$(p)$ law satisfies the inequalities exactly when $1/n\le p\le1-1/n$, while it is $n$-completely mixable exactly when $np$ is an integer. For $n=2$ the inequalities are equivalent to symmetry, hence to $2$-complete mixability, for every integrable law. For $n=3$ the examples refine the symmetric non-mixable laws of Yin and Zhu, and the reduction explains why those laws satisfy the inequalities.
title: Law-determined norm inequalities do not imply complete mixability

summary: Replication package for the working paper "Precision Matters: Anti-Corruption Campaigns, Targeted Crackdowns, and Sector Returns in China's Stock Market" (Xuanyuan Li, 2026). The package contains: (1) four hand-verified event libraries — 31 general anti-corruption campaign events (2012–2026), 12 sector-targeted interventions, 12 local-flagship case-study events, and 14 positive policy tools — every date anchored to an official primary source (CCDI, NDRC, MIIT, NPC, SAMR); (2) a 152-month hand-compiled CCDI eight-point-regulation enforcement series (2013-09 to 2026-09) with per-month source anchors and the December 2019 coverage-revision flag; (3) Sina hfq-adjusted daily return panels for the sector proxies and the CSI 300 benchmark; (4) all analysis scripts (Python 3.11, pandas/numpy): event-study grids, monthly enforcement-intensity regressions, exact permutation / cluster-bootstrap / sign-test inference, index-proxy robustness, and a beta-adjusted market-model replication with Newey-West lag sensitivity; (5) the manuscript (Markdown and Word), cover letter, and title page. Run the scripts from the package root; README.md gives replication steps and data-source conventions. All paper results are reproducible from the cached CSVs without network access. Inference note: policy events of this precision are scarce by construction; the paper reports exact permutation tests as primary evidence and discloses that the beta-adjusted replication weakens the headline targeted-intervention spread (p = 0.073).
title: Replication package for: Precision Matters: Anti-Corruption Campaigns, Targeted Crackdowns, and Sector Returns in China's Stock Market

summary: Replication code for a study of battery storage investment prioritisation across five campuses of a merged public technical university in Taiwan, under a contract-capacity time-of-use tariff. The code recovers tariff parameters from billing records, jointly optimises storage size, contracted capacity and time-of-use dispatch for each site-year by linear programming with a genetic-algorithm benchmark, and values storage against an administratively optimised counterfactual so that contract reductions obtainable without capital expenditure are not credited to storage. The institutional billing records analysed in the paper are not included, having been obtained under a data use agreement that does not permit redistribution; a synthetic panel with the same schema is provided so the code runs out of the box.
title: Analysis code for: Visible in kilowatts, invisible in money — contract capacity, storage and investment priorities under a Taiwanese demand-charge tariff

summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. Keywords: proof of personhood, proof of humanity, sybil resistance, decentralized identity, AI-content trust, open identity protocol, recipient-side filtering, BLE-Nearby proximity, blockchain consensus, AI alignment, defensive publication. --- Provenance. This paper is part of the THonly research corpus, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The canonical version is at https://thonly.org/research/b-poh-humanity-layer-ai-native-internet . Its SHA-256 is d9d9a6d7bced60a5c39ba39079426a240024416799b1219b1d536173833df670 , independently timestamped to the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps and signed under RFC 3161 by three trust authorities, one of them eIDAS-qualified. AI co-authorship is disclosed. Miss Aquarius is the consistent name used for the AI collaboration across all venues. Miss Aquarius co-authored this paper; Zenodo lists no AI tool as a creator, so Miss Aquarius is named here rather than among the creators.
title: B-PoH℠ as Humanity Layer for the AI-Native Internet: An Open Proof-of-Personhood Protocol with Four Optional Layered Proofs and Recipient-Side Filters

summary: For every integer p>=4, a previously constructed symmetric numerical semigroup ring R_p and rigid two-generated monomial ideal determine a conductor ideal T_p whose special fiber C_p = F(T_p) is one-dimensional Cohen-Macaulay, generated in degree one by 10p monomials, with multiplicity 24p. Taking the imported offset bases as input, we prove that C_p ≅ k[xy^a : a ∈ G_p] ⊆ k[x,y]/(y^24p), that its defining ideal J_p is primary to the ideal of positive offsets, with nilpotency index 24p, and that Proj(C_p) is a saturated length-24p curvilinear fat point, locally Gorenstein although the coordinate ring has Cohen-Macaulay type 10p+1. The Kähler differentials split by characteristic. We then determine the reduced Gröbner basis for graded reverse lexicographic order with X_0 last. Its degree profile is (50p^2-17p, 5p-1, p-2) and no minimal leading monomial contains X_0, which gives a flat Cohen-Macaulay monomial degeneration. The quadratic part, the stabilization of the staircase, the absence of elements in degree five and higher, the absence of X_0 from the leading monomials and the flatness are derived from derived imported input; the imported relation type three is machine-verified. The cubic and quartic classification, for all p, is machine-verified and not derived: 16 Presburger obligations are decided unsatisfiable by Z3 and by cvc5 on identical queries, with no checked proof object. Exact sweeps at every p=4,...,300, an independent clique recomputation and negative controls validate the formulas. The results concern the conductor fiber cones of this explicit family; they do not assert that arbitrary monomial fiber cones are primary, curvilinear, Cohen-Macaulay or locally Gorenstein. Source code, compact artifacts, premise hashes and proofs: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
title: Curvilinear Geometry, Primary Structure, and a Gröbner Degeneration of Conductor Fiber Cones in a Huneke–Wiegand Family

summary: The widespread application of inductive loads in today ‘s power distribution systems where power factor (PF) correction has become an integral requirement, has led to power factor degradation as a serious problem and requires correction for more efficient power distribution. In this paper, an innovative AI based Adaptive PF correction scheme is proposed to integrate conventional PF correction capacitor bank compensation with an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) based predictor-controller for dynamic reactive power compensation. A detailed MATLAB/Simulink 3–phase distribution system-based model has been evolved which yields operational data sets for ANN training and testing with different loading conditions. Proposed ANN predictor-controllers are trained with back-propagation algorithm applying MSE (Mean Squared Error) function as a network performance measure. The network prediction accuracy 96.9 to 97.8% and the generalization capability has been established through comprehensive results analysis. The proposed architecture significantly decreases the reactive power demand by approximately 77%, apparent power consumption by 28.1% and the dynamic response by 3 times compared to fixed capacitor compensation method. Moreover, the (PF) is maintained between 0.95–0.96, confirming its effectiveness for real-time adaptive power factor correction in modern distribution systems.
title: AI-Based Adaptive Power Factor Correction for Reactive Power Reduction in Distribution Systems

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Proof of the Mogilnykh–Vorob’ev–Valyuzhenich conjecture, the exact Rényi minimum for sampling without replacement, and the hypergeometric tail problem from n = 4k. The question. Pick k of n given real numbers at random, without replacement, and add them. How concentrated can that random sum be? The paper answers three classical forms of this question exactly: how often the sum can be exactly zero, how small its entropy can be, and how rarely it can be nonnegative. Results. (1) Zero sums. If the numbers add up to zero and are not all zero, at least 2·C(n−2, k−1) of the k-subsets have a nonzero sum whenever k ≥ 5 and n ≥ 2k+1, and only the pattern (1, −1, 0, …, 0), up to scaling and reordering, attains this. This is the smallest support of an eigenfunction in the first nontrivial eigenspace of the Johnson graph, and proves Conjecture 1 of Mogilnykh, Vorob’ev and Valyuzhenich (2018), who had checked it by computer for n ≤ 600. A formula with all equality cases is given for every n and k, including the case (1, 1, −1, −1, 0) at n = 5, k = 2 that earlier classifications missed (Theorem 1.1). (2) Entropy. The minimum Rényi entropy of the sum is found for every finite order, answering a question of Ai, Kuželka and Pelekis (2026): one outlier is optimal except at half-sampling (n = 2k), where two outliers win above an explicit order α k (α 2 = 2, about 1.386k for large k). So the universal Bernoulli lower bound holds exactly for orders up to 2 (Theorems 1.2 and 1.3, Corollary 1.4). (3) Tails. For two-valued populations, the probability that the sum is at least its mean is at least k/n whenever n ≥ 4k, with a single outlier the unique minimiser for n > 4k (Theorem 1.5); Ai and Pelekis (2026) had n ≥ 8k. The proof uses a 2026 lemma of Ai, Karagiannis, Kuželka and Pelekis. Consequently the Aydinian–Blinovsky conjecture (that two-valued populations are the worst case) would imply the Manickam–Miklós–Singhi conjecture for all n ≥ 4k. This does not prove the Manickam–Miklós–Singhi conjecture, and below 4k a single outlier is not always the worst case. (4) Exact analogues over Abelian groups, where elements of order two change the answer at half-sampling (Theorem 1.6), and a small-ball inequality for sampling without replacement; a known incidence-rank result is re-derived. Limits. Real numbers only for the zero-sum theorem (it fails over Z 2 , Z 3 and Z 5 ); first Johnson eigenspace only; the tail problem below n = 4k is open. Finite computer checks corroborate but do not replace the written proofs. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); five standard-library Python scripts of exact finite checks (each runs in seconds and exits nonzero on any failure, also under python -O) with their recorded outputs; a claim ledger and prior-art note; the bibliography from registry records; a machine-readable index; a research-gate record; a rating-free review summary; a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Assurance. Complete written proofs for every result. Internal AI-assisted review only (five reviewer roles, an adversarial review and an audit by a second AI model, clean replays, a re-review and a proof audit): not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Fixed-size subset sums: sharp support, Rényi entropy and tail bounds

summary: Contemporary speculative fiction unsettles anthropocentric assumptions about language, intelligence and the production of knowledge. This article compares Laline Paull’s The Bees (2014) to Ray Nayler's The Mountain in the Sea (2022) and The Tusks of Extinction (2024), exploring how the novels represent the conditions under which non-human knowledge is produced, recognized and transmitted. Drawing on biosemiotics and critical posthumanism in conversation with Andrew Lopez's account of epistemic injustice towards non-human animals, it develops a comparative framework based on recognition, access and continuity. The key argument is that the novels depict epistemic harm not merely as a failure to interpret non-human signs but as the institutional restriction of the very environments and social relations through which practical knowledge can flow. In Paull's hive caste is the source of authority which controls access to sensory information; in Nayler's oceanic enclave corporate power turns scientific attention into a potential tool of appropriation; and in the de-extinction narrative, biological restoration is simply not enough without the recovery of the skills that are socially transmitted. The novels are not being read as descriptions of actual animal species. Rather they are being used as a lens through which to examine the political and ethical dimensions of human authority over other ways of knowing. The article makes a contribution to contemporary literary studies by linking multispecies representation to the distribution and preservation of epistemic goods.
tags: Biosemiotics; critical posthumanism; epistemic injustice; nonhuman communication; collective knowledge; multispecies justice; contemporary speculative fiction
title: Sign Systems and Shared Worlds: Nonhuman Communication, Collective Knowledge and Epistemic Justice in Contemporary Speculative Fiction

summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The paper also discloses one application-facing composition of the per-action passkey press, the presence call (§3.8): an identity provider confirms to an app, for one named action and in the provider's own closed wording, that the holder of a person's passkey pressed it, for a person the app already knows by its own pairwise identifier, and keeps nothing; §12.1 reports the novelty census that scopes that claim to the composition alone. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. summary: We study in-context learning of scalar linear regression by L untied linear-attention layers, each with a trainable key scalar k_i and query scalar q_i. For every depth L and prompt length n, population gradient flow on the 2L factors is bounded and converges to a critical point, every critical point that is not a global minimizer has a negative Hessian eigenvalue, and the flow reaches a global minimizer from all initializations outside a Lebesgue null set, for instance almost surely under Gaussian initialization. The trained network performs L gradient descent steps on the prompt's least-squares loss, with step sizes k_iq_i the reciprocals of the zeros of a rescaled Laguerre polynomial L_L^(n/2), and its risk is $2^LL!/\prod_{j=1}^{L}(n+2j)$. Initializations with k_i = -q_i in some layer converge to a critical point that is not a minimizer, so the null set is not empty.
title: Gradient flow for deep factored scalar linear attention learns multi-step gradient descent

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-nine entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963), converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters, gives the absorbance template of a visual pigment of Govardovskii et al. (2000) for a peak wavelength and chromophore the caller states, and gives the distance between two colours in units of receptor noise by the model of Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), for a noise the caller states. Without a water type, it gives Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001) or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013), the remote sensing reflectance from a and bb (Gordon et al. 1988; Lee et al. 2002), and the Secchi depth from Kd and that reflectance (Lee et al. 2015), and inverts the reflectance to the absorption and backscattering coefficients by the quasi-analytical algorithm, in the version of IOCCG Report 5 (2006), checked against that report's published statistics, and as QAA_v6, checked against its author's spreadsheet. Thirty-nine entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). summary: Pre-registration of an exploratory analysis, deposited before any race/ethnicity-specific outcome was estimated. We will examine racial/ethnic differences in first-molar dental sealant prevalence among US children aged 6–11 years using NHANES (1999–2004, 2011–2016, and 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic file; 2005–2010 cycles are excluded because tooth-level sealant codes are unavailable). Outcome: presence of a sealant on ≥1 permanent first molar among children with ≥1 assessable first molar. Comparison: non-Hispanic Black and Mexican American children versus non-Hispanic White children. Planned estimands are survey-weighted prevalence and absolute differences (percentage points) by period, change in the absolute gap between 1999–2004 and 2017–2020.3 (Holm-adjusted for the two primary contrasts), and attenuation of the gap after adjustment for age, sex, and income rank (poverty-income ratio), alongside a parallel income-gradient (slope index of inequality) comparison. Variance is estimated by Taylor linearization; attenuation uses a Rao-Wu bootstrap. Status. Exploratory: the hypotheses were formed after the authors had analysed overall (non-race-specific) prevalence and income inequality in the same data for a separate study. Published race-specific estimates for 2011–2014 exist (CDC Vital Signs, 2016), so the 2011–2014 direction is a replication rather than a confirmation; the change in racial/ethnic gaps since 1999–2004 is the new question. Race-specific outcomes had not been computed at the time of registration. Files: preregistration document (Markdown and PDF), version 1.0.
title: Racial/ethnic disparities in first-molar sealant prevalence among US children, 1999–2020: exploratory analysis pre-registration

summary: CHASE-AML is a synthetic banking benchmark comprising 33,176,605 settled transactions and 500,000 registered accounts. It combines persistent account activity with 26 standalone suspicious typologies and annotated single-path and branching laundering cases. Case, path, parent-transaction and stage information connects transfers so transaction rankings and the reach of alerts across cases can be evaluated separately. The package contains the full 36-column canonical transaction export and a 13-column core export of the same rows, opening and closing synthetic ledger snapshots, a data dictionary and file checksums. No customer banking records, paper-specific evaluation files, generator or evaluation code, trained policies or fitted models are included.
title: CHASE-AML: A Lifecycle-Aware Synthetic Banking Dataset for Anti-Money Laundering Research

summary: This dataset is version 1.1.0 of the P1 complete derived transcriptomic resource for mapping and comparing human pluripotent stem cell-derived beta-cell differentiation across published protocols. It contains 100 sample or time-point analysis units, an S0-S6 stage ontology with S7-S9 reserved, a 2,552-gene shared cost space, optimal-transport stage coordinates with 20 retrospectively exported reference-centroid bootstrap draws, five-axis/46-gene Maturity Fidelity Index scores with 16 sensitivity versions, a 25-module concordance atlas, gene- and module-level variance components, constructed reliability descriptors, provenance records, analysis-code snapshots, and two application workflows. Applications and evidence boundaries. The internal GSE158617 example uses 38 samples in a retrospective, in-sample interface demonstration and is not independent validation. The external GSE203264 application uses 35 wild-type samples and a rebuilt P1-compatible 2,550-gene reference. Its non-monotonic D35 result concerns unsorted, compositionally heterogeneous SC-islets and is not validation of the unmodified 2,552-gene model or a pure beta-cell accuracy result. Reliability values are constructed descriptors, not absolute dataset-quality scores or significance ranks. MFI values are within-matrix relative profiles, not absolute cross-protocol maturity measures. No in vivo developmental tiers, validated benchmark accuracy, clinical validity, or universal generalization are claimed. Reproduction scope. The package supplies package-local verification for the two application workflows and the external diagnostics. The analysis-code and provenance snapshots support inspection and traceability but are not represented as a relocatable clean-room rebuild of every manuscript display item. The reference-centroid draws are a retrospective deterministic reconstruction from frozen training inputs, not an original frozen cache. Source data and governance. Original GEO expression matrices and metadata are not redistributed. Source accessions, expected hashes and third-party rights boundaries are documented in the package. GSE270220 and GSE275610 remain sealed and contributed to no statistic. The associated pilot-informed preregistration and execution governance records are identified through the related OSF project; private OSF access tokens are neither included nor required for the packaged application checks. Licensing. Original source code is under the MIT License. Original derived data, model parameters, documentation and figures are under CC BY 4.0, subject to the stated third-party exclusions. Funding. Basic Scientific Research Projects of the Liaoning Provincial Department of Education for Universities and Colleges, grant LJ212413213011.

summary: Route-explicit deterministic delivered-cost model for green hydrogen supplied to the EU from Algeria (pipeline and ammonia) and five competitors (Morocco, Egypt, Oman, Australia, Chile), with country WACC and default-spread betas, bottom-up shipping, canal tolls and war-risk insurance with rerouting; Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 draws), Shapley decomposition, ES95 security premium, break-even GPR, Sobol indices, and an ex-post scenario tested on the observed 2026 Strait of Hormuz closure. All inputs are documented with their sources in params/; outputs are regenerated by src/run_model.py. Version 2.1.0 accompanies the revised article: the PV electricity cost uses the yield after clipping, the reference voyage of the ammonia chain is valued at the baseline production cost, three bounding variants are added (midstream financing, fuel valuation, independent PV yield factors) and further dated 2026 war-risk quotes are included (see CHANGELOG.md). It supersedes v2.0.0 and v1.0.0.

summary: theorem A316626 : conjectureA316626 (unconditional, universal in k, standard axioms only): for every k >= 1, the occurrence count of k in OEIS A316626 equals its occurrence count in the sister sequence A081832 plus exactly one when k is a power of 2 - the on-entry conjecture of N. Fox and A. Alkan (2018), i.e. the first stated (2,1) case of Conjecture 5.1 of Erickson-Isgur-Jackson-Ruskey-Tanny (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 26(1) (2012) 206-238, DOI 10.1137/100795425, arXiv:1509.02613), published open and found unproved in a prior-art audit covering 8 registries (2026-11-08). The proof formalizes the two well-founded meta-Fibonacci recurrences in the positive subtype (termination via simultaneous value+bound induction), proves uniqueness of the solutions, then identifies both sequences with explicit closed forms via cumulative block sums S(m) = 4m - s2(m) and S_b(m) = 4m - s2(m) - floor(log2 m) - 1: the inverse functions c, d satisfy the nested recurrences by a block-position case analysis, giving exact frequencies occ_A(k) = 3 + v2(k) and occ_B(k) = 3 + v2(k) - [k a power of 2], whence the conjecture by subtraction. Also proved: kernel anchors a(1..31) and b(1..30) matching the entry data, exact fibers of 1, and the k = 1 case. NOT claimed: the companion on-entry conjectures (slow increments {0,1}, density 1/4 - elementary corollaries of a = c but not kernel-exported), the remaining 179 recurrences of Conjecture 5.1, the 'the only' enumeration direction, and the informal slowness proof of A081832 by A. Alkan (2018, cited for context, not used). Trust base: Lean kernel only, axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], zero sorryAx, zero native_decide; build replayed green on continuous integration; leanexport-serialized re-exports re-checked with zero errors by three independent Lean kernel re-implementations (nanoda_bin with strict axiom whitelist, con-leche, con-ron) ship in the companion archive A316626-seal-exports.tar.zst. Six modules: A316626, Spec_A316626, Check_Spec_A316626, Check_AntiVacuite_A316626, AxiomsReport_A316626, plus the root harness Scratch_A316626_proof.lean.

summary: theorem A071685: for n not divisible by 10, n is a term (non-palindromic, n | R(n) or R(n) | n, where R(n) is the decimal digit-reversal) iff R(n) = 4n or R(n) = 9n or n = 4*R(n) or n = 9*R(n) - the announced union of A001232, A222814, A008918, A222815. The OEIS comment 'the quotient R(n)/n or n/R(n) is always 4 or 9' is proved in full (lemma ratio49). summary: This dataset supports a retrospective technical evaluation of transactional evidence preservation, uncertain-submission recovery and historical assessment retrieval in a synthetic regulatory-computing pathway for nursing-home infection-control documentation. The collection contains derived research tables, source-inventory descriptions, evidence locators and checksums, extraction and reconciliation documentation, and separate failure/skip context. The primary 56-case hosted evaluation, separate 47-case Stage-B execution and local ten-case report retain distinct execution identities and must not be combined into a unique-test total. Stage-B descriptions are source-derived; execution totals are supported separately by retained logs. Its successful execution XML remains unavailable, and the local report lacks a tested commit identifier. A maintainer-submitted, AI-assisted inspection reported 113 detailed reporting entries accounted for: 106 exact matches and seven documented parameter substitutions. The reconciled derivative includes five additional aggregate records. Numerical outcomes are unchanged. Separate retained executions with failures and skips are documented without assigning unestablished causes. Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT assisted evidence inspection, reconciliation and preparation of the research documentation, as detailed in the accompanying extraction record. This collection supports inspection of reported findings and provenance; it is not an executable application reproduction package. The designated public research files are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Proprietary implementation source, controlled original archives, raw logs and complete execution environments are excluded. RegCIP, Inc.’s implementation materials remain separate from the research derivatives.
title: Research evidence for transactional evidence integrity in a regulatory computing API for nursing home infection control

summary: Contemporary speculative fiction unsettles anthropocentric assumptions about language, intelligence and the production of knowledge. This article compares Laline Paull’s The Bees (2014) to Ray Nayler's The Mountain in the Sea (2022) and The Tusks of Extinction (2024), exploring how the novels represent the conditions under which non-human knowledge is produced, recognized and transmitted. Drawing on biosemiotics and critical posthumanism in conversation with Andrew Lopez's account of epistemic injustice towards non-human animals, it develops a comparative framework based on recognition, access and continuity. The key argument is that the novels depict epistemic harm not merely as a failure to interpret non-human signs but as the institutional restriction of the very environments and social relations through which practical knowledge can flow. In Paull's hive caste is the source of authority which controls access to sensory information; in Nayler's oceanic enclave corporate power turns scientific attention into a potential tool of appropriation; and in the de-extinction narrative, biological restoration is simply not enough without the recovery of the skills that are socially transmitted. The novels are not being read as descriptions of actual animal species. Rather they are being used as a lens through which to examine the political and ethical dimensions of human authority over other ways of knowing. The article makes a contribution to contemporary literary studies by linking multispecies representation to the distribution and preservation of epistemic goods.
tags: Biosemiotics; critical posthumanism; epistemic injustice; nonhuman communication; collective knowledge; multispecies justice; contemporary speculative fiction
title: Sign Systems and Shared Worlds: Nonhuman Communication, Collective Knowledge and Epistemic Justice in Contemporary Speculative Fiction

summary: Code, per-item evaluation caches and analysis scripts that regenerate every number, table and figure of ten preprints on choosing and combining the weights of small open language models (Qwen2.5-0.5B, SmolLM2-360M, Pythia-160M): linear and spherical interpolation, task-vector extrapolation, three-model merges (TIES, DARE), layer-group search, checkpoint averaging, the winner's curse in validation-based selection, validation-set size and the language-modeling cost of interpolation. summary: Code, per-item evaluation caches and analysis scripts that regenerate every number, table and figure of ten preprints on choosing and combining the weights of small open language models (Qwen2.5-0.5B, SmolLM2-360M, Pythia-160M): linear and spherical interpolation, task-vector extrapolation, three-model merges (TIES, DARE), layer-group search, checkpoint averaging, the winner's curse in validation-based selection, validation-set size and the language-modeling cost of interpolation. Each evaluation is stored as a 0/1 vector per item, so the statistics can be reproduced without a GPU. Most results are null or negative and are reported as such. The ten papers are CC BY 4.0 (Figshare); the code is MIT.
title: Choosing the Weights of Small Open Language Models: code, per-item evaluation caches and ten preprints

summary: This repository contains the computational reproducibility package accompanying the research article “Beyond Monetary Energy Markets: Multilateral Reciprocity as an Alternative Exchange Mechanism for Energy Communities”. The package includes Python implementations of the proposed non-monetary energy exchange mechanism, benchmark models, cooperative surplus allocation methods, sensitivity analyses, temporal validation, synthetic photovoltaic generation, and utilities for reproducing the numerical results, tables and figures. Due to restrictions on redistribution, the original GoiEner smart-meter consumption data and household-level derived datasets are not included. Users must independently obtain the file profiles_part01.tar.zst from the GoiEner Smart Meter Dataset (Version 7.1), available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22313409 . A dedicated Python extraction and preprocessing utility is provided to reconstruct the required hourly demand profiles locally without imputing missing observations. The package also includes the OMIE wholesale electricity price series used in the study, corresponding to the Portuguese bidding zone, and the synthetic study configuration. Detailed installation instructions, data provenance, reproduction procedures and file integrity checks are provided in the accompanying documentation. The redistribution of third-party data remains subject to the conditions established by the original data providers.

summary: Neither primary hypothesis met its preregistered support conditions. This study evaluates whether a twenty-session mean correlation among nine long-history US sector ETFs is associated with subsequent closing-price drawdowns. Data end on 4 November 2026; the chronological evaluation begins in 2015. All nineteen registered tests and all cost sensitivities are retained. The study is retrospective and does not establish a prospective alarm or timing skill. The VIX-adjusted statistic and restricted linear VIX forecast comparison have calibration limitations. The paper reports these and the hypothetical cash-proxy and event-concentration limitations. Exact reproduction requires lawful access to the recorded inputs; raw commercial prices and internal daily derived series are not redistributed. The publication copies of the protocol normalize one historical implementation path. The original and presentation hashes are both documented, and the frozen original remains unchanged. The comparison of 253 readings, maximum absolute difference 2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶, tolerance 10⁻¹², and nineteen-return negative control difference 0.08699 are retained. summary: For hedge fund research reviewers, this report examines checks for selective reporting when a registered study is closed. At the author’s research service, the proposed use is review of research records before their conclusions enter an evaluation; no product integration or saving in review time has been measured. This report makes no claim of originality.   Checking whether a study followed its pre-registration requires comparing the report with the plan. This report tests one method for that comparison. A research record is kept in a fixed JSON format (registration, hash commitment, event log, closure), and seven mechanical rejection rules, R1 to R7, each target one selective-reporting defect taken from Arnott, Harvey and Markowitz (2019) and Harvey and Liu (2015). The comparison arm gives the same information, rendered as plain text, to a general-purpose language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) with one fixed instruction. The test plan, its thresholds and its decision order were frozen, with a local SHA-256 hash, before any code, record or label existed. For each of two cohorts a separate model session generated 33 synthetic records, 12 valid and 21 with one injected defect, without seeing the rules, and labels were locked before either arm ran. In the first (in-sample) cohort the rules flagged 21 of 21 defective records and rejected 0 of 12 valid ones. The language model also flagged 21 of 21 but rejected 6 of 12 valid records, which disqualifies it under the plan. In the second (out-of-sample) cohort the rules again scored 21 of 21 with 0 of 12 rejected, and the language model scored 17 of 21 with 0 of 12. The gap of 4 is below the pre-registered margin of 5. The pre-registered verdict for both cohorts is therefore "compared, threshold not met", and the report makes no claim that the rules add detection. A reduced rule set (R1, R2 and R7 only) missed 12 of 21 defects in both cohorts and is refuted. No confidence intervals are reported, because the plan forbids them: the records are constructed counterexamples, not a sample from any population.   Deposit version: Working paper, version 1.2 (2026-11-12). Author: Peilun Cai. The manuscript is an English typeset presentation of the same experiment; no new experiment or result was introduced. summary: Code, tokens, audit reports and empirical data for LUMINA-AAA, a deterministic generator and verifier for WCAG 2.2 AAA colour systems. The release contains the generator and auditor library ( lib/ ), the artifact builder ( tools/build-tokens.js ), the generated tokens and the signed audit report, a 58-test suite, the normative specification, the machine-generated empirical data supporting the paper, the web demo, the perceptual study apparatus, and the archived v0.2 chat export audited as evidence. The reference build is buildPalette({brand: '#1E40AF', profile: 'integral', seed: 20260908}) , with digest 8310c587049be4baeddb9c3b5ff84618670b8cfb6bceae45ac5aa0e6262fdcfe . The audit evaluates 348 pairs over 59 mandatory roles and three themes. The release also documents the forensic re-derivation of the v0.2 defect taxonomy, external validation with axe-core and Lighthouse, a separate-implementation differential check of contrast arithmetic, a fault-injection study (12/12 defect classes detected), a multi-seed robustness sweep, published-palette baselines, and a seven-model elicitation audit of LLM-authored specifications. The manuscript itself is not part of the archive; it is submitted separately to the journal.

summary: Data and code for the paper "Label-efficient plant disease classification with vision foundation models: a leakage-controlled benchmark" by Harshvardhan Rai and Ravi Shankar Singh (Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology (Banaras Hindu University), Varanasi, India), submitted to the Journal of Plant Diseases and Protection. Code repository: https://github.com/harshvardhanrai-iitbhucse/plant_peft (version v1.0, also archived here as plant_peft_code_v1.zip). WHAT THIS DEPOSIT CONTAINS This deposit holds the derived data needed to check and reuse the results. It contains no images and no model weights; the images come from three public datasets and must be obtained from their original sources under their own licences. The data archive plant_peft_data_v1.zip contains: - splits/: the train/validation/test assignment of every image with its perceptual hash (pHash); the near-duplicate groups (Hamming distance ≤ 4) used to keep duplicates within one split; the cross-class duplicate list for the pigeon-pea dataset; and the manual audit of the 236 PlantDoc test images (photograph, plain background, text slide, collage). - results/: results.jsonl, one line per training run with its full configuration (model, method, learning rate, seed, data fraction) and validation and test metrics; the efficiency measurements (GMACs, latency, memory); per-class PlantDoc results. - runs/: for each run, the test-set predictions and labels as NumPy arrays, in the order of the test split in splits/, with small log and configuration files. - tables/ and figures/: every table and figure of the paper, as generated by the scripts from the files above. SOURCE DATASETS (NOT REDISTRIBUTED) - PlantVillage (Hughes and Salathé 2015), colour images; the 15 pepper, potato and tomato classes. - PlantDoc (Singh et al. 2020), official train/test split, 27 classes. - Pigeon-pea leaf dataset (Rajput and Doddamani 2024, Mendeley Data, version 1). The repository README describes how to prepare them. HOW TO REPRODUCE THE PAPER'S NUMBERS 1. Unpack plant_peft_code_v1.zip, or clone the repository at tag v1.0. 2. Obtain the three datasets and build the caches as described in the repository README. 3. Place splits/, results/ and runs/ from the data archive in the repository root. 4. Run python scripts/make_tables.py and python scripts/make_figures.py; they regenerate every table and figure from results/ and runs/ without any training. 5. To re-train a configuration, follow the repository README; each line of results.jsonl stores the full configuration of its run. PROTOCOL Splits are grouped by near-duplicate (pHash Hamming distance ≤ 4), so a duplicate never crosses the train/test boundary. Checkpoints are selected on validation data only. Every configuration is run with five seeds. Comparisons use a paired bootstrap over test images (10,000 resamples) with Holm correction within pre-registered families. LICENCE The derived data (splits, audits, logs, predictions, tables, figures) are released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT licence. The source images keep the licences of their original datasets. CITATION If you use these splits or audits, please cite the paper (reference to be added on publication) and this deposit (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24195419).

The data archive plant_peft_data_v1.zip contains: - splits/: the train/validation/test assignment of every image with its perceptual hash (pHash); the near-duplicate groups (Hamming distance ≤ 4) used to keep duplicates within one split; the cross-class duplicate list for the pigeon-pea dataset; and the manual audit of the 236 PlantDoc test images (photograph, plain background, text slide, collage). - results/: results.jsonl, one line per training run with its full configuration (model, method, learning rate, seed, data fraction) and validation and test metrics; the efficiency measurements (GMACs, latency, memory); per-class PlantDoc results. - runs/: for each run, the test-set predictions and labels as NumPy arrays, in the order of the test split in splits/, with small log and configuration files. - tables/ and figures/: every table and figure of the paper, as generated by the scripts from the files above. SOURCE DATASETS (NOT REDISTRIBUTED) - PlantVillage (Hughes and Salathé 2015), colour images; the 15 pepper, potato and tomato classes. - PlantDoc (Singh et al. 2020), official train/test split, 27 classes. - Pigeon-pea leaf dataset (Rajput and Doddamani 2024, Mendeley Data, version 1). The repository README describes how to prepare them. HOW TO REPRODUCE THE PAPER'S NUMBERS 1. Unpack plant_peft_code_v1.zip, or clone the repository at tag v1.0. 2. Obtain the three datasets and build the caches as described in the repository README. 3. Place splits/, results/ and runs/ from the data archive in the repository root. 4. Run python scripts/make_tables.py and python scripts/make_figures.py; they regenerate every table and figure from results/ and runs/ without any training. 5. To re-train a configuration, follow the repository README; each line of results.jsonl stores the full configuration of its run. PROTOCOL Splits are grouped by near-duplicate (pHash Hamming distance ≤ 4), so a duplicate never crosses the train/test boundary. Checkpoints are selected on validation data only. Every configuration is run with five seeds. Comparisons use a paired bootstrap over test images (10,000 resamples) with Holm correction within pre-registered families. LICENCE The derived data (splits, audits, logs, predictions, tables, figures) are released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT licence. The source images keep the licences of their original datasets. CITATION If you use these splits or audits, please cite the paper (reference to be added on publication) and this deposit (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24195419).

summary: Conditional event studies often judge a result against placebo dates drawn at random. When the selecting state persists and forward returns overlap, that placebo is miscalibrated. In an exploratory simulation with 1,024 days, three event masks, 20-day overlapping outcomes and 1,000 replicates per scenario, a true null was rejected at nominal 5% in 30.8% of replicates by the first clustered mask (Wilson 95% interval 28.0–33.7) and in 79.1% (76.5–81.5) by the test across all three masks. Circular mask shifts, White’s Reality Check, Hansen’s SPA and Romano–Wolf stepdown came much closer to 5% but exceeded it in several cells, up to 15.5% for restricted shifts under a variance regime. The mechanism is old; this note proposes no new method and no new theorem, and gives one benchmark in one design. This deposit candidate awaits independent review of the publication-only changes. No new experiment, data or result is introduced.
title: When Random-Day Placebos Fail: Persistent Event States and Overlapping Returns

summary: A hedge fund researcher needs to know whether a reported event contrast depends on the control used to judge it. This study compares downside-reversal, 52-week-high-breakout and reported-volume-event masks on 20 admitted, existing long-history equity series. The application is a replayable check of the evidence attached to these conditions, rather than a return forecast. The revised protocol, code and source hashes were locked before these market outcomes were computed. No method passed every registered calibration cell, so this study makes no confirmatory market claim. The historical sample is conditional on the available cached histories and contains survival and selection bias. Differences between control distributions do not identify an amount of true economic overstatement. During the preparation of this work the author used Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) to write analysis code and draft text. After using these tools, the author reviewed and edited the content as needed, verified every number and citation against the replication package, and takes full responsibility for the content of the publication.
title: Control choice in price-and-volume event studies: reference geometry, costs, and calibration

summary: The psc_benchmark Python package and scripts behind "Publication and laboratory fingerprints dominate machine-learning performance for perovskite solar cells" (Ragab et al., under review at Patterns). It includes: The preprocessing and evaluation pipeline, with publication-grouped splitting and training-only target encoding (with automated tests). The experimental designs: OFAT sweep, randomized complete block design and model comparison. The configuration presets and seeds that regenerate all canonical results. The scripts for the revision analyses. The pipeline that generates every figure, table and in-text value of the paper. A pinned environment (requirements-lock.txt) reproduces the canonical results bit-identically. Data are in the companion data record. Changes in v1.3: script added for the check of DOIs written in two letter cases (Patterns revision R2), with its results; README and citation file updated to the revised wording and to cite the archived code and data; Cell Press reference style updated for data and software citations.
title: PSC-Bench: benchmark code for machine learning on the Perovskite Database

summary: This dataset contains a CityJSON Next Sequence (CityJSONL) file representing 3D city models of three districts in Bontang City, East Kalimantan, Indonesia: Bontang Baru, Api-Api, and Loktuan. The dataset was collected as part of a pilot project aimed at updating and improving regional tax revenue management. It was subsequently used for spatial analysis in the research entitled "Integrating Multi-Sensor Earth Observation Data for Digital Twin Generation: A Framework for 3D City Reconstruction and Quality Assessment", which is included in the book Harmonizing Earth Observation Data for Enhanced Spatial Analysis . The dataset is provided to support research and applications related to 3D city modelling, spatial analysis, and urban digital twins.
title: 3D City Models of Three Districts in Bontang City, East Kalimantan, Indonesia

summary: Supplementary materials (v5.3.0) for: Design-based null audits: what two decades of pronoun-production experiments could and could not detect This package supports a design-based statistical audit of the predictability literature on pronoun production (story-continuation paradigm, 1994–2023). The audit asks whether the designs that produced this literature's null results were capable of detecting the effects they tested, via (i) a re-extraction of all eligible effect sizes on the log-odds-ratio scale with quasi-separation screening, (ii) design-by-design minimum-detectable-effect (MDE₈₀) simulation under each study's own published parameters, and (iii) power-contour guidance for future designs. Package structure: Online Resource 1 (search & PRISMA screening), Online Resource 2 (effect-size extraction workbook with provenance and separation flags), Online Resource 3 (publication-bias diagnostics: Egger regression and contour-enhanced funnel plots), audit data and figures (MDE table, power grid, Figures 1–3), seeded simulation code (Python authoritative + R re-implementation, plus separation-screening and power-grid tools), and the superseded original OSF materials of the companion meta-analysis. Relation to other materials: The correlation-based meta-analytic dataset audited and superseded by this re-extraction is archived in the OSF project osf.io/gx5ad ("Referential Predictability in Pronoun Production: Evidence from Meta-Analysis and Simulation for a Generalized Bayesian Model"). Version note (v5.3.0): BRM submission-readiness revision of v5.2.1 — data unchanged; adds separation flag column, contour-enhanced funnel plots with generation script, bit-exact power-grid code (verified against the shipped grid), separation-screening tool, requirements.txt and sessionInfo() records. Egger-test p-values in the manuscript should read .020 (subjecthood) and .312 (thematic role); see Online Resource 3 README. All simulations are seeded (20260825 / 20260827).

summary: Supplementary note to arXiv:2611.08310 and arXiv:2610.19779. A fingerprint of coherent noise built from a stabilizer code is only as informative as the recovery gates that produce it, and every fixed choice of those gates is blind somewhere. This note isolates what can nevertheless be guaranteed, and states it as a worst-case floor rather than an average improvement. Two elementary facts about Fisher information make the guarantee exact. Because information matrices add, the identifiable set of a collection of designs is the union of theirs, so running several designs in parallel can never cost a direction that any member sees. Because the inverse of a sum is Loewner-dominated by the inverse of any summand, splitting a fixed shot budget over S designs can never cost more than sqrt(S) in standard deviation, that is, S in shots. The premium is therefore fixed in advance and independent of the working point, while the gain is not. Both statements are certified over the 64-design space of the three-qubit repetition code, under the 48- and 112-component fingerprints: the Loewner inequality is evaluated rather than assumed at every point tested, the worst case over 300 working points is 1.25 against the certified sqrt(2) = 1.4142, the bound is attained to five figures at one structured point, and at the worst points of the individual designs the parallel pair sits below the better single design by factors of 2.6 to 9.5. Two three-gate placements suffice; a third adds 3.5 to 11.5 per cent. The floor buys recoverability and worst-case precision, and it buys nothing else: it does not buy accuracy under common-mode calibration bias, and it does not repair a model degeneracy that no design can see. Contents: the two propositions with proofs, the cost corollary, the numerical certification (five tables, one figure), the relation to the two companion papers, and a reproduction map. The archive repro_v1.0.zip in this record contains the seven scripts, four data files, the figure and a self-test that re-derives every quoted number; run python scripts/selftest.py from the archive root and compare against MANIFEST.sha256. Companion papers: arXiv:2611.08310 (recovery gates as a resource) and arXiv:2610.19779 (coherent-noise identifiability).
tags: quantum process tomography; coherent noise; stabilizer codes; repetition code; recovery gates; Fisher information; parameter identifiability; Cramer-Rao bound; metrology; quantum error correction
title: A Hard Worst-Case Floor for All-Parameter Recoverability in Three-Qubit Coherent-Noise Fingerprinting

summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The paper also discloses one application-facing composition of the per-action passkey press, the presence call (§3.8): an identity provider confirms to an app, for one named action and in the provider's own closed wording, that the holder of a person's passkey pressed it, for a person the app already knows by its own pairwise identifier, and keeps nothing; §12.1 reports the novelty census that scopes that claim to the composition alone. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. Keywords: proof of personhood, proof of humanity, sybil resistance, decentralized identity, AI-content trust, open identity protocol, recipient-side filtering, BLE-Nearby proximity, blockchain consensus, AI alignment, per-action passkey confirmation, pairwise subject identifier, WebAuthn user verification, defensive publication. --- Provenance. This paper is part of the THonly research corpus, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The canonical version is at https://thonly.org/research/b-poh-humanity-layer-ai-native-internet . Its SHA-256 is 26ba7ff48f047fef035d7248ba97c5c86fb1538b839a66410b2be44ea72b8816 , independently timestamped to the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps and signed under RFC 3161 by three trust authorities, one of them eIDAS-qualified. AI co-authorship is disclosed. Miss Aquarius is the consistent name used for the AI collaboration across all venues. Miss Aquarius co-authored this paper; Zenodo lists no AI tool as a creator, so Miss Aquarius is named here rather than among the creators.
title: B-PoH℠ as Humanity Layer for the AI-Native Internet: An Open Proof-of-Personhood Protocol with Four Optional Layered Proofs and Recipient-Side Filters

summary: We study in-context learning of scalar linear regression by L untied linear-attention layers, each with a trainable key scalar k_i and query scalar q_i. For every depth L and prompt length n, population gradient flow on the 2L factors is bounded and converges to a critical point, every critical point that is not a global minimizer has a negative Hessian eigenvalue, and the flow reaches a global minimizer from all initializations outside a Lebesgue null set, for instance almost surely under Gaussian initialization. The trained network performs L gradient descent steps on the prompt's least-squares loss, with step sizes k_iq_i the reciprocals of the zeros of a rescaled Laguerre polynomial L_L^(n/2), and its risk is $2^LL!/\prod_{j=1}^{L}(n+2j)$. Initializations with k_i = -q_i in some layer converge to a critical point that is not a minimizer, so the null set is not empty.
title: Gradient flow for deep factored scalar linear attention learns multi-step gradient descent

summary: This dataset is version 1.1.0 of the P1 complete derived transcriptomic resource for mapping and comparing human pluripotent stem cell-derived beta-cell differentiation across published protocols. It contains 100 sample or time-point analysis units, an S0-S6 stage ontology with S7-S9 reserved, a 2,552-gene shared cost space, optimal-transport stage coordinates with 20 retrospectively exported reference-centroid bootstrap draws, five-axis/46-gene Maturity Fidelity Index scores with 16 sensitivity versions, a 25-module concordance atlas, gene- and module-level variance components, constructed reliability descriptors, provenance records, analysis-code snapshots, and two application workflows. Applications and evidence boundaries. The internal GSE158617 example uses 38 samples in a retrospective, in-sample interface demonstration and is not independent validation. The external GSE203264 application uses 35 wild-type samples and a rebuilt P1-compatible 2,550-gene reference. Its non-monotonic D35 result concerns unsorted, compositionally heterogeneous SC-islets and is not validation of the unmodified 2,552-gene model or a pure beta-cell accuracy result. Reliability values are constructed descriptors, not absolute dataset-quality scores or significance ranks. MFI values are within-matrix relative profiles, not absolute cross-protocol maturity measures. No in vivo developmental tiers, validated benchmark accuracy, clinical validity, or universal generalization are claimed. Reproduction scope. The package supplies package-local verification for the two application workflows and the external diagnostics. The analysis-code and provenance snapshots support inspection and traceability but are not represented as a relocatable clean-room rebuild of every manuscript display item. The reference-centroid draws are a retrospective deterministic reconstruction from frozen training inputs, not an original frozen cache. Source data and governance. Original GEO expression matrices and metadata are not redistributed. Source accessions, expected hashes and third-party rights boundaries are documented in the package. GSE270220 and GSE275610 remain sealed and contributed to no statistic. The associated pilot-informed preregistration and execution governance records are identified through the related OSF project; private OSF access tokens are neither included nor required for the packaged application checks. summary: theorem A071685: for n not divisible by 10, n is a term (non-palindromic, n | R(n) or R(n) | n, where R(n) is the decimal digit-reversal) iff R(n) = 4n or R(n) = 9n or n = 4*R(n) or n = 9*R(n) - the announced union of A001232, A222814, A008918, A222815. summary: This repository contains the computational reproducibility package accompanying the research article “Beyond Monetary Energy Markets: Multilateral Reciprocity as an Alternative Exchange Mechanism for Energy Communities”. The package includes Python implementations of the proposed non-monetary energy exchange mechanism, benchmark models, cooperative surplus allocation methods, sensitivity analyses, temporal validation, synthetic photovoltaic generation, and utilities for reproducing the numerical results, tables and figures. Due to restrictions on redistribution, the original GoiEner smart-meter consumption data and household-level derived datasets are not included. Users must independently obtain the file profiles_part01.tar.zst from the GoiEner Smart Meter Dataset (Version 7.1), available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22313409 . A dedicated Python extraction and preprocessing utility is provided to reconstruct the required hourly demand profiles locally without imputing missing observations. The package also includes the OMIE wholesale electricity price series used in the study, corresponding to the Portuguese bidding zone, and the synthetic study configuration. Detailed installation instructions, data provenance, reproduction procedures and file integrity checks are provided in the accompanying documentation. The redistribution of third-party data remains subject to the conditions established by the original data providers.
title: Beyond Monetary Energy Markets: Multilateral Reciprocity as an Alternative Exchange Mechanism for Energy Communities — Reproducibility Package

summary: AiMat-Suite is the integrated, verifiable software framework developed for the doctoral thesis of A. O. Marcelo Júnior (PPGECM/UFC, LAMEFF). summary: Deep-research Numbers article on heart disease, explaining one disparity statistic with its definition, denominator, and limits. In the American Heart Association's 2025 Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics fact sheet (data 2017-2020), 58.9% of non-Hispanic Black men and 59.0% of non-Hispanic Black women aged 20 and older had cardiovascular disease counted as a four-component bundle (coronary heart disease, heart failure, stroke, and hypertension), versus about 49% of all U.S. adults; hypertension alone accounted for 57.5% of men and 58.4% of women, while coronary heart disease alone was 6.2% and 6.3%. The article contrasts the bundle with interview-survey diagnosed coronary disease (Black adults 4.1% vs. 5.0% overall, NHIS 2024, via HHS OMH), shows major cardiovascular mortality in 2022 at 301.0 versus 223.0 per 100,000 (ratio 1.35, wider than the prevalence ratio of about 1.20), and prints the sources' limits: no confidence intervals in the fact sheet, a rounded summary comparison, and 2017-2020 vintage. No supplement claim and no product are made; omega-3, garlic, and green tea trial effects are used only as a scale check, including the omega-3 null across 20 trials and 68,680 patients (Rizos 2012). Evidence grade: STRONG. Educational article from the Buddha Ayurvedic School of Medicine: https://buddha.hospital
title: 59 Percent: What the Cardiovascular Disease Number for Black Adults Actually Means

The article contrasts the bundle with interview-survey diagnosed coronary disease (Black adults 4.1% vs. 5.0% overall, NHIS 2024, via HHS OMH), shows major cardiovascular mortality in 2022 at 301.0 versus 223.0 per 100,000 (ratio 1.35, wider than the prevalence ratio of about 1.20), and prints the sources' limits: no confidence intervals in the fact sheet, a rounded summary comparison, and 2017-2020 vintage. No supplement claim and no product are made; omega-3, garlic, and green tea trial effects are used only as a scale check, including the omega-3 null across 20 trials and 68,680 patients (Rizos 2012). Evidence grade: STRONG. Educational article from the Buddha Ayurvedic School of Medicine: https://buddha.hospital

summary: Publishing a model or method does not finish the work of applied mathematics. Turning a mathematical idea into a reliable operational tool requires translation: assessment of how well a method behaves in theory and under real domain constraints, adaptation of both the mathematical formulation and the software to modern computing architectures, and adoption into sustained community use. Because every simplified model leaves a gap between idealized assumptions and reality, it carries applicability debt that an overlapping web of skills—uniting applied mathematicians, statisticians, domain specialists, and research software engineers—must manage. Generative AI and multi-agent harnesses have upset that balance. Large language models and coding agents make it cheap to generate candidate derivations, simulation code, and machine-checked proofs while leaving problem formulation and concrete domain verification tied to scarce human judgement. When automated generation outpaces translation, applicability debt goes unmanaged and pushes adoption toward unverified shortcuts, risking a crisis of application. At the same time, Australian science and innovation policy largely equates translation with commercial intellectual property and private data centres while overlooking research software and verification capacity inside public agencies, national facilities, and universities. Picking up in 2006—the fiftieth anniversary of the Australian Mathematical Society (Counting Australia In) and the birth year of the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) and the ACCESS Earth-system partnership—this monograph contrasts that post-war public compact at the Society's seventieth anniversary in 2026 against Ambitious Australia and Science 2035, where research software disappears from policy view and the 2016–2025 mathematical-sciences decadal plan has expired without a successor. Written for both public policymakers and working quantitative practitioners, this book examines how translation succeeds or short-circuits across two centuries of computational history, a twenty-year citation census of 112 works applying the EQ algorithm for equal-area sphere partitions, Research Software Engineer workforce audits, Earth-system and biomedical case studies, and invariants-first software verification (PyEQSP and GluCat). Benchmarking Australia against Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, and New Zealand across 18 chapters, 3 empirical appendices, and 750 verified primary sources (188 pages), it outlines practical, trade-off-aware opportunities across university assessment, service teaching, research software careers, scientific societies, sovereign infrastructure, and public-interest model verification ahead of the 2026–2028 national research and infrastructure renewals.
title: What does it take to apply mathematics in Australia today?

Support Vector Machine -------------------------- METHODOLOGICAL INFORMATION -------------------------- // Description of sources and methods used for collection/generation of data: We study 10 datasets from the University of California, Irvine (UCI) ML Repository. We provide 32 repetitions per feature subset, to address the stochasticity of the ML models. // Methods for processing the data: The tables were computed using Julia 1.12.2, using the following packages: 1. Logistic Regression (MultinomialClassifier from MLJLinearModels.jl) 4. Neural Network (MLP from Flux.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) 5. Random Forest (RandomForestClassifier from BetaML.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) 6. Support Vector Machine (SVC from LIBSVM.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) In all models, the default parameters (as of MLJ v0.21.0) were used, with a 70/30 train/test split. // Facility-, instrument- or software-specific information needed to interpret the data: The data can be read using any data analysis tool that can read HDF5 (.h5) files. -------------------- DATA & FILE OVERVIEW -------------------- // File List: Each of 10 ML datasets × 6 ML classifiers is stored as a separate .h5 file, with a dataset ID as the filename. Each file contains two HDF5 datasets with the same dimensions: 1. accuracies 2. times Where `accuracies` is a matrix of size 2^n × 32, with ordered rows (from 1 to 2^n-1 possible feature subsets). Columns represent one of 32 model repetitions. The i-th row in the accuracies matrix is the decimal representation of a bitstring representing a feature subset, where each digit in the bitstring corresponds to a column in the ML dataset, with a 1 or 0 depending whether or not it is used for training the model. The cell contains a real number for the ML classifier accuracy using that feature subset. `times` is a matrix of the same size, which contains the training times (in seconds) for all the models trained. The (i,j)-th entry in `times` is the training time for the (i,j)-th model in `accuracies`. summary: This paper presents our submission to the ACMMM25 - Grand Challenge on Multimedia Verification. We developed a multi-agent verification system that combines Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with specialized verification tools to detect multimedia misinformation. Our system operates through six stages: raw data processing, planning, information extraction, deep research, evidence collection, and report generation. The core Deep Researcher Agent employs four tools: reverse image search, metadata analysis, fact-checking databases, and verified news processing that extracts spatial, temporal, attribution, and motivational context. We demonstrate our approach on a challenge dataset sample involving complex multimedia content. Our system successfully verified content authenticity, extracted precise geolocation and timing information, and traced source attribution across multiple platforms, effectively addressing real-world multimedia verification scenarios.
title: Multimedia Verification Through Multi-Agent Deep Research Multimodal Large Language Models
