summary: Abstract This integrative research synthesis develops a candidate relational architecture across quantum foundations, physical history, persistent organization, relational time, and the recovery problem for spacetime. Its method is unification by decomposition : constraint, weighting, singular factualization, and retention are treated as distinct operations with distinct evidential burdens. Key Analyses & Framework Quantum Foundations & Entanglement: The double slit separates coherent alternatives, receiver-defined effects, Born weighting, and the $n = 1$ record. The Sorkin hierarchy and reconstruction literature delimit what is already formally known and leave open the physical motivation for second-order weighting. Entanglement is analyzed through a missing-loss audit: spatial routing, operational differentiation, and dynamical decoupling do not by themselves demonstrate ontological severance of a nonfactorizable joint state. Ontology & Event-Factualization: Primitive factualization is treated as a technical event-ontology posit, with fundamental agency as a stronger interpretive hypothesis (alongside objective stochasticity, Bohmian completion, Everettian branching, and collapse dynamics as comparison classes). A present-state coherence veto prevents absolute factualization while coherence-bearing degrees of freedom remain causally accessible to future interactions in which their phase relation can again matter. Retained factual consequences provide the bridge to physical history, memory, differential persistence, and increasingly organized agency. Downstream Physics & Empirical Testing: Transition and stabilization are treated as relational roles of one field-energy reality rather than new substances. The synthesis incorporates a fully exposed prospective transition-stabilization kill test in a driven liquid-to-vapor system and preserves planetary, gravitational, and spacetime extensions as explicitly conditional research branches. Methodological Stance: No universal master equation is claimed. The program is a structured ontology, audit, and research architecture whose modules must earn mathematical or empirical closure independently. Philosophical Extensions (Dual-Aspect Hypothesis): A further dual-aspect factualist hypothesis, with a panexperiential extension, distinguishes the publicly accessible objective face of factual processes from a minimally subjective first-person-like aspect associated with irreducible factual resolution. This is presented as a stronger ontological interpretation, not as an experimentally established consequence. It does not identify an elementary subjective aspect with a subject, mind, or consciousness. Complex biological agency is treated as potentially nested and hierarchically integrated, while the combination of elementary subjective loci into a unified subject is left as an explicit unresolved problem.
title: Unification by Decomposition: The Dualverse — From Quantum Factualization and Physical Memory to Hierarchical Individuality and Spacetime

summary: A negative and methodological result on Edward Elgar's Dorabella cipher (87 arc symbols, 14 July 1897). Thirty decipherment hypotheses were each tested against shuffled-symbol nulls and enciphered-English controls; all were ruled out or disfavoured. About 10% drawing slips reduce a standard substitution solver from 97% to about 57% accuracy on 87-letter controls, so earlier "not English" verdicts do not cover a carelessly drawn cipher; a slip-tolerant solver places Dorabella above all shuffles but below all English controls. Neighbouring arcs that are 180° flips of each other are strongly over-represented (27 of 86 against 12.6 expected, p ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵). The cipher is not solved. AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) was used in transcription, decipherment, checking and drafting, under the author's direction; it is disclosed in the text. No archival images are reproduced.
title: Elgar's Dorabella cipher (14 July 1897): thirty hypothesis tests with shuffled and enciphered controls, a slip-tolerance loophole, and an excess of opposed neighbouring arcs

summary: RSE-AS: Research Code, Trained SAC Models, and Evaluation Results for Renewable Microgrid Energy Management This repository accompanies the research study entitled “Causality-Aware Economic Action Selection for Battery-Constrained Microgrid Energy Management: A Computational Trade-off Between Soft Actor-Critic and Model Predictive Control.” It provides the original research code, five pretrained Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) models, experimental evaluation results, and additional numerical verification artifacts for Causality-Aware Risk-Sensitive Economic Action Selection (RSE-AS) . RSE-AS is a post-policy economic action-selection mechanism that evaluates battery-feasible candidate actions using chronologically available forecasts, economic scoring, and uncertainty-dependent regularization without retraining the underlying SAC policies. Repository Contents Original research archive (Version 1) Research notebooks: Two Google Colab notebooks documenting the research workflow and dataset preparation. Pretrained SAC models: Five saved policies corresponding to random seeds 42, 43, 44, 45, and 46, each trained for 100,000 environment interactions. Chronological evaluation: Results for validation in 2021, full-year testing in 2022, and the available 8,753 hourly observations from 2023. Distribution-shift evaluation: Results under increased electricity demand (+20%), reduced photovoltaic (PV) generation (−30%), increased electricity tariffs (+50%), and combined perturbations. Ablation analysis: Comparisons among RSE-AS, Economic-Only, Fixed attenuation, Adaptive attenuation, and unmodified SAC actions. Statistical analysis: Seed-level results, paired cost differences, nominal confidence intervals, and exact two-sided sign tests. Documentation: README, software requirements, reproducibility notes, data-source attribution, and licensing information. Additional verification archive (Version 2) reproduce_rse_2023.py — Python source code for the numerical replay audit. RSE_AS_2023_hourly_all_seeds.csv — Hourly replay trajectories for five frozen SAC policies. replay_vs_original.csv — Comparison of replayed and previously recorded results. verification_report.csv — Results of the 16 implemented verification checks. verification_metadata.json — Evaluation configuration, numerical discrepancies, and software environment information. README_VERIFICATION.md — Documentation of the additional audit and its limitations. The Version 2 verification materials are included in RSE_AS_2023_Verification_Update.zip , alongside the retained original research archive. Experimental Configuration The investigated grid-connected microgrid includes a battery energy storage system with the following parameters: Nominal battery capacity: 200 kWh . Maximum charging/discharging power: 50 kW . State-of-charge (SOC) limits: 20%–90% . Charging and discharging efficiencies: 95% . Nominal initial SOC: 50% . Dispatch interval: 1 hour . SAC observation dimension: 12 . SAC action dimension: 1 . The SAC policies were trained using the 2017–2020 dataset, with 2021 reserved for validation and controller development. The complete 2022 period was used for primary chronological testing, while the available 2023 observations provided an additional evaluation period. The 2023 data were examined during research development and are not presented as a previously untouched holdout. summary: Version 1.14.0 (2026-11-14) replaces the height increment rule with a fitted height increment equation (the rule is kept as the fallback) and adds a crown base equation, a comparison with stand-level mortality forms (none adopted), and two long-term assessment metrics, with their scripts, logs and the rules written before fitting, in final_equations_20261114.zip , and supplement v127. The height, maximum stand density, diameter increment and mortality equations of version 1.13.1 are unchanged; projected height and assumed volume changed. Version 1.13.1 (2026-11-13) adds five checks of the relative-density system (benchmark with every equation refitted without the plot's installation fold, joint bootstrap of installations, the mortality equation under three death rules, benchmark after thinning, and equation S1 without the 53 Kap plots) with their scripts, logs and the inputs the scripts read, in final_equations_20261113.zip , and supplement v125. The equations and coefficients of version 1.13.0 are unchanged. Version 1.13.0 (11 November 2026) adds an annual individual-tree growth and mortality system for Acacia koa A. Gray ( koa_step_rdbyi.R and koa_rdbyi_equations.csv , both inside final_equations_20261111.zip ) that supersedes the v105final engine. An audit found that the v105final engine applies calibration multipliers, a height blend and a self-thinning step that the earlier supplement does not describe; see README.md. The new system applies the fitted equations as estimated. Diameter increment and mortality depend on relative density, the stand density index of live koa over a maximum that is predicted from the Biomass Yield Index and origin or supplied by the user. summary: The rapid growth of blockchain networks has raised concerns about their environmental sustainability, yet existing assessments are fragmented and often rely on problematic metrics or unverifiable self-reported data. This article addresses these gaps by combining quantitative measures of annual energy consumption and carbon emissions with a qualitative assessment of sustainability initiatives. Using data from the Crypto Carbon Ratings Institute (CCRI) and corporate sustainability reports, we evaluate Bitcoin, Ethereum, Binance Chain, XRP, Cardano, Solana, Dogecoin, Polygon, and Polkadot, and benchmark their operational footprints against those of Visa and Mastercard as representatives of traditional payment systems. Results show wide variation in sustainability performance: Proof-of-Stake networks exhibit substantially lower energy use and carbon intensity than Proof-of-Work systems, while transparency and reporting practices differ significantly across projects. This research contributes to the sustainability discourse by providing one of the first systematic comparisons between blockchain networks and incumbent payment systems, identifying methodological challenges in sustainability accounting, and advancing policy recommendations for standardized reporting, third-party verification, and energy-efficient design. This is the published version of: Mabrouk, H., Paul, L., & Wild, D. (2026). Sustainability Metrics and Disclosure Alignment in Blockchain Networks. Blockchain and Cryptocurrency, 4(1), 1–9. IFSA Publishing, S. L. Originally published on 23 March 2026. Original article: https://bc-ifsa-journal.com/p_bc_21.html Deposited under the journal’s Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license (CC BY 4.0).
title: Sustainability Metrics and Disclosure Alignment in Blockchain Networks

summary: Data and code that reproduce every number, table and figure in the manuscript "What Do Indonesian Artificial Intelligence Courses Teach That Industry Asks For? A Multi-University Curriculum Audit That Accounts for Lecturer Disagreement" (submitted to Computer Applications in Engineering Education). The study compares 953 course learning outcomes from 71 AI-related courses at 19 Indonesian universities with 840 requirement sentences from 51 AI job postings. A multilingual sentence-embedding model (paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2) finds the closest match in both directions, and similarity is converted into the probability that a lecturer would accept the match, using judgements from four faculty validators and a lead researcher, under six judgement standards and three calibration curve shapes. Curriculum relevance, demand coverage and their harmonic mean (alignment) are reported for the corpus, universities, Bloom levels, AI-relevance tiers, courses and skills, with cluster-bootstrap intervals, size controls, cross-validation of the calibration curves and a verb-swap check. Contents: paper4_replication.zip holds the anonymised data (universities coded U01 to U19, courses C01 to C71), the expert labels (cosine similarity, labels and job-statement group only; the texts of the judged pairs are not included), one Google Colab script (code/paper4_replication.py) and a README that maps each output file to the table or figure it produces. paper4_results.zip holds the outputs of the published run, and similarity_matrix.npy the 953 x 840 cosine similarity matrix. Raw validator forms contain personal data and are not released.
title: Replication package for: What Do Indonesian Artificial Intelligence Courses Teach That Industry Asks For? A Multi-University Curriculum Audit That Accounts for Lecturer Disagreement

summary: Experimental data from tests on timber–concrete composite beam–floor slab joints, carried out at PEMADE (Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Lugo Campus) with the project's own test procedure within the FrameTCC project. Three specimens were tested (J1–J3), each representing the intersection of two floor slab sections on a beam. Each test comprised two load cycles, loading to failure and unloading. The first cycle of J2 is not discussed in the related manuscript. For each record (the unloading of J1 is in a separate record, so there are ten), the dataset provides the time series of applied load, actuator stroke, the vertical displacement at mid-length measured by two transducers and the slip between the flanges of the floor slabs and the flange of the beam measured by four transducers, sampled at intervals of about 0.28 s, as CSV files (10 files). It also includes the processing workbook of each record, the maximum load of each record, the mass and failure mode of each specimen and 15 selected photographs with descriptions, five per specimen. It also contains nine digital image correlation (DIC) projects (created with GOM Software 2017), described in dic.csv together with the free software that can open them, and the calibration report of the DIC system. The results are discussed in the manuscript «Continuity effect over beams of timber-concrete composite floor slabs» (under review; doi:10.5281/zenodo.24142933).
title: FrameTCC 4.1 – Tests on timber–concrete composite beam–floor slab joints: test data and DIC

summary: Experimental data from four-point bending tests on cross-laminated timber–concrete composite floors, carried out at PEMADE (Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Lugo Campus) following EN 408 within the FrameTCC project. Three floor elements were tested (F1–F3), 6.10 m long with a span of 6.00 m. F1 and F2 were loaded to failure; F3 was loaded twice up to 60 kN without failure (F3a and F3b) and was then used in the long-term test of dataset 2.4, so there are four records. For each record, the dataset provides the time series of applied load, actuator stroke, mid-span deflection, local deflection over 1500 mm and the slip between concrete and timber at both ends, sampled at intervals of about 0.28 s, as CSV files (4 files). It also includes the processing workbook of each record, the values obtained (maximum load, loads and readings at two load levels, and local and global bending stiffness), the failure mode of F1 and F2 and 15 selected photographs with descriptions, at least four per floor. It also contains the digital image correlation (DIC) projects of F1, F2 and F3a (created with GOM Software 2017; the second cycle of F3 was not recorded with DIC), described in dic.csv together with the free software that can open them, and the calibration report of the DIC system. The results are discussed in Martín-Gutiérrez, Suárez-Riestra and Otero-Chans (2026), Structures 88, 111857 (doi:10.1016/j.istruc.2026.111857). The package follows the FrameTCC data standard v7: a README, metadata files (test, specimens, channels, publications, SHA-256 manifest and changelog), the converted test data as CSV files and the other files described above. Time is given relative to the start of each acquisition; no calendar dates are included. Original acquisition files are kept unmodified by the project and are not published.
title: FrameTCC 2.2 – Four-point bending tests on cross-laminated timber–concrete composite floors (EN 408): test data and DIC

summary: Analysis panel of 32 Indonesian provinces over 2020-2025, assembled from six editions of Statistik Indonesia (BPS) and from Indeks Pembangunan Manusia 2025, together with the extraction scripts, the 15 data-verification checks, the estimation code for the five specifications and the province-trend extensions, and the executed notebooks. summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: for 1 < p < 2 this paper finds the exact Schatten-norm constant for sums of matrix moduli when there are at least as many matrices as the matrix size, gives a new general upper bound ((1+√m)/2) 1−1/p , and certifies in exact arithmetic that rank-one matrices do not give the answer to Lee’s two-matrix problem. The question. For numbers, |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b|. A matrix A has a natural absolute value |A| = (A*A) 1/2 , but for matrices the size of a sum can exceed the size of the sum of the absolute values. Measuring size by the Schatten p-norm (p = 1 is the trace norm, p = 2 the Frobenius norm), one asks for the smallest constant c with ‖A 1 +…+A m ‖ p ≤ c ‖|A 1 |+…+|A m |‖ p . What was known. Eun-Young Lee (2010, 2012) asked for the best constant for two matrices. Lin and Zhang (2022) settled p = 2; Tang and Zhang extended the question to m matrices and conjectured a formula; Qiu (2026) proved it for p ≥ 2; below p = 2 the formula fails, by counterexamples of Zeng, Liu and Ratnavelu, of Pang and of Qiu, all built from rank-one matrices. The survey of Bourin and Zhang (2026) lists the range 1 < p < 2 as open. Results (1 < p < 2, n-by-n matrices). (1) When m ≥ n the best constant is an explicit one-variable maximum D p,n ; it depends only on the rank of the sum of the moduli, every equality case is classified, and for m < n the constant is strictly smaller. Consequently the best constant for rank-one summands is D p,min(m,n) in every dimension. (2) The best constant is log-convex in 1/p, so interpolating between p = 1 and p = 2 gives the dimension-free bound ((1+√m)/2) 1−1/p , better than the previous m (p−1)/(2p) for every m ≥ 2 (for two matrices at p = 3/2: 1.0648 instead of 1.1225, while the true value is at least 1.0364). (3) For two 3-by-3 matrices a computer-assisted proof in exact rational and interval arithmetic shows that the best rank-one value is beaten at nine exponents between 11/10 and 17/10. How. The sum is written as a product of two block matrices and Hölder’s inequality is applied; the problem reduces to comparing two Rényi entropies of the spectrum, whose extremal shape is one large eigenvalue and the rest equal. This extends T. Zhang’s Frobenius-norm argument; the matching examples are Pang’s, with a re-tuned parameter. Limits. The exact constant for two matrices of arbitrary size (Lee’s problem) for 1 < p < 2 remains open, as does the case m < n; the interpolation bound is not sharp; the certified excess over the rank-one value is tiny (about 10 −5 to 10 −7 ) and covers nine specific exponents, not an interval. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF) with Figure 1; the certificate script certify_rank_gap.py with its exact rational witnesses; verify_schatten.py (128 numerical checks of the scalar constant, equality families, adversarial searches, the bounds table and asymptotics, with negative controls); the figure script; recorded outputs; the bibliography from registry records; a machine-readable index; a research-gate record; a rating-free review summary; a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Assurance. Written proofs, except one computer-assisted proof in exact arithmetic (Proposition 2.5). Internal AI-assisted review only (five reviewer roles, an adversarial review and audit by a second AI model, a clean replay, a re-review and a proof audit): not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Sharp constants for sums of matrix moduli when 1<p<2

summary: The Brina Gap measures the difference between the growth a company can self-finance and the growth its market price already assumes.  Its fundamental arm is the sustainable-growth ceiling,  g f  = ROIC × Reinvestment Rate; its pricing arm is the market-implied growth  g *, recovered from a reverse discounted-cash-flow on enterprise value. Both come from public filings, so the Gap makes the market's embedded growth expectation explicit — mechanically, reproducibly, and without an analyst's private valuation. Stated in growth units, it is the only kind of valuation claim that can be checked against what firms later deliver —  and it checks out. On the complete point-in-time S&P 500 (2010–2024, survivorship-free), the market-implied growth  g * genuinely tracks the growth firms subsequently realize (correlation ≈ 0.4–0.5, nearly unbiased at the 10-year horizon) and is robust across independent recovery methods (Spearman 0.73–1.00).  The Brina Gap is a detector of over-extrapolated growth expectations:  the market systematically over-extrapolates growth — the calibration slope sits below one at every horizon — and the median firm priced for high growth under-delivers what its price implies (≈ 26% priced in vs ≈ 22% realized).  Head-to-head against the classical Margin of Safety, the Gap is mechanical and falsifiable where the Margin of Safety is not, nearly orthogonal to it in cross-section, and more accurate on the one directional test both can take (+3.9 points, p ≈ .004; the Gap's expensive-side calls were correct 58.9% of the time on the full universe).  Among all pure valuation metrics tested — book-to-market, earnings yield, EPV, the Margin of Safety — the Brina Gap ranks first, and it is the only one whose central claim can be verified at all.  Its practical form is the  Brina Matrix , which crosses the Gap's pricing read with fundamental quality and yields one rule that survives every specification tested:  "cheap" is only a bargain when quality is high — cheap plus low quality is the value trap, the worst-performing cell in the sample. We are equally explicit about the limits: the fundamental arm is a conservative anchor, not a forecast; and the Gap — like every metric in the companion audit, the Margin of Safety included — is not a standalone return signal, which is exactly what efficiency logic predicts for any transparent, filings-based measure, in the most pricing-hostile decade on record. Data and code are published: a per-call outcomes file and a one-command verifier reproduce every headline number (see below). Verify the headline numbers yourself (added in v3.0.1). directional_outcomes_v3.0.csv lists all 1,504 directional calls on the complete point-in-time S&P 500, 2010–2024, delisted and acquired firms included (CRSP-style). Running python3 verify_headline_claims.py (Python standard library only) recomputes: • Stocks the Brina Gap clearly flagged as priced too high trailed the S&P 500 over the next five years in 546 of 927 cases (58.9%; a coin flip gives 50%). Exact one-sided binomial p = 3.3×10⁻⁸: if the warnings were coin flips, a record this good would come up about once in 30 million tries. • On the same 1,504 calls the classic Margin of Safety scored 50.9% (chance); the Gap 54.8%: +3.9 points, year-clustered bootstrap p = 0.0038. • Value Trap calls: 59.5% (207 of 348). The Gap's "cheap" calls were at chance (48.2%), as the paper reports. The paper claims no standalone return edge (over every stock, sign only: 52.4%). See README_VERIFY.md. Two parts:  Part I — the paper (the construct, its theory, the validity battery, the Brina Matrix); Part II — the complete empirical record (directional tests, robustness, failure modes, pre-registered refinements).  Supersedes v1.0 and v2.0; their d
title: The Brina Gap: A Framework for Identifying Growth Mispricing in Equity Markets

summary: Replication package for the working paper "Precision Matters: Anti-Corruption Campaigns, Targeted Crackdowns, and Sector Returns in China's Stock Market" (Xuanyuan Li, 2026). The package contains: (1) four hand-verified event libraries — 31 general anti-corruption campaign events (2012–2026), 12 sector-targeted interventions, 12 local-flagship case-study events, and 14 positive policy tools — every date anchored to an official primary source (CCDI, NDRC, MIIT, NPC, SAMR); (2) a 152-month hand-compiled CCDI eight-point-regulation enforcement series (2013-09 to 2026-09) with per-month source anchors and the December 2019 coverage-revision flag; (3) Sina hfq-adjusted daily return panels for the sector proxies and the CSI 300 benchmark; (4) all analysis scripts (Python 3.11, pandas/numpy): event-study grids, monthly enforcement-intensity regressions, exact permutation / cluster-bootstrap / sign-test inference, index-proxy robustness, and a beta-adjusted market-model replication with Newey-West lag sensitivity; (5) the manuscript (Markdown and Word), cover letter, and title page. Run the scripts from the package root; README.md gives replication steps and data-source conventions. All paper results are reproducible from the cached CSVs without network access. Inference note: policy events of this precision are scarce by construction; the paper reports exact permutation tests as primary evidence and discloses that the beta-adjusted replication weakens the headline targeted-intervention spread (p = 0.073).
title: Replication package for: Precision Matters: Anti-Corruption Campaigns, Targeted Crackdowns, and Sector Returns in China's Stock Market

summary: Replication code for a study of battery storage investment prioritisation across five campuses of a merged public technical university in Taiwan, under a contract-capacity time-of-use tariff. The code recovers tariff parameters from billing records, jointly optimises storage size, contracted capacity and time-of-use dispatch for each site-year by linear programming with a genetic-algorithm benchmark, and values storage against an administratively optimised counterfactual so that contract reductions obtainable without capital expenditure are not credited to storage. The institutional billing records analysed in the paper are not included, having been obtained under a data use agreement that does not permit redistribution; a synthetic panel with the same schema is provided so the code runs out of the box.
title: Analysis code for: Visible in kilowatts, invisible in money — contract capacity, storage and investment priorities under a Taiwanese demand-charge tariff

summary: Measurement data and analysis code for maximum independent set (MIS) written as a single penalty (QUBO) objective and run on quantum annealers (D-Wave Advantage_system6 and Advantage2_system1) and gate-model processors (IBM Heron r3 and Nighthawk r2) through a QAOA circuit. The deposit contains: measurement count histograms of every executed circuit and annealer read set, with the executed angles, compiled depth, two-qubit gate counts and physical layouts; job ledgers and submission plans; the calibration snapshot each gate-model batch ran under; noiseless state-vector results for the same circuits; the instance generator (every instance is a pure function of size, fill fraction and seed) for king-lattice graphs, random 3-regular graphs, Erdős–Rényi graphs and heavy-hex induced subgraphs; the analysed tables; four hardware jobs whose predictions and criteria were written before submission, with the written designs and plan hashes; and the analysis scripts. reproduce.py recomputes derived quantities from the deposited tables offline. Not included: per-shot bitstrings (the provider returns count histograms), compiled circuit files (rebuilt from instance, angles and transpiler seed), optimizer per-evaluation traces and annealer embeddings. Account identifiers and budget statements were removed; the redactions are listed. The record is one zip archive ( zenodo_deposit.zip , directory structure preserved) with the README.md and a SHA-256 checksum list of every archived file alongside. Code: MIT ( LICENSE-code.txt in the archive). Data, tables and documents: CC BY 4.0.
title: Measurement data and analysis code: maximum independent set under a penalty objective on quantum annealers and gate-model processors

summary: This record provides MATLAB code, processed inputs and Source Data supporting the manuscript “Tectonic pump closes the evolutionary loop for long-buried subseafloor microbes.” The software archive includes poroelastic fluid-flow modeling and its benchmark, fluid and cell source budgets, and analyses of Costa Rica microbial communities and seismicity, including partial Spearman correlations controlling for temperature and pH. The accompanying Source Data archive contains the numerical data underlying the main-text and supplementary figures and tables. summary: Computational detection of intertextuality has so far used individual features such as word n-grams, edit distance, or word embeddings to identify text reuse or allusion, with only limited efforts to combine two such features for improved detection. This article presents Tesserae V6, a freely available platform that searches, weights, and combines into a single fused score ten distinct signals: shared headwords; a single shared headword; identical surface forms; character-trigram sound similarity; near-identical strings by edit distance; shared meaning by sentence embedding; curated cross-headword synonym pairs; matching dependency-tree patterns at shared headwords; identical dependency frames without any shared word; and shared rare words. The fused score also incorporates word-rarity weighting from corpus-wide frequencies. On the founding Lucan–Vergil benchmark, the previous V3 lexical baseline recovered about 27% of known parallels. Against five commentator-attested benchmarks comprising 862 parallel passages from Latin epic, the new fused V6 system recovered 91.5% in its full ranked output. Of the top distinct results for the Lucan–Vergil comparison, 79% (34 of 43) are meaningful instances of intertextuality. The platform was built by a classicist directing a sequence of AI coding assistants in natural language, with no traditional programming, and with each stage of development checked against the same benchmarks. The platform is available at https://tesserae.caset.buffalo.edu . This preprint has not been peer reviewed.
title: Feature Fusion for Computational Intertextuality Detection in Tesserae V6

summary: MakeCOO is a Wolfram Language command-line package that constructs a stoichiometric matrix from reaction definitions. It represents each reversible reaction as separate forward and reverse records and constructs a matrix with chemical species as rows and directed reactions as columns. It also exports the species list and directed reaction table. This archive contains MakeCOO version 0.3.0, the version used to construct the stoichiometric matrix in the anaerobic Mn(II) oxidation case study. It includes the source code, documentation, example inputs and tests, and the shared Utils/IO.wl file. The software is distributed under the MIT License. If you use MakeCOO in research, please cite the accompanying article by Mayumi Seto and Yuya Tsukamoto in Geomicrobiology Journal ( https://doi.org/10.1080/01490451.2026.2762317 ).
title: MakeCOO: Stoichiometric matrix construction from reaction definitions

summary: This dataset supports a retrospective technical evaluation of transactional evidence preservation, uncertain-submission recovery and historical assessment retrieval in a synthetic regulatory-computing pathway for nursing-home infection-control documentation. The collection contains derived research tables, source-inventory descriptions, evidence locators and checksums, extraction and reconciliation documentation, and separate failure/skip context. The primary 56-case hosted evaluation, separate 47-case Stage-B execution and local ten-case report retain distinct execution identities and must not be combined into a unique-test total. Stage-B descriptions are source-derived; execution totals are supported separately by retained logs. Its successful execution XML remains unavailable, and the local report lacks a tested commit identifier. A maintainer-submitted, AI-assisted inspection reported 113 detailed reporting entries accounted for: 106 exact matches and seven documented parameter substitutions. The reconciled derivative includes five additional aggregate records. Numerical outcomes are unchanged. Separate retained executions with failures and skips are documented without assigning unestablished causes. Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT assisted evidence inspection, reconciliation and preparation of the research documentation, as detailed in the accompanying extraction record. This collection supports inspection of reported findings and provenance; it is not an executable application reproduction package. The designated public research files are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Proprietary implementation source, controlled original archives, raw logs and complete execution environments are excluded. RegCIP, Inc.’s implementation materials remain separate from the research derivatives.
title: Research evidence for transactional evidence integrity in a regulatory computing API for nursing home infection control

summary: Code, partition manifests and per-image predictions supporting the audit and leakage-controlled re-evaluation of the 4,217-image Eye Disease Retinal Images collection.   Contents: the provenance and integrity audit; the manifests defining every evaluation arm image by image (image-level, patient-grouped, size-matched, source-matched, the common test set and the six leave-one-source-out splits); the training and evaluation code; stored per-image class probabilities for every run; the shortcut probes; and the visual adjudication verdicts for all 335 cross-label near-duplicate candidates.   The image collection itself is not redistributed here. It is available at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/python16/eye-disease-retinal-images and the manifests reference it by relative path.
title: Acquisition source confounds a widely used retinal fundus benchmark: audit, partitions and per-run predictions

summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. Keywords: proof of personhood, proof of humanity, sybil resistance, decentralized identity, AI-content trust, open identity protocol, recipient-side filtering, BLE-Nearby proximity, blockchain consensus, AI alignment, defensive publication. --- Provenance. This paper is part of the THonly research corpus, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The canonical version is at https://thonly.org/research/b-poh-humanity-layer-ai-native-internet . Its SHA-256 is d9d9a6d7bced60a5c39ba39079426a240024416799b1219b1d536173833df670 , independently timestamped to the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps and signed under RFC 3161 by three trust authorities, one of them eIDAS-qualified. AI co-authorship is disclosed. Miss Aquarius is the consistent name used for the AI collaboration across all venues. Miss Aquarius co-authored this paper; Zenodo lists no AI tool as a creator, so Miss Aquarius is named here rather than among the creators.
title: B-PoH℠ as Humanity Layer for the AI-Native Internet: An Open Proof-of-Personhood Protocol with Four Optional Layered Proofs and Recipient-Side Filters

summary: For every integer p>=4, a previously constructed symmetric numerical semigroup ring R_p and rigid two-generated monomial ideal determine a conductor ideal T_p whose special fiber C_p = F(T_p) is one-dimensional Cohen-Macaulay, generated in degree one by 10p monomials, with multiplicity 24p. Taking the imported offset bases as input, we prove that C_p ≅ k[xy^a : a ∈ G_p] ⊆ k[x,y]/(y^24p), that its defining ideal J_p is primary to the ideal of positive offsets, with nilpotency index 24p, and that Proj(C_p) is a saturated length-24p curvilinear fat point, locally Gorenstein although the coordinate ring has Cohen-Macaulay type 10p+1. The Kähler differentials split by characteristic. We then determine the reduced Gröbner basis for graded reverse lexicographic order with X_0 last. Its degree profile is (50p^2-17p, 5p-1, p-2) and no minimal leading monomial contains X_0, which gives a flat Cohen-Macaulay monomial degeneration. The quadratic part, the stabilization of the staircase, the absence of elements in degree five and higher, the absence of X_0 from the leading monomials and the flatness are derived from derived imported input; the imported relation type three is machine-verified. The cubic and quartic classification, for all p, is machine-verified and not derived: 16 Presburger obligations are decided unsatisfiable by Z3 and by cvc5 on identical queries, with no checked proof object. Exact sweeps at every p=4,...,300, an independent clique recomputation and negative controls validate the formulas. The results concern the conductor fiber cones of this explicit family; they do not assert that arbitrary monomial fiber cones are primary, curvilinear, Cohen-Macaulay or locally Gorenstein. Source code, compact artifacts, premise hashes and proofs: https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_RESEARCH .
title: Curvilinear Geometry, Primary Structure, and a Gröbner Degeneration of Conductor Fiber Cones in a Huneke–Wiegand Family

summary: The widespread application of inductive loads in today ‘s power distribution systems where power factor (PF) correction has become an integral requirement, has led to power factor degradation as a serious problem and requires correction for more efficient power distribution. In this paper, an innovative AI based Adaptive PF correction scheme is proposed to integrate conventional PF correction capacitor bank compensation with an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) based predictor-controller for dynamic reactive power compensation. A detailed MATLAB/Simulink 3–phase distribution system-based model has been evolved which yields operational data sets for ANN training and testing with different loading conditions. Proposed ANN predictor-controllers are trained with back-propagation algorithm applying MSE (Mean Squared Error) function as a network performance measure. The network prediction accuracy 96.9 to 97.8% and the generalization capability has been established through comprehensive results analysis. The proposed architecture significantly decreases the reactive power demand by approximately 77%, apparent power consumption by 28.1% and the dynamic response by 3 times compared to fixed capacitor compensation method. Moreover, the (PF) is maintained between 0.95–0.96, confirming its effectiveness for real-time adaptive power factor correction in modern distribution systems.
title: AI-Based Adaptive Power Factor Correction for Reactive Power Reduction in Distribution Systems

summary: Supplementary note to arXiv:2611.08310 and arXiv:2610.19779. A fingerprint of coherent noise built from a stabilizer code is only as informative as the recovery gates that produce it, and every fixed choice of those gates is blind somewhere. This note isolates what can nevertheless be guaranteed, and states it as a worst-case floor rather than an average improvement. Two elementary facts about Fisher information make the guarantee exact. Because information matrices add, the identifiable set of a collection of designs is the union of theirs, so running several designs in parallel can never cost a direction that any member sees. Because the inverse of a sum is Loewner-dominated by the inverse of any summand, splitting a fixed shot budget over S designs can never cost more than sqrt(S) in standard deviation, that is, S in shots. The premium is therefore fixed in advance and independent of the working point, while the gain is not. Both statements are certified over the 64-design space of the three-qubit repetition code, under the 48- and 112-component fingerprints: the Loewner inequality is evaluated rather than assumed at every point tested, the worst case over 300 working points is 1.25 against the certified sqrt(2) = 1.4142, the bound is attained to five figures at one structured point, and at the worst points of the individual designs the parallel pair sits below the better single design by factors of 2.6 to 9.5. Two three-gate placements suffice; a third adds 3.5 to 11.5 per cent. The floor buys recoverability and worst-case precision, and it buys nothing else: it does not buy accuracy under common-mode calibration bias, and it does not repair a model degeneracy that no design can see. Contents: the two propositions with proofs, the cost corollary, the numerical certification (five tables, one figure), the relation to the two companion papers, and a reproduction map. The archive repro_v1.0.zip in this record contains the seven scripts, four data files, the figure and a self-test that re-derives every quoted number; run python scripts/selftest.py from the archive root and compare against MANIFEST.sha256. Companion papers: arXiv:2611.08310 (recovery gates as a resource) and arXiv:2610.19779 (coherent-noise identifiability).
tags: quantum process tomography; coherent noise; stabilizer codes; repetition code; recovery gates; Fisher information; parameter identifiability; Cramer-Rao bound; metrology; quantum error correction
title: A Hard Worst-Case Floor for All-Parameter Recoverability in Three-Qubit Coherent-Noise Fingerprinting

summary: Contemporary speculative fiction unsettles anthropocentric assumptions about language, intelligence and the production of knowledge. This article compares Laline Paull’s The Bees (2014) to Ray Nayler's The Mountain in the Sea (2022) and The Tusks of Extinction (2024), exploring how the novels represent the conditions under which non-human knowledge is produced, recognized and transmitted. Drawing on biosemiotics and critical posthumanism in conversation with Andrew Lopez's account of epistemic injustice towards non-human animals, it develops a comparative framework based on recognition, access and continuity. The key argument is that the novels depict epistemic harm not merely as a failure to interpret non-human signs but as the institutional restriction of the very environments and social relations through which practical knowledge can flow. In Paull's hive caste is the source of authority which controls access to sensory information; in Nayler's oceanic enclave corporate power turns scientific attention into a potential tool of appropriation; and in the de-extinction narrative, biological restoration is simply not enough without the recovery of the skills that are socially transmitted. The novels are not being read as descriptions of actual animal species. Rather they are being used as a lens through which to examine the political and ethical dimensions of human authority over other ways of knowing. The article makes a contribution to contemporary literary studies by linking multispecies representation to the distribution and preservation of epistemic goods.
tags: Biosemiotics; critical posthumanism; epistemic injustice; nonhuman communication; collective knowledge; multispecies justice; contemporary speculative fiction
title: Sign Systems and Shared Worlds: Nonhuman Communication, Collective Knowledge and Epistemic Justice in Contemporary Speculative Fiction

summary: Enterprise database systems face data-loss risks that come from operational errors, system failures and security incidents. MySQL binary logs give tools for data replication and point-in-time recovery, yet many organizations do not use them fully for recovery. This study proposes an automated, schema-aware MySQL binary-log recovery framework that integrates log discovery, dependency-aware recovery planning, database reconstruction, and validation into a unified enterprise restoration pipeline. The framework explains how to read binary-log formats, how to run recovery steps automatically and how to use performance-boosting tactics learned from well-known recovery models such as ARIES write-ahead logging, log-structured storage and event sourcing. The framework was tested in four failure scenarios and compared with the usual backup-and-restore approach. In those tests, the recovery time dropped by about 65%, meaning the framework needed only about one-third of the baseline time. A real-world check compared each recovered field to the printed reference invoice: 99.7% of the fields matched exactly, and every financial total was correct. The only error was a single non-financial field. This work gives reusable tools for people who care about database reliability, and it offers a clear map of failure types and a step-by-step method for bringing MySQL databases back to life. The proposed approach differs from conventional binary-log recovery methods by providing an end-to-end automated workflow with schema awareness and independent validation of recovered data.
title: Advanced MySQL Binary Log-Based Data Recovery

summary: Analysis package for a study of copy-specific assignment at the two 23S rRNA copies of Helicobacter pylori . The package contains the seventeen supplementary tables, the analysis and figure code, the recorded software versions, the reconstruction log for the long-read alignments, and a per-read phase-evidence table. What is reproducible. The six-criterion classification of 103 matched isolates is re-runnable and every verdict was re-derived from the counts with zero mismatches. The reference metadata for all cited works is captured from Europe PMC and every DOI was verified against its record. The figures are generated by script and each passes a programmatic overlap, clipping and text-on-line audit before export. The short-read counts at the two A2143 coordinates are reproduced from the archived alignment, whose header records the exact command and tool versions. What is not. The original NCBI query string and its date were not retained, so the cohort cannot be rebuilt verbatim; per-accession inclusion flags are given instead. The barrnap installation originally used on the analysis machine is missing a Perl module and does not run; the rRNA copy numbers were therefore archived values in earlier versions and are re-derived with barrnap 1.10.5 in this version. The original parameter sets for two of the three long-read procedures were not retained; those procedures were re-run and both original and re-run values are reported side by side and never pooled. One cell of the long-read table reproduces exactly; the others do not, and this is stated in the manuscript. Changes in version 4. The package matches the manuscript. All thirteen supplementary tables are present, including Supplementary Tables S12 and S13, which were absent from the previous version, and Supplementary Table S1 now carries the genome length and assembly level of all 1,483 retained genomes rather than leaving those columns empty. A new Supplementary Table S1b lists the seven excluded genomes that could be recovered from local storage, with their lengths; the genome-length window is 1.5 to 1.7 Mb and this version states the evidence that fixes its bounds. Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. The four control reference sequences are deposited under results/marker_control/. Changes in version 6. This version restores the complete file set. The previous version was published from an incomplete upload, so most of the figures, several of the supplementary tables and part of the analysis code were missing from that record. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files and this package has 134, so the package is now deposited as a single archive, hp23s_copy_assignment_package.zip , which holds every file at the path it occupies in the source repository; this README, the SHA-256 manifest and the archive of rRNA calls and copy sequences are additionally placed loose in the record. From version 10 the manuscript itself is not deposited, in the archive or loose. Every member of the archive is listed in SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256, and that manifest is regenerated here, which corrects the entry for this README (the previous manifest had been computed before the last edit of the file). DOI.txt now lists the version DOIs, and the data-availability sentence in the manuscript names the concept DOI rather than one version, so that it cannot point at a superseded record. Changes in version 7. This version is a manuscript round: the text is rebuilt from the same locked data by the same script, and no reported value changes. Three defects in the supplementary apparatus are correcte
title: Long reads assign a 23S rRNA resistance allele to one of the two copies in Helicobacter pylori; a complete short-read assembly does not

summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The paper also discloses one application-facing composition of the per-action passkey press, the presence call (§3.8): an identity provider confirms to an app, for one named action and in the provider's own closed wording, that the holder of a person's passkey pressed it, for a person the app already knows by its own pairwise identifier, and keeps nothing; §12.1 reports the novelty census that scopes that claim to the composition alone. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. summary: Pre-registration of an exploratory analysis, deposited before any race/ethnicity-specific outcome was estimated. We will examine racial/ethnic differences in first-molar dental sealant prevalence among US children aged 6–11 years using NHANES (1999–2004, 2011–2016, and 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic file; 2005–2010 cycles are excluded because tooth-level sealant codes are unavailable). Outcome: presence of a sealant on ≥1 permanent first molar among children with ≥1 assessable first molar. Comparison: non-Hispanic Black and Mexican American children versus non-Hispanic White children. Planned estimands are survey-weighted prevalence and absolute differences (percentage points) by period, change in the absolute gap between 1999–2004 and 2017–2020.3 (Holm-adjusted for the two primary contrasts), and attenuation of the gap after adjustment for age, sex, and income rank (poverty-income ratio), alongside a parallel income-gradient (slope index of inequality) comparison. Variance is estimated by Taylor linearization; attenuation uses a Rao-Wu bootstrap. Status. Exploratory: the hypotheses were formed after the authors had analysed overall (non-race-specific) prevalence and income inequality in the same data for a separate study. Published race-specific estimates for 2011–2014 exist (CDC Vital Signs, 2016), so the 2011–2014 direction is a replication rather than a confirmation; the change in racial/ethnic gaps since 1999–2004 is the new question. Race-specific outcomes had not been computed at the time of registration. Files: preregistration document (Markdown and PDF), version 1.0.
title: Racial/ethnic disparities in first-molar sealant prevalence among US children, 1999–2020: exploratory analysis pre-registration

summary: CHASE-AML is a synthetic banking benchmark comprising 33,176,605 settled transactions and 500,000 registered accounts. It combines persistent account activity with 26 standalone suspicious typologies and annotated single-path and branching laundering cases. Case, path, parent-transaction and stage information connects transfers so transaction rankings and the reach of alerts across cases can be evaluated separately. The package contains the full 36-column canonical transaction export and a 13-column core export of the same rows, opening and closing synthetic ledger snapshots, a data dictionary and file checksums. No customer banking records, paper-specific evaluation files, generator or evaluation code, trained policies or fitted models are included.
title: CHASE-AML: A Lifecycle-Aware Synthetic Banking Dataset for Anti-Money Laundering Research

summary: This dataset is version 1.1.0 of the P1 complete derived transcriptomic resource for mapping and comparing human pluripotent stem cell-derived beta-cell differentiation across published protocols. It contains 100 sample or time-point analysis units, an S0-S6 stage ontology with S7-S9 reserved, a 2,552-gene shared cost space, optimal-transport stage coordinates with 20 retrospectively exported reference-centroid bootstrap draws, five-axis/46-gene Maturity Fidelity Index scores with 16 sensitivity versions, a 25-module concordance atlas, gene- and module-level variance components, constructed reliability descriptors, provenance records, analysis-code snapshots, and two application workflows. Applications and evidence boundaries. The internal GSE158617 example uses 38 samples in a retrospective, in-sample interface demonstration and is not independent validation. The external GSE203264 application uses 35 wild-type samples and a rebuilt P1-compatible 2,550-gene reference. Its non-monotonic D35 result concerns unsorted, compositionally heterogeneous SC-islets and is not validation of the unmodified 2,552-gene model or a pure beta-cell accuracy result. Reliability values are constructed descriptors, not absolute dataset-quality scores or significance ranks. MFI values are within-matrix relative profiles, not absolute cross-protocol maturity measures. No in vivo developmental tiers, validated benchmark accuracy, clinical validity, or universal generalization are claimed. Reproduction scope. The package supplies package-local verification for the two application workflows and the external diagnostics. The analysis-code and provenance snapshots support inspection and traceability but are not represented as a relocatable clean-room rebuild of every manuscript display item. The reference-centroid draws are a retrospective deterministic reconstruction from frozen training inputs, not an original frozen cache. Source data and governance. Original GEO expression matrices and metadata are not redistributed. Source accessions, expected hashes and third-party rights boundaries are documented in the package. GSE270220 and GSE275610 remain sealed and contributed to no statistic. The associated pilot-informed preregistration and execution governance records are identified through the related OSF project; private OSF access tokens are neither included nor required for the packaged application checks. Licensing. Original source code is under the MIT License. Original derived data, model parameters, documentation and figures are under CC BY 4.0, subject to the stated third-party exclusions. Funding. Basic Scientific Research Projects of the Liaoning Provincial Department of Education for Universities and Colleges, grant LJ212413213011.

summary: Route-explicit deterministic delivered-cost model for green hydrogen supplied to the EU from Algeria (pipeline and ammonia) and five competitors (Morocco, Egypt, Oman, Australia, Chile), with country WACC and default-spread betas, bottom-up shipping, canal tolls and war-risk insurance with rerouting; Monte Carlo simulation (10,000 draws), Shapley decomposition, ES95 security premium, break-even GPR, Sobol indices, and an ex-post scenario tested on the observed 2026 Strait of Hormuz closure. All inputs are documented with their sources in params/; outputs are regenerated by src/run_model.py. Version 2.1.0 accompanies the revised article: the PV electricity cost uses the yield after clipping, the reference voyage of the ammonia chain is valued at the baseline production cost, three bounding variants are added (midstream financing, fuel valuation, independent PV yield factors) and further dated 2026 war-risk quotes are included (see CHANGELOG.md). It supersedes v2.0.0 and v1.0.0.

summary: theorem A316626 : conjectureA316626 (unconditional, universal in k, standard axioms only): for every k >= 1, the occurrence count of k in OEIS A316626 equals its occurrence count in the sister sequence A081832 plus exactly one when k is a power of 2 - the on-entry conjecture of N. Fox and A. Alkan (2018), i.e. the first stated (2,1) case of Conjecture 5.1 of Erickson-Isgur-Jackson-Ruskey-Tanny (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 26(1) (2012) 206-238, DOI 10.1137/100795425, arXiv:1509.02613), published open and found unproved in a prior-art audit covering 8 registries (2026-11-08). The proof formalizes the two well-founded meta-Fibonacci recurrences in the positive subtype (termination via simultaneous value+bound induction), proves uniqueness of the solutions, then identifies both sequences with explicit closed forms via cumulative block sums S(m) = 4m - s2(m) and S_b(m) = 4m - s2(m) - floor(log2 m) - 1: the inverse functions c, d satisfy the nested recurrences by a block-position case analysis, giving exact frequencies occ_A(k) = 3 + v2(k) and occ_B(k) = 3 + v2(k) - [k a power of 2], whence the conjecture by subtraction. Also proved: kernel anchors a(1..31) and b(1..30) matching the entry data, exact fibers of 1, and the k = 1 case. NOT claimed: the companion on-entry conjectures (slow increments {0,1}, density 1/4 - elementary corollaries of a = c but not kernel-exported), the remaining 179 recurrences of Conjecture 5.1, the 'the only' enumeration direction, and the informal slowness proof of A081832 by A. Alkan (2018, cited for context, not used). Trust base: Lean kernel only, axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], zero sorryAx, zero native_decide; build replayed green on continuous integration; leanexport-serialized re-exports re-checked with zero errors by three independent Lean kernel re-implementations (nanoda_bin with strict axiom whitelist, con-leche, con-ron) ship in the companion archive A316626-seal-exports.tar.zst. Six modules: A316626, Spec_A316626, Check_Spec_A316626, Check_AntiVacuite_A316626, AxiomsReport_A316626, plus the root harness Scratch_A316626_proof.lean.
title: A316626 - EJIRT Conjecture 5.1 (occurrence counts vs A081832) proved: certified formalization (Lean 4)

summary: theorem A071685: for n not divisible by 10, n is a term (non-palindromic, n | R(n) or R(n) | n, where R(n) is the decimal digit-reversal) iff R(n) = 4n or R(n) = 9n or n = 4*R(n) or n = 9*R(n) - the announced union of A001232, A222814, A008918, A222815. The OEIS comment 'the quotient R(n)/n or n/R(n) is always 4 or 9' is proved in full (lemma ratio49). Kernel-verified anchors: 1089 is the least term; the 26 values listed on the entry are all terms; Dale's conjecture (every term mod 100 in {1,12,78,89}) is verified on those 26 entry terms. The general Dale conjecture, Chandler's counting formula 4*Fib(floor((n-2)/2)), and the completeness of the 26 listed values are not proved here, documented not claimed. Trust base: standard axioms only; zero native_decide.
title: OEIS A071685: Reverse multiples with quotient in {4,9} proved

summary: This repository contains the computational reproducibility package accompanying the research article “Beyond Monetary Energy Markets: Multilateral Reciprocity as an Alternative Exchange Mechanism for Energy Communities”. The package includes Python implementations of the proposed non-monetary energy exchange mechanism, benchmark models, cooperative surplus allocation methods, sensitivity analyses, temporal validation, synthetic photovoltaic generation, and utilities for reproducing the numerical results, tables and figures. Due to restrictions on redistribution, the original GoiEner smart-meter consumption data and household-level derived datasets are not included. Users must independently obtain the file profiles_part01.tar.zst from the GoiEner Smart Meter Dataset (Version 7.1), available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22313409 . A dedicated Python extraction and preprocessing utility is provided to reconstruct the required hourly demand profiles locally without imputing missing observations. The package also includes the OMIE wholesale electricity price series used in the study, corresponding to the Portuguese bidding zone, and the synthetic study configuration. Detailed installation instructions, data provenance, reproduction procedures and file integrity checks are provided in the accompanying documentation. The redistribution of third-party data remains subject to the conditions established by the original data providers.
title: Beyond Monetary Energy Markets: Multilateral Reciprocity as an Alternative Exchange Mechanism for Energy Communities — Reproducibility Package

summary: For hedge fund research reviewers, this report examines checks for selective reporting when a registered study is closed. At the author’s research service, the proposed use is review of research records before their conclusions enter an evaluation; no product integration or saving in review time has been measured. This report makes no claim of originality.   Checking whether a study followed its pre-registration requires comparing the report with the plan. This report tests one method for that comparison. A research record is kept in a fixed JSON format (registration, hash commitment, event log, closure), and seven mechanical rejection rules, R1 to R7, each target one selective-reporting defect taken from Arnott, Harvey and Markowitz (2019) and Harvey and Liu (2015). The comparison arm gives the same information, rendered as plain text, to a general-purpose language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) with one fixed instruction. The test plan, its thresholds and its decision order were frozen, with a local SHA-256 hash, before any code, record or label existed. For each of two cohorts a separate model session generated 33 synthetic records, 12 valid and 21 with one injected defect, without seeing the rules, and labels were locked before either arm ran. In the first (in-sample) cohort the rules flagged 21 of 21 defective records and rejected 0 of 12 valid ones. The language model also flagged 21 of 21 but rejected 6 of 12 valid records, which disqualifies it under the plan. In the second (out-of-sample) cohort the rules again scored 21 of 21 with 0 of 12 rejected, and the language model scored 17 of 21 with 0 of 12. The gap of 4 is below the pre-registered margin of 5. The pre-registered verdict for both cohorts is therefore "compared, threshold not met", and the report makes no claim that the rules add detection. A reduced rule set (R1, R2 and R7 only) missed 12 of 21 defects in both cohorts and is refuted. No confidence intervals are reported, because the plan forbids them: the records are constructed counterexamples, not a sample from any population.   Deposit version: Working paper, version 1.2 (2026-11-12). Author: Peilun Cai. The manuscript is an English typeset presentation of the same experiment; no new experiment or result was introduced. PDF SHA-256: 6da6d6add0672e74bdad8b2c575268f6876434460b440da4cf868135e9425a21. Replication archive SHA-256: 5bba143768793c187a1c29c35e08a588c50697a0a47883341d75d252e57625ac. Original-language records available on request, verifiable against listed SHA-256. The original historical review is withheld; its scope and findings are represented by an English reproduction summary. The source and PDF are supplied separately. Funding: none. summary: Data and code for the paper "Label-efficient plant disease classification with vision foundation models: a leakage-controlled benchmark" by Harshvardhan Rai and Ravi Shankar Singh (Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology (Banaras Hindu University), Varanasi, India), submitted to the Journal of Plant Diseases and Protection. Code repository: https://github.com/harshvardhanrai-iitbhucse/plant_peft (version v1.0, also archived here as plant_peft_code_v1.zip). WHAT THIS DEPOSIT CONTAINS This deposit holds the derived data needed to check and reuse the results. It contains no images and no model weights; the images come from three public datasets and must be obtained from their original sources under their own licences. The data archive plant_peft_data_v1.zip contains: - splits/: the train/validation/test assignment of every image with its perceptual hash (pHash); the near-duplicate groups (Hamming distance ≤ 4) used to keep duplicates within one split; the cross-class duplicate list for the pigeon-pea dataset; and the manual audit of the 236 PlantDoc test images (photograph, plain background, text slide, collage). - results/: results.jsonl, one line per training run with its full configuration (model, method, learning rate, seed, data fraction) and validation and test metrics; the efficiency measurements (GMACs, latency, memory); per-class PlantDoc results. - runs/: for each run, the test-set predictions and labels as NumPy arrays, in the order of the test split in splits/, with small log and configuration files. - tables/ and figures/: every table and figure of the paper, as generated by the scripts from the files above. SOURCE DATASETS (NOT REDISTRIBUTED) - PlantVillage (Hughes and Salathé 2015), colour images; the 15 pepper, potato and tomato classes. - PlantDoc (Singh et al. 2020), official train/test split, 27 classes. - Pigeon-pea leaf dataset (Rajput and Doddamani 2024, Mendeley Data, version 1). The repository README describes how to prepare them. HOW TO REPRODUCE THE PAPER'S NUMBERS 1. Unpack plant_peft_code_v1.zip, or clone the repository at tag v1.0. 2. Obtain the three datasets and build the caches as described in the repository README. 3. Place splits/, results/ and runs/ from the data archive in the repository root. 4. Run python scripts/make_tables.py and python scripts/make_figures.py; they regenerate every table and figure from results/ and runs/ without any training. 5. To re-train a configuration, follow the repository README; each line of results.jsonl stores the full configuration of its run. PROTOCOL Splits are grouped by near-duplicate (pHash Hamming distance ≤ 4), so a duplicate never crosses the train/test boundary. Checkpoints are selected on validation data only. Every configuration is run with five seeds. Comparisons use a paired bootstrap over test images (10,000 resamples) with Holm correction within pre-registered families. LICENCE The derived data (splits, audits, logs, predictions, tables, figures) are released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT licence. The source images keep the licences of their original datasets. CITATION If you use these splits or audits, please cite the paper (reference to be added on publication) and this deposit (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24195419).
title: Data and code for: Label-efficient plant disease classification with vision foundation models: a leakage-controlled benchmark

summary: Conditional event studies often judge a result against placebo dates drawn at random. When the selecting state persists and forward returns overlap, that placebo is miscalibrated. In an exploratory simulation with 1,024 days, three event masks, 20-day overlapping outcomes and 1,000 replicates per scenario, a true null was rejected at nominal 5% in 30.8% of replicates by the first clustered mask (Wilson 95% interval 28.0–33.7) and in 79.1% (76.5–81.5) by the test across all three masks. Circular mask shifts, White’s Reality Check, Hansen’s SPA and Romano–Wolf stepdown came much closer to 5% but exceeded it in several cells, up to 15.5% for restricted shifts under a variance regime. The mechanism is old; this note proposes no new method and no new theorem, and gives one benchmark in one design. This deposit candidate awaits independent review of the publication-only changes. No new experiment, data or result is introduced.
title: When Random-Day Placebos Fail: Persistent Event States and Overlapping Returns

summary: A hedge fund researcher needs to know whether a reported event contrast depends on the control used to judge it. This study compares downside-reversal, 52-week-high-breakout and reported-volume-event masks on 20 admitted, existing long-history equity series. The application is a replayable check of the evidence attached to these conditions, rather than a return forecast. The revised protocol, code and source hashes were locked before these market outcomes were computed. No method passed every registered calibration cell, so this study makes no confirmatory market claim. The historical sample is conditional on the available cached histories and contains survival and selection bias. Differences between control distributions do not identify an amount of true economic overstatement. During the preparation of this work the author used Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) to write analysis code and draft text. After using these tools, the author reviewed and edited the content as needed, verified every number and citation against the replication package, and takes full responsibility for the content of the publication.
title: Control choice in price-and-volume event studies: reference geometry, costs, and calibration

summary: Analysis package for a study of copy-specific assignment at the two 23S rRNA copies of Helicobacter pylori . The package contains the eighteen supplementary tables, the analysis and figure code, the recorded software versions, the reconstruction log for the long-read alignments, and a per-read phase-evidence table. What is reproducible. The six-criterion classification of 103 matched isolates is re-runnable and every verdict was re-derived from the counts with zero mismatches. The reference metadata for all cited works is captured from Europe PMC and every DOI was verified against its record. The figures are generated by script and each passes a programmatic overlap, clipping and text-on-line audit before export. The short-read counts at the two A2143 coordinates are reproduced from the archived alignment, whose header records the exact command and tool versions. What is not. The original NCBI query string and its date were not retained, so the cohort cannot be rebuilt verbatim; per-accession inclusion flags are given instead. The barrnap installation originally used on the analysis machine is missing a Perl module and does not run; the rRNA copy numbers were therefore archived values in earlier versions and are re-derived with barrnap 1.10.5 in this version. The original parameter sets for two of the three long-read procedures were not retained; those procedures were re-run and both original and re-run values are reported side by side and never pooled. One cell of the long-read table reproduces exactly; the others do not, and this is stated in the manuscript. Changes in version 4. The package matches the manuscript. All thirteen supplementary tables are present, including Supplementary Tables S12 and S13, which were absent from the previous version, and Supplementary Table S1 now carries the genome length and assembly level of all 1,483 retained genomes rather than leaving those columns empty. A new Supplementary Table S1b lists the seven excluded genomes that could be recovered from local storage, with their lengths; the genome-length window is 1.5 to 1.7 Mb and this version states the evidence that fixes its bounds. Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. The four control reference sequences are deposited under results/marker_control/. Changes in version 6. This version restores the complete file set. The previous version was published from an incomplete upload, so most of the figures, several of the supplementary tables and part of the analysis code were missing from that record. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files and this package has 134, so the package is now deposited as a single archive, hp23s_copy_assignment_package.zip , which holds every file at the path it occupies in the source repository; this README, the SHA-256 manifest and the archive of rRNA calls and copy sequences are additionally placed loose in the record. From version 10 the manuscript itself is not deposited, in the archive or loose. Every member of the archive is listed in SHA256SUMS.txt with its SHA-256, and that manifest is regenerated here, which corrects the entry for this README (the previous manifest had been computed before the last edit of the file). DOI.txt now lists the version DOIs, and the data-availability sentence in the manuscript names the concept DOI rather than one version, so that it cannot point at a superseded record. Changes in version 7. This version is a manuscript round: the text is rebuilt from the same locked data by the same script, and no reported value changes. Three defects in the supplementary apparatus are corrected
title: Long reads assign a 23S rRNA resistance allele to one of the two copies in Helicobacter pylori; a complete short-read assembly does not
