summary: AiMat-Suite is the integrated, verifiable software framework developed for the doctoral thesis of A. O. Marcelo Júnior (PPGECM/UFC, LAMEFF). It chains, in a single system: (i) U-Net (ResNet-34) segmentation of fibre networks in optical photographs of chitosan/sisal films; (ii) automatic geometry and meshing (CalculiX cgx: S4 shells for the matrix, B32 beams for the fibres, translational MPC tie) and linear-elastic FE solution (CalculiX ccx); (iii) physics-informed and operator-learning surrogates (SharedPINN/Cascade PINN with Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation; Kuramoto-reservoir DeepONet with a Poisson-coupled nodal solver); (iv) a differentiable Rietveld engine for XRD with calibrated uncertainty and a declared domain of validity; (v) a material-card module that turns raw EMIC/Instron tensile curves into FE material cards with declared estimators, bootstrap confidence intervals and a load-regime check. Version 3.1.1 is the thesis reference release. The platform was developed in two stages: the aiMat MVP (2023–2025), which automated the image → model → simulation chain and produced the 2025 Materials Research papers, and AiMat-Suite (2026), which adds an operator-verification module (digitisation-invariance criterion), material cards built from tensile curves, the X-ray diffraction module, image-conditioned surrogates and zero-shot transfer to 217 microstructures. In AiMat-Suite the FE deck generator uses the translational fibre–matrix tie ( areampc 123 ), the choice supported by the digitisation-invariance criterion; matrix E = 13.67 MPa / ν = 0.35 from the tested plasticised film; fibre E = 9.3 GPa (sensitivity 31 GPa) / ν = 0.153; line load q = 1.75 kN/m applied as F = q·L_edge in N; static linear analysis; *NODE FILE, OUTPUT=2D . The provenance of every parameter is recorded in packages/fem/src/aiMat/calculix/materials.py . The MVP protocol (six-DOF tie, MVP material cards and load) is kept as legacy to reproduce the 2025 papers. packages/fem/reexecucao_v13/ contains the full re-execution of microstructures M1–M6 (decks, displacement fields, SHA-256 hashes) and of 220 image-derived microstructures, plus a test that rebuilds and solves M1 with ccx (E_eff within 0.5 % of the deposited value). The suite ships 170 Python modules and 90 tests ( scripts/verify.sh ). Changes in 3.1.1. (i) The coupled nodal solver and reservoir-readout ablation used in Sections 5.5.3.3–5.5.3.4 of the thesis ( packages/newton_oir/oir/phase_field_coupled.py , phase_field_sparse.py , metrics.py , hybrid_readout.py and experiments/ex31_v62_ablation_full.py ) were missing from 3.1.0 and are restored unchanged from the repository history; (ii) re-executions of 30 Oct–1 Nov 2026 are added under packages/fem/reexecucao_v13/ : surrogates on the AiMat-Suite fields, normalisation by the image-derived fibre fraction, sensitivity to shell thickness and beam diameter, and a complementary re-execution (reservoir readouts, coupled solver, leave-one-out and Wilcoxon on the AiMat-Suite fields; 660 CalculiX runs of the 220 image-derived cases with pure matrix, 9.3 GPa and 31 GPa fibres); (iii) SHA-256 manifests are computed on the LF-normalised files as versioned. Erratum to 3.1.0: its description states 210 Python modules; the 3.1.0 archive contains 154 (verify.sh count). Dependencies: Python ≥ 3.10, numpy/scipy/scikit-image/opencv (core); PyTorch (segmentation, PINNs, DRX AI routes); JAX (Rietveld engine); CalculiX 2.17 (FE). Abaqus is required only by the optional XFEM module ( packages/fem/src/abaqus/ ) and is not part of the open-source chain. Licence: MIT (integration and packages/drx ); datasets under assets/ are CC-BY-4.0. Companion archive (15 Nov 2026). AiMat-Suite-v3.1.1-tese_complemento.zip adds the trained U-Net weights (ResNet-34 encoder; partition by photograph and by crop) and the script and CSV that reproduce Tables 4 and 5 of the thesis (fibre diameter and total length on predicted versus annotated masks, 13 photographs, at the photograph resolu

summary: Publishing a model or method does not finish the work of applied mathematics. Turning a mathematical idea into a reliable operational tool requires translation: assessment of how well a method behaves in theory and under real domain constraints, adaptation of both the mathematical formulation and the software to modern computing architectures, and adoption into sustained community use. Because every simplified model leaves a gap between idealized assumptions and reality, it carries applicability debt that an overlapping web of skills—uniting applied mathematicians, statisticians, domain specialists, and research software engineers—must manage. Generative AI and multi-agent harnesses have upset that balance. Large language models and coding agents make it cheap to generate candidate derivations, simulation code, and machine-checked proofs while leaving problem formulation and concrete domain verification tied to scarce human judgement. When automated generation outpaces translation, applicability debt goes unmanaged and pushes adoption toward unverified shortcuts, risking a crisis of application. At the same time, Australian science and innovation policy largely equates translation with commercial intellectual property and private data centres while overlooking research software and verification capacity inside public agencies, national facilities, and universities. Picking up in 2006—the fiftieth anniversary of the Australian Mathematical Society (Counting Australia In) and the birth year of the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) and the ACCESS Earth-system partnership—this monograph contrasts that post-war public compact at the Society's seventieth anniversary in 2026 against Ambitious Australia and Science 2035, where research software disappears from policy view and the 2016–2025 mathematical-sciences decadal plan has expired without a successor. Written for both public policymakers and working quantitative practitioners, this book examines how translation succeeds or short-circuits across two centuries of computational history, a twenty-year citation census of 112 works applying the EQ algorithm for equal-area sphere partitions, Research Software Engineer workforce audits, Earth-system and biomedical case studies, and invariants-first software verification (PyEQSP and GluCat). Benchmarking Australia against Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, and New Zealand across 18 chapters, 3 empirical appendices, and 750 verified primary sources (188 pages), it outlines practical, trade-off-aware opportunities across university assessment, service teaching, research software careers, scientific societies, sovereign infrastructure, and public-interest model verification ahead of the 2026–2028 national research and infrastructure renewals.
title: What does it take to apply mathematics in Australia today?

summary: This README file was generated on [2026-11-15] (YYYY-MM-DD) Last updated: [2026-11-15]. ------------------- GENERAL INFORMATION ------------------- // Title of Dataset: Replication data for: Surrogate-Assisted Heuristic Search: An Empirical Study of Feature Selection for Classification // DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24248202 // Data Type: Numeric data as .h5 files. // Date of data collection/generation: 2026-09-22 (YYYY-MM-DD). // Description of dataset: This dataset contains replication data for the paper Surrogate-Assisted Heuristic Search: An Empirical Study of Feature Selection for Classification. It contains accuracy and training cost tables of well-known classification datasets from The UCI Machine Learning Repository. These tables comprise the accuracy for all feature subsets, i.e., all column combinations, obtained by six classifiers: 1. Decision Tree 2. k-Nearest Neighbors 3. Logistic Regression 4. Neural Network 5. Random Forest 6. Support Vector Machine -------------------------- METHODOLOGICAL INFORMATION -------------------------- // Description of sources and methods used for collection/generation of data: We study 10 datasets from the University of California, Irvine (UCI) ML Repository. On each dataset, we train all classifiers and compute an accuracy table that comprises all possible 2^n subsets of features, where n is the number of columns in the dataset. We provide 32 repetitions per feature subset, to address the stochasticity of the ML models. // Methods for processing the data: The tables were computed using Julia 1.12.2, using the following packages: 1. Decision Tree (DecisionTreeClassifier from BetaML.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) 2. k-Nearest Neighbors (KNNClassifier from NearestNeighbors.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) 3. Logistic Regression (MultinomialClassifier from MLJLinearModels.jl) 4. Neural Network (MLP from Flux.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) 5. Random Forest (RandomForestClassifier from BetaML.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) 6. Support Vector Machine (SVC from LIBSVM.jl and its MLJ.jl interface) In all models, the default parameters (as of MLJ v0.21.0) were used, with a 70/30 train/test split. // Facility-, instrument- or software-specific information needed to interpret the data: The data can be read using any data analysis tool that can read HDF5 (.h5) files. -------------------- DATA & FILE OVERVIEW -------------------- // File List: Each of 10 ML datasets × 6 ML classifiers is stored as a separate .h5 file, with a dataset ID as the filename. Each file contains two HDF5 datasets with the same dimensions: 1. accuracies 2. times Where `accuracies` is a matrix of size 2^n × 32, with ordered rows (from 1 to 2^n-1 possible feature subsets). Columns represent one of 32 model repetitions. The i-th row in the accuracies matrix is the decimal representation of a bitstring representing a feature subset, where each digit in the bitstring corresponds to a column in the ML dataset, with a 1 or 0 depending whether or not it is used for training the model. The cell contains a real number for the ML classifier accuracy using that feature subset. `times` is a matrix of the same size, which contains the training times (in seconds) for all the models trained. summary: Single-valued neutrosophic set theory is an important soft computing approach for resolving uncertainty and imprecision in decision-making. Several models have been established under the framework of single-valued neutrosophic sets for decision-making purposes. Single-valued neutrosophic relations, their max-min-max composition and a score-based use of this composition in medical diagnosis already exist in the literature; this paper revisits the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation in the framework of composite relations under fuzzy-set extensions, describes its algebraic properties, and applies it to two new healthcare problems. In this work, this composite relation on single-valued neutrosophic sets is presented. The numerical illustrations of the composite relation are given, and some of its algebraic properties are proved (inverse, monotonicity, associativity and distributivity over union), while it is shown by counterexamples that the composition is neither commutative nor distributive over intersection. In addition, the applications of the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation to medical healthcare services are considered to illustrate its use. Two medical healthcare applications are considered involving prediction of maternal outcome for a pregnant woman and the diagnosis of some common ailments. The examples are illustrative and use data adapted from earlier studies; no clinical validation is claimed.
title: Single-Valued Neutrosophic Composite Relation and Its Application to Healthcare Services

summary: Emissions figures in ship weather routing rest on regulatory and market data that change with new legal acts and markets. Maintaining them by hand is slow and prone to plausible errors. This paper presents the Data Steward, an agent built on a large language model that maintains these data in EcoRouter, a workbench for ship weather routing. The agent changes a value that calculations use only through an approved proposal. Deterministic tools take over the tasks that the model performs unreliably, such as reading area boundaries from legal texts, and checks run as workflows of small steps with an outcome for every item. The contribution to artificial intelligence is the design of an agent that maintains regulatory reference data under human control, together with a method for evaluating such an agent. The engineering application is the maintenance of the regulatory data on which a ship-routing tool computes emissions and regulatory costs. In a controlled test with 40 errors injected into the data that a full check covers, the Steward corrected 36 to 38 in three runs, against 20 to 28 for the same model alone with web search. In three full checks of the live data, 96 to 99 % of judged items were correct. A person who took no part in building EcoRouter found 57 of the 59 approved values correct. The results show that a commercial language model can maintain regulatory reference data with few errors once the tasks it performs unreliably are moved into deterministic code. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Version 1. The records of the tests are published as a dataset: 10.5281/zenodo.24251511. Use of AI: during the preparation of this work the author used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) in order to correct the text, check its grammar, to create the tables and figures from the author's records, and to check the statements about EcoRouter against its source code. The same assistant also helped to run tests 1 and 3, to judge their results against the acts and publishers, to prepare the person's sheet for test 2 and to aggregate the results of the three tests. It did only the tasks that the author gave it, under the author's control. The author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for it. Language models are also part of the research itself: Section 5 of the paper states which model the Data Steward ran on and which AI assistant judged its results.
title: A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence" by Jingyang Li (School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, China). summary: The records of the tests reported in the preprint "A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation" (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24250853). The Data Steward is an agent built on a large language model that keeps the emissions-regulation data of EcoRouter, a weather-routing tool, current. It proposes changes, and an administrator approves them. The files hold every message EcoRouter sent the agent and every answer, its proposals, the outcome of every item checked, and the judgement of each item and proposal against its act or publisher. - Test 1: three full checks of the live data, checks 1, 2 and 3. - Test 2: a person's check of the 59 values approved in test 1: the values, the instructions given to the person, the person's sheet, the key and the result. - Test 3: nine runs on a copy of the data with injected errors. A1 to A3 are the agent as built, B1 to B3 the same model alone with web search, and E1 to E3 a check of the EU ETS exemptions. Beside the runs: the answer key, the random draw of the errors with its seed, the changes that made the test copy, and the result of each run. - Severity: the rule that grades every wrong result as high, medium or small, the grade of each, and EcoRouter's value catalogue. E-mail addresses and names are replaced by codes. CONTENTS.md lists every file and the test it belongs to. The ZIP keeps the folder tree. These files are the output of the language-model agent evaluated in the paper, gpt-5.5 (version 2026-04-24) in Microsoft Foundry, and the judgements of its work, made by an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) under the author's control, as Section 5 of the paper describes. They are research data on that agent. Some proposals carry area boundaries from Marine Regions: Flanders Marine Institute (2026), MarineRegions.org, licensed under CC BY. Some carry place positions from OpenStreetMap: © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License, https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright.

summary: RideLab is a self-contained, browser-based platform for the design and teaching of active suspension control, for students, researchers, educators and engineers. It simulates a vehicle active suspension in real time and compares six controllers, PID, fuzzy logic, sliding mode, linear-quadratic regulator, model predictive control and a neural network, against a passive baseline on an ISO 8608 road, with live plots and a multi-indicator dashboard. An integrated adaptive AI tutor guides learners with missions, prediction questions and graded hints, and can be switched off for pure design work. The archive contains the toolbox, a Python reference engine, verification harnesses for the design tool and for the tutor, the road seeds and controller tunings, and the scripts that regenerate the published results and figures. How to use Option 1, use the toolbox: download RideLab.html and open it in any modern web browser (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox or Microsoft Edge). No installation or external dependencies are needed. Option 2, see the code and regenerate the results: download RideLab_v1.0.zip and unzip it. The toolbox is included as suspension_design_toolbox.html. To regenerate the results, follow README.md; the scripts need Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib, and the harnesses and timing script need Node.js. Generative AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) assisted in developing the software; the author verified all results against the reference engine. Access to the files is granted on request.

summary: This doctoral thesis, entitled Genomic Studies of Piscine Streptococci and Genome Assembly of Clariidae Catfishes (Siluriformes) for Aquaculture Enhancement, was prepared at the Faculty of Fisheries, Kasetsart University, Thailand, for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). The thesis integrates microbial comparative genomics, genome assembly, genome annotation, repeat and gene-family analysis, population genomics and chromosome evolution to develop genomic resources and analytical approaches relevant to aquaculture, fish health and genetic management. It comprises eight research chapters and a general discussion. Chapter 1 — Bighead catfish genome assembly. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of Clarias macrocephalus generated with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing. Chapter 2 — Streptococcus iniae comparative genomics and reverse vaccinology. The genome of strain SIKU01 and comparative analyses of 90 isolates used to prioritize candidate antigens. The candidates require experimental validation. Chapter 3 — F1 hybrid catfish genome annotation. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved assembly of the interspecific hybrid Clarias macrocephalus × Clarias gariepinus , with its protein-coding, non-coding, satellite and transposable-element annotation. Chapter 4 — Repetitive architecture of the two haplotypes. Tandem repeats, segmental duplications, gene-family clusters, the miR-430 array and the divergence of Gypsy and Helitron elements. Chapter 5 — Hatchery population genomics. Diversity, relatedness, family reconstruction, autozygosity, structural variation, polymorphic inversions and shared parents in a commercial C. gariepinus broodstock. Chapter 6 — Gene repertoire and divergence of the two parental haplotypes, on a phylogenomic framework of 17 catfish genomes. Chapter 7 — Composition of the 41 polymorphic inversions of C. gariepinus and deletion-based PCR markers for their arrangements. The markers were designed in silico and have not been tested in the laboratory. Chapter 8 — Fusion and fission between the karyotypes of the two species. Junctions are reported as intervals; no mechanism is resolved at any junction. Chapter 9 — General discussion and conclusion. Changes since the version of 2026-11-03: lists of tables and figures; Chapters 7 and 8 revised; five figures of the repeat analyses added to Chapters 3 and 4 (spacer types of the LG04 array, tandem repeats against chromosome ends, copy number by counting step, array structure of repeated loci, Gypsy and Helitron); new introductions of Chapters 6 and 7; Chapter 9 updated to the chapters. summary: This doctoral thesis, entitled Genomic Studies of Piscine Streptococci and Genome Assembly of Clariidae Catfishes (Siluriformes) for Aquaculture Enhancement, was prepared at the Faculty of Fisheries, Kasetsart University, Thailand, for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). The thesis integrates microbial comparative genomics, genome assembly, genome annotation, repeat and gene-family analysis, population genomics and chromosome evolution to develop genomic resources and analytical approaches relevant to aquaculture, fish health and genetic management. It comprises eight research chapters and a general discussion. Chapter 1 — Bighead catfish genome assembly. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of Clarias macrocephalus generated with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing. Chapter 2 — Streptococcus iniae comparative genomics and reverse vaccinology. The genome of strain SIKU01 and comparative analyses of 90 isolates used to prioritize candidate antigens. The candidates require experimental validation. Chapter 3 — F1 hybrid catfish genome annotation. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved assembly of the interspecific hybrid Clarias macrocephalus × Clarias gariepinus , with its protein-coding, non-coding, satellite and transposable-element annotation. Chapter 4 — Repetitive architecture of the two haplotypes. Tandem repeats, segmental duplications, gene-family clusters, the miR-430 array and the divergence of Gypsy and Helitron elements. Chapter 5 — Hatchery population genomics. Diversity, relatedness, family reconstruction, autozygosity, structural variation, polymorphic inversions and shared parents in a commercial C. gariepinus broodstock. Chapter 6 — Gene repertoire and divergence of the two parental haplotypes, on a phylogenomic framework of 17 catfish genomes. Chapter 7 — Composition of the 41 polymorphic inversions of C. gariepinus and deletion-based PCR markers for their arrangements. The markers were designed in silico and have not been tested in the laboratory. Chapter 8 — Fusion and fission between the karyotypes of the two species. Junctions are reported as intervals; no mechanism is resolved at any junction. Chapter 9 — General discussion and conclusion. summary: This repository provides analysis code, aggregate results and supporting documentation for the manuscript “Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana.” The study uses Ghana Living Standards Survey Round 7 (GLSS 7), conducted in 2016/17, to examine associations between earnings, observable employment conditions and employment-change intentions across Ghana’s ten survey-era regions. Employment-change intentions distinguish wanting to change jobs, take an additional job or change current-job conditions. The materials include Stata scripts for survey-weighted earnings, job-quality, binary-logit and multinomial-logit models; regional interaction analyses; and Python scripts for data construction and machine-learning prediction. The repository also contains aggregate statistical tables, figures, variable documentation, sample-construction summaries, reproduction instructions and file checksums. Respondent-level survey data and individual prediction records are excluded. Researchers must obtain the underlying GLSS 7 data from the Ghana Statistical Service under its applicable access conditions. The supplied code and results are preserved without re-estimation. Reproduction requirements and outstanding limitations including unavailable original software-version information and two inventory files required for raw-data reconstruction are documented in the package. The findings describe conditional associations and predictive relationships, not causal effects.
title: Replication Materials for Pay, Job Quality and Employment Change Intentions among Paid Workers in Ghana

A strong oil-matched control can reveal that supposed botanical superiority originated in a residual cosolvent or in surfactant concentration. An independent laboratory must be able to identify the same marker molecules before accepting the morphology. F047: A mean radius is a poor description of a diverse droplet world An intensity-weighted DLS peak can be ruled by a small number of large scatterers. Number-weighted counts and volume-weighted oil fractions answer different questions. The same mean hydrodynamic diameter can belong to two populations with different rare large-droplet tails, different oil mass distribution and different stability trajectories. This is why the tenth family refuses a one-number specification. A richer experiment defines the droplet population at the moment of collection, after a controlled dilution, and after thermal aging. An unblinded analyst can always find the prettiest distribution. A credible research method should make a high-tail or poorly fitting distribution visible even when it defeats the preferred recipe. F048: The useful interface and the hazardous excess may coexist A surfactant occupies the oil-water interface, exchanges with water and may assemble into micelles at concentrations above its relevant critical aggregation threshold. Shrinking droplets increases total interface area. Yet simply adding more surfactant can increase the bioavailable free fraction without ensuring superior film coverage. A formulation might therefore look beautiful and remain unsuitable for a qualified reconstructed epidermis comparison. The laboratory must measure adsorbed, dissolved, micellar, degraded and container-associated amounts. Co-solvent and preservative must enter the competition as separate interventions. A single elevated-temperature hold cannot be treated as a certificate of ambient shelf life. Repeated heating-cooling loops can generate hysteresis even when they return to an identical endpoint temperature. Each produces a different laboratory question. At least one independent real-time lot is needed to test whether accelerated aging forecasts actual storage behavior. F050: Nonclinical skin compatibility is an evidence contract A reconstructed human epidermis model is a defined surrogate, not a human wearer. Botanical pigments, reducing molecules and surfactants can distort common viability assays. The proper design uses a matched oil-and-surfactant vehicle, an independent exposure dose per tissue area, qualified tissue integrity, color interference controls and noncompensatory refusal conditions. A lower cytokine concentration can arise from fewer living cells. A higher local skin-associated chemical signal may arise from barrier injury or unwashed surface material. summary: This dataset contains hydrological model inputs, simulation outputs, spatial data, analysis code and reproducibility materials for the Mandena coastal mineral-sand mining basin near Taolagnaro, southeastern Madagascar. The SWAT+ simulation period covers 1987–2022, including a warm-up period of 1987–1992. The principal analysis covers 1993–2022, with an additional analysis window ending in 2020. Auxiliary source datasets may extend beyond these periods. The archive includes basin, mining-area, reference-area and hydrological response unit geometries; elevation, land-cover and soil-class rasters; meteorological inputs and rainfall-processing materials; model configuration files; annual and monthly hydrological outputs; scenario definitions; numerical results; scientific figures; and documentation describing data structures, model formulations and analytical methods. Source materials for the independent evapotranspiration comparison include MODIS MOD16A2GF Collection 061 data and associated quality and spatial-support information. The experiment registry defines 35 simulation configurations. These include standard and coupled surface–soil water formulations, static composite parameter-perturbation scenarios, individual parameter-family experiments, rainfall-forcing alternatives, identity experiments and dated synthetic interventions. The parameter families are curve number, overland roughness, leaf area, biomass, residue cover and soil available water capacity. Perturbations target a documented selection of 158 hydrological response units. The dated synthetic intermediate intervention begins on 1 January 2008. Temporal analyses examine simulated mining–reference contrasts using BACI-style and interrupted time-series formulations. The baseline uses static land-cover and soil configurations; its temporal contrasts describe outputs from that configuration. Dated interventions are imposed numerical experiments rather than reconstructions of historical mining disturbance. The analytical materials include annual step, trend, segmented and ramp regressions; alternative breakpoint and pre-intervention placebo analyses; heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent inference; confidence intervals and Holm multiplicity adjustments; monthly and quarterly analyses; conditional detectability and minimum-detectable-effect calculations; block-bootstrap experiments; residual and influence diagnostics; and sensitivity to reference selection, spatial support, analysis period, forcing and parameter configuration. Spatial analyses document polygon coverage, HRU intersections, shared supports, the representativeness of selected HRUs, and differences in configured soil, vegetation and terrain characteristics. Water-balance diagnostics include annual export-based assessments and high-precision daily coupled-budget checks for the documented diagnostic period. Evapotranspiration comparisons report results under alternative quality and spatial-support filters. The archive provides model source code, Windows AMD64 executables, Python analysis scripts, offline dependency wheels for Python 3.12, experiment-specific inputs and outputs, file inventories, checksum manifests and execution instructions. The main entry point supports file-integrity verification, simulation execution and analysis regeneration. Reproducibility testing completed all 35 registered simulation configurations and confirmed numerical agreement for three designated summary tables using an absolute tolerance of 10⁻⁶ and a relative tolerance of 10⁻⁹. Author-created data and documentation are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. The MIT licence applies to the robust-statistics component identified in the archive. Third-party data, model components and software dependencies retain their respective licences, attribution requirements and copyright notices.
title: Mandena hydrological simulations, data and analysis

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask whether numerical histories shape generation, whether process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls, and whether learning from construction histories improves the next corpus and the learner trained on it. Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: POLYPHENOL-LIPID COUPLING SCIENCE F096-F100 | Family 20 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch  |  33 x STARLI  |  Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: molecular interface binding, oil-peroxide kinetics, polyphenol redox depletion, genuine lipid nanocarrier co-loading, and nonclinical barrier/viability evidence. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F096-F100; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of polyphenol-lipid-botanical causation F096 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Interfacial Binding at the Limit: primary endpoint apparent binding constant K_app (L/mol). Fair comparator: free polyphenol alone, free oil/lipid alone, missing-component mixtures and matched blank liposomes. Disqualifying counterexample: surface adsorption, self-quenching, polyphenol autoxidation, incomplete recovery or bilayer disruption masquerading as molecular binding. F097 - Botanical Polyphenol-Plant Oil Antioxidant Coupling at the Limit: primary endpoint plant-oil peroxide formation rate (meq peroxide/kg oil per h). Fair comparator: polyphenol-free oil, oil-free polyphenol, matched vehicle, dark isothermal control and tocopherol reference. Disqualifying counterexample: autooxidation, probe quenching, transient induction-period selection or peroxide breakdown without suppressed secondary oxidation. F098 - Lipid Oxidation and Botanical Polyphenol Activity at the Limit: primary endpoint slope of polyphenol depletion versus lipid oxidation (prespecified native units). Fair comparator: unprotected oil, polyphenol without oil, oxidized-polyphenol spike and matched light-oxygen factorial controls. Disqualifying counterexample: reverse causality, time-confounded oxidation, ion suppression or antioxidant depletion without protection of the lipid phase. F099 - Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Nano-Codelivery at the Limit: primary endpoint true co-loading fraction (%) of independently qualified polyphenol and lipid compartments. Fair comparator: free botanical in oil, empty carriers, equal-total-mass physically blended carriers and independent single-loaded formulations. Disqualifying counterexample: adsorption to particle surface, unseparated micelles, centrifugation loss or fluorescent overlap mistaken for shared nanocarrier loading. F100 - Barrier Evidence for Botanical Polyphenol-Lipid Formulations at the Limit: primary endpoint joint qualified barrier-surrogate effect and RhE viability (%), reported separately. Fair comparator: vehicle-matched control, polyphenol-only, lipid-only, blank carrier and positive reference irritant. Disqualifying counterexample: optical-probe self-quenching, surface occlusion, damaged RhE tissue, dye interference or unmatched vehicle causing false barrier evidence. Methodological introduction F096: apparent interfacial association is not proof of binding Different redox states and lipids require independent molecular identity. A change in fluorescence or oil-water partition can arise from self-quenching, adsorption or photochemical loss. An apparent binding constant must survive reversible washout, recovery checks and a separately measured lipid interface area. F098: oxidative depletion and lipid preservation are different A statistical slope between polyphenol depletion and lipid oxidation is a descriptive estimate, not a causal mechanism. summary: Version 1.1.0 of the reproducible research repository accompanying the manuscript: "Operative treatment of pyogenic spondylodiscitis in German hospitals: patient selection, hospital size, and in-hospital mortality" This release adds a cell-level reconstruction of the hospital tables (bed-size class × ownership). The InEK DatenBrowser combines some cells of these tables into a residual row, differently in each query and not only for small counts, so the displayed cells give numerators and denominators that do not match. The reconstruction (analysis/05b_hospital_reconstruction.py) resolves the hidden cells under the containment constraints between the four queries of each year; reported values are medians over 2000 feasible reconstructions, with ranges over these and 2000 extreme reconstructions (fixed seed). With the reconstruction, the operative share is 28.2% in hospitals with fewer than 300 beds and 63.7% in hospitals with 1000 beds or more (version 1.0.0: 27.9% and 65.2%). The risk ratio stratified by data year and hospital bed-size category is 1.02 (95% CI 0.96–1.08), and by data year and ownership 1.08 (1.01–1.14). Also added: hospital-stratified risk ratios, article tables, figure data and key numbers (analysis/06_reported_quantities.py) and the article figures (analysis/07_article_figures.py). All other results are unchanged. Intraspinal abscess (G06.1) is now labelled intraspinal empyema. The underlying hospital data are publicly accessible through the InEK DatenBrowser. Original query outputs are not redistributed; they can be regenerated from the documented query specification.
title: Operative treatment and in-hospital mortality in pyogenic spondylodiscitis: query protocol, analysis code and derived results

summary: Markov chains for a Bayesian inverse problem with a 100-parameter Karhunen-Loeve log permeability field and an elliptic PDE, following P. G. Constantine, C. Kent and T. Bui-Thanh, "Accelerating Markov chain Monte Carlo with active subspaces", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 38(5):A2779-A2805, 2016, doi:10.1137/15M1042127. pde_mcmc_chains.npz (load with numpy.load, no pickle) holds the synthetic data, the misfit gradients at 1000 prior samples and their active subspace, 20 random-walk Metropolis chains and 4 + 4 active-variable chains (reductions), and a grid of the misfit on the active variables. kl-short.npz is the Karhunen-Loeve basis the model uses. generate_data.py in the repository regenerates the chains from saved seeds. These files are deposited as the full-size archive of the data set uq_benchmarks/PDE_Inverse_Problem_MCMC in the as-data-sets repository ( https://github.com/paulcon/as-data-sets/tree/main/uq_benchmarks/PDE_Inverse_Problem_MCMC ), a collection of Jupyter notebooks that apply active subspaces (parameter-space dimension reduction) to science and engineering models. The notebook there analyzes these data; its DATA.md documents every file, column, unit and unknown. The repository keeps each file under 10 MB, so it ships the same arrays split into files under 10 MB. License: CC BY 4.0. Cite Constantine, Kent and Bui-Thanh (2016).
title: Markov chain Monte Carlo on the active variables of a PDE inverse problem: chains, subspace and grid

summary: BOTANICAL SHEET-MASK SCIENCE: FROM SERUM CHEMISTRY TO VERIFIED WET CONTACT F121-F125 | Family 25 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch | 33 x STARLI | Edition v1.0 / November 2026 Five integrated nonclinical research themes: storage marker integrity, lyocell sorption, three-dimensional wet contact, mass-based evaporation and qualified reconstructed-epidermis evidence. Scope and scientific authority This long-form technical notebook is a proposed investigation, not a laboratory or cosmetic product performance report. The primary source is the 817-page STARLI Botanical Master Blueprint v1.0, Family25 F121-F125; older Mothers F12 and F28 provide method and evidence constraints. The numerical charts are synthetic hypotheses. Chinese materia medica inspires provenance, processing and compound questions, not a biological proof. Claims about a commercial sheet mask, sensitive-skin suitability and humans would need independent ethically and legally appropriate evidence. Five different objects, five different vetoes F121 - Botanical Sheet-Mask Serum Active Stability at the Limit. Native measurement: stored mask-serum marker retention (%). Fair reference: equal-formula serum stored in an inert vessel, blank lyocell, matched nonwoven mask and light/dark paired packaging. Disqualifying rival: adsorption onto cellulose, packaging migration, altered extract recovery, optical co-elution or oxygen-driven degradation. F122 - Lyocell–Botanical Serum Adsorption at the Limit. Native measurement: identified botanical marker adsorbed on lyocell (mg/g). Fair reference: matched nonwoven material, no-sheet serum reservoir, same-area inert substrate and prewetted lyocell control. Disqualifying rival: surface liquid mistaken for bonded sorbate, unequal sheet density, incomplete desorption or retained marker counted as delivered. F123 - Botanical Mask Conformability and Liquid Distribution at the Limit. Native measurement: verified face-surface wet-contact area (cm2). Fair reference: shape-matched nonwoven mask, same-serum container exposure, equal-load flat phantom and reversed sheet orientation. Disqualifying rival: pressure shadows mistaken for contact, pixel threshold bias, droplet pooling in folds or high contact area with low local transfer. F124 - Botanical Mask Wear Time and Evaporation at the Limit. Native measurement: evaporation mass flux (g/m2/h). Fair reference: no-sheet serum film, humidity-matched nonwoven, impermeable occlusive reference and evaporation-free gravimetric blank. Disqualifying rival: short-term occlusion masquerades as barrier repair, variable wet area, edge leakage or ambient humidity drift. F125 - Botanical Nano-Sheet-Mask Sensitive-Skin Tolerability at the Limit. Native measurement: qualified reconstructed epidermis viability (%) and marker exposure (microg/cm2). Fair reference: same-contact-time matched serum alone, blank lyocell, nonwoven sheet with matched vehicle and qualified positive-irritant reference. Disqualifying rival: pigmented botanicals distort viability reagent, local occlusion hides evaporation, tissue necrosis mimics reduced flux or uncontrolled dose. Methodological sources and foundations Five independent scientific identities under one mask F121 tests marker retention through storage without confusing cellulose sorption with degradation. F122 resolves lyocell-bound and freely available serum markers. F123 measures the genuine 3D wet-contact area and spatial transfer rather than a photographic silhouette. F124 reconstructs evaporation by mass, time, true area and environmental gradients. F125 tests qualified RhE viability only with chemically verified exposure, matched vehicle and cell-free interference controls. None of the five outputs substitutes for another. F121: chemical stability versus package partition A marker lost from the liquid phase may reside inside lyocell, on packaging film, in a precipitate or as a true degradation product. The difference is decisive. I

Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. A five-part chain of source-resolved peptide, carrier and nonclinical evidence F111 - Plant Peptide Extraction Stability at the Limit: primary endpoint sequence-resolved HPLC peptide retention (%). Fair comparator: authenticated free peptide, dark isothermal batch, deoxygenated vehicle and equal-solvent extraction control. F112 - Plant Peptide-Botanical Polyphenol Binding at the Limit: primary endpoint chemically verified peptide-polyphenol bound fraction (%). F113 - Botanical Peptide Nanocarrier Protection at the Limit: primary endpoint parent peptide survival after external protease challenge (%). Fair comparator: free peptide, surface-spiked empty carrier, blank carrier with enzyme, and matched no-enzyme reference. Disqualifying counterexample: inhibited protease masquerading as protection, peptide surface adsorption, incomplete fractionation or analytical recovery loss. F114 - Plant Peptide Enzymatic Degradation Control at the Limit: primary endpoint peptide degradation half-life (h) under a qualified protease assay. Disqualifying counterexample: enzyme inactivation, substrate depletion, product detector saturation, adsorption loss or photochemical decay mistaken for proteolysis. F115 - Skin Compatibility Evidence for Botanical Peptide Blends at the Limit: primary endpoint qualified RhE tissue viability (%) and separately specified irritation surrogate. Fair comparator: vehicle-matched blank, peptide-free carrier, free peptide, polyphenol-free equal carrier and validated irritant reference. Disqualifying counterexample: colored peptide assay interference, tissue nonviability, contact occlusion, vehicle osmolality or cytokine nonspecificity. Methodological introduction F111: sequence-resolved chromatographic stability A single HPLC retention value can hide amino-acid sequence substitution, peak coelution or instrument suppression. The critical falsifying world contains a stable-looking HPLC signal while the true peptide has already fragmented. Source and analytical identities must be separable before a stability claim is meaningful. summary: In the loop-erased ant process of Kious, Mailler and Schapira, ants walk in turn from a nest $N$ to a food source $F$ on a finite graph, and each ant reinforces the loop-erasure of its time-reversed trajectory. Kious, Mailler and Schapira conjectured that the weight of an edge grows linearly exactly when the edge lies on a geodesic from $N$ to $F$. Let $G_\ell$ consist of a triangle $N,u,v$ and two paths of $\ell$ edges, from $u$ to $F$ and from $v$ to $F$. On $G_\ell$ the normalised weights converge almost surely, and the limit on the edge $uv$ is $(1-1/\ell)\rho(1-\rho)$ for a non-degenerate random variable $\rho$ with values in $(0,1)$. For $\ell\ge2$ this edge lies on no geodesic, so the conjecture fails; for $\ell=1$, the losange, the edge dies. The same statements hold for the forward-loop-erased process of Armfield and Mailler, which has the same law.
title: A non-geodesic edge that survives in the loop-erased ant process

summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.
title: BasisSimulator.jl: Open-source polychromatic CT simulation with a GPU-portable reconstruction stack

summary: Analysis code (code only; no data) for the manuscript "Where are deaths in the Republic of Korea certified with ill-defined causes, and which specific causes are recorded less often there?". Scripts build sex- and age-standardised expected deaths for ill-defined causes of death (ICD-10 R00-R99) in 229 districts, 2011-2024, run pre-specified substitution analyses against specific causes, fit Bayesian negative binomial spatio-temporal models with R-INLA, and generate every number, table and figure in the manuscript. All source statistics are public aggregate data from Statistics Korea and other national sources; processed data are available from the author on reasonable request.
title: Ill-defined causes of death and their inverse relation with specific causes across districts of the Republic of Korea, 2011-2024: analysis code
