title: BOTANICAL CERAMIDE AND BARRIER-LIPID SCIENCE F106-F110 | Family 22 | Civilizational Scientific Research Notebook White Rainbow Epoch | 33 x STARLI | Edition v1.0 / November 2026 A companion to the 819-page integrated research atlas: botanical-active/ceramide precipitation, three-lipid mole-fraction order, lamellar repeat spacing, spatial delivery and viable-model water-loss evidence. Editorial scope and safety boundary This is a prospective research design, not a report of completed experiments. The graphical response surfaces are synthetic and reproducible. Traditional materia-medica scholarship is used as a source of research questions, not as a substitute for evidence of human tolerance or cosmetic efficacy. Source-lineage and the native endpoints are inherited from the 817-page STARLI Master Blueprint F106-F110; the narrative and candidate models are newly elaborated research proposals. A five-part chain of authenticated botanical, lamellar and barrier evidence F106 - Botanical Active-Ceramide Compatibility at the Limit: primary endpoint botanical-active / ceramide precipitation fraction (%). Fair comparator: full-lipid reference, active-only, ceramide-only, matched vehicle and equal-oil nonlamellar controls. Disqualifying counterexample: color/turbidity interference, precipitated cholesterol, pH-triggered crystal formation, non-specific surface adsorption, pigment scattering. F107 - Ceramide-Cholesterol-Fatty Acid Ratios at the Limit: primary endpoint lamellar-order parameter (dimensionless) under defined three-lipid mole ratios. Fair comparator: matched single-lipid omissions, equimass nonlamellar dispersions and same-total-lipid reference. Disqualifying counterexample: bulk lipid crystallization masquerading as lamellar order, peak overlap, crystal orientation and off-ratio total-solids change. F108 - Botanical Lipid Lamellar Structure Formation at the Limit: primary endpoint lamellar-domain repeat spacing (nm) with reported scattering resolution. Fair comparator: equal-total-lipid disordered reference, reordered lipid mixture and water-activity-matched blank. Disqualifying counterexample: instrument q-calibration drift, sample thickness, cholesterol crystals, preferred orientation or hydration swelling misassigned to layered structure. F109 - Botanical Barrier Lipid Nanodelivery at the Limit: primary endpoint coefficient of variation of component distribution in a nonclinical lipid model (%). Fair comparator: equal-lipid nonlamellar vehicle, matched blank nanocarrier, free-active mixture and depth-attenuation reference. Disqualifying counterexample: fluorescent dye decoupling, light attenuation, optical scatter, surface contamination mistaken for depth deposition. F110 - Barrier Recovery Evidence for Botanical-Ceramide Blends at the Limit: primary endpoint qualified nonclinical water-loss flux (g/m2/h), with independent RhE viability (%). Fair comparator: equal-lipid vehicle, occlusive inert reference, missing-ceramide arm, full-lipid reference and sham-treated qualified RhE. Disqualifying counterexample: temporary occlusive masking, chamber acclimation, humidity drift, damaged or nonviable tissue, incomplete evaporation correction.

summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional attention, but rotary position embeddings (RoPE) still confine them to a fixed pretraining window. Existing training-free extrapolation, notably LongLLaDA, copies NTK-based RoPE scaling from autoregressive (AR) models and applies one static, length-only transform at every position and denoising step. That transplant ignores a signal unique to dLLMs: the evolving mask pattern of the partially decoded sequence. We propose Mask-Pattern Position Augmentation (MPPA). MPPA linearly interpolates indices into the pretrained window, then adds a per-position, per-step offset from cumulative mask density. The offset restores rotary phase resolution that interpolation collapses, and it shrinks as tokens are committed, so late steps see near-clean interpolated geometry. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at twice its 4096-token window, MPPA reduces perplexity from 19.51 under standard decoding to 3.12 at 8192 tokens, below the in-window figure, with 100% passkey retrieval and unchanged needle-in-a-haystack accuracy. These preliminary $2\times$ results motivate mask-conditioned position engineering as a diffusion-native path to long-context generation.
title: Mask-Pattern Position Augmentation: Training-Free Long-Context Extrapolation for Diffusion LLMs

summary: We investigate a failed filament eruption and associated coronal heating in NOAA Active Region 12353 on 2015 May 23, focusing on the relationship between magnetic confinement and external reconnection. Coordinated observations from the Goode Solar Telescope and the Solar Dynamics Observatory, together with nonlinear force-free field extrapolations, allow us to trace the event from the merging of two low-lying filamentary structures to the failed eruption of the resulting elongated filament. Before the rapid rise, the modeled flux rope had entered a regime susceptible to kink instability, while low-atmospheric internal reconnection had already occurred; both may have contributed to the initial acceleration. The rising flux rope remained below the torus instability threshold and was confined by a strong, asymmetric overlying field that compressed it against the overlying loops. An elongated interface brightening, bidirectional plasmoid-like motions, newly brightened loop systems, and progressive weakening of the filament are consistent with external reconnection that changed the magnetic connectivity, removed magnetic flux from the rope, and disrupted its coherent structure. Differential emission measure analysis indicates that the external reconnection heated the active region loop system. A transient, localized structure with high-temperature emission was observed at the interaction interface, consistent with the expected location of a current sheet associated with external reconnection. These results suggest that the strong confining field halted the filament eruption and sustained the interface compression required for current sheet formation, enabling external reconnection to disrupt the flux rope and heat the active region loop system.
title: A Failed Filament Eruption and Associated Active Region Heating Driven by External Magnetic Reconnection

summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.
title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems

summary: We show that cyclic fatigue can occur in a system whose elements behave elastically up to an irreversible failure threshold, without plasticity, friction, or any time-dependent process. The model represents a weak interface between two elastic bodies loaded in shear. Under sufficiently large cyclic loading below the static failure threshold, a pre-existing flaw advances progressively, by a few lattice spacings per cycle. Two conditions are needed for this behavior: each bond fails more easily under one sense of the shear than the opposite, and the shear must be reversed during the cycle by an amount large enough to break bonds that have not yet failed. The model thus identifies the minimal conditions for an intrinsic, plasticity-free fatigue mechanism. Such conditions may be met at interfaces and weak planes subjected to strongly reversed shear, as in fretting, rolling contact, and reversed torsion, or in cyclic shear of cemented granular materials.
title: Fatigue crack growth without plasticity under cyclically reversed shear

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an integral part of wireless systems, yet much of today's wireless AI remains task-specific and reactive, with models typically trained to map current observations to predefined outputs or reconstruct observed data. While effective for individual tasks, such approaches provide limited support for learning what is predictable, reusable, and transferable in dynamic wireless environments. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) offers a different perspective by learning predictive representations in latent space that capture informative structure in the observations. In this article, we introduce Communication JEPA (CommJEPA) as a communication-oriented framework for predictive representation learning. The central idea is bidirectional. JEPA can equip wireless systems with predictive representations for capturing latent channel and environmental dynamics, integrating heterogeneous observations, adapting to changing conditions, and supporting future decisions. Conversely, the physical structure, partial observability, multiple time scales, action-dependent evolution, and resource constraints of wireless systems motivate new communication-aware JEPA designs. We develop this mutual perspective, organize the resulting design space, and discuss representative JEPA-based wireless instantiations for prediction and control. We further highlight open challenges toward scalable, interactive, and predictive wireless intelligence.
title: CommJEPA: When Predictive Representation Learning Meets Wireless Intelligence

summary: This dataset contains the code, data and experimental records supporting "Privacy-Aware Personalized Scheduling of Behind-the-Meter Energy Storage via an Edge-Resident Large Language Model." It covers natural-language request interpretation, condition validation and mapping, load-dependent robust scheduling, independent schedule verification, nominal recovery and execution-layer grid import enforcement. The scheduling data comprise 72 household-day profiles from six households and six request scenarios. Four methods receiving user conditions are evaluated under three forecast configurations, producing 5,184 daily trajectories and 124,416 hourly planning steps. Four corresponding planners with the user conditions removed add 864 trajectories and 20,736 steps; each trajectory is evaluated against six requests, yielding 5,184 no-personalization request evaluations. The current formal comparison therefore contains 6,048 trajectories, 145,152 planning steps and 10,368 request evaluations. Development runs, degradation-cost sensitivity experiments and separate reproducibility checks are also included. The main absolute-calibration comparison gives actual complete success rates of 55.32% for no-personalization nominal rolling scheduling and 94.21% for the proposed method, with mean daily operating costs of 5.2964 and 5.3631 USD2022, respectively. Costs combine electricity purchases under the constructed time-of-use tariff with throughput-based degradation costs. User clock times and tariff periods follow Europe/Berlin within fixed 24-hour UTC simulation windows. Language materials include prompts, request texts, saved responses, reference annotations and scoring code for the 80-request controlled benchmark, 240-request stress benchmark and 30-request extended benchmark, together with paired prompt-development records. Device records cover inference, request-to-schedule integration, resource monitoring and rolling scheduling on RK3588. The release provides source code, frozen inputs, raw results, machine-readable tables, independent data checks and a unified desktop reproduction entry point for Tables 1-10 and S1 and Figures 1-6 and S1. A result index links each output to its inputs and scripts. Dependency specifications, RK3588 operating instructions, component licenses and SHA-256 checksums accompany the archive. Research code is distributed under the MIT License. Research data, derived results and figures use CC BY 4.0; third-party materials retain their accompanying licenses. Household data source: Open Power System Data, Data Package Household Data, version 2020-04-15, https://data.open-power-system-data.org/household_data/2020-04-15/.
title: Data and Code for Privacy-Aware Personalized Scheduling of Behind-the-Meter Energy Storage via an Edge-Resident Large Language Model

summary: This paper develops a distributed inverse-optimal fixed-time integral reinforcement learning framework for unknown nonlinear leader-follower multi-agent systems. The proposed method first reconstructs the unknown agent dynamics from finite integral data. Based on the identified dynamics, a distributed inverse-optimal formulation is constructed by prescribing a desired fixed-time value function and recovering a compatible running cost. A critic-only integral reinforcement learning architecture is then developed using current integral data and finitely informative experience-replay data, thereby avoiding the persistent-excitation requirement. Practical fixed-time convergence of the critic-weight errors is established in the presence of identification and function-approximation residuals. Finally, a network-level composite Lyapunov analysis proves practical fixed-time leader-following consensus of the true unknown nonlinear multi-agent system. Numerical simulations are provided to validate the developed theory.
title: Inverse-Optimal Fixed-Time Integral Reinforcement Learning for Unknown Nonlinear Leader-Follower Multi-Agent Systems

summary: Graph-based observability analysis runs in seconds where Lie-derivative tests take hours, but it answers only one question: is the system observable or not. It cannot say how well a given set of measurements supports state reconstruction. This paper extends the graph-based approach with symbolic observability coefficients computed from a symbolic Jacobian of the state-space equations, in which every dependency is classified as constant, nonlinear polynomial, or rational. We show that the coefficient tracks the analytical observability determinant of the Lie-derivative approach: it is zero when the determinant vanishes, lies strictly between zero and one when the determinant depends on the state, and equals one when the determinant is a nonzero constant. We apply the method to a seven-state synchronous machine and to the 21-state Western System Coordinating Council nine-bus system under several synchrophasor measurement configurations. On the nine-bus system, the coefficient grows from 0.0952 with one PMU to 0.1905 with two and 0.2857 with three, and the whole analysis runs in under five seconds. Configurations with the same number of PMUs receive the same coefficient, yet an unscented Kalman filter estimates the states with different accuracy for each. The symbolic coefficient therefore grades measurement sets beyond identifying root strongly connected components, while telling PMU locations apart still requires the numerical parameters of the system.
title: Beyond Yes or No: Grading Observability of Power System Dynamic States with Symbolic Coefficients

summary: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.
title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions

summary: Talagrand's convolution conjecture, recently proven by J. Lu, S. Guo, and E. Fang, concerns the smoothing properties of the heat semigroup on $\{-1,1\}^N$. We follow their perturbed coupled reverse-heat approach to generalize the theorem to tensor powers of irreducible continuous-time Markov semigroups on finite state spaces. Specifically, let $(S_t)_{t\geq0}$ be the semigroup of an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite state space $G_0$ with stationary distribution $π$. Then, for every $τ>0$, there exists a finite constant $C_{τ,S,π}<\infty$ such that, for every $N\geq1$, every nonnegative function $f:G_0^N\to[0,\infty)$, and every $η>1$, \begin{align*} π^{\otimes N}\left(S_τ^{\otimes N}f>η\int_{G_0^N}f\,dπ^{\otimes N}\right)\leq\frac{C_{τ,S,π}}{η\sqrt{\logη}}, \end{align*} where the constant is independent of $N$, $f$, and $η$. Most of the machinery developed by Lu, Guo, and Fang transfers cleanly, but since probability distributions on $|G_0|$ elements are not determined by their mean for $|G_0|>2$, we must use explicit terminal bridge laws to find a dimension-independent bound for the terminal-discrepancy estimate. We have formalized our result in Lean 4. The formalization is publicly available.
title: Talagrand's Convolution Bound for Tensor Powers of Finite-State Markov Semigroups

summary: RF fingerprinting benchmarks report how well a classifier separates transmitters, not whether that separability reflects the individual unit or its hardware family. We compare a benchmark's real hardware grouping with size-matched random groupings of the same devices, using calibrated, unclipped variational lower bounds under label-blind, device-level cross-fitting on devices never seen in training. On WiSig (OFDM Wi-Fi), the generation grouping exceeded all 999 matched random groupings (permutation p = 0.001, the resolution floor), although no grouping attained a positive certified bound, and the direction survives removing channel equalization. A preregistered replication on a LoRa corpus (chirp spread spectrum, three hardware models), with a front-end frozen on synthetic data, again exceeded all 999 (p = 0.001), and two sensitivity analyses judged by a reversal rule fixed in advance did not reverse the direction. This is a directional replication only: the excess magnitude reflects a miscalibrated null, the chain-rule decomposition leaves a residual of +0.296 bits, and capture order is undocumented. In a same-model corpus of 122 ESP32 radios, a temperature-calibrated held-out bound of +3.338 bits (label entropy 6.931 bits) indicates substantial device-specific identity, not separable from per-device capture-session effects; relying on the calibrated bound was decided after the uncalibrated bound changed sign. On synthetic transmitters a high-capacity convolutional decoder reaches 98.5% of a known 6-bit ceiling, and the audit protocol leaves chain-rule residuals of +0.072 bits (synthetic, fixed physical features) and +0.060 bits (WiSig, audit features). Two further corpora were excluded by preregistered ingest gates. Across WiSig and LoRa, hardware-family groupings consistently produced stronger identity-associated signal than size-matched random groupings.
title: What Does an RF Fingerprint Identify? A Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Hardware-Family-Associated and Unit-Level Signal

summary: Cataloguing a Roman Imperial coin involves reading its legends and identifying its imagery in order to match it to an entry in the standard reference catalogue. Previous work has automated individual parts of this process, such as identifying the issuer or recognizing reverse motifs, by formulating each part as a classification task over a predefined set of labels. We instead formulate coin description as image-to-text generation and adapt an open-weight vision-language model (VLM), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, to four tasks: transcribing the obverse and reverse legends, and describing the obverse and reverse imagery. To obtain training data, we convert approximately 30,000 auction records into structured image-text pairs. We separate the two sides of each coin, extract and normalize legends and descriptions, and standardize obverse descriptions against a bust-type taxonomy. We then train a separate low-rank adapter for each task on a single 20GB GPU, and evaluate each task with metrics that we define to capture the key components of numismatic descriptions. The adapted models outperform both the unadapted base model and GPT-4.1 on all four tasks, reducing the normalized edit distance of legend transcriptions by over 40% relative to GPT-4.1. The improvement is smaller, but still present, on legends absent from the training data.
title: From Classification to Generation: Vision-Language Models for Roman Imperial Coin Description

summary: TripLibre is an open-source, local-first iOS application designed for personal mobility tracking and travel behavior research. It records location data in the background, reconstructs daily travel activities into visits, trips, transportation modes, and trip chains. It allows users to review and correct inferred travel records. The application supports exporting structured mobility datasets in CSV, JSON, GeoJSON, and SQLite formats, with a Python loader for further analysis. By combining automated GPS-based travel detection with user-controlled data management, TripLibre aims to lower the technical and financial barriers to collecting travel behavior data. Its broader vision is to provide researchers, educational institutions, and resource-constrained communities with an accessible and adaptable alternative to proprietary travel survey technologies, while preserving individual control over sensitive location information. Documentation: https://triplibre.hhtdiary.org/docs/
title: TripLibre: An Open-Source, Privacy-First Travel Diary for Mobility Research

summary: SPECIMEN 1.0.0 SPECIMEN's first stable release (tracker #7) provides workflows for automated, strain-specific genome-scale metabolic model reconstruction and curation: HQTB: Build a model from a high-quality template and an annotated genome. CMPB: Extend and curate a CarveMe model using refineGEMs and ModelPolisher. 🔧 Fixes Corrected CLI parameter handling for analysis and smoothing. Fixed validation commands and selection of individual validation tests. Restored MetaNetX setup, including missing-table detection and download chunk-size handling. Fixed batch HQTB execution across genome subdirectories and temporary configuration handling. 📖 Documentation and usability Revised workflow descriptions, configuration guidance, installation instructions, and CLI documentation. Updated workflow diagrams, logos, and README badges. Refreshed the workflow tutorial and removed outdated notebooks. Fixed documentation build dependencies. 🚧 Project maintenance Added contribution guidelines, issue templates, a pull request template, and a code of conduct. Added a Docker Hub publishing workflow with a CLI smoke test. Added automated dependency security updates. 🟢 Scope The workflows have been tested on prokaryotic genomes. BiGG remains the best-supported namespace; feedback on other namespaces is welcome. The new PGAB workflow is under development. Full changelog: v0.0.dev3 → v1.0.0
title: draeger-lab/SPECIMEN: SPECIMEN 1.0.0 - first full release

summary: Access. Restricted: the metadata is public and the files are visible to the depositor and to the Zenodo accounts thomas@digitalethercomputing.com and wasi@digitalethercomputing.com only. This record holds data and trained checkpoints only. It contains no source code and no third-party model weights. Data and checkpoints for the manuscript on inverse-folding distillation for foldable RNA (Bhat, Ul-Kabir, Islam, Caulfield; Digital Ether Computing LLC). A grammar proposes secondary-structure scaffolds, inverse folding writes sequences onto them, a ViennaRNA refold keeps the sequences that fold into a stable, well-defined structure, and a small masked-diffusion language model (AptaLM, 21 M parameters) is trained on the survivors. The files below are every dataset and every trained checkpoint behind the manuscript's tables and figures. Sequences are 10–80 nt over A, C, G, U. Subdivisions (files) aptalm_synthetic_cohort.tar.zst – the synthetic cohort. corpora/screened_pool.jsonl is the screened synthetic pool (about 3.8 million sequences, each with its target dot-bracket, ViennaRNA energy terms, structure descriptors, generating stream, and screen label; screened_pool_streams.json counts the streams). The training corpora built from it: IF (338,049 sequences, natural length profile), PoolBins (338,049, the pool's own length profile), IF-34k and IF-100k (size subsets of IF ), IF-Cond (the IF sequences paired with their ViennaRNA minimum-free-energy structures, as conditioning input), and RF (338,049 sequences from grammar structures filled with random nucleotides, then passed through the same refold screen; the no-inverse-folding control). IF-matched and RF-matched are the synthetic arms of a composition-matched trio (164,559 sequences each, equal counts in 189 length-by-GC cells). Also the structure reference refs/train_passer_ss.jsonl (15,000 pool sequences folded with ViennaRNA) and 5,000-sequence samples of IF and RF . aptalm_natural_cohort.tar.zst – the natural cohort, derived only from RNAcentral. natural_rep90.jsonl is the non-redundant natural reference (1,735,854 sequences, 10–80 nt, one representative per 90% identity cluster; each row carries its RNAcentral URS accession), natural_all.jsonl a capped per-RNA-type sample, and the corpora Nat (338,049, the same length profile as IF ), NatScreen (338,049, natural sequences passed through the pool's fold screen), and Nat-matched (the natural arm of the matched trio), with the structure reference refs/natural_rep90_ss.jsonl (15,000 sequences folded with ViennaRNA) and a 5,000-sequence sample of Nat . aptalm_aptamer_references.tar.zst – refs/aptamer_core_analysis.jsonl : 637 published aptamers used only as an evaluation reference, never for training. 583 rows are from the UTexas Aptamer Database (September 2023 snapshot; primer-stripped to the random region; 515 of them 10–80 nt) and 54 rows are native aptamer models from RNAapt3D. aptalm_checkpoints.tar.zst – 19 trained checkpoints, weights/ablations/*.pt , each the epoch with the lowest validation loss. LLaDA-style masked diffusion (AptaLM): AptaLM (full pool), AptaLM-IF , AptaLM-IF-seed1 , AptaLM-Nat , AptaLM-Nat-seed1 , AptaLM-RF , AptaLM-RF-seed1 , AptaLM-NatScreen , AptaLM-PoolBins , AptaLM-34k , AptaLM-100k , AptaLM-IF-matched , AptaLM-Nat-matched , AptaLM-RF-matched (each named after its training corpus); AptaLM-FT10 and AptaLM-FT30 ( AptaLM-Nat fine-tuned on IF for 10 and 30 epochs); AptaLM-Cond (structure-conditioned, trained on IF-Cond ). Autoregressive Llama-style control (LlamaRNA, 20.5 M parameters): AptaLM-AR ( IF ) and AptaLM-AR-Nat ( Nat ). SHA256SUMS.txt – checksums of the four archives. Where the data come from Natural sequences : RNAcentral active collection, release 26.0 (15 September 2025), rnacentral_active.fasta , 40,712,942 sequences, downloaded 2026-06-07; filtered to 10–80 nt over A, C, G, U, exact duplicates removed, clustered with MMseqs2 (Steinegg
title: AptaLM: synthetic and natural RNA cohorts, aptamer references, and model checkpoints

summary: Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors and turn-taking failures. Advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction, but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings continue to be far too prevalent. This short paper looks back at earlier methods for improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today, arguing that multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.
title: Robots That Talk Too Much and Don't Listen Enough

summary: The brain-skull interface governs the boundary/contact conditions of the brain in computational head models, yet its mechanical behaviour remains poorly characterised experimentally. We characterised the brain-skull interface by testing brain-skull complex samples (skull bone, meninges and brain tissue in their native arrangement) excised from 19 sheep cadaver heads under uniaxial tension and compression at strain rates of 0.002, 0.02 and 0.2 s$^{-1}$ and simple shear at 0.02 s$^{-1}$. Histology confirmed that the meningeal layers remained intact and attached to the brain and skull after excision. We acquired magnetic resonance images of every sample, reconstructed their geometry and developed a sample-specific finite element model of each experiment. We represented the brain tissue using a second-order Ogden hyperelastic model and the brain-skull interface using a cohesive zone model. Using inverse finite element analysis, we first calibrated the brain tissue parameters for each subject. Keeping these parameters fixed, we then identified the interface parameters from the corresponding brain-skull complex specimen. The brain tissue shear modulus increased with strain rate from 0.94 $\pm$ 0.16 kPa at 0.002 s$^{-1}$ to 1.60 $\pm$ 0.30 kPa at 0.2 s$^{-1}$. In contrast, the interface properties (maximum normal traction 2.35 $\pm$ 0.81 kPa, maximum tangential traction 4.14 $\pm$ 0.97 kPa, and fracture energy 0.35 $\pm$ 0.14 N m$^{-1}$) showed no significant dependence on strain rate or loading mode. In all samples, failure occurred within the subarachnoid space. Neither a rigid brain-skull connection nor frictionless sliding contact with separation reproduced the measured mechanical response or failure mode of the brain-skull interface. Our experimentally derived cohesive zone model provides a realistic representation of the brain-skull interface for computational head models.
title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear

summary: Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model's density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.
title: Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss

summary: Federated learning experiments can produce reasonable-looking results even when the experiment implementation differs from the intended experimental protocol. Small errors in configuration, data partitioning, aggregation, randomness, evaluation, or checkpoint recovery may therefore affect a comparison without causing the program to fail. We present FedBrew, a research codebase for controlled and reproducible federated learning experiments. Its focus is controlled simulation with checks of specified conditions of the intended experimental protocol. FedBrew uses configuration checks, identifiable client data partitions, checkpoint recovery checks, self-describing run records, and development-time checks of scientific conditions. These checks assess, for example, whether client partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and aggregation weights match the prescribed rule; numerical and recovery checks examine non-finite client model states and interrupted runs. The same structure also provides clear extension points and automated checks for new algorithms, datasets, models, and tasks, whether they are added by researchers or AI coding agents. FedBrew therefore supports reproducible and inspectable FL experiments through checks of specified software and scientific conditions and the run records associated with reported results.
title: Paper-Faithful Federated Learning: Scientific Checks for Practitioner and Agent Development

summary: Version 3 — published 13 November 2026. This release includes the GB1 model-identity correction described below. This archive contains the manuscript-adopted results supporting the evaluation of full-parameter domain-specific unsupervised fine-tuning (DS-UFT) of ESM-2 650M. It includes sequence pseudo-perplexity, contact prediction, secondary-structure prediction and GB1 mutational-effect prediction results, adopted supplementary controls, confidence intervals, figure assets, executable analysis code and SHA-256 file manifests. GB1 results use validation-selected configurations; unused exploratory and test-selected alternatives are excluded. The archive includes 85 adopted checkpoint files: 30 secondary-structure heads, five L2 contact heads, 35 frozen-representation GB1 heads and 15 GB1 SFT trainable-parameter checkpoints. Full pretrained/DS-UFT backbone checkpoints and complete third-party databases are not bundled; verified external backbone references and loading requirements are provided. Model-identity correction: The two adopted mean-pooled GB1 conditions previously labeled PF00076_05 and PF00076_09 actually used PF00067_05 and PF00067_09. Checkpoint hashes and direct embedding reproduction verified the identity. Corresponding labels, Figure S7, head paths and backbone references are corrected; predictions, performance estimates, confidence intervals and fitted weight bytes are unchanged. The two affected candidate-corpus overlap comparisons are recomputed using the correct PF00067 collections. Genuine PF00076 experiments in other tasks are unaffected. See the archive provenance for scope and limitations. This release supports reconstruction of the included results, not end-to-end reproduction of every historical training workflow. Code: DS-UFT-Benchmark . Version-series DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23045593 .
title: DS-UFT-Benchmark: Data supporting the evaluation of domain-specific unsupervised fine-tuning of ESM-2 650M

summary: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.
title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning

summary: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.
title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning

summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression

summary: Analog in-memory computing offers the potential to accelerate approximate inverse preconditioning, but hardware errors can degrade preconditioners designed in digital arithmetic. We develop an analog-digital preconditioner for symmetric positive-definite linear systems that combines analog block Jacobi with a small digital low-rank residual correction. The correction space is constructed by probing the same programmed analog arrays used in the solve, targeting errors from both the coupling omitted by block Jacobi and persistent hardware perturbations. Under a random linear-operator model, we separate the programmed-mean error from fresh read fluctuations, distinguish the effects of copy averaging and repeated reads, and quantify the sampling accuracy of columnwise probing. Under a centered additive write-noise model, we also derive a computable regularization threshold and identify the approximation error introduced by the regularization shift. Experiments with an analog hardware simulator show that programming errors can change the directions that block Jacobi reduces poorly. In the tested comparisons with significant programming errors, learning the correction space from the programmed copies reduces FGMRES iteration counts relative to construction from digital block Jacobi.
title: Noise-Adaptive Analog-Digital Preconditioning

summary: We study recovery of an initial state from dynamical samples of a trajectory driven by unknown additive forcing. Measurements against both the original sensors and their images under the adjoint nominal evolution yield one-step residuals that cancel the initial state exactly. These residuals separate forcing estimation from initial-state reconstruction. For a centered Gaussian forcing model with fixed covariance parameters, we combine Gaussian conditioning with canonical dual-frame reconstruction and derive an exact unconditional second-moment identity, including the correlation between the forcing-estimation error and the measurement noise. We also obtain high-probability bounds and identify the irreducible forcing uncertainty through a conditional covariance in the geometry induced by the prior. A hierarchy of augmented sensor systems separates the role of sampling depth in forcing visibility from that of the observation horizon in nominal observability. An image-transport experiment and finite-dimensional and periodic-convolution experiments illustrate the residual correction and the separate roles of sampling depth and observation horizon.
title: Augmented Dynamical Sampling under unmodeled Forcing

summary: Can the spatial correlations of a quantum environment be revealed through work extraction? We address this question using two harmonic-oscillator detectors coupled to either an accelerated vacuum or a matched inertial thermal field. We establish a quantitative connection between the spatial correlations of the environment and the equilibrium Gaussian ergotropy, showing that the leading extractable work is governed by a response-weighted spatial correlation. Although the two environments have identical local spectra, their different spatial correlations give rise to distinct work responses. We further identify a finite-distance blind point at which a single measurement configuration fails to distinguish the two environments. By reversing the direct coupling between the detectors, we develop a two-setting scheme that removes this ambiguity and reconstructs the underlying spatial correlations from work measurements. This reconstruction remains effective beyond the weak-coupling regime. We also show that spatial correlations can provide additional global work even when the detector pair is separable, demonstrating that entanglement is not a necessary resource for this advantage. Finally, we investigate the transient evolution of Gaussian ergotropy and reveal its oscillatory decay and dependence on acceleration and detector parameters. Our results establish Gaussian ergotropy as an operational probe of spatial correlations in bosonic environments.
title: Gaussian ergotropy and spatial correlations: accelerated vacuum versus a thermal field

summary: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.
title: CT-RespGeomLib: Deterministic reconstruction of CT airway masks into editable,port-matched lumen geometry

summary: SignalAudit-QD is a reproducible audit resource for testing whether a dated public signal adds information beyond query history in a fixed 20-term U.S. AI panel. It aligns two archived Google Trends extractions with eight USPTO AI-patent publication streams and releases origin-indexed predictions, paired losses, provenance, executable tests, and tamper-evident run manifests. Both inputs are retrospective reconstructions obtained after the modeled 2020--2023 origins; the task is therefore a pseudo-origin assay within frozen measurement vintages, not a historical deployment simulation. In the designated one-month comparison, adding a two-component patent block to a level ridge changes macro mean absolute error by +0.0012 Trends points, with conditional 95% moving-block interval [-0.0363,+0.0387]. This establishes neither aggregate benefit nor equivalence. Alternative dimensions, semantic mapping, patent definitions, a second extraction, and a three-month horizon remain unresolved; persistence-anchored and nonlinear hosts instead show model-specific worsening, tiny for the anchored fit. Matched timing controls expose availability assumptions, while a planted-signal assay detects only the largest tested injection. A within-query high-interest alert demonstrates the released interface but not online utility. The contribution is a bounded negative case study and an extensible evidence schema for auditing external-signal claims in temporal information retrieval.
title: SignalAudit-QD: A Reproducible Audit Resource for External Signals in AI-Query Forecasting

summary: Gravitational-wave observations have opened new opportunities to study massive object events like merging binary black holes. When combined with electromagnetic counterparts, accurate localization of gravitational-wave sources could allow us to identify their host galaxies and carry out follow-up studies, such as study the environment of merging black holes and determine the Hubble constant. One of the possible methods for precise localization is strong gravitational-wave lensing. Previous studies have considered strong gravitational-wave lensing with galaxy lenses. However, galaxy clusters have yet to be investigated due to the complexity of their mass structures. Here we take the list of known cluster lenses from the Hubble Frontier Fields, simulate lensing properties of gravitational waves from their reconstructions as they would be observed by the ground-based gravitational-wave detectors. When same model family is used in simulation and localization, we find that the correct lens is identified for around 90\% of the simulated events. We also show that the source positions within the cluster can be pinpointed at sub-arcsecond precision with an estimate on source redshift. When we marginalize over all possible lens models for the clusters, the lens identification and localizations remain valid as long as the correct lens model is contained in the available cluster lens models. However, most localization attempts fail at initialization if the correct cluster model is excluded. These tests establish a proof of concept of localization under idealized conditions, while more work is needed to understand the cluster lens modeling discrepancies and reconstruction bias to validate the approach further.
title: Localization of gravitational-wave source behind galaxy clusters by gravitational-wave lensing

summary: This paper investigates the global geometry of loxodromes and loxodromic curves on surfaces of revolution in $\mathbb{R}^3$. A loxodrome is a regular curve avoiding the poles and making a constant directed angle with the meridians. To allow curves to reach or pass through poles, we introduce loxodromic curves, whose pole-free interior portions are loxodromes. The directed azimuths of these portions agree modulo $π$. We classify surfaces of revolution into four types based on the number of poles and whether the profile curve is closed: cylinder-like, torus-like, paraboloid-like, and sphere-like. For cylinder-like surfaces, every maximal loxodromic curve other than a parallel is non-self-intersecting. For torus-like surfaces, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves are closed or dense according to the rationality of their rotation numbers. For paraboloid-like and sphere-like surfaces, only maximal meridians can pass smoothly through poles, while nonmeridional, nonparallel maximal loxodromic curves have poles as endpoints. We derive the differential equations for arc-length-parametrized loxodromes and introduce coordinates in which they are represented by straight lines. We solve the direct and inverse problems for loxodromic segments on all four surface types and give criteria for maximal loxodromic curves to be geodesics. We show that diffeomorphisms preserving maximal loxodromic curves preserve surface type and that their inverses preserve such curves. These maps preserve maximal meridians and parallels on surfaces with poles, but need not do so on pole-free surfaces. We characterize azimuth-consistent diffeomorphisms and, for cylinder-like surfaces, establish criteria for conformality and isometry. In particular, azimuth-consistent diffeomorphisms are conformal when both surfaces have poles.
title: Classification and Geometry of Loxodromic Curves on Surfaces of Revolution in Three-Dimensional Euclidean Space

summary: Machine learning coupled with device simulation is widely used to optimize thin-film solar cells, but almost exclusively in the forward direction, from device parameters to predicted performance. The inverse problem encountered after fabrication, namely identifying the mechanism that limits a given device, is still addressed by manual inspection of characterization data. In this work, both directions are examined for lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells using approximately 42,000 SCAPS-1D simulations. Replacing the Spiro-OMeTAD hole transport layer with CuI increases the simulated power conversion efficiency from 19.6\% to 21.6\%, almost entirely through the fill factor. Surrogate models trained and tested on a factorial parameter grid substantially overstate their predictive accuracy. An XGBoost regressor attains $R^2 = 0.9997$ on held-out grid points but only 0.58 on independently sampled devices, whereas training on a Latin hypercube design of comparable size restores $R^2 = 0.995$. For the inverse problem, a multi-label classifier identifies which of six degradation mechanisms are present from simulated temperature- and illumination-dependent open-circuit-voltage measurements. It achieves a macro $F_1$ score of 0.938, compared to 0.687 for a calibrated physics-rule baseline. The classifier does not, however, generalize to combinations of mechanisms absent from the training set.
title: Interpretable machine learning diagnosis of degradation mechanisms in lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells from temperature- and illumination-dependent electrical measurements

summary: Accurate photometric-redshift estimation and calibration of the weak-lensing point-spread function (PSF) for Euclid require complementary ground-based optical imaging with high photometric precision and spatial homogeneity. The Organisation Unit for External Data (OU-EXT) integrates heterogeneous ground-based surveys into the Euclid Science Ground Segment (SGS), delivering uniformly calibrated, co-added images, and associated PSF models. To minimise systematics in spectral energy distribution (SED) reconstruction and photometric-redshift estimation, these data must achieve relative photometric stability at the $\sim$10 mmag level on Euclid-tile scales. We present the ground-based imaging component of Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), comprising $\sim2500$ deg$^2$ across the wide, deep, and auxiliary fields. We summarise the OU-EXT production workflow and validation framework, and quantify the achieved data quality of the co-added products in terms of depth, photometric zero-point stability, and spatial colour homogeneity. In the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the point-source $10σ$ depths in the $griz$ bands reach 24.8/24.3/24.0/23.0 AB mag, with the deep fields extending 1--2 magnitudes deeper. Most EWS DR1 tiles meet the 10 mmag relative photometric requirement, with 1.1% and 1.5% showing offsets exceeding 50 mmag in the northern and southern hemispheres, respectively. Spatial colour variations remain typically below 5--10 mmag across the southern EWS footprint, while larger residual structures of 10--25 mmag appear in some northern regions. These results demonstrate that the EXT production chain provides a largely homogeneous framework for integrating ground-based datasets into Euclid, while identifying calibration and co-addition limitations that have to be addressed in DR2 to meet the mission's most stringent cosmological requirements. (Abridged)
title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Colouring Euclid with external ground-based imaging data

summary: CREAM v1.1 provides an ensemble reconstruction of East Asian summer monsoon circulation for May–September 1855–1907, constrained by monthly wet-day counts from the historical Seoul Cheugugi rain-gauge record through offline ensemble data assimilation. The dataset contains frozen prior and posterior ensemble-mean anomaly fields for sea-level pressure (SLP), 850-hPa geopotential height (Z850), and zonal and meridional winds (U850 and V850) on a global T42 grid (64 latitudes × 128 longitudes), together with point-wise posterior ensemble standard deviations. Anomalies are referenced to the historical ensemble’s own 1855–1907 monthly climatology. A separate file, CREAM_v1.1_prior_members.nc , provides the ten GOGA prior ensemble members used in the reconstruction as full fields, together with this reference climatology. These allow users to examine the prior ensemble and recover model-referenced absolute prior and posterior mean fields on valid grid cells. The package also includes the western North Pacific subtropical high (WNPSH) western-edge index, per-year 5 × 5 monthly index covariance matrices, monthly Z850 reliability grades, historical and modern observation records, a provenance-based observation-error budget, assimilation feedback, and verification results. The assimilated historical wet-day counts incorporate eight adjudicated daily readings supplied with the observations. Python production, analysis, and figure-generation scripts, numerical figure inputs, four worked examples, and reproducibility documentation are provided. Posterior field-level ensemble members and full field covariance matrices are not included. CREAM v1.1 is a weakly constrained reconstruction intended primarily for WNPSH-index, seasonal, and epoch-scale analyses. In the development-exposed 2015–2024 modern holdout, near-Korea monthly Z850 root-mean-square error (RMSE), evaluated against NCEP/NCAR R1, improves by 1.6% relative to the SST-forced prior (95% confidence interval: +0.4 to +2.7%), although absolute monthly-field RMSE remains above climatology. The supplied reliability grades assess improvement over the prior for specified monthly Z850 composites within the East Asian evaluation domain; they do not certify absolute accuracy, other variables, or seasonal and epoch averages. May–June monthly fields are not recommended for use. WNPSH seasonal uncertainty derived from the supplied monthly covariance matrices represents conditional ensemble uncertainty and does not include stationarity or model-structure errors. Development exposure and recommended-use limitations are documented in the accompanying materials. The supplied numerical inputs support manuscript-figure rendering and selected verification and confidence-interval calculations without rerunning the full assimilation. The fourth worked example checks the released prior ensemble against the frozen product and reproduces a selected year’s assimilation update over the WNPSH Z850 index region. Full field-level production requires adapting the supplied scripts’ archive loaders and configuring paths. The original production script also retrains the observation operator using external NCEP/NCAR R1 fields; reusing the packaged operator-space observations and observation-error variances instead requires an additional code adaptation. Modern verification and other full-pipeline analyses require additional external AGCM and reanalysis inputs, as described in REPRODUCE.md . The ten historical prior members are included, but the broader raw AGCM archive and most external reanalysis source fields are not. The manuscript and rendered figure files are not distributed in this package. CREAM-authored data, code, and documentation are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) license. KMA-derived files retain the Korea Open Government License Type 1 and attribution to the Korea Meteorological Administration. The included NOAA
title: CREAM v1.1: Cheugugi-constrained ensemble reconstruction of East Asian summer monsoon circulation, 1855–1907

summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.
title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization

summary: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.
title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models

summary: We study $d$-dimensional quantum linear bandits with bounded rewards, where the learner selects an action and queries its quantum reward oracle or its inverse in each round. For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $Ω(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $Ω(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cramér--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.
title: Regret Bounds for Quantum Linear Bandits

summary: The manuscript gives a proposed learning algorithm for an unknown polynomially sparse Pauli Hamiltonian of operator norm at most one, using only forward evolution queries whose durations are all at least a fixed positive constant T. It obtains maximum coefficient error epsilon with constant success probability and total evolution time polynomial in the qubit number and sparsity, divided by epsilon, up to logarithmic factors. Circuit and classical processing costs are polynomial; constants may depend on T. The construction uses a two-time residual inverse and does not assume controlled access to, or the inverse of, the unknown evolution. This deposit preserves the website manuscript, version 1.0, dated 1 October 2026, by Yuxuan Zhang. It is a complete proof candidate with internal review and supporting checks; independent expert verification and exhaustive priority confirmation remain outstanding. Website and supporting material: https://yuxuanzhang1995.github.io/agentic-research/fixed-duration-hamiltonian-learning/ QIQC original: https://qiqc-op.com/problem/op_30954594cf01ebb3/
title: Heisenberg-scaling sparse Hamiltonian learning with a fixed minimum query duration

summary: CylOn is a framework allowing to reconstruct HEP experiments tracks on multiple backends.
title: CylOn: An(other) Geometry Agnostic Framework for Heterogenous Track Reconstruction

summary: Frozen pre-registration of a study that compares smoke-dependent exit choice in pyFDS-Evac (JuPedSim coupled with FDS 6.10.1) with survivor exit-use data from The Station Nightclub fire (Fahy et al. 2011, Table 2). It was frozen before the first production FDS fire run. This archive is the source tree of the pyFDS-Evac repository at tag station-prereg-v1 (commit aaeda1f3). The directory assets/station_prereg/ contains: preregistration.md: targets, registered criteria and bands, run design, arms and sensitivities, fire inputs, outputs already seen, failure policy, and changes from the study plan; freeze_record.md: software versions, build, run and scoring commands for every arm, and seeds; fds/: the six FDS input decks (0.2 m central, low and high yields, ±15 s HRR shift; 0.1 m grid check), their generator, and the HRR curve digitised from NIST NCSTAR 2 Fig. 5-42; SHA256SUMS: checksums of these files, the scenario configs, the scoring script and uv.lock. The study is a comparison with survivor exit-use data, not a validation and not a forensic reconstruction. Any registered criterion that fails will be reported as a disclosed failure.
title: Pre-registration of the Station Nightclub coupled fire–evacuation study with pyFDS-Evac (station-prereg-v1)

summary: What information about environmental memory must a quantum controller retain to guarantee a specified computational output? This preprint formulates that question in terms of task-sufficient process representations, intervention-valid predictions, stochastic clock laws, and explicit resource accounting. The central requirement is to preserve the outcomes and costs of the permitted decisions, with a stated accuracy contract and a finite-sample certificate. The paper connects two complementary lines of analysis. An operational construction studies Gaussian dephasing and controlled qubit tasks. A separate stochastic-clock analysis studies direct and inverse time changes, fractional relaxation, and the information that temporal coarse graining must transport. These constructions address related modelling questions but are not identified as a single microscopic noise model. The main elements are: Identical uncontrolled channels, different controlled responses. A continuum of Gaussian phase processes has the same uncontrolled coherence at every time and zero Breuer-Laine-Piilo backflow, yet different spin-echo responses. The construction shows why an uncontrolled channel family alone can fail to determine an intervention-dependent control decision. Task-sufficient equivalence and resource contracts. The manuscript defines a contract functional collecting accepted-output moments, acceptance probabilities, and physical costs over a declared policy family. Its finite linear task quotient identifies distinctions relevant to those predictions. Approximate sufficiency is accompanied by stability bounds that expose the sensitivity of conditional guarantees to low acceptance probabilities and small feasibility margins. Simultaneous finite-policy certification. Conservative confidence bounds certify conditional task bias and expected cost per accepted outcome after selection among a fixed, finite set of candidate policies. The assumptions include independent reset attempts, bounded observations and costs, and a trusted ideal reference. Failure to certify a candidate is explicitly distinguished from proof that no feasible physical policy exists. An explicit coarse-graining framework for stochastic clocks. The proposed decorated phase space records the process, permitted policy family, observable set, and clock law. The clock component transports stable laws under their natural scaling and relates domains of attraction to regular variation of waiting-time tails. Within the stated two-parameter clock-and-coupling family, the relaxation-rate direction scales with eigenvalue c^alpha. These clock results are placed in the established probabilistic renormalization literature; they do not establish hyperbolicity or convergence for the full decorated operator. A reset-sensitive fractional-relaxation calculation. Direct subordination of a quantum dynamical semigroup is distinguished from inverse-stable time change. For the latter, the paper compares uninterrupted evolution with independent renewal of the hidden clock and relevant environment. At half order and dimensionless rate one, the exact erfcx representation gives the short-time defect Delta(h) ~ 0.660989212585294 sqrt(h). The difference concerns the declared reset protocols, rather than a general assertion that every physical gate resets its environment. The reported classical benchmark uses ten candidate policies with explicit pulse depolarisation and separate X- and Z-expectation contracts. At the quasistatic endpoint, midpoint echo increases average identity-gate fidelity from 0.789293 to 0.990050. The fidelity crossover near r = 0.0467883 is distinct from the stricter X-task feasibility threshold r >= 0.9688074. For the selected Z-task input, dephasing is harmless and unnecessary echo pulses reduce the expectation. Conventional calibrated echo matches the best tested control performance; calibration, sampling, rejected attempts, and amortisation remain part of the resource account. Two q
title: Task-Sufficient Memory under Stochastic Clocks: Coarse-graining operators, fixed points, and finite-policy certification

summary: Companion research materials for the manuscript “First-passage asymptotics and identifiability in reflected damage-threshold models with growing drift, with an application to dietary-switching survival” by Bowen Xu, Ning Tang and Jiaying Li. The archive contains source code, archived inputs and results, post hoc descriptive summaries, mathematical statements and proofs, manuscript sources, documented numerical and statistical protocols, and provenance records. Independent density-solver agreement is limited to the reported converged ranges; unresolved trajectories and earlier failures are retained. The fly-record application is exploratory, and all panel distribution-free simultaneous bands include zero. Same-code reproduction is not independent scientific validation. The proofs have not been reviewed by a human mathematician, and an independent statistical assessment has not been completed. AI-use and author-contribution statements are included in the manuscript and archive. Original code is licensed under MIT. Original documentation and derived outputs are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Original Dryad records retain CC0 and source attribution; file-specific licence scopes are described in LICENSES.md. Original data: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.3xsj3txcn ; original article: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aay3047 . All three authors are designated equal contributors. Bowen Xu is listed first and is the corresponding author (bxu666@stanford.edu). This work received no specific funding. The authors declare no competing interests.
title: Code, frozen results and mathematical proofs for: First-passage asymptotics and identifiability in reflected damage-threshold models with growing drift, with an application to dietary-switching survival

summary: This report and reproducibility package examine how a specified receiver determines which distinctions in a supplied nested quantum state become accessible in its measurement records. Two nonorthogonal states with unequal 70/30 population weights and opposite coherence have identical reduced states on every nonempty proper subset of their encoded registers. Measurements confined to those subsets cannot distinguish the candidates. Local equatorial measurements followed by comparison of their records reveal a joint parity contrast, whose accessibility depends on the receiver phase. For the worked two-register example, equal-prior single-trial discrimination succeeds with probability 95.83% under ideal retention and 79.33% with independent 80% retention at each receiver. These probabilities include incomplete records. Blind receiver settings and complete dephasing provide distinct zero-contrast controls. The report also establishes reconstruction from three real quantities within a known two-dimensional encoded subspace. A support-leakage counterexample demonstrates why this reconstruction does not extend to unrestricted states. All sixteen numerical check families pass, including 5,130 proper-subset comparisons. A verification run reproduces the archived scientific results exactly. The package includes the report, executable code, fixed configuration, numerical results, probability tables, figures, equation sources, report builder and checksums. This is an analytic and computational benchmark within declared quantum states and measurement models. It provides a bounded example of receiver-dependent information access and candidate-state identification; it does not constitute experimental validation or derive a physical mechanism of nesting.
title: Receiver Distinguishability of Nested States

summary: GPU-native Julia framework for CT and photon-counting CT simulation, reconstruction, and quantitative spectral imaging. Provides distance-driven forward projection (with Siddon ray tracing as an alternative), polychromatic Beer-Lambert physics with vendor-realistic detector response (MC-derived LUTs for GE Gemstone scintillator and Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha CdTe), FDK, helical WFBP and hybrid iterative reconstruction, sinogram and image-domain beam-hardening correction, projection-domain dual-kVp and PCCT material decomposition (K-channel profile likelihood, Cong 2022), spectral denoising, and virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI + Grant 2014 Mono+) — all dispatching transparently across CPU, Metal, CUDA, and ROCm via AcceleratedKernels.jl.
