The original parameter sets for two of the three long-read procedures were not retained; those procedures were re-run and both original and re-run values are reported side by side and never pooled. One cell of the long-read table reproduces exactly; the others do not, and this is stated in the manuscript. Changes in version 4. The package matches the manuscript. All thirteen supplementary tables are present, including Supplementary Tables S12 and S13, which were absent from the previous version, and Supplementary Table S1 now carries the genome length and assembly level of all 1,483 retained genomes rather than leaving those columns empty. A new Supplementary Table S1b lists the seven excluded genomes that could be recovered from local storage, with their lengths; the genome-length window is 1.5 to 1.7 Mb and this version states the evidence that fixes its bounds. Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. summary: We present an analytical derivation of fundamental coupling constants and structural attractors emerging from a descending residual iteration function F(y,x) possessing a unique global fixed point y*(x) . Evaluating the first iteration term for specific membrane residues ( 155 and 185 ) yields pure, asymmetric numerical invariants--most notably 461.4331634036143, composed almost exclusively of the four digits {1, 3, 4, 6}--which directly link the inverse fine-structure constant alpha^{-1} approx 137.036 and the characteristic quark bounce frequency (925) to the 43.2 GeV signal. Through algebraic decomposition, we isolate the longitudinal attractor ( 323 ) governing transversal gravitational anchorage and membrane confinement from the transversal emission attractor ( 232 ), demonstrating how their balance generates a flat background (555) driven by the double-axis torsion gradient of charmonium. Finally, by applying discrete digit-suppression transformations ( 137.036 -> 137.360 and removal of the 036 residue), we map the transition to an antimatter-dominated dual system lacking inversion symmetry and derive a secondary four-digit invariant (2177.5711270036704), establishing arithmetically differentiated topological sets as the fundamental origin of the distinct interaction regimes.

Obtain public-use files and documentation from the CDC NIS-Teen data and documentation page . The package contains code and aggregate outputs only.

summary: The biological response of the body is a fundamental adaptation mechanism underlying the diagnosis and evaluation of the effectiveness of therapeutic interventions. Regardless of the registration methods used, whether instrumental or clinical, medical practice relies on an objective assessment of the response of the body's functional systems to internal and external stimuli. The article discusses the concept of biological response as a universal criterion combining the approaches of evidence-based and holistic medicine. An analytical review of scientific publications and theoretical concepts devoted to the physiology of adaptation and self-regulation of the body has been conducted. The study is based on an analysis of the theories of homeostasis, stress, and functional systems (W. Cannon, G. Selye, P.K. Anokhin, C. Pert), as well as modern concepts of neuroendocrine, autonomic, and immune regulation. Methods of biological response registration used in osteopathy, applied kinesiology, traditional Chinese medicine, and other holistic fields are considered. A universal sequence of biological response formation has been systematized, including afferent synthesis, assessment of compliance with the physiological norm, initiation of adaptive reactions, executive action, and reverse afferentation. It is shown that various diagnostic approaches use a single physiological feedback mechanism, differing mainly in the ways of registering the response. The modern physiological justification for holistic diagnostic methods, including muscle testing, osteopathic listening, and pulse diagnostics of traditional Chinese medicine, is presented. The data on the relationship of pulse wave characteristics with the state of the autonomic nervous system and hemodynamic parameters are considered. The biological response of the body is a universal diagnostic and therapeutic criterion reflecting the state of functional systems and the effectiveness of therapeutic interventions. The unity of the mechanisms of formation and registration of the biological response allows us to consider it as a methodological basis for the integration of evidence-based and holistic medicine. The use of feedback principles helps to increase the personalization, safety, and validity of diagnostic and therapeutic measures.
title: The Biological Response of the Body as a Universal Diagnostic and Therapeutic Tool

summary: Tools that claim to detect emerging research topics are rarely judged on their own lists. Our main contribution is a protocol that makes such judgement possible. A bet freezes four things before its verdict can be known: the date of the photograph, the population of candidates, the verdict rule, and the comparison with chance drawn among the same candidates. The list has a fixed length, is read on two axes (champions and failures) against a computed ceiling, and is sealed by cryptographic fingerprint; sealing proves that a list existed at a date, not that it is right. A topic is a champion if its yearly volume of records triples within three years and reaches 100, a failure if it falls by 30%. We apply the protocol to one detector on PubMed/MEDLINE, in three separate blocks. On a retrospective benchmark (2017-2022), chance among the candidates yields 26.7 champions and 15.1 failures out of 120 slots; the detector yields 85 and 3, and under nine pre-registered variants of the verdict rule its champions stay between 2.5 and 5.0 times chance, with no more failures. The detector was developed with these verdicts known, and its specification is not published. Prospective validation rests on six sealed bets, judged in early 2029 and early 2030; only bets 5 and 6 test exactly the instrument of the benchmark. A secondary, exploratory study applies the same judge to eight research funders: under exact name matching, which may disadvantage grant texts, the detector's lists are more concentrated in future champions than the twenty topics named in the most grants of each funder (70.8% against 20.8% to 35.8%, chance 22.3%). We document data defects, negative results and the limits of each comparison.
title: Sealed bets on emerging research topics: a protocol for judging early detection, applied to a detector and to eight research funders

summary: Capability benchmarks measure what large language models can do, but not whether their recommendations remain appropriate as decision conditions change. This paper proposes a trajectory-based measurement framework and prospective validation protocol for artificial wisdom, defined behaviorally as context-sensitive regulation of judgment. Versioned reference specifications determine admissible responses and transition materiality before evaluation. Seven stage-level criteria assess judgment under current conditions, while two transition components assess material-update adequacy and commitment-preserving stability. Stability requires prior adequacy; switching within registered commitment classes is permitted, and persistent error earns no stability credit. A nine-component profile is primary, with a secondary bottleneck score and separate critical-failure reporting. Three simplified simulations examine precision, bottleneck estimation, and sensitivity to model-family count. A single-criterion simulation met its precision criteria at 24 scenarios per domain. Near a bottleneck tie, the estimated minimum had a downward bias of 0.55 points at that size. A simplified incremental-prediction simulation detected a Brier improvement of 0.027 with probabilities of .508 and .742 using eight and twelve families, respectively; it does not establish power for the operational protocol. An exploratory predecessor-rubric study comprising 71 evaluation records illustrates aggregation sensitivity but does not validate the proposed instrument. The twelve-family target remains provisional pending feasibility assessment and calibration of the complete analysis. Whether the profile predicts independent decision outcomes beyond capability remains an open empirical question.
title: Evaluating Artificial Wisdom (AW): A Trajectory-Based Framework for Context-Sensitive Decision Regulation

summary: Objective: Choosing between noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS) and invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for acute respiratory failure is a time-sensitive decision. Although guidelines provide population-level guidance, it remains unclear who benefits more from NIRS than IMV. The standard outcome, ventilator-free days at 28 days (VFD-28), scores death and prolonged ventilation equally, and current estimators do not distinguish between them. We developed and validated a censoring-aware Digital Twin framework for Individualized Treatment Effects of Non-Invasive Respiratory Support (DINIRS) to estimate individualized treatment effects (ITEs) that capture both mortality and ventilation duration. Materials and Methods: We emulated a target trial in 5,336 MIMIC-IV patients and trained DINIRS on 23 baseline clinical variables measured during the first 24 ICU hours. A transformer encoder with a survival attention gate decomposed VFD-28 into survival probability and conditional ventilation duration. A cross-fitted, doubly robust learner estimated ITEs. We externally validated DINIRS in 2,540 patients from the multi-site eICU-CRD dataset without retraining. Results: The DINIRS policy achieved a mean benefit of 2.07 ventilator-free days per patient (207 per 100 patients) compared with observed practice. Predicted NIRS benefit was higher among patients with less organ dysfunction (88.4% versus 49.0%) and persisted across hypoxemia severity. External validation reproduced this pattern. Discussion: The NIRS benefit stemmed from shorter ventilation among survivors rather than from reduced mortality, indicating that avoiding intubation-associated complications was the primary mechanism. Conclusion: Prospective validation is needed before these estimates inform treatment decisions. The decomposition framework can be extended beyond respiratory support to any zero-inflated composite outcome.
title: A Digital Twin for Individualized Treatment Effects of Non-Invasive Respiratory Support Strategies (DINIRS)

summary: Large language model research agents can connect literature retrieval, analysis code, and manuscript preparation, but coherent output does not establish scientific validity. We developed Plato-Bio, a biology-routed extension of the open Plato/Denario architecture that couples explicit workflow states with provenance records, citation checks, claim-to-evidence links, scoped file writes, and publication gates. A source audit identified and repaired three defects that could distort evaluation: loss of task domain in the default factory, omission of declared method signals from scoring, and evidence sidecars that lacked the drafted-claim denominator. On the current clean revision, the full Python suite completed with 931 passes, six skips, and no failures or errors; targeted biology, genomics, evidence/citation, and adversarial-safety suites likewise completed without failure. We evaluated two narrow use cases. In a frozen historical rediscovery task, independent pre-1986 literature bridges ranked the later-studied relation between fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon first; TF-IDF ranked it second and corpus frequency third. This single curated task measures retrospective ranking, not prospective discovery. In a separate comparison of AlphaFold models with experimental structures for 15 human proteins, 11 targets had high-confidence-core C-alpha RMSD below 1 Angstrom (median 0.501 Angstrom). Four targets exceeded 2 Angstrom, and confidence masking reduced the SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Angstrom over 74 residues. The workflow emitted 27 traceable discrepancy regions, all retained as unvalidated hypotheses. Plato-Bio therefore provides reproducible software contracts and auditable screening baselines; broader claims of agent efficacy or biological novelty require preregistered evaluation, independent review, and prospective validation.
title: Plato-Bio: verification-first biological novelty screening with temporal rediscovery and structural benchmarks

summary: The study examines the physiological adaptation of boxers to mid-altitude conditions (1,800‒2,200 m above sea level) and substantiates the need to individualize training loads based on functional markers: blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), heart rate (HR), lactate levels, and maximum oxygen consumption (VO2). The article presents the results of a pedagogical experiment involving 24 qualified boxers (CMS and MS), divided into control and experimental groups. The experimental methodology included real-time monitoring of functional markers and real-time adjustment of the weekly microcycle. Following a 4-week high-altitude training camp, the experimental group demonstrated a significant increase in VO2 by 6.8%, hemoglobin concentration by 4.3%, and an improvement in the heart rate recovery index by 34.4% compared to the control group (p<0.05). The obtained data demonstrate the high efficiency of an individualized approach to load planning in midaltitude areas and are recommended for use in the training of highly qualified athletes.
title: Individualization of Boxing Training Loads in Middle-Altitude Conditions Based on Functional Adaptation Markers.

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: We develop a price-based framework for stochastic portfolio theory in which trading strategies are generated from nominal price weights and evaluated relative to a price-weighted benchmark. Stock splits and reverse splits induce jumps in the generating weights without changing the value of existing investments. In a semimartingale market with predictable adjustment events, we incorporate the corresponding share adjustments into the self-financing condition and construct additively and multiplicatively generated strategies with explicit jump-corrected wealth decompositions. For additive generation, an entropy-based example exhibits relative wealth tending to $-\infty$ almost surely under repeated splits, demonstrating why the usual argument for long-horizon relative arbitrage does not extend directly. We also show that advance adjustment information alone provides no model-free guarantee of improved performance for functionally generated portfolios. For multiplicative generation, wealth-preserving restarts retain the classical portfolio allocation evaluated at the current price weights. We also establish a correspondence with the capitalization-based framework that preserves absolute wealth and yields a strategy-independent benchmark conversion. We illustrate the framework using daily NYSE data, comparing price- and capitalization-weighted benchmarks and the corresponding diversity-weighted portfolios across price- and capitalization-selected universes.
title: A Price-Based Framework for Stochastic Portfolio Theory

summary: We present a systematic study of the quantum phase transition from a Dirac semimetal to an antiferromagnetic Mott insulator in the honeycomb-lattice Hubbard model, using finite-temperature auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) simulations. Given the dynamical critical exponent $z=1$ at criticality, we scale the inverse temperature $β$ with the linear system size $L$, i.e., $βt=L$ (with $t$ as the hopping amplitude), to approach the thermodynamic and zero-temperature limits simultaneously. On the algorithmic front, we generalize the fast Fourier transform in path propagation to multi-sublattice systems and employ the delayed update technique in configuration updates to accelerate the AFQMC simulations. These advances enable us to access unprecedented system sizes of up to $3528$ sites (with $L=42$ and $βt = 42$). We additionally use twist-averaged boundary conditions to reduce the finite-size effects in computed observables. On the physical side, we determine the Dirac quantum criticality via finite-size scaling analysis of the spin correlations and off-diagonal single-particle Green's function, and locate the critical point at $U_c/t=3.731(4)$ with the critical exponents $ν=1.097(7)$, $η_φ=0.72(2)$ and $η_ψ=0.155(6)$. We further corroborate the critical point by examining several relevant quantities, including the quasiparticle weight, Fermi-liquid parameter, charge compressibility, $U$-derivative of double occupancy, and fidelity susceptibility. Our work establishes an independent benchmark for the chiral Heisenberg Gross-Neveu-Yukawa criticality in the honeycomb Hubbard model, offering a complementary perspective to previous ground-state simulations.
title: Finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo study of Dirac quantum criticality: Algorithmic advances and comprehensive analysis

summary: Many existing Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions on mobile devices rely on an extensive collection of sensitive data, raising privacy concerns and often requiring storage for both context and model improvement. Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) aims to address this by emphasizing mobile device integration and a privacy-first design. The central claim of PCC is that it does not store any user data and that user input and user accounts are unlinkable. While most of the PCC system specifications are public, compiled binaries add a layer of opaqueness. There are no reproducible builds, and there are no symbols within those binaries, creating potential discrepancies between the specification and what is shipped to the user. Additionally, the underlying models and interfaces for querying PCC are not openly accessible, limiting academic evaluation of model properties, such as accuracy. This poses a challenge in assessing whether a privacy-preserving approach like PCC is actually trustworthy while also providing high-quality answers. We are the first to reverse-engineer the PCC implementation on mobile devices to evaluate privacy aspects and to open its non-public interfaces on local devices to support custom PCC queries. We demonstrate this level of access beyond Apple's intended use cases by independently benchmarking the PCC model. We enable future research by making our PCC benchmarking framework publicly available.
title: Unlocking Apple's Private Cloud Compute: An Analysis of Privacy-Preserving Artificial Intelligence

summary: This paper presents our submission to the ACMMM25 - Grand Challenge on Multimedia Verification. We developed a multi-agent verification system that combines Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with specialized verification tools to detect multimedia misinformation. Our system operates through six stages: raw data processing, planning, information extraction, deep research, evidence collection, and report generation. The core Deep Researcher Agent employs four tools: reverse image search, metadata analysis, fact-checking databases, and verified news processing that extracts spatial, temporal, attribution, and motivational context. We demonstrate our approach on a challenge dataset sample involving complex multimedia content. Our system successfully verified content authenticity, extracted precise geolocation and timing information, and traced source attribution across multiple platforms, effectively addressing real-world multimedia verification scenarios.
title: Multimedia Verification Through Multi-Agent Deep Research Multimodal Large Language Models

summary: Herrero García, José Luis. “La reivindicación marroquí y la soberanía española sobre Ceuta y Melilla.” Boletín CODESEL , vol. 2, no. 11, Oct. 2026, pp. 1–15. ISSN 3045-7750 LEGAL REVIEW The territorial claims advanced by the Kingdom of Morocco concerning Ceuta, Melilla and the remaining Spanish territories in North Africa constitute a particularly complex controversy at the intersection of international public law, historical sovereignty, territorial integrity, decolonisation and European security. Although these claims are frequently presented through the political vocabulary of colonial restitution and national reunification, their historical and legal foundations require examination beyond the geographical proximity of the disputed territories or the nationalist narratives surrounding Morocco's independence. In this extensive historical and juridical study, José Luis Herrero García undertakes a systematic examination of Moroccan territorial revisionism and the legal continuity of Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. His principal argument challenges the doctrine of Greater Morocco by distinguishing premodern religious allegiances, dynastic dominion and military expansion from the legal characteristics of territorial sovereignty under contemporary international law. Through the combined analysis of medieval political formations, historical treaties, constitutional provisions, international judicial reasoning and European institutional practice, the article develops a comprehensive interpretation of the historical and legal circumstances supporting Spain's position. The significance of the study extends beyond the bilateral dispute, raising fundamental questions concerning the construction of historical territorial titles, the stability of international borders and the limitations imposed by international law upon irredentist claims. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. The discussion of the Almoravids emphasises their origins among Saharan Berber communities associated with territories situated in present-day Mauritania, thereby questioning the assumption that their subsequent expansion establishes a uniquely Moroccan historical entitlement. summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 43 examines the governance and evidence requirements that arise when artificial intelligence influences consequential business decisions. The paper defines a decision chain of custody as a controlled, verifiable record connecting the information used, systems involved, applicable policies, delegated authority, approvals, execution and preserved evidence behind an AI-influenced decision. Its central operating test is independent reconstruction: an authorised reviewer should be able to determine what happened, which authority permitted the action and how the resulting business state was verified without relying on the original operator's memory. The analysis distinguishes decision custody from related concepts including accuracy, explainability, data lineage, observability and content provenance. It argues that these controls answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable forms of transparency. Content provenance might identify the history of a digital asset, for example, while providing no evidence that a user held authority to approve a payment or that the resulting transaction was correctly executed. The paper proposes eight linked evidence domains for consequential AI-influenced decisions: information received, intelligence used, rules applied, tools invoked, state changed, authority held, outcome approved and evidence preserved. These domains connect through a shared decision identifier and are intended to preserve relationships between initial inputs, policy evaluation, delegated authority, approval, execution and verified outcome. Particular attention is given to the moment of commitment, when an AI-generated recommendation becomes an external or financial business action. The paper argues that approvals must remain linked to the material terms ultimately executed. Changes to amount, recipient, purpose or other material conditions require a defined re-evaluation path rather than reliance on an earlier approval. The paper also addresses delegation across multiple agents and systems, retry behaviour, transaction reconciliation, evidence integrity, retention, human oversight and supplier evidence obligations. It distinguishes reconstruction from reproduction and outcome verification, noting that exact reproduction of stochastic model output is neither always possible nor necessary for reconstructing observable system behaviour. Three cases illustrate different dimensions of the argument. IBM provides company-reported evidence of reduced data-clearance processing time within an integrated governance programme. HSBC demonstrates large-scale financial-crime detection alongside explainable and auditable investigative outputs. AstraZeneca provides published evidence concerning the organisational scope and challenges of ethics-based AI auditing. summary: The Brina Gap measures the difference between the growth a company can self-finance and the growth its market price already assumes.  Its fundamental arm is the sustainable-growth ceiling,  g f  = ROIC × Reinvestment Rate; its pricing arm is the market-implied growth  g *, recovered from a reverse discounted-cash-flow on enterprise value. Both come from public filings, so the Gap makes the market's embedded growth expectation explicit — mechanically, reproducibly, and without an analyst's private valuation. Stated in growth units, it is the only kind of valuation claim that can be checked against what firms later deliver —  and it checks out. On the complete point-in-time S&P 500 (2010–2024, survivorship-free), the market-implied growth  g * genuinely tracks the growth firms subsequently realize (correlation ≈ 0.4–0.5, nearly unbiased at the 10-year horizon) and is robust across independent recovery methods (Spearman 0.73–1.00).  The Brina Gap is a detector of over-extrapolated growth expectations:  the market systematically over-extrapolates growth — the calibration slope sits below one at every horizon — and the median firm priced for high growth under-delivers what its price implies (≈ 26% priced in vs ≈ 22% realized).  Head-to-head against the classical Margin of Safety, the Gap is mechanical and falsifiable where the Margin of Safety is not, nearly orthogonal to it in cross-section, and more accurate on the one directional test both can take (+3.9 points, p ≈ .004; the Gap's expensive-side calls were correct 58.9% of the time on the full universe).  Among all pure valuation metrics tested — book-to-market, earnings yield, EPV, the Margin of Safety — the Brina Gap ranks first, and it is the only one whose central claim can be verified at all.  Its practical form is the  Brina Matrix , which crosses the Gap's pricing read with fundamental quality and yields one rule that survives every specification tested:  "cheap" is only a bargain when quality is high — cheap plus low quality is the value trap, the worst-performing cell in the sample. We are equally explicit about the limits: the fundamental arm is a conservative anchor, not a forecast; and the Gap — like every metric in the companion audit, the Margin of Safety included — is not a standalone return signal, which is exactly what efficiency logic predicts for any transparent, filings-based measure, in the most pricing-hostile decade on record. Data and code are published: a per-call outcomes file and a one-command verifier reproduce every headline number (see below). Verify the headline numbers yourself (added in v3.0.1). directional_outcomes_v3.0.csv lists all 1,504 directional calls on the complete point-in-time S&P 500, 2010–2024, delisted and acquired firms included (CRSP-style). Running python3 verify_headline_claims.py (Python standard library only) recomputes: • Stocks the Brina Gap clearly flagged as priced too high trailed the S&P 500 over the next five years in 546 of 927 cases (58.9%; a coin flip gives 50%). Exact one-sided binomial p = 3.3×10⁻⁸: if the warnings were coin flips, a record this good would come up about once in 30 million tries. • On the same 1,504 calls the classic Margin of Safety scored 50.9% (chance); the Gap 54.8%: +3.9 points, year-clustered bootstrap p = 0.0038. • Value Trap calls: 59.5% (207 of 348). The Gap's "cheap" calls were at chance (48.2%), as the paper reports. The paper claims no standalone return edge (over every stock, sign only: 52.4%). See README_VERIFY.md. summary: Supplementary note to arXiv:2611.08310 and arXiv:2610.19779. A fingerprint of coherent noise built from a stabilizer code is only as informative as the recovery gates that produce it, and every fixed choice of those gates is blind somewhere. This note isolates what can nevertheless be guaranteed, and states it as a worst-case floor rather than an average improvement. Two elementary facts about Fisher information make the guarantee exact. Because information matrices add, the identifiable set of a collection of designs is the union of theirs, so running several designs in parallel can never cost a direction that any member sees. Because the inverse of a sum is Loewner-dominated by the inverse of any summand, splitting a fixed shot budget over S designs can never cost more than sqrt(S) in standard deviation, that is, S in shots. The premium is therefore fixed in advance and independent of the working point, while the gain is not. Both statements are certified over the 64-design space of the three-qubit repetition code, under the 48- and 112-component fingerprints: the Loewner inequality is evaluated rather than assumed at every point tested, the worst case over 300 working points is 1.25 against the certified sqrt(2) = 1.4142, the bound is attained to five figures at one structured point, and at the worst points of the individual designs the parallel pair sits below the better single design by factors of 2.6 to 9.5. Two three-gate placements suffice; a third adds 3.5 to 11.5 per cent. The floor buys recoverability and worst-case precision, and it buys nothing else: it does not buy accuracy under common-mode calibration bias, and it does not repair a model degeneracy that no design can see. Contents: the two propositions with proofs, the cost corollary, the numerical certification (five tables, one figure), the relation to the two companion papers, and a reproduction map. The archive repro_v1.0.zip in this record contains the seven scripts, four data files, the figure and a self-test that re-derives every quoted number; run python scripts/selftest.py from the archive root and compare against MANIFEST.sha256. Companion papers: arXiv:2611.08310 (recovery gates as a resource) and arXiv:2610.19779 (coherent-noise identifiability).

summary: Contemporary speculative fiction unsettles anthropocentric assumptions about language, intelligence and the production of knowledge. This article compares Laline Paull’s The Bees (2014) to Ray Nayler's The Mountain in the Sea (2022) and The Tusks of Extinction (2024), exploring how the novels represent the conditions under which non-human knowledge is produced, recognized and transmitted. Drawing on biosemiotics and critical posthumanism in conversation with Andrew Lopez's account of epistemic injustice towards non-human animals, it develops a comparative framework based on recognition, access and continuity. The key argument is that the novels depict epistemic harm not merely as a failure to interpret non-human signs but as the institutional restriction of the very environments and social relations through which practical knowledge can flow. In Paull's hive caste is the source of authority which controls access to sensory information; in Nayler's oceanic enclave corporate power turns scientific attention into a potential tool of appropriation; and in the de-extinction narrative, biological restoration is simply not enough without the recovery of the skills that are socially transmitted. The novels are not being read as descriptions of actual animal species. Rather they are being used as a lens through which to examine the political and ethical dimensions of human authority over other ways of knowing. The article makes a contribution to contemporary literary studies by linking multispecies representation to the distribution and preservation of epistemic goods.

title: Sign Systems and Shared Worlds: Nonhuman Communication, Collective Knowledge and Epistemic Justice in Contemporary Speculative Fiction

summary: Enterprise database systems face data-loss risks that come from operational errors, system failures and security incidents. MySQL binary logs give tools for data replication and point-in-time recovery, yet many organizations do not use them fully for recovery. This study proposes an automated, schema-aware MySQL binary-log recovery framework that integrates log discovery, dependency-aware recovery planning, database reconstruction, and validation into a unified enterprise restoration pipeline. The framework explains how to read binary-log formats, how to run recovery steps automatically and how to use performance-boosting tactics learned from well-known recovery models such as ARIES write-ahead logging, log-structured storage and event sourcing. The framework was tested in four failure scenarios and compared with the usual backup-and-restore approach. In those tests, the recovery time dropped by about 65%, meaning the framework needed only about one-third of the baseline time. A real-world check compared each recovered field to the printed reference invoice: 99.7% of the fields matched exactly, and every financial total was correct. The only error was a single non-financial field. This work gives reusable tools for people who care about database reliability, and it offers a clear map of failure types and a step-by-step method for bringing MySQL databases back to life. The proposed approach differs from conventional binary-log recovery methods by providing an end-to-end automated workflow with schema awareness and independent validation of recovered data.
title: Advanced MySQL Binary Log-Based Data Recovery

summary: The internet's prevailing identity-and-authentication systems were designed for account ownership, not for proving authentic human presence at the moment of digital interaction. As generative AI makes synthesized content indistinguishable from human-produced content, every platform that depends on a distinction between human and machine participation faces a sybil-resistance problem the existing identity stack cannot solve. Proof of Humanity ℠ (PoH℠) is an open protocol for proving authentic human presence at the moment of action, structured as four optional layered proofs (passkey-per-action, witness-and-document-attested kinship graph, continuous breath-signature liveness, DNA-verified kinship lineage) surfaced as depth on a user profile, paired with recipient-side filters that route the spam-cost decision to the parties who bear it. B-PoH℠ is HeartBank's reference deployment of the PoH protocol — brand-family-prefixed by the project's B-prefix convention, the way Let's Encrypt is a specific certificate authority implementing the SSL/TLS protocol. This paper specifies the protocol architecture, the recipient-filter mechanism, the BLE-Nearby proximity verification path that preserves location privacy, the bilateral-uncacheable-anonymity property, and the placement of B-PoH℠ beside Proof of Work and Proof of Stake as a proof bounded by humanness, in the line of earlier proof-of-personhood work (§12) — the proof-of-X primitive that fits the era when compute and capital have both become AI-commodified, leaving humanness as a scarce resource AI cannot readily manufacture. The paper also discloses one application-facing composition of the per-action passkey press, the presence call (§3.8): an identity provider confirms to an app, for one named action and in the provider's own closed wording, that the holder of a person's passkey pressed it, for a person the app already knows by its own pairwise identifier, and keeps nothing; §12.1 reports the novelty census that scopes that claim to the composition alone. The protocol is offered defensively to the commons under CC0; the authors and HeartBank® will not seek patent on the protocol specification or any portion thereof. Trademark rights on specific marks ( Proof of Humanity ℠ , PoH℠ , B-PoH℠ , Aquarius℠ , HeartBank® , the B-heart logo) are separately and explicitly reserved. Keywords: proof of personhood, proof of humanity, sybil resistance, decentralized identity, AI-content trust, open identity protocol, recipient-side filtering, BLE-Nearby proximity, blockchain consensus, AI alignment, per-action passkey confirmation, pairwise subject identifier, WebAuthn user verification, defensive publication. --- Provenance. summary: This dataset is version 1.1.0 of the P1 complete derived transcriptomic resource for mapping and comparing human pluripotent stem cell-derived beta-cell differentiation across published protocols. It contains 100 sample or time-point analysis units, an S0-S6 stage ontology with S7-S9 reserved, a 2,552-gene shared cost space, optimal-transport stage coordinates with 20 retrospectively exported reference-centroid bootstrap draws, five-axis/46-gene Maturity Fidelity Index scores with 16 sensitivity versions, a 25-module concordance atlas, gene- and module-level variance components, constructed reliability descriptors, provenance records, analysis-code snapshots, and two application workflows. Applications and evidence boundaries. The internal GSE158617 example uses 38 samples in a retrospective, in-sample interface demonstration and is not independent validation. The external GSE203264 application uses 35 wild-type samples and a rebuilt P1-compatible 2,550-gene reference. Its non-monotonic D35 result concerns unsorted, compositionally heterogeneous SC-islets and is not validation of the unmodified 2,552-gene model or a pure beta-cell accuracy result. Reliability values are constructed descriptors, not absolute dataset-quality scores or significance ranks. MFI values are within-matrix relative profiles, not absolute cross-protocol maturity measures. No in vivo developmental tiers, validated benchmark accuracy, clinical validity, or universal generalization are claimed. Reproduction scope. The package supplies package-local verification for the two application workflows and the external diagnostics. The analysis-code and provenance snapshots support inspection and traceability but are not represented as a relocatable clean-room rebuild of every manuscript display item. The reference-centroid draws are a retrospective deterministic reconstruction from frozen training inputs, not an original frozen cache. Source data and governance. Original GEO expression matrices and metadata are not redistributed. Source accessions, expected hashes and third-party rights boundaries are documented in the package. GSE270220 and GSE275610 remain sealed and contributed to no statistic. The associated pilot-informed preregistration and execution governance records are identified through the related OSF project; private OSF access tokens are neither included nor required for the packaged application checks. Licensing. Original source code is under the MIT License. Original derived data, model parameters, documentation and figures are under CC BY 4.0, subject to the stated third-party exclusions. Funding. Basic Scientific Research Projects of the Liaoning Provincial Department of Education for Universities and Colleges, grant LJ212413213011.
title: P1 complete derived transcriptomic resource for cross-protocol beta-cell differentiation analysis

summary: theorem A316626 : conjectureA316626 (unconditional, universal in k, standard axioms only): for every k >= 1, the occurrence count of k in OEIS A316626 equals its occurrence count in the sister sequence A081832 plus exactly one when k is a power of 2 - the on-entry conjecture of N. Fox and A. Alkan (2018), i.e. the first stated (2,1) case of Conjecture 5.1 of Erickson-Isgur-Jackson-Ruskey-Tanny (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 26(1) (2012) 206-238, DOI 10.1137/100795425, arXiv:1509.02613), published open and found unproved in a prior-art audit covering 8 registries (2026-11-08). Also proved: kernel anchors a(1..31) and b(1..30) matching the entry data, exact fibers of 1, and the k = 1 case. NOT claimed: the companion on-entry conjectures (slow increments {0,1}, density 1/4 - elementary corollaries of a = c but not kernel-exported), the remaining 179 recurrences of Conjecture 5.1, the 'the only' enumeration direction, and the informal slowness proof of A081832 by A. Alkan (2018, cited for context, not used). summary: For hedge fund research reviewers, this report examines checks for selective reporting when a registered study is closed. At the author’s research service, the proposed use is review of research records before their conclusions enter an evaluation; no product integration or saving in review time has been measured. This report makes no claim of originality.   Checking whether a study followed its pre-registration requires comparing the report with the plan. This report tests one method for that comparison. A research record is kept in a fixed JSON format (registration, hash commitment, event log, closure), and seven mechanical rejection rules, R1 to R7, each target one selective-reporting defect taken from Arnott, Harvey and Markowitz (2019) and Harvey and Liu (2015). The comparison arm gives the same information, rendered as plain text, to a general-purpose language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) with one fixed instruction. The test plan, its thresholds and its decision order were frozen, with a local SHA-256 hash, before any code, record or label existed. For each of two cohorts a separate model session generated 33 synthetic records, 12 valid and 21 with one injected defect, without seeing the rules, and labels were locked before either arm ran. In the first (in-sample) cohort the rules flagged 21 of 21 defective records and rejected 0 of 12 valid ones. The language model also flagged 21 of 21 but rejected 6 of 12 valid records, which disqualifies it under the plan. In the second (out-of-sample) cohort the rules again scored 21 of 21 with 0 of 12 rejected, and the language model scored 17 of 21 with 0 of 12. The gap of 4 is below the pre-registered margin of 5. The pre-registered verdict for both cohorts is therefore "compared, threshold not met", and the report makes no claim that the rules add detection. A reduced rule set (R1, R2 and R7 only) missed 12 of 21 defects in both cohorts and is refuted. No confidence intervals are reported, because the plan forbids them: the records are constructed counterexamples, not a sample from any population.   Deposit version: Working paper, version 1.2 (2026-11-12). Three new scripts are included: the marker-control experiment (scripts 26 and 27), in which the single copy-differentiating base of the isolate was set to A in both copies, to C in both, to T in both, and exchanged between them, with the reads realigned to each control; and the structural diagnostic of the two 26695 23S copies (script 28), which reports that copy 1 contains no ambiguous base while copy 2 contains one N at genome position 1,475,696. The four control reference sequences are deposited under results/marker_control/. Changes in version 6. This version restores the complete file set. The previous version was published from an incomplete upload, so most of the figures, several of the supplementary tables and part of the analysis code were missing from that record. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files and this package has 134, so the package is now deposited as a single archive, hp23s_copy_assignment_package.zip , which holds every file at the path it occupies in the source repository; this README, the SHA-256 manifest and the archive of rRNA calls and copy sequences are additionally placed loose in the record. Three defects in the supplementary apparatus are corrected
title: Long reads assign a 23S rRNA resistance allele to one of the two copies in Helicobacter pylori; a complete short-read assembly does not

summary: This dataset contains a CityJSON Next Sequence (CityJSONL) file representing 3D city models of three districts in Bontang City, East Kalimantan, Indonesia: Bontang Baru, Api-Api, and Loktuan. The dataset was collected as part of a pilot project aimed at updating and improving regional tax revenue management. It was subsequently used for spatial analysis in the research entitled "Integrating Multi-Sensor Earth Observation Data for Digital Twin Generation: A Framework for 3D City Reconstruction and Quality Assessment", which is included in the book Harmonizing Earth Observation Data for Enhanced Spatial Analysis . The dataset is provided to support research and applications related to 3D city modelling, spatial analysis, and urban digital twins.

summary: AiMat-Suite is the integrated, verifiable software framework developed for the doctoral thesis of A. O. Marcelo Júnior (PPGECM/UFC, LAMEFF). It chains, in a single system: (i) U-Net (ResNet-34) segmentation of fibre networks in optical photographs of chitosan/sisal films; (ii) automatic geometry and meshing (CalculiX cgx: S4 shells for the matrix, B32 beams for the fibres, translational MPC tie) and linear-elastic FE solution (CalculiX ccx); (iii) physics-informed and operator-learning surrogates (SharedPINN/Cascade PINN with Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation; Kuramoto-reservoir DeepONet with a Poisson-coupled nodal solver); (iv) a differentiable Rietveld engine for XRD with calibrated uncertainty and a declared domain of validity; (v) a material-card module that turns raw EMIC/Instron tensile curves into FE material cards with declared estimators, bootstrap confidence intervals and a load-regime check. Version 3.1.1 is the thesis reference release. The platform was developed in two stages: the aiMat MVP (2023–2025), which automated the image → model → simulation chain and produced the 2025 Materials Research papers, and AiMat-Suite (2026), which adds an operator-verification module (digitisation-invariance criterion), material cards built from tensile curves, the X-ray diffraction module, image-conditioned surrogates and zero-shot transfer to 217 microstructures. In AiMat-Suite the FE deck generator uses the translational fibre–matrix tie ( areampc 123 ), the choice supported by the digitisation-invariance criterion; matrix E = 13.67 MPa / ν = 0.35 from the tested plasticised film; fibre E = 9.3 GPa (sensitivity 31 GPa) / ν = 0.153; line load q = 1.75 kN/m applied as F = q·L_edge in N; static linear analysis; *NODE FILE, OUTPUT=2D . The provenance of every parameter is recorded in packages/fem/src/aiMat/calculix/materials.py . The MVP protocol (six-DOF tie, MVP material cards and load) is kept as legacy to reproduce the 2025 papers. packages/fem/reexecucao_v13/ contains the full re-execution of microstructures M1–M6 (decks, displacement fields, SHA-256 hashes) and of 220 image-derived microstructures, plus a test that rebuilds and solves M1 with ccx (E_eff within 0.5 % of the deposited value). The suite ships 170 Python modules and 90 tests ( scripts/verify.sh ). Changes in 3.1.1. (i) The coupled nodal solver and reservoir-readout ablation used in Sections 5.5.3.3–5.5.3.4 of the thesis ( packages/newton_oir/oir/phase_field_coupled.py , phase_field_sparse.py , metrics.py , hybrid_readout.py and experiments/ex31_v62_ablation_full.py ) were missing from 3.1.0 and are restored unchanged from the repository history; (ii) re-executions of 30 Oct–1 Nov 2026 are added under packages/fem/reexecucao_v13/ : surrogates on the AiMat-Suite fields, normalisation by the image-derived fibre fraction, sensitivity to shell thickness and beam diameter, and a complementary re-execution (reservoir readouts, coupled solver, leave-one-out and Wilcoxon on the AiMat-Suite fields; 660 CalculiX runs of the 220 image-derived cases with pure matrix, 9.3 GPa and 31 GPa fibres); (iii) SHA-256 manifests are computed on the LF-normalised files as versioned. Erratum to 3.1.0: its description states 210 Python modules; the 3.1.0 archive contains 154 (verify.sh count). Dependencies: Python ≥ 3.10, numpy/scipy/scikit-image/opencv (core); PyTorch (segmentation, PINNs, DRX AI routes); JAX (Rietveld engine); CalculiX 2.17 (FE). Abaqus is required only by the optional XFEM module ( packages/fem/src/abaqus/ ) and is not part of the open-source chain. Licence: MIT (integration and packages/drx ); datasets under assets/ are CC-BY-4.0. Companion archive (15 Nov 2026). AiMat-Suite-v3.1.1-tese_complemento.zip adds the trained U-Net weights (ResNet-34 encoder; partition by photograph and by crop) and the script and CSV that reproduce Tables 4 and 5 of the thesis (fibre diameter and total length on predicted versus annotated masks, 13 photographs, at the photograph resolu

summary: Single-valued neutrosophic set theory is an important soft computing approach for resolving uncertainty and imprecision in decision-making. Several models have been established under the framework of single-valued neutrosophic sets for decision-making purposes. Single-valued neutrosophic relations, their max-min-max composition and a score-based use of this composition in medical diagnosis already exist in the literature; this paper revisits the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation in the framework of composite relations under fuzzy-set extensions, describes its algebraic properties, and applies it to two new healthcare problems. In this work, this composite relation on single-valued neutrosophic sets is presented. The numerical illustrations of the composite relation are given, and some of its algebraic properties are proved (inverse, monotonicity, associativity and distributivity over union), while it is shown by counterexamples that the composition is neither commutative nor distributive over intersection. In addition, the applications of the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation to medical healthcare services are considered to illustrate its use. Two medical healthcare applications are considered involving prediction of maternal outcome for a pregnant woman and the diagnosis of some common ailments. The examples are illustrative and use data adapted from earlier studies; no clinical validation is claimed.
title: Single-Valued Neutrosophic Composite Relation and Its Application to Healthcare Services

summary: Emissions figures in ship weather routing rest on regulatory and market data that change with new legal acts and markets. Maintaining them by hand is slow and prone to plausible errors. This paper presents the Data Steward, an agent built on a large language model that maintains these data in EcoRouter, a workbench for ship weather routing. The agent changes a value that calculations use only through an approved proposal. Deterministic tools take over the tasks that the model performs unreliably, such as reading area boundaries from legal texts, and checks run as workflows of small steps with an outcome for every item. The contribution to artificial intelligence is the design of an agent that maintains regulatory reference data under human control, together with a method for evaluating such an agent. The engineering application is the maintenance of the regulatory data on which a ship-routing tool computes emissions and regulatory costs. In a controlled test with 40 errors injected into the data that a full check covers, the Steward corrected 36 to 38 in three runs, against 20 to 28 for the same model alone with web search. In three full checks of the live data, 96 to 99 % of judged items were correct. A person who took no part in building EcoRouter found 57 of the 59 approved values correct. The results show that a commercial language model can maintain regulatory reference data with few errors once the tasks it performs unreliably are moved into deterministic code. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Version 1. The records of the tests are published as a dataset: 10.5281/zenodo.24251511. Use of AI: during the preparation of this work the author used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) in order to correct the text, check its grammar, to create the tables and figures from the author's records, and to check the statements about EcoRouter against its source code. The same assistant also helped to run tests 1 and 3, to judge their results against the acts and publishers, to prepare the person's sheet for test 2 and to aggregate the results of the three tests. It did only the tasks that the author gave it, under the author's control. The author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for it. Language models are also part of the research itself: Section 5 of the paper states which model the Data Steward ran on and which AI assistant judged its results.
title: A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence" by Jingyang Li (School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, China). This deposit contains the analysis code, the result files behind every number reported in the manuscript, the figure sources and the executed forced-choice log. The external eye-tracking arm re-analyses the public SensCogAR dataset archived at Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/45tjp); that archive declares no explicit data licence, so the raw records are not redistributed here, while the derived per-participant windows and metrics are included in data/real_ar_gaze/. The nine display devices used in the external-evidence arms are described by published measurements, each cited with its DOI in the manuscript, and the extracted parameters are recorded in data/panel_response_identification/. The target display panel and the human observers of the perceptual arm were not measured, so no raw panel or eye-tracker record exists for them. Contents: code/ (analysis, verification, simulation and figure scripts plus the LaTeX typesetting pipeline), data/ (the JSON, CSV and Markdown result files behind every number), manuscript_en_jsid_template.md (manuscript source), perceptual_experiment_protocol.md, AUDIT_citations.md, README.md, LICENSE.txt and CITATION.cff. Reproducing the results: ``` export JSID_MD='manuscript_en_jsid_template.md' python code/verify_manuscript_numbers.py    # CHECKED 404 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_tables_6_9.py           # TABLES 6-9 CHECKED 252 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_data_provenance.py      # per-device DOI and tau audit python code/verify_figure_resolution.py    # 600 dpi plate check ``` Licence: data and documentation CC BY 4.0; code MIT. Please cite the article above; a CITATION.cff file is included in this deposit.
title: Data and code for: Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence

summary: The records of the tests reported in the preprint "A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation" (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24250853). The Data Steward is an agent built on a large language model that keeps the emissions-regulation data of EcoRouter, a weather-routing tool, current. It proposes changes, and an administrator approves them. The files hold every message EcoRouter sent the agent and every answer, its proposals, the outcome of every item checked, and the judgement of each item and proposal against its act or publisher. - Test 1: three full checks of the live data, checks 1, 2 and 3. - Test 2: a person's check of the 59 values approved in test 1: the values, the instructions given to the person, the person's sheet, the key and the result. - Test 3: nine runs on a copy of the data with injected errors. A1 to A3 are the agent as built, B1 to B3 the same model alone with web search, and E1 to E3 a check of the EU ETS exemptions. Beside the runs: the answer key, the random draw of the errors with its seed, the changes that made the test copy, and the result of each run. - Severity: the rule that grades every wrong result as high, medium or small, the grade of each, and EcoRouter's value catalogue. E-mail addresses and names are replaced by codes. CONTENTS.md lists every file and the test it belongs to. The ZIP keeps the folder tree. These files are the output of the language-model agent evaluated in the paper, gpt-5.5 (version 2026-04-24) in Microsoft Foundry, and the judgements of its work, made by an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) under the author's control, as Section 5 of the paper describes. They are research data on that agent. Some proposals carry area boundaries from Marine Regions: Flanders Marine Institute (2026), MarineRegions.org, licensed under CC BY. Some carry place positions from OpenStreetMap: © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License, https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright.
title: Records of the tests of a language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool

summary: This doctoral thesis, entitled Genomic Studies of Piscine Streptococci and Genome Assembly of Clariidae Catfishes (Siluriformes) for Aquaculture Enhancement, was prepared at the Faculty of Fisheries, Kasetsart University, Thailand, for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). The thesis integrates microbial comparative genomics, genome assembly, genome annotation, repeat and gene-family analysis, population genomics and chromosome evolution to develop genomic resources and analytical approaches relevant to aquaculture, fish health and genetic management. It comprises eight research chapters and a general discussion. Chapter 1 — Bighead catfish genome assembly. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of Clarias macrocephalus generated with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing. Chapter 2 — Streptococcus iniae comparative genomics and reverse vaccinology. The genome of strain SIKU01 and comparative analyses of 90 isolates used to prioritize candidate antigens. The candidates require experimental validation. Chapter 3 — F1 hybrid catfish genome annotation. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved assembly of the interspecific hybrid Clarias macrocephalus × Clarias gariepinus , with its protein-coding, non-coding, satellite and transposable-element annotation. Chapter 4 — Repetitive architecture of the two haplotypes. Tandem repeats, segmental duplications, gene-family clusters, the miR-430 array and the divergence of Gypsy and Helitron elements. Chapter 5 — Hatchery population genomics. Diversity, relatedness, family reconstruction, autozygosity, structural variation, polymorphic inversions and shared parents in a commercial C. gariepinus broodstock. Chapter 6 — Gene repertoire and divergence of the two parental haplotypes, on a phylogenomic framework of 17 catfish genomes. Chapter 7 — Composition of the 41 polymorphic inversions of C. gariepinus and deletion-based PCR markers for their arrangements. The markers were designed in silico and have not been tested in the laboratory. Chapter 8 — Fusion and fission between the karyotypes of the two species. Junctions are reported as intervals; no mechanism is resolved at any junction. Chapter 9 — General discussion and conclusion. Changes since the version of 2026-11-03: lists of tables and figures; Chapters 7 and 8 revised; five figures of the repeat analyses added to Chapters 3 and 4 (spacer types of the LG04 array, tandem repeats against chromosome ends, copy number by counting step, array structure of repeated loci, Gypsy and Helitron); new introductions of Chapters 6 and 7; Chapter 9 updated to the chapters. Several chapters are working versions of manuscripts in preparation. Institution: Kasetsart University, Faculty of Fisheries, Thailand. Degree: Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). Related publications, data, code and accessions Chapter 1, bighead catfish ( Clarias macrocephalus ). Article: 10.1038/s41597-025-06325-6 . Data record: 10.5281/zenodo.14826876 . Code: github.com/Isoris/fClaMac . NCBI BioProjects PRJNA1121957 , PRJNA1132508 , PRJNA1159889 , PRJNA1159890 ; GenBank JBLWMO000000000 and JBLWMP000000000 . Chapter 2, Streptococcus iniae SIKU01. Data record with the manuscript: 10.5281/zenodo.15264953 . Code: github.com/Isoris/SIKU01_prioritization . NCBI BioProject PRJNA933632 ; GenBank CP121692.1 . Chapters 3 to 8, F 1 hybrid catfish and hatchery broodstock. Manuscript record (in preparation): 10.5281/zenodo.24249285 . Genome assembly and annotation: 10.5281/zenodo.14864260 . Hatchery population genomics and comparative analyses: 10.5281/zenodo.21639188 . Code: github.com/Isoris/fClaHyb , github.com/Isoris/SatChain , github.com/Isoris/BroodLink . summary: We present an analytical derivation of fundamental coupling constants and structural attractors emerging from a descending residual iteration function F(y,x) possessing a unique global fixed point y*(x) . Evaluating the first iteration term for specific membrane residues ( 155 and 185 ) yields pure, asymmetric numerical invariants--most notably 461.4331634036143, composed almost exclusively of the four digits {1, 3, 4, 6}--which directly link the inverse fine-structure constant alpha^{-1} approx 137.036 and the characteristic quark bounce frequency (925) to the 43.2 GeV signal. Through algebraic decomposition, we isolate the longitudinal attractor ( 323 ) governing transversal gravitational anchorage and membrane confinement from the transversal emission attractor ( 232 ), demonstrating how their balance generates a flat background (555) driven by the double-axis torsion gradient of charmonium. Finally, by applying discrete digit-suppression transformations ( 137.036 -> 137.360 and removal of the 036 residue), we map the transition to an antimatter-dominated dual system lacking inversion symmetry and derive a secondary four-digit invariant (2177.5711270036704), establishing arithmetically differentiated topological sets as the fundamental origin of the distinct interaction regimes.

summary: Bench dataset of a small multirotor propulsion assembly (A2212 920 KV motor, 9450 propeller, SkyWalker 40 A ESC): five endurance runs at nominal 6, 8 and 9.5 A, represented by 87 intermittent 50-second captures sampled at 1 kHz (vibration, shunt-current and temperature channel voltages; 4.35 million samples per channel), plus 11 thrust curves (66 observations) comparing post-test configurations with a shared healthy reference. The package contains the original MAT files, value-identical raw-voltage CSV exports, run and capture metadata with session identifiers and quality flags, derived features, technical-validation outputs, and Python scripts that reproduce every table and figure of the associated data descriptor, including operating-condition controls, permutation tests and grouped-validation comparisons. Known limitations (unobserved gaps, unresolved current calibration, temperature-channel excursions, shared thrust reference and unverified physical failure endpoints) are documented in README.md and metadata/quality_flags.csv. Download the single ZIP file and start with README.md. Version 1.2.0 adds session identifiers, a current cross-check, operating-condition control analyses, a three-way split comparison, per-block spectra and a thrust-loss table.
title: UAV Propulsion Endurance Dataset: Vibration, Current, Temperature and Thrust Measurements of a Small Multirotor Propulsion System

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Partial Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. As a result, some sites have WAV files with 0 bytes of data or timestamps outside the range of probable recording times. Procedures used by the Eclipse Soundscapes team to process audio data for its purposes are outlined in the Data Management reports located in the Eclipse Soundscapes Zenodo community. Data with 0 bytes of data were included for completeness. When possible, all site-specific files, including the audio files, are included in a single zip file for ease of download. If a single zip file upload was not possible due to upload or bandwidth limitations, audio files are included in multiple zip files based on the day of the observation. summary: Version 1.14.1 (2026-11-15) fits the height curve and the height increment equation jointly, so that they share one site-dependent asymptote (22.5 m at the median site of natural stands, 95% interval 21.2 to 24.1 m), and adds a two-stage ingrowth rate for natural stands as a scenario assumption, with their scripts, logs and the rules written before each test, in final_equations_20261115.zip , and supplement v128. The maximum stand density, crown base, diameter increment and mortality equations of version 1.14.0 are unchanged; projected height and assumed volume changed, and natural-stand projections changed through ingrowth. Version 1.14.0 (2026-11-14) replaces the height increment rule with a fitted height increment equation (the rule is kept as the fallback) and adds a crown base equation, a comparison with stand-level mortality forms (none adopted), and two long-term assessment metrics, with their scripts, logs and the rules written before fitting, in final_equations_20261114.zip , and supplement v127. The height, maximum stand density, diameter increment and mortality equations of version 1.13.1 are unchanged; projected height and assumed volume changed. Version 1.13.1 (2026-11-13) adds five checks of the relative-density system (benchmark with every equation refitted without the plot's installation fold, joint bootstrap of installations, the mortality equation under three death rules, benchmark after thinning, and equation S1 without the 53 Kap plots) with their scripts, logs and the inputs the scripts read, in final_equations_20261113.zip , and supplement v125. The equations and coefficients of version 1.13.0 are unchanged. Version 1.13.0 (11 November 2026) adds an annual individual-tree growth and mortality system for Acacia koa A. Gray ( koa_step_rdbyi.R and koa_rdbyi_equations.csv , both inside final_equations_20261111.zip ) that supersedes the v105final engine. An audit found that the v105final engine applies calibration multipliers, a height blend and a self-thinning step that the earlier supplement does not describe; see README.md. The new system applies the fitted equations as estimated. Diameter increment and mortality depend on relative density, the stand density index of live koa over a maximum that is predicted from the Biomass Yield Index and origin or supplied by the user. Mortality intervals that end in or span a thinning removal year of a PSP installation are censored, because the PSP database records thinned stems as dead. The rule written before the test did not prefer a maximum that varies with the Biomass Yield Index over a single value; it was adopted for consistency between fitting and use, and the README reports every test, including those that fail. No volume equation is fitted and carbon is not computed. The supplement PDF in this version is supplement v124, which describes this system. All other files are unchanged. Version 1.12.2 (7 November 2026) replaces koa_supplemental.pdf with supplement v123, the supplement submitted with the manuscript to Forest Ecosystems (reporting corrections only). The engine, parameters, frames and numbers are unchanged; see README.md. Version 1.12.1 (6 November 2026) adds koa_frames.sqlite , the stand, plot and tree frames of 1.12.0 as one SQLite database (320, 768 and 16,914 rows; md5-checked against this record), and build_sqlite_v2.py , its builder. On 7 November 2026 koa_supplemental.pdf was replaced with supplement v120, the supplement of the manuscript as submitted to Forest Ecosystems (reporting corrections only); the engine, parameters, frames and computed outputs are those of 1.12.0. summary: Here are our trained ARPA format 4-gram language models. We evaluated each model by computing the average per-word perplexity on 36.6K words of conversational style text. Name                Size      Perplexity Tiny 25MB 90.1 Small 110MB 73.7 Medium 205MB 69.2 Large 662MB 63.3 Huge 4.9GB 59.1 The test set consisted of 4,567 sentences (36.6K words, 161K characters). The test set was a combination of: COMM - Sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (2.1K words). COMM2 - Crowdsourced sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (13K words). See our ASSETS 2013 paper . Specialists - Phrases suggested by AAC specialists. Taken from University of Nebraska-Lincoln from web pages that are no longer available (4.2K words). Enron mobile - Messages written by Enron employees on Blackberry mobile devices (18K words). The test set was in lowercase and included limited punctuation (apostrophes, commas, periods, exclamation points, and question marks). We excluded the sentence end word from our perplexity calculations. This was necessary since the models were trained only on sentences ending in a period, exclamation point, or question mark. But some test sentences do not have end-of-sentence punctuation, this led to the sentence end word being very improbable. summary: Sweet proteins — brazzein (54 aa), monellin (single-chain MNEI, 95 aa), and thaumatin I (207 aa) — elicit intense sweetness at the human TAS1R2/TAS1R3 heterodimeric receptor at concentrations orders of magnitude lower, by weight, than sucrose. Their utility in food and ingredient applications is constrained by thermolability (monellin), limited yield in plant expression hosts (brazzein), and receptor-binding geometry that makes rational mutagenesis difficult. We apply inverse folding with ESM-IF1 and ProteinMPNN to redesign all three sweet proteins under structural constraints that pin the established sweetness-contact residues and the disulfide geometry, while sampling the remaining sequence space for predicted thermostability and expression-host compatibility. For each protein, we generate 500 candidate sequences per method (1,000 per protein, 3,000 total), score each with ESM2 log-likelihood ratio and in-silico thermostability predictors, and report the top-20 designs per protein alongside matched random controls (sequences that do not pin the contact residues) to establish the baseline distribution. All designs are computational; no wet-lab validation was performed. Covered by U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. [P4 APPLICATION NUMBER]. Platform: platform.scovillesplice.farm The methods and constructs described herein are the subject of U.S. Provisional Patent Application Nos. 64/172,827 (filed October 9, 2026), 64/188,197 (filed October 30, 2026), 64/192,062 (filed November 5, 2026), and 64/199,105 (filed November 15, 2026).

Their utility in food and ingredient applications is constrained by thermolability (monellin), limited yield in plant expression hosts (brazzein), and receptor-binding geometry that makes rational mutagenesis difficult. We apply inverse folding with ESM-IF1 and ProteinMPNN to redesign all three sweet proteins under structural constraints that pin the established sweetness-contact residues and the disulfide geometry, while sampling the remaining sequence space for predicted thermostability and expression-host compatibility. For each protein, we generate 500 candidate sequences per method (1,000 per protein, 3,000 total), score each with ESM2 log-likelihood ratio and in-silico thermostability predictors, and report the top-20 designs per protein alongside matched random controls (sequences that do not pin the contact residues) to establish the baseline distribution. All designs are computational; no wet-lab validation was performed. Covered by U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. [P4 APPLICATION NUMBER]. Platform: platform.scovillesplice.farm The methods and constructs described herein are the subject of U.S. Provisional Patent Application Nos. 64/172,827 (filed October 9, 2026), 64/188,197 (filed October 30, 2026), 64/192,062 (filed November 5, 2026), and 64/199,105 (filed November 15, 2026).

summary: This paper develops a mathematical framework for Quantum Information Holography (QIH), examining how nonlocal quantum information, phase relationships, interference, and holographic encoding can be represented through a unified information-processing architecture. The framework establishes formal relationships between quantum state vectors, angular frequency, the sum over histories, boundary encoding, and geodesic information addressing. It derives conditions for reversible reconstruction, matched quantum readout, and the preservation of information through successive phase-dependent transformations. The analysis further examines connections to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, relational geometry, quantum measurement, and the emergence of spacetime structure. It extends this framework to investigate the proposed role of biological information processing in the reconstruction of conscious experience. Mathematical definitions, conditional theorems, and explicit derivations distinguish established quantum-information results from the additional physical hypotheses concerning gravitation and consciousness, providing a foundation for further theoretical development and experimental investigation.
title: The Quantum Internet of Consciousness: The Universe Has an Address
