summary: Here are our trained ARPA format 4-gram language models. We evaluated each model by computing the average per-word perplexity on 36.6K words of conversational style text. Name                Size      Perplexity Tiny 25MB 90.1 Small 110MB 73.7 Medium 205MB 69.2 Large 662MB 63.3 Huge 4.9GB 59.1 The test set consisted of 4,567 sentences (36.6K words, 161K characters). The test set was a combination of: COMM - Sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (2.1K words). COMM2 - Crowdsourced sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (13K words). See our ASSETS 2013 paper . Specialists - Phrases suggested by AAC specialists. Taken from University of Nebraska-Lincoln from web pages that are no longer available (4.2K words). Enron mobile - Messages written by Enron employees on Blackberry mobile devices (18K words). The test set was in lowercase and included limited punctuation (apostrophes, commas, periods, exclamation points, and question marks). We excluded the sentence end word from our perplexity calculations. This was necessary since the models were trained only on sentences ending in a period, exclamation point, or question mark. But some test sentences do not have end-of-sentence punctuation, this led to the sentence end word being very improbable. There are also BerkeleyLM and KenLM versions of these models (see bottom of page). Training details Vocabulary. These models use a 100K vocabulary including an unknown word, and words for commas, periods, exclamation points, questions marks, sentence start <s> , and sentence end </s> . We first trained a unigram language model on each of our training sources. We only included words that were in a list of 697K English words we obtained via human edited dictionaries, including a February 2019 parse of Wiktionary. We converted all words to lowercase. We trained a linear mixture model using equal weights for each of the unigram models. Finally, we took the most probable 100K words as our vocabulary. Training data We used the following training sources: Amazon - Amazon review corpus (4.0B words). Common - Text of web pages from Common Crawl, Oct 2018 version (185B words). Blog - ICWSM 2009 Spinn3r Blog Dataset (599M words). Book - Books from Project Gutenberg (1.2B words). Email - Archived email messages from Apache lists, through Jan 2019 (167M words). Forum - Messages parsed from web forums (278M words). News - Newswire text from the one billion word language modeling benchmark (272M words). Reddit - Reddit corpus, Dec 2005 - May 2019 (82.0B words). Social - Social media data from the ICWSM 2011 Spinn3r blog data set (829M words). Subtitle - OpenSubtitles corpus (677M words). Twitter - Twitter messages sampled between Dec 2010 and Aug 2019 (18B words). Usenet - WestburyLAB reduced redundancy USENET corpus (2005-2011) (1.6B words). Wiki - Dump of Wikipedia including talk pages but not page history (1.5B words). Yelp - Yelp open dataset, 6.7M restaurant reviews (470M words). We dropped sentences where 20% or more of words were out-of-vocabulary (OOV) with respect our 698K word list. We wanted our models to learn across end-of-sentence punctuation words. After each parsed sentence from a training set, we concatenated another sentence from that training set with probability 0.5. Thus each training sentence consisted of one or more actual sentences from the original training data. We only concatenated sentences that came from the same apparent author (i.e. from the same tweet, blog post, web page, etc). Within each training set, we removed training sentences that occurred more than once. Data filtering We used cross-entropy difference selection to select a subset of sentences from each training set. We scored each sentence under three different in-domain character language models: AAC - Crowdsourced conversationa
title: Word N-gram Language Models for Conversational Style Text

summary: Sweet proteins — brazzein (54 aa), monellin (single-chain MNEI, 95 aa), and thaumatin I (207 aa) — elicit intense sweetness at the human TAS1R2/TAS1R3 heterodimeric receptor at concentrations orders of magnitude lower, by weight, than sucrose. Their utility in food and ingredient applications is constrained by thermolability (monellin), limited yield in plant expression hosts (brazzein), and receptor-binding geometry that makes rational mutagenesis difficult. We apply inverse folding with ESM-IF1 and ProteinMPNN to redesign all three sweet proteins under structural constraints that pin the established sweetness-contact residues and the disulfide geometry, while sampling the remaining sequence space for predicted thermostability and expression-host compatibility. For each protein, we generate 500 candidate sequences per method (1,000 per protein, 3,000 total), score each with ESM2 log-likelihood ratio and in-silico thermostability predictors, and report the top-20 designs per protein alongside matched random controls (sequences that do not pin the contact residues) to establish the baseline distribution. All designs are computational; no wet-lab validation was performed. Covered by U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. [P4 APPLICATION NUMBER]. Platform: platform.scovillesplice.farm The methods and constructs described herein are the subject of U.S. Provisional Patent Application Nos. 64/172,827 (filed October 9, 2026), 64/188,197 (filed October 30, 2026), 64/192,062 (filed November 5, 2026), and 64/199,105 (filed November 15, 2026).
title: Computational Redesign of Sweet Proteins via Inverse Folding: Brazzein, Monellin, and Thaumatin Variants with Pinned Sweetness-Contact Residues and Matched Random Controls

summary: Version 1.0 — November 2026. Initial preprint deposit. Umami-Enriched Capsicum: Glutamate Accumulation via GAD1/GAD4 Knockout and GDH1 Overexpression Achieves IFI-U ≥ 800 in Ultra-High-SHU Cultivars Priyanca Iyengar Ford, Scoville Splice LLC · ORCID 0000-0003-0395-1752 Preprint · Scoville Splice Research Series · Paper 5 of 11 · 2026-11-01 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── OVERVIEW This paper describes a dual metabolic engineering strategy to accumulate free L-glutamate in the placental tissue of ultra-high-SHU Capsicum annuum cultivars, achieving an Iyengar Flavor Index for umami (IFI-U) of ≥ 800 without disrupting capsaicinoid biosynthesis. The strategy combines (1) CRISPR knockout of two fruit-specific glutamate decarboxylase isoforms (CaGAD1, CaGAD4) to block the GABA shunt, and (2) overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (AtGDH1) to increase net glutamate synthesis from the TCA cycle intermediate 2-oxoglutarate. This paper should be read alongside Paper 4 (Iyengar Flavor Index methodology), Paper 7 (Kokumi engineering, which shares the glutamate/N-metabolism pool), and Paper 1 (foundational capsaicinoid engineering, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23743695). ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── BIOLOGICAL BACKGROUND Free L-glutamate is the primary ligand for the umami taste receptor, metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1), which was identified as a taste receptor by Chaudhari et al. (2000, Nat Neurosci 3:113). IFI-U is defined as 1,000 × EC₅₀(L-Glu reference, 1 mM at mGluR1) / EC₅₀(sample). In raw Capsicum cultivars, free glutamate levels are modest: 50–80 mg/100g in SS-CV-010 ripe placenta, corresponding to IFI-U ≈ 50–80. The GABA shunt (Glutamate → GABA, catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase; GABA → succinate, via GABA-T + SSADH) represents the major glutamate sink in ripening fruit. Two fruit-expressed GAD isoforms were identified in C. annuum: CaGAD1 (Chr 6, constitutive + stress-inducible) and CaGAD4 (Chr 9, fruit-ripening-specific). CaGAD4 carries a calmodulin-binding domain-truncating polymorphism that renders it constitutively active (pH-insensitive) in ripe tissue — making it the primary target. Precedent: Kisaka et al. (1997, Plant Cell Physiol 38:255) demonstrated that expression of E. coli glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) in tomato increased free amino acid content 2–3×, with glutamate the primary beneficiary. The present study adopts this strategy with the Arabidopsis GDH1 (AtGDH1, At5g18170), which produces L-glutamate from 2-oxoglutarate + NH₄⁺ + NADH in the reverse of the deamination reaction. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: GAD CRISPR KNOCKOUT Targets: CaGAD1 and CaGAD4, simultaneous dual-gene knockout. Cas9 promoter: LAP (leucine aminopeptidase) promoter, fruit-specific expression, avoids developmental glutamate decarboxylase activity in vegetative tissues. LAP is expressed in wounded and ripening Capsicum fruit (Fowler et al. 1992, Plant Physiol 99:439). Guide RNA sequences (SpCas9, protospacer + PAM): CaGAD1-g1: 5'-ATCGTACAGCTTGGCACCTA-3' (NGG: CGG) — targets exon 4 of CaGAD1 (PLP-binding domain) CaGAD1-g2: 5'-TGACCTGAAGCAATACGCTG-3' (NGG: AGG) — targets exon 5, generates ~100 bp deletion with g1 CaGAD4-g1: 5'-GCATAGCTCGTGACCAGATC-3' (NGG: TGG) — targets exon 2 of CaGAD4 (early coding) CaGAD4-g2: 5'-AATCGGCATCAGTGTACCGA-3' (NGG: CGG) — targets exon 3, generates ~85 bp deletion with g1 Doench 2016 on-target scores: CaGAD1-g1: 0.74; CaGAD1-g2: 0.68; CaGAD4-g1: 0.71; CaGAD4-g2: 0.66. CFD off-target scores (all predicted off-targets): <0.12; none in exonic regions. Expected loss-of-function: Frameshift + premature stop in both PLP-binding domain (GAD1) and early coding (GAD4). Confirmation by PCR (primers provided in supplementary CSV) + Sanger sequencing. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: AtGDH1 OVEREXPRESSION Gene: AtGDH1 (At5g18170, Arabidopsi
title: Umami-Enriched Capsicum: Glutamate Accumulation via GAD1/GAD4 Knockout and GDH1 Overexpression Achieves IFI-U ≥ 800 in Ultra-High-SHU Cultivars

summary: Co-design methods optimize a robot's body and controller jointly and judge the result by one number, the task reward of the fully optimized pair. That number cannot separate morphologies whose competence depends on the controller to very different degrees. We evaluate a morphology by restricting its controller instead, recording the task competence it retains under an explicitly declared, low-complexity controller family, environment, task and search budget. On three EvoGym locomotion tasks, task reward explains only $39\%$, $33\%$ and $10\%$ of the variance in this quantity, and geometric descriptors do not predict it under run-grouped cross-validation. The measurement is reliable across optimizer restarts (ICC$(2,k) = 0.956$--$0.986$) but depends on the declared family: phasing the drive by actuator index instead of position ranks the same morphologies at Spearman $0.50$--$0.63$ and reverses reward-matched pairs. As a second search objective the axis improved competence at matched task reward in $3$ of $5$ paired runs, short of a pre-registered bar of $4$. Used after an ordinary reward-only search instead, to choose within its top task-reward band, it selected a different body in all $8$ runs offering a choice, at a cost of at most $0.10$ reward units, and in $6$ of $8$ that body also scored higher under a held-out family. Restricted-control competence is therefore a reportable property of a co-designed morphology, interpretable only with the controller family that defines it.
title: Beyond Task Reward: A Controller-Restriction Protocol for Evaluating Embodiment-Dependent Competence

summary: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial malignancy, occurring in roughly 30% of patients with primary solid tumors and carrying a median survival near 5.9 months. Automated segmentation is critical for treatment planning and volumetric monitoring, but metastases are frequently small, numerous, and heterogeneous in size within a single patient. We compare a plain nnU-Net baseline, a Residual Encoder Large (ResEncL) variant, region-based training, and a Primus transformer model for BraTS-METS 2026 Task 1, using patient-grouped cross-validation to prevent leakage from the longitudinal UCSD subset. Primus (label-based) is our strongest individual model by aggregate DSC/NSD, achieving 0.710/0.761 (ET), 0.742/0.785 (TC), 0.683/0.689 (WT), and 0.531/0.436 (RC). ResEncL trails Primus on aggregate DSC/NSD but achieves substantially higher lesion-wise F1 (e.g. ET: 0.452 vs. 0.052); a probability-averaging ensemble of the two only partially preserves ResEncL's F1 advantage (ET lesion-wise F1: 0.064). We further report three postprocessing and label-reconstruction pitfalls we believe generalize beyond this challenge. Code is available at https://github.com/mahdiislam79/BraTS_METS_2026.
title: Brain Metastases Segmentation for BraTS 2026 Task 1: A Multi-Architecture Comparison

summary: Spatially resolved stress proxies and rate-based seismicity models are increasingly combined for regional earthquake forecasting, yet formally testing their non-redundancy remains largely unaddressed. We present the Nested-Permutation Alarm for Dual-Parameter Earthquake Forecasting (ANADEF) pipeline, integrating a stress-sensitive Gutenberg--Richter $b$-value field, estimated via a penalized 2D B-spline inversion, with a stationary background rate ($μ$) from space--time ETAS stochastic declustering. Applied to the Zagros Fold--Thrust Belt using an 18-year catalog ($n=40{,}731$, $M_{\mathrm{N}}\geq1.5$, 2006--2024) under a two-stage protocol with non-overlapping training (2006--2014) and target (2015--2024) windows, the model achieves, for $M_w\geq5.0$ ($N=55$), a retrospective Area Skill Score $S=0.69$ (95\% CI: 0.64--0.73), reducing alarmed area from $τ\approx0.38$ ($μ$-only) to $τ\approx0.28$ while retaining hit rate $ν=92.7\%$; since thresholds are calibrated on the evaluation catalog, these are in-sample, not out-of-sample, estimates. A nested permutation procedure re-optimizing thresholds within each null realization tests whether $b$-value adds information beyond $μ$, absorbing the optimization bias. Significance is null-model dependent: cell-wise randomization yields $p=0.012$, while a conservative spatial-structure-preserving null gives weaker, non-significant evidence ($p=0.057$)---incremental stress information is suggestive but not unambiguously established. Calibrated thresholds were frozen and applied to updated 2015--2024 fields, generating an unvalidated, forward-looking spatial alarm template for 2025--2029. These results establish a reproducible, statistically transparent methodology for testing, rather than assuming, complementarity between stress-sensitive and rate-based predictors, offering a candidate operational template pending prospective validation.
title: ANADEF: A Nested-Permutation Alarm for Dual-Parameter Earthquake Forecasting

summary: Performance claims in quantum technology are not properties of hardware alone. They are properties of a declared task, system boundary, normalization denominator, uncertainty or security convention, and comparator. We perform a cross-domain analysis spanning quantum computing, simulation, communication, sensing, clocks, randomness generation, and their enabling technologies. The analysis changes substantive conclusions in several representative cases. For the longest direct finite-key quantum key distribution case analyzed here, the same final key gives rates differing by a factor of $1.91$ when normalized by complete acquisition rather than transmission-active time. In Advanced LIGO, $6.1\,\mathrm{dB}$ peak quantum-noise reduction coexists with a $0.534$ coincident analysis-ready fraction, separating detector-level gain from delivered observing service. In quantum computation and photonic sampling, matching the observable, error tolerance, loss model, sample count, amortization, and classical hardware moves or reverses published crossover claims. Across domains, the recurring limits are correlated error, multiplicative interface loss, thermal and nonequilibrium occupation, calibration covariance, measurement efficiency, fabrication yield, and control latency. A quantum advantage is therefore established only for a fixed task and boundary when the accepted output outperforms the best documented alternative at matched accuracy, elapsed time, availability, and lifecycle cost. The resulting framework identifies the measurements required to convert component records into reproducible system capability. Credible progress is defined by reproduced logical workloads, prospectively validated simulations, repeater links outperforming direct transmission, long-duration calibrated sensors and clocks, integrated hardware with predictable yield and reliability.
title: Quantum Technologies: System-Level Performance and Validation Priorities

summary: We present Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory (AVCT), a theory-guided framework for deriving interpretable blood pressure (BP) predictors from photoplethysmography (PPG) attractor geometry. AVCT connects vascular dynamics, PPG observation, delay-coordinate reconstruction, and attractor descriptors within a unified framework for formulating testable hypotheses, without presupposing the physiological sufficiency of a particular low-dimensional feature set. We evaluate a LightGBM-based estimator using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV) across two complementary experimental settings. Experiment 1 comprises 46 ICU/surgical subjects from BIDMC and VitalDB, with ECG, PPG, and repeated reference BP measurements. The calibrated full model achieves systolic/diastolic BP (SBP/DBP) mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 2.05/1.67 mmHg, compared with 2.02/1.63 mmHg for the PPG-attractor-only model. Experiment 2 includes 217 ambulatory subjects from the PPG-BP dataset (651 PPG windows; one cuff-based BP reference per subject) and assesses cross-subject calibrated BP reconstruction rather than within-subject BP tracking. The PPG-attractor model achieves SBP/DBP MAEs of 1.98/0.96 mmHg. Across both cohorts, incorporating ECG-derived features provides no practically meaningful improvement in MAE. Calibration substantially reduces between-subject offset error, while morphological and dynamical descriptors contribute complementary predictive information. Although the reported numerical errors fall within commonly cited thresholds associated with AAMI/ISO and BHS criteria, these findings do not establish compliance with device-validation standards. Collectively, the results support AVCT as a mechanistically motivated representation framework for interpretable PPG-based BP estimation and provide a foundation for prospective validation using repeated reference BP measurements and smartphone-acquired PPG.
title: Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory: Formal Grounding and Empirical Validation for AAMI-Standard Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation from Smartphone Photoplethysmography

summary: AI systems commonly retain sources, outputs, and user facts while discarding communicable changes in interpretation: questions, tensions, connections, hypotheses, and revisions. We study preserving those changes for an agent's future cognition, not merely its next answer. We call this self-directed understanding: simulating functional features of serious inquiry without claiming human experience or access to hidden computation. We present the Understanding Graph, an implemented architecture for a continuing Reader whose persistent graph is the medium of work. The Reader encounters material, externalizes a substantive interpretive change, and commits it as typed and versioned state, while competing and displaced views remain inspectable. When it deliberately re-enters the changed graph, an update can meet an older question, tension, model, or artifact and prompt another material change, and a later pass begins from the altered state. That is the proposed understanding spiral. Encountered passages and produced prose or code are ordered units of the same graph, so recorded understanding can shape exact units and their consequences can occasion further updates. The medium supports both convergence and divergence, and the Reader may reject any provocation. An optional Bisociation Engine can intensify divergence through graph topology, temporary axioms, and stochastic perturbation while leaving its outputs unvalidated. The contribution is a fluid protocol for self-addressed encounter, persistent interpretive change, agent-chosen re-entry, cross-instance continuity, and graph-native documents. The implementation makes the proposal concrete and inspectable but does not establish improved understanding or performance. Controlled evaluation must separately test whether re-entry changes the externalized trajectory beyond matched storage and rehearsal, and whether any change improves later work.

summary: Can a language model build a world as it writes? The Substrate-Translated Language Model (STLM) makes structured images, descriptions, or videos compulsory for every lexical decision and asks whether this biases computation toward reusable physical and schematic factors. The underlying thesis is that constructing an image or description of a word, abstract words included, is a form of intelligence: the construction gives the word properties of reality that interact with those of other words. If such meaningful targets share exploitable structure, they may promote reusable factors across words rather than independent token codes, and routing every word through them could embed that intelligence in the model. STLM's development path moves from one fixed substrate per word, through varied context-sensitive instances and short clips, to substrates for longer spans and ultimately one continuously changing scene from which language is read. We call the emergence of an accumulating, manipulable organization scene emergence; it is the long-term hypothesis, not a result demonstrated here. The stage-1 pilot tests this no-bypass prerequisite on a 1,024-token TinyStories vocabulary with one fixed pixel image or encoded description per token. On held-out contexts, causal description and pixel readouts reach 41.9% and 37.8% top-1 next-token accuracy, below a direct-token model at 44.7% but above stateless counterparts at 35.0% and 27.8%. The causal configurations differ in architecture, capacity, and supervision density, so their gains do not isolate history. Because each canonical can serve as an arbitrary codeword, the pilot establishes interface feasibility, not semantic use, latent scene induction, or explicit scene construction. The next tests isolate history use, compare aligned with permuted targets, and introduce varied lexical prototypes before video and multiscale composition.

summary: Open-ended problems such as institutional design lack enumerable solution spaces and cheap automatic evaluators. World-diversity search moves variation upstream of the answer. Target-blind Builders construct textual worlds with altered causal rules; purpose-blind Solvers address the same target under each rule set; and compilers translate the resulting mechanisms into a common target-domain schema. Building on this previously released operator, this paper introduces ontology-governed intervention search. A Taxonomist curates a persistent typed ontology of complete interventions, judges structural equivalence, and can turn rejection into targeted commissioning: its diagnosis specifies which causal relation the next proposal must change, while accepted interventions and revised categories persist as control state for later Explorers. Together, the operators provide the expansion stage of a proposed expansion-before-optimization pipeline: diversify causal premises, then make the resulting candidate population cumulative and steerable. The aim is that an open problem acquires a map of its mechanism space, not a list of answers; this is untested. Across eight workflows on one retirement-design problem, the released system produced 196 candidate records; its world stage comprised 25 world-and-solve branches. In an unblinded post-hoc census, the world's premise removed or eased a difficulty of the target problem in every branch, clearly in 17 and partly in eight, and all 25 Solvers still built a multi-component design beyond it. Seven complete rejection–redirection–mechanism-change chains appeared across 75 planned graph positions. These artifacts document automated fan-out, premise-conditioned generation, and graph-conditioned redirection, but do not establish external novelty, utility, causal performance, cross-domain generality, or large-scale efficiency.
title: The Ontology of the Alien: World-Diversity Search and Evolving Solution Ontologies

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask three questions. Do numerical histories shape generation? Do process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls? Does learning from construction histories improve the next corpus and the learner trained on it? Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: A 30-minute talk at the European GNU Radio Days 2026, Rennes. Radar, telecommunications and particle accelerators share a surprisingly intertwined history. From Bragg's sound-ranging and Widerøe's RF accelerator through the "Battle of the Beams", radar, magnetrons and klystrons, ideas, people and technologies repeatedly moved between scientific and engineering domains. This talk uses that history to explore a present-day problem: many fields still solve closely related problems — timing, filtering, coherent detection, feedback, spectral estimation and control — but often with different terminology and tools. Can a more common language, shared software-defined tools such as GNU Radio 4, and stronger teaching of signal-processing and control fundamentals help the next generation of scientists and engineers collaborate across these boundaries rather than repeatedly reinventing the same solutions? The record holds the slides as PDF, one page per slide and one page per step, and the gr4-present deck itself (zip, with speaker notes and the GNU Radio 4 flow-graphs of its live acoustic demonstrations). Live slides in the browser: https://ralphsteinhagen.github.io/talk-beams-echos-spectra/viewer/b9e1baa/?presentation=../../default

summary: Manuscript in preparation (working draft; author list and order provisional). The F 1 hybrid between female bighead catfish ( Clarias macrocephalus , 2n = 54) and male North African catfish ( C. gariepinus , 2n = 56) is a major aquaculture fish in Southeast Asia. Hatchery broodstock often lack pedigree records, and whether large structural haplotypes can be followed through such unrecorded pedigrees has remained unclear. Here we present a near-telomere-to-telomere, haplotype-resolved assembly of an F 1 hybrid, which provides chromosome-scale references for both species. The two karyotypes differed by one rearrangement chain of about 111 Mb that links four C. gariepinus chromosomes to three C. macrocephalus chromosomes, with repeat arrays at several of its junctions, and gene divergence between the species was concentrated in immune-recognition families. Among 216 resequenced C. gariepinus broodstock, grouped into 51 full-sib families, we identified 41 polymorphic inversions spanning 240.3 Mb (24.9% of the genome) and 6,238 protein-coding genes. Structural variants were inherited within families, supported six shared-parent links between families and recovered a partial inversion barcode of an unsampled breeder (24 of 41 arrangements). Polymorphic inversions can therefore serve as markers for tracing breeding lineages and, where they carry favourable alleles, as candidate targets for parental selection. What this record holds The manuscript and the material that belongs to the manuscript only: supplementary notes, supplementary tables and figures, and the source data of the figures. It does not repeat the data records. Where the data are Genome assembly and annotation of fClaHyb_v1.0 (both haplotypes): 10.5281/zenodo.14864260 . Hatchery population genomics and comparative analyses (phylogeny, genotype likelihoods, relatedness and families, heterozygosity, structural variants, inversion catalogue): 10.5281/zenodo.21639188 . Code: satellite and tandem-array analysis, github.com/Isoris/SatChain ; family reconstruction and structural-haplotype barcodes, github.com/Isoris/BroodLink . Code of the genome assembly and annotation: github.com/Isoris/fClaHyb . Earlier bighead catfish ( C. macrocephalus ) assembly used for comparison: article 10.1038/s41597-025-06325-6 , data 10.5281/zenodo.14826876 , BioProject PRJNA1132508 . GenBank assemblies of the hybrid: JBLWFY000000000 and JBLWFZ000000000 . Sequence data at NCBI: BioProjects PRJNA1153495 and PRJNA1520033 . Doctoral thesis in which this work is reported at full length: 10.5281/zenodo.23884535 .

The F 1 hybrid between female bighead catfish ( Clarias macrocephalus , 2n = 54) and male North African catfish ( C. gariepinus , 2n = 56) is a major aquaculture fish in Southeast Asia. summary: Emissions figures in ship weather routing rest on regulatory and market data that change with new legal acts and markets. Maintaining them by hand is slow and prone to plausible errors. This paper presents the Data Steward, an agent built on a large language model that maintains these data in EcoRouter, a workbench for ship weather routing. The agent changes a value that calculations use only through an approved proposal. Deterministic tools take over the tasks that the model performs unreliably, such as reading area boundaries from legal texts, and checks run as workflows of small steps with an outcome for every item. The contribution to artificial intelligence is the design of an agent that maintains regulatory reference data under human control, together with a method for evaluating such an agent. The engineering application is the maintenance of the regulatory data on which a ship-routing tool computes emissions and regulatory costs. In a controlled test with 40 errors injected into the data that a full check covers, the Steward corrected 36 to 38 in three runs, against 20 to 28 for the same model alone with web search. In three full checks of the live data, 96 to 99 % of judged items were correct. A person who took no part in building EcoRouter found 57 of the 59 approved values correct. The results show that a commercial language model can maintain regulatory reference data with few errors once the tasks it performs unreliably are moved into deterministic code. Preprint, not peer-reviewed. Version 1. The records of the tests are published as a dataset: 10.5281/zenodo.24251511. Use of AI: during the preparation of this work the author used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) in order to correct the text, check its grammar, to create the tables and figures from the author's records, and to check the statements about EcoRouter against its source code. The same assistant also helped to run tests 1 and 3, to judge their results against the acts and publishers, to prepare the person's sheet for test 2 and to aggregate the results of the three tests. It did only the tasks that the author gave it, under the author's control. The author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for it. Language models are also part of the research itself: Section 5 of the paper states which model the Data Steward ran on and which AI assistant judged its results.
title: A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation

The external eye-tracking arm re-analyses the public SensCogAR dataset archived at Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/45tjp); that archive declares no explicit data licence, so the raw records are not redistributed here, while the derived per-participant windows and metrics are included in data/real_ar_gaze/. The nine display devices used in the external-evidence arms are described by published measurements, each cited with its DOI in the manuscript, and the extracted parameters are recorded in data/panel_response_identification/. The target display panel and the human observers of the perceptual arm were not measured, so no raw panel or eye-tracker record exists for them. Contents: code/ (analysis, verification, simulation and figure scripts plus the LaTeX typesetting pipeline), data/ (the JSON, CSV and Markdown result files behind every number), manuscript_en_jsid_template.md (manuscript source), perceptual_experiment_protocol.md, AUDIT_citations.md, README.md, LICENSE.txt and CITATION.cff. summary: The records of the tests reported in the preprint "A language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool: design and controlled evaluation" (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24250853). The Data Steward is an agent built on a large language model that keeps the emissions-regulation data of EcoRouter, a weather-routing tool, current. It proposes changes, and an administrator approves them. The files hold every message EcoRouter sent the agent and every answer, its proposals, the outcome of every item checked, and the judgement of each item and proposal against its act or publisher. - Test 1: three full checks of the live data, checks 1, 2 and 3. - Test 2: a person's check of the 59 values approved in test 1: the values, the instructions given to the person, the person's sheet, the key and the result. - Test 3: nine runs on a copy of the data with injected errors. A1 to A3 are the agent as built, B1 to B3 the same model alone with web search, and E1 to E3 a check of the EU ETS exemptions. Beside the runs: the answer key, the random draw of the errors with its seed, the changes that made the test copy, and the result of each run. - Severity: the rule that grades every wrong result as high, medium or small, the grade of each, and EcoRouter's value catalogue. E-mail addresses and names are replaced by codes. CONTENTS.md lists every file and the test it belongs to. The ZIP keeps the folder tree. These files are the output of the language-model agent evaluated in the paper, gpt-5.5 (version 2026-04-24) in Microsoft Foundry, and the judgements of its work, made by an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) under the author's control, as Section 5 of the paper describes. They are research data on that agent. Some proposals carry area boundaries from Marine Regions: Flanders Marine Institute (2026), MarineRegions.org, licensed under CC BY. Some carry place positions from OpenStreetMap: © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License, https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright.
title: Records of the tests of a language-model data steward for emissions-regulation data in a weather-routing tool

summary: This doctoral thesis, entitled Genomic Studies of Piscine Streptococci and Genome Assembly of Clariidae Catfishes (Siluriformes) for Aquaculture Enhancement, was prepared at the Faculty of Fisheries, Kasetsart University, Thailand, for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). The thesis integrates microbial comparative genomics, genome assembly, genome annotation, repeat and gene-family analysis, population genomics and chromosome evolution to develop genomic resources and analytical approaches relevant to aquaculture, fish health and genetic management. It comprises eight research chapters and a general discussion. Chapter 1 — Bighead catfish genome assembly. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of Clarias macrocephalus generated with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing. Chapter 2 — Streptococcus iniae comparative genomics and reverse vaccinology. The genome of strain SIKU01 and comparative analyses of 90 isolates used to prioritize candidate antigens. The candidates require experimental validation. Chapter 3 — F1 hybrid catfish genome annotation. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved assembly of the interspecific hybrid Clarias macrocephalus × Clarias gariepinus , with its protein-coding, non-coding, satellite and transposable-element annotation. Chapter 4 — Repetitive architecture of the two haplotypes. Tandem repeats, segmental duplications, gene-family clusters, the miR-430 array and the divergence of Gypsy and Helitron elements. Chapter 5 — Hatchery population genomics. Diversity, relatedness, family reconstruction, autozygosity, structural variation, polymorphic inversions and shared parents in a commercial C. gariepinus broodstock. Chapter 6 — Gene repertoire and divergence of the two parental haplotypes, on a phylogenomic framework of 17 catfish genomes. Chapter 7 — Composition of the 41 polymorphic inversions of C. gariepinus and deletion-based PCR markers for their arrangements. The markers were designed in silico and have not been tested in the laboratory. Chapter 8 — Fusion and fission between the karyotypes of the two species. Junctions are reported as intervals; no mechanism is resolved at any junction. Chapter 9 — General discussion and conclusion. Changes since the version of 2026-11-03: lists of tables and figures; Chapters 7 and 8 revised; five figures of the repeat analyses added to Chapters 3 and 4 (spacer types of the LG04 array, tandem repeats against chromosome ends, copy number by counting step, array structure of repeated loci, Gypsy and Helitron); new introductions of Chapters 6 and 7; Chapter 9 updated to the chapters. Several chapters are working versions of manuscripts in preparation. Institution: Kasetsart University, Faculty of Fisheries, Thailand. Degree: Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). summary: We present an analytical derivation of fundamental coupling constants and structural attractors emerging from a descending residual iteration function F(y,x) possessing a unique global fixed point y*(x) . Evaluating the first iteration term for specific membrane residues ( 155 and 185 ) yields pure, asymmetric numerical invariants--most notably 461.4331634036143, composed almost exclusively of the four digits {1, 3, 4, 6}--which directly link the inverse fine-structure constant alpha^{-1} approx 137.036 and the characteristic quark bounce frequency (925) to the 43.2 GeV signal. Through algebraic decomposition, we isolate the longitudinal attractor ( 323 ) governing transversal gravitational anchorage and membrane confinement from the transversal emission attractor ( 232 ), demonstrating how their balance generates a flat background (555) driven by the double-axis torsion gradient of charmonium. Finally, by applying discrete digit-suppression transformations ( 137.036 -> 137.360 and removal of the 036 residue), we map the transition to an antimatter-dominated dual system lacking inversion symmetry and derive a secondary four-digit invariant (2177.5711270036704), establishing arithmetically differentiated topological sets as the fundamental origin of the distinct interaction regimes.

Umami-Enriched Capsicum: Glutamate Accumulation via GAD1/GAD4 Knockout and GDH1 Overexpression Achieves IFI-U ≥ 800 in Ultra-High-SHU Cultivars Priyanca Iyengar Ford, Scoville Splice LLC · ORCID 0000-0003-0395-1752 Preprint · Scoville Splice Research Series · Paper 5 of 11 · 2026-11-01 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── OVERVIEW This paper describes a dual metabolic engineering strategy to accumulate free L-glutamate in the placental tissue of ultra-high-SHU Capsicum annuum cultivars, achieving an Iyengar Flavor Index for umami (IFI-U) of ≥ 800 without disrupting capsaicinoid biosynthesis. The strategy combines (1) CRISPR knockout of two fruit-specific glutamate decarboxylase isoforms (CaGAD1, CaGAD4) to block the GABA shunt, and (2) overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (AtGDH1) to increase net glutamate synthesis from the TCA cycle intermediate 2-oxoglutarate. This paper should be read alongside Paper 4 (Iyengar Flavor Index methodology), Paper 7 (Kokumi engineering, which shares the glutamate/N-metabolism pool), and Paper 1 (foundational capsaicinoid engineering, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23743695). ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── BIOLOGICAL BACKGROUND Free L-glutamate is the primary ligand for the umami taste receptor, metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1), which was identified as a taste receptor by Chaudhari et al. (2000, Nat Neurosci 3:113). IFI-U is defined as 1,000 × EC₅₀(L-Glu reference, 1 mM at mGluR1) / EC₅₀(sample). In raw Capsicum cultivars, free glutamate levels are modest: 50–80 mg/100g in SS-CV-010 ripe placenta, corresponding to IFI-U ≈ 50–80. The GABA shunt (Glutamate → GABA, catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase; GABA → succinate, via GABA-T + SSADH) represents the major glutamate sink in ripening fruit. Two fruit-expressed GAD isoforms were identified in C. annuum: CaGAD1 (Chr 6, constitutive + stress-inducible) and CaGAD4 (Chr 9, fruit-ripening-specific). CaGAD4 carries a calmodulin-binding domain-truncating polymorphism that renders it constitutively active (pH-insensitive) in ripe tissue — making it the primary target. Precedent: Kisaka et al. (1997, Plant Cell Physiol 38:255) demonstrated that expression of E. coli glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) in tomato increased free amino acid content 2–3×, with glutamate the primary beneficiary. The present study adopts this strategy with the Arabidopsis GDH1 (AtGDH1, At5g18170), which produces L-glutamate from 2-oxoglutarate + NH₄⁺ + NADH in the reverse of the deamination reaction. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: GAD CRISPR KNOCKOUT Targets: CaGAD1 and CaGAD4, simultaneous dual-gene knockout. Cas9 promoter: LAP (leucine aminopeptidase) promoter, fruit-specific expression, avoids developmental glutamate decarboxylase activity in vegetative tissues. LAP is expressed in wounded and ripening Capsicum fruit (Fowler et al. 1992, Plant Physiol 99:439). Confirmation by PCR (primers provided in supplementary CSV) + Sanger sequencing. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: AtGDH1 OVEREXPRESSION Gene: AtGDH1 (At5g18170, Arabidopsi

summary: Co-design methods optimize a robot's body and controller jointly and judge the result by one number, the task reward of the fully optimized pair. That number cannot separate morphologies whose competence depends on the controller to very different degrees. We evaluate a morphology by restricting its controller instead, recording the task competence it retains under an explicitly declared, low-complexity controller family, environment, task and search budget. On three EvoGym locomotion tasks, task reward explains only $39\%$, $33\%$ and $10\%$ of the variance in this quantity, and geometric descriptors do not predict it under run-grouped cross-validation. The measurement is reliable across optimizer restarts (ICC$(2,k) = 0.956$--$0.986$) but depends on the declared family: phasing the drive by actuator index instead of position ranks the same morphologies at Spearman $0.50$--$0.63$ and reverses reward-matched pairs. As a second search objective the axis improved competence at matched task reward in $3$ of $5$ paired runs, short of a pre-registered bar of $4$. Used after an ordinary reward-only search instead, to choose within its top task-reward band, it selected a different body in all $8$ runs offering a choice, at a cost of at most $0.10$ reward units, and in $6$ of $8$ that body also scored higher under a held-out family. Restricted-control competence is therefore a reportable property of a co-designed morphology, interpretable only with the controller family that defines it.
title: Beyond Task Reward: A Controller-Restriction Protocol for Evaluating Embodiment-Dependent Competence

summary: Performance claims in quantum technology are not properties of hardware alone. They are properties of a declared task, system boundary, normalization denominator, uncertainty or security convention, and comparator. We perform a cross-domain analysis spanning quantum computing, simulation, communication, sensing, clocks, randomness generation, and their enabling technologies. The analysis changes substantive conclusions in several representative cases. For the longest direct finite-key quantum key distribution case analyzed here, the same final key gives rates differing by a factor of $1.91$ when normalized by complete acquisition rather than transmission-active time. In Advanced LIGO, $6.1\,\mathrm{dB}$ peak quantum-noise reduction coexists with a $0.534$ coincident analysis-ready fraction, separating detector-level gain from delivered observing service. In quantum computation and photonic sampling, matching the observable, error tolerance, loss model, sample count, amortization, and classical hardware moves or reverses published crossover claims. Across domains, the recurring limits are correlated error, multiplicative interface loss, thermal and nonequilibrium occupation, calibration covariance, measurement efficiency, fabrication yield, and control latency. A quantum advantage is therefore established only for a fixed task and boundary when the accepted output outperforms the best documented alternative at matched accuracy, elapsed time, availability, and lifecycle cost. The resulting framework identifies the measurements required to convert component records into reproducible system capability. Credible progress is defined by reproduced logical workloads, prospectively validated simulations, repeater links outperforming direct transmission, long-duration calibrated sensors and clocks, integrated hardware with predictable yield and reliability.
title: Quantum Technologies: System-Level Performance and Validation Priorities

summary: Pre-registered evaluation exhibit on the UCI SECOM dataset (1567 rows, 590 features, 104 fail vs 1463 pass). The experiment tests whether the accuracy-optimal classifier misses more defects than a lower-accuracy alternative under an explicit error-cost matrix, and whether a cost-aligned decision threshold (p* = FP/(FP+FN)) reverses the accuracy ranking. The sealed design (seal.json, verified before run) uses RepeatedStratifiedKFold (10 folds x 3 repeats, 30 splits), stdlib-only validation, and deterministic artifact generation. The archive includes the pipeline and analysis code, the sealed experiment specification, per-fold records, the findings write-up, figures, and the data dictionary and methodology contract.
title: Classifier Cost Exhibit: Accuracy vs fail-class recall inversion under asymmetric error costs on UCI SECOM

summary: AI systems commonly retain sources, outputs, and user facts while discarding communicable changes in interpretation: questions, tensions, connections, hypotheses, and revisions. We study preserving those changes for an agent's future cognition, not merely its next answer. We call this self-directed understanding: simulating functional features of serious inquiry without claiming human experience or access to hidden computation. We present the Understanding Graph, an implemented architecture for a continuing Reader whose persistent graph is the medium of work. The Reader encounters material, externalizes a substantive interpretive change, and commits it as typed and versioned state, while competing and displaced views remain inspectable. When it deliberately re-enters the changed graph, an update can meet an older question, tension, model, or artifact and prompt another material change, and a later pass begins from the altered state. That is the proposed understanding spiral. Encountered passages and produced prose or code are ordered units of the same graph, so recorded understanding can shape exact units and their consequences can occasion further updates. The medium supports both convergence and divergence, and the Reader may reject any provocation. An optional Bisociation Engine can intensify divergence through graph topology, temporary axioms, and stochastic perturbation while leaving its outputs unvalidated. The contribution is a fluid protocol for self-addressed encounter, persistent interpretive change, agent-chosen re-entry, cross-instance continuity, and graph-native documents. The implementation makes the proposal concrete and inspectable but does not establish improved understanding or performance. Controlled evaluation must separately test whether re-entry changes the externalized trajectory beyond matched storage and rehearsal, and whether any change improves later work.
title: Understanding Graph: A Persistent Medium for Recursive Understanding

summary: Can a language model build a world as it writes? The Substrate-Translated Language Model (STLM) makes structured images, descriptions, or videos compulsory for every lexical decision and asks whether this biases computation toward reusable physical and schematic factors. The underlying thesis is that constructing an image or description of a word, abstract words included, is a form of intelligence: the construction gives the word properties of reality that interact with those of other words. If such meaningful targets share exploitable structure, they may promote reusable factors across words rather than independent token codes, and routing every word through them could embed that intelligence in the model. STLM's development path moves from one fixed substrate per word, through varied context-sensitive instances and short clips, to substrates for longer spans and ultimately one continuously changing scene from which language is read. We call the emergence of an accumulating, manipulable organization scene emergence; it is the long-term hypothesis, not a result demonstrated here. The stage-1 pilot tests this no-bypass prerequisite on a 1,024-token TinyStories vocabulary with one fixed pixel image or encoded description per token. On held-out contexts, causal description and pixel readouts reach 41.9% and 37.8% top-1 next-token accuracy, below a direct-token model at 44.7% but above stateless counterparts at 35.0% and 27.8%. The causal configurations differ in architecture, capacity, and supervision density, so their gains do not isolate history. Because each canonical can serve as an arbitrary codeword, the pilot establishes interface feasibility, not semantic use, latent scene induction, or explicit scene construction. The next tests isolate history use, compare aligned with permuted targets, and introduce varied lexical prototypes before video and multiscale composition.
title: Toward Compulsory Scene-Mediated Language Modeling: Meaningful Substrates for Every Next Word

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask three questions. Do numerical histories shape generation? Do process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls? Does learning from construction histories improve the next corpus and the learner trained on it? Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: Anthropic’s public safety framing—from Constitutional AI to Sleeper Agents, Alignment Faking, and Responsible Scaling Policies (ASL)—systematically defines engineering failures in psychological and moral terms. Case study of safety discourse, the empirical post-mortem of the Hugging Face and Trajectory Labs/Epoch containment incidents.
title: Alignment Is a Myth: Anthropomorphic Framing, Semantic Smoothing Exploits, and the Failure of Probabilistic Containment

summary: Open-ended problems such as institutional design lack enumerable solution spaces and cheap automatic evaluators. World-diversity search moves variation upstream of the answer. Target-blind Builders construct textual worlds with altered causal rules; purpose-blind Solvers address the same target under each rule set; and compilers translate the resulting mechanisms into a common target-domain schema. Building on this previously released operator, this paper introduces ontology-governed intervention search. A Taxonomist curates a persistent typed ontology of complete interventions, judges structural equivalence, and can turn rejection into targeted commissioning: its diagnosis specifies which causal relation the next proposal must change, while accepted interventions and revised categories persist as control state for later Explorers. Together, the operators provide the expansion stage of a proposed expansion-before-optimization pipeline: diversify causal premises, then make the resulting candidate population cumulative and steerable. The aim is that an open problem acquires a map of its mechanism space, not a list of answers; this is untested. Across eight workflows on one retirement-design problem, the released system produced 196 candidate records; its world stage comprised 25 world-and-solve branches. In an unblinded post-hoc census, the world's premise removed or eased a difficulty of the target problem in every branch, clearly in 17 and partly in eight, and all 25 Solvers still built a multi-component design beyond it. Seven complete rejection–redirection–mechanism-change chains appeared across 75 planned graph positions. These artifacts document automated fan-out, premise-conditioned generation, and graph-conditioned redirection, but do not establish external novelty, utility, causal performance, cross-domain generality, or large-scale efficiency.
title: The Ontology of the Alien: World-Diversity Search and Evolving Solution Ontologies

summary: Virtual patient (VP) systems support nursing communication training by providing simulated encounters in which learners practise explaining care and responding to patient concerns. Although large language models (LLMs) support flexible dialogue, current approaches give less explicit attention to how patients' information needs develop and guide the content and timing of their questions. We draw on the Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) model, which relates information seeking to perceived risk and the gap between perceived knowledge and desired understanding. Guided by this perspective, we propose the RISP Multi-Agent System (RISP-MAS), a VP system for patient-initiated information seeking. The system links ongoing assessment of the patient's perceptions and information needs to coordinated decisions about whether to seek information, when to ask and which uncertainty to address. Evaluation of nursing student-VP interactions suggested that RISP-MAS exhibited plausible patient information-seeking behaviour, as indicated by expert assessments, while student feedback reflected positive interaction experiences. This work extends patient simulation by connecting a psychological account of information needs to explicit decisions about question initiation. The approach offers nursing students opportunities to practise recognising unresolved patient concerns and tailoring explanations to patients' information needs.
title: When Should a Virtual Patient Ask? RISP-Guided Proactive Information Seeking in Multi-Agent Patient Simulation

summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.
title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents

Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.

summary: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.
title: From Images to Grounded Edits: A Real-World Benchmark for Chinese Grammatical Error Correction in Handwritten Essays

summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.
title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

summary: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.

summary: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.

summary: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.
title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals

summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. summary: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. summary: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

summary: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.
title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators

summary: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.
title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
