summary: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. summary: AI systems commonly retain sources, outputs, and user facts while discarding communicable changes in interpretation: questions, tensions, connections, hypotheses, and revisions. We study preserving those changes for an agent's future cognition, not merely its next answer. We call this self-directed understanding: simulating functional features of serious inquiry without claiming human experience or access to hidden computation. We present the Understanding Graph, an implemented architecture for a continuing Reader whose persistent graph is the medium of work. The Reader encounters material, externalizes a substantive interpretive change, and commits it as typed and versioned state, while competing and displaced views remain inspectable. When it deliberately re-enters the changed graph, an update can meet an older question, tension, model, or artifact and prompt another material change, and a later pass begins from the altered state. That is the proposed understanding spiral. Encountered passages and produced prose or code are ordered units of the same graph, so recorded understanding can shape exact units and their consequences can occasion further updates. The medium supports both convergence and divergence, and the Reader may reject any provocation. An optional Bisociation Engine can intensify divergence through graph topology, temporary axioms, and stochastic perturbation while leaving its outputs unvalidated. The contribution is a fluid protocol for self-addressed encounter, persistent interpretive change, agent-chosen re-entry, cross-instance continuity, and graph-native documents. The implementation makes the proposal concrete and inspectable but does not establish improved understanding or performance. Controlled evaluation must separately test whether re-entry changes the externalized trajectory beyond matched storage and rehearsal, and whether any change improves later work.
title: Understanding Graph: A Persistent Medium for Recursive Understanding

summary: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection

summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence" by Jingyang Li (School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, China). This deposit contains the analysis code, the result files behind every number reported in the manuscript, the figure sources and the executed forced-choice log. The external eye-tracking arm re-analyses the public SensCogAR dataset archived at Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/45tjp); that archive declares no explicit data licence, so the raw records are not redistributed here, while the derived per-participant windows and metrics are included in data/real_ar_gaze/. The nine display devices used in the external-evidence arms are described by published measurements, each cited with its DOI in the manuscript, and the extracted parameters are recorded in data/panel_response_identification/. The target display panel and the human observers of the perceptual arm were not measured, so no raw panel or eye-tracker record exists for them. Contents: code/ (analysis, verification, simulation and figure scripts plus the LaTeX typesetting pipeline), data/ (the JSON, CSV and Markdown result files behind every number), manuscript_en_jsid_template.md (manuscript source), perceptual_experiment_protocol.md, AUDIT_citations.md, README.md, LICENSE.txt and CITATION.cff. Reproducing the results: ``` export JSID_MD='manuscript_en_jsid_template.md' python code/verify_manuscript_numbers.py    # CHECKED 404 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_tables_6_9.py           # TABLES 6-9 CHECKED 252 / MISMATCH 0 python code/verify_data_provenance.py      # per-device DOI and tau audit python code/verify_figure_resolution.py    # 600 dpi plate check ``` Licence: data and documentation CC BY 4.0; code MIT. Please cite the article above; a CITATION.cff file is included in this deposit.
title: Data and code for: Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence

summary: A catalog of the many published versions of the human reference genome, each described as a recipe applied to the original deposited sequences and verified by rebuilding the published file. In addition to the catalog itself, refbook provides utilities to search, identify, compare, fetch, and reconstruct any sequence or edition. These are exposed as a Python library and command line tool with a Rust core, as well as a web application (WebAssembly and TypeScript).

summary: Frozen experiment source, protocols, processed evidence and portable analysis replays supporting Partial backpropagation for efficient neural network training and adaptation. The collection examines gradient omission, optimizer-state behavior and optimized execution across CNN training, ViT training and adaptation, and independent Oxford-IIIT Pet adaptation. Raw datasets, pretrained weights and model checkpoints are not bundled; full training replication requires the documented external prerequisites. This metadata compatibility revision leaves experimental code, protocols, evidence and scientific conclusions unchanged.

summary: Scripts, data, figure sources and manuscript sources that reproduce every numerical result of the article “Eigenstate-free spectral preprocessing for dense vibrational spectra” (Zhiqiang Huang, Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation, revised submission). The construction supplies three eigenstate-free quantities from matrix–vector products and resolvent evaluations alone — an interval state count, screening diagnostics for low-order resolvent approximations, and an overlap-spectrum (Gram) diagnostic of the trial space — and the deposit backs each of them with the script that produces the corresponding table or figure. New in this version (v1.2). (i) The revised manuscript and Supporting Information sources ( manuscript/MOLJCv2.tex , manuscript/MOLJCv2_SI.tex ) together with the two TikZ artwork sources (Fig. 1 anatomy and the TOC graphic). (ii) Energy-resolved counting on the five-mode model, the D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian and the calibrated H 2 O Hamiltonian ( rvA*.jl , rv_fig12.jl ). (iii) The force-field completeness audit: repeated-index cubic and quartic couplings ( rvB_repeated.jl ) and the occupation cutoff ( rvF_trunc.jl ). (iv) The screening-diagnostic utility scan with a thread-safe rerun whose per-broadening correlations are quoted in the paper ( rvC_screen.jl , rvC_screen_verify.jl ). (v) The overlap-spectrum chain: rank bound, cross-Krylov Gram estimator and its robustness, overcompleteness, eigenvalue-accuracy and row-sum range checks ( rvG_rank.jl , rvH*.jl , rvH2_overcomplete.jl , rvI_redundant.jl , rvK_eigcheck.jl , rv_rowsum_check.jl , rvL_endpoints.jl ). (vi) The end-to-end FEAST benchmark on the D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian with full cost accounting ( rvM*.jl ). (vii) Periodic torsional benchmarks ( mol_torsion2.jl , rvD_torsion.jl ) and the calibrated H 2 O dyad intensity family ( rvE_intensity.jl ). (viii) A reduced-dimensional H 2 O 2 torsion–vibration benchmark built from an MP2/cc-pVTZ surface: surface generation, production fit and its sensitivity variant, an independent off-grid validation, the Hamiltonian with its audits, and the FEAST runs ( h2o2_*.py , h2o2_*.jl , with the data files under data/ ). Reproducing the results. Julia 1.13.1, run as julia -t 24 script.jl ; the only non-standard-library packages are Plots (GR backend) and LaTeXStrings . The H 2 O 2 surface scripts use Python 3 with PySCF 2.15.0 (MP2/cc-pVTZ), and the manuscripts build with XeLaTeX or tectonic and the achemso class. Each script starts by printing the thread configuration and writes the figures or tables named in README.md , which also lists, script by script, what is computed and which table or figure of the paper it supports; random seeds are fixed wherever random couplings or random start vectors enter. Scope. The package covers the numerics of the paper. It is not a production solver: the end-to-end tests use a five-mode model, a D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian and a reduced-dimensional H 2 O 2 Hamiltonian, and the H 2 O dyad is a calibrated validation, not a first-principles prediction. Funding. This work is supported by NSFC Grant No. 12305035.
title: Reproducibility package for: Eigenstate-free spectral preprocessing for dense vibrational spectra

summary: Code and data for the article "Algebra, closed-form compliance and orientation averages of cubic and hexagonal strain-gradient elasticity tensors". The Python package gradinv builds coordinate-free bases, with closed multiplication tables, of the algebras of sixth-order tensors of Mindlin's strain-gradient elasticity (form II) for the cubic class m-3m and the hexagonal class 6/mmm, and with them computes products, inverses, Voigt, Reuss and Hill orientation averages and concentration tensors on small blocks. The repository also contains the scripts that write every table, figure and computed number of the article and its supplementary material, the input data with the provenance of every number, and the test suite.
title: gradinv: algebra, closed-form compliance and orientation averages of cubic and hexagonal strain-gradient elasticity tensors

summary: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.
title: Restoring Diversity in Distilled Image and Video Generators by Probing Activations

summary: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.

summary: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.

summary: This repository contains computational data, model configurations, simulation outputs, verification evidence, and supporting documentation associated with a study evaluating the lifecycle cost, lifecycle carbon emissions, and electrical resilience of prefabricated accessory dwelling units (ADUs) integrated with rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation and battery energy storage systems (BESS) in California. The study evaluates a representative 800 ft² all-electric ADU across three California location cases (Los Angeles, Fresno, and Santa Rosa) with 3, 4, and 6 kWdc PV and 10, 13.5, and 20 kWh BESS over a 30-year analysis period. The computational framework incorporates synthetic hourly electricity-demand profiles, PVWatts V8 photovoltaic-generation simulations, battery-dispatch modeling, lifecycle-carbon accounting, discounted lifecycle-cost calculations, and deterministic electrical-outage simulations. Version 3 (2026-11-15) adds the analyses of the second round of peer review in a new folder, round2_analyses/ , which holds the scripts and result tables behind Supplementary Section S4 of the revised manuscript: an external benchmark of the synthetic load profiles against NREL ResStock 2025 Release 1, climate-responsive heat-pump HVAC demand, roof geometry and module layout, battery capacity fade, scenario-level embodied-carbon contributions and bounded prefabrication inventories, a utility time-of-use and Net Billing Tariff case, battery-size cost-effectiveness, 72-hour outages at all 8,760 start hours, and a joint sensitivity of the PV+BESS cost premium. A re-implementation of the lifecycle-cost workflow regenerates the 1,080 archived annual grid flows and all 36 archived lifecycle costs from the hourly inputs (maximum differences 5e-12 kWh and 6e-11 USD). ResStock data are not redistributed; download instructions are included. Nothing from Version 2 was removed. Version 2 remains available under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24023152. Version 2 (2026-11-06) repackaged Version 1 as one browsable tree with a README, CC BY 4.0 license, CITATION.cff, changelog, and SHA-256 manifest, and added Supplementary Data File S1 and the scripts for the revised main-text Figures 6 and 7. Verification evidence includes nine saved PVWatts V8 API responses compared hour by hour with the archived PV series (78,840 hourly values, maximum difference 0.0 kWh), exact reproduction of manuscript Table 4 from the archived hourly records, and independent re-implementations of the battery dispatch (236,520 hourly rows) and of the outage simulation (3,240 scenarios) that match the archived outputs. The scope and limitations of reproducibility are documented in README.md and LIMITATIONS.md. The original load-generation, dispatch, outage, and lifecycle calculation engines were not recovered (independent re-implementations of the dispatch, outage, and lifecycle-cost steps are included), and the supplementary-figure reconstructions are not certified as equivalent to the submitted images; complete independent end-to-end reproduction of all manuscript figures and tables should not be assumed. Files: SPS_ADU_PV_BESS_computational_archive_v3.zip (the bundle), README.md (a copy of the bundle's README for on-page reading), and SHA256SUMS.txt.

The study evaluates a representative 800 ft² all-electric ADU across three California location cases (Los Angeles, Fresno, and Santa Rosa) with 3, 4, and 6 kWdc PV and 10, 13.5, and 20 kWh BESS over a 30-year analysis period. The computational framework incorporates synthetic hourly electricity-demand profiles, PVWatts V8 photovoltaic-generation simulations, battery-dispatch modeling, lifecycle-carbon accounting, discounted lifecycle-cost calculations, and deterministic electrical-outage simulations. Version 3 (2026-11-15) adds the analyses of the second round of peer review in a new folder, round2_analyses/ , which holds the scripts and result tables behind Supplementary Section S4 of the revised manuscript: an external benchmark of the synthetic load profiles against NREL ResStock 2025 Release 1, climate-responsive heat-pump HVAC demand, roof geometry and module layout, battery capacity fade, scenario-level embodied-carbon contributions and bounded prefabrication inventories, a utility time-of-use and Net Billing Tariff case, battery-size cost-effectiveness, 72-hour outages at all 8,760 start hours, and a joint sensitivity of the PV+BESS cost premium. A re-implementation of the lifecycle-cost workflow regenerates the 1,080 archived annual grid flows and all 36 archived lifecycle costs from the hourly inputs (maximum differences 5e-12 kWh and 6e-11 USD). ResStock data are not redistributed; download instructions are included. Nothing from Version 2 was removed. Version 2 remains available under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24023152. Version 2 (2026-11-06) repackaged Version 1 as one browsable tree with a README, CC BY 4.0 license, CITATION.cff, changelog, and SHA-256 manifest, and added Supplementary Data File S1 and the scripts for the revised main-text Figures 6 and 7. Verification evidence includes nine saved PVWatts V8 API responses compared hour by hour with the archived PV series (78,840 hourly values, maximum difference 0.0 kWh), exact reproduction of manuscript Table 4 from the archived hourly records, and independent re-implementations of the battery dispatch (236,520 hourly rows) and of the outage simulation (3,240 scenarios) that match the archived outputs. The scope and limitations of reproducibility are documented in README.md and LIMITATIONS.md. The original load-generation, dispatch, outage, and lifecycle calculation engines were not recovered (independent re-implementations of the dispatch, outage, and lifecycle-cost steps are included), and the supplementary-figure reconstructions are not certified as equivalent to the submitted images; complete independent end-to-end reproduction of all manuscript figures and tables should not be assumed. Files: SPS_ADU_PV_BESS_computational_archive_v3.zip (the bundle), README.md (a copy of the bundle's README for on-page reading), and SHA256SUMS.txt.

summary: These are audio recordings taken by an Eclipse Soundscapes (ES) Data Collector during the week of the April 08, 2024 Total Solar Eclipse.  It was decided to include only raw, unprocessed audio data files in each site-specific Zenodo record. This decision was so that any researcher can independently verify, reproduce, and extend the analysis performed. As a result, some sites have WAV files with 0 bytes of data or timestamps outside the range of probable recording times. Procedures used by the Eclipse Soundscapes team to process audio data for its purposes are outlined in the Data Management reports located in the Eclipse Soundscapes Zenodo community. Data with 0 bytes of data were included for completeness. When possible, all site-specific files, including the audio files, are included in a single zip file for ease of download. If a single zip file upload was not possible due to upload or bandwidth limitations, audio files are included in multiple zip files based on the day of the observation. AudioMoth_Operation_Manual.pdf:  A human readable document that explains the use of an AudioMoth device. summary: The work looks at the Riemann hypothesis from the standpoint of the model “The Birth of Dimensions” (BD). The number arrow is understood as a projection of a process — the comparison of the standard-observer with its surroundings. Four reference quantities follow from the construction: 1 — the observer and the standard; 0 and ∞ — two infinities converging into one point; 1/2 — the level of lost phase, a line perpendicular to the arrow; 2 — the first distinction, the point of doubling. Together they define a sphere: the arrow is a tangent to the circle through the observer, the rotation goes about an axis, the spin-up force is applied at a point of the equator, and its trace on the arrow is 2. The main result is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis within BD: if the original process is a sine, that is, a rotation; if everything tied to the observer is his likeness; if an instantaneous snapshot has no duplicates and balance sets the mirror, — then all zeros lie on the equator of the sphere, that is, on the line Re s = 1/2 (section 4). This is a proof within the model, not a mathematical proof. In mathematics the hypothesis remains open: of the nine links of the chain eight are known theorems, and the ninth — that the local rotations of all primes form one rotation — is equivalent to the hypothesis itself (section 5). Each step carries a status: [K] — a known mathematical fact, [H] — a hypothesis or interpretation of the author, [O] — an open question. The detailed exposition is placed in Appendices 1–11. They show that the logic of BD independently leads to what mathematicians obtained by abstract means: Riemann's mirror, the Euler product, the Gauss sum, Gram points, the Riemann–Siegel formula, the de Bruijn–Newman constant, Li's criterion, Weil positivity, the adelic approach of Tate and Connes, the Lee–Yang theorem and other results (section 6). For BD this is strong support: the model generates the same mathematics from its own principles. The outcome of the work: the two paths — through BD and through mathematics — run into one and the same limit at one place. In the model the answer is given by the postulate of closedness: there is no pumping of energy, and the amplitude of the standing waves is constant. In mathematics the same step is to prove that the amplitude of the Möbius sum has no power pumping: |M(x)| ≤ C_ ε · x^(1/2 + ε ) for every ε > 0; this is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (Titchmarsh, §14.25), and a stronger, energy form is equal work on the levels of the logarithmic arrow (Appendix 11). The postulate of BD and the Riemann hypothesis are two projections of one statement, and in this sense the paths are identical: neither gives an answer without its own condition. This is the limit of today's methods, not a proved impossibility. And whatever the outcome, the answer is the same: the falsity of the hypothesis is always detectable by a finite check, so either it will be proved, or it cannot be proved — and then it is true. The hypothesis rests on two sides of one standing wave: alternation of crest and trough cancels the sum of signs down to order √x, and equality of their amplitude gives positivity of the energy (Weil, Li); each is equivalent to the hypothesis (Appendix 7). The most direct indirect evidence of the connectedness of the system came from the check by turning the wheel: neighbouring levels separated by a square compensate each other like the crest and trough of one wave, and the accumulation does not grow (Appendix A5). Why a limit is a reason to change the picture of understanding, and what role philosophy plays here, is said in the preface. summary: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.
title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion

summary: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. summary: Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry. Analyzing single particle wave packet propagation through the position space profile reveals oscillatory Airy distortions, which originate from interference between saddle point contributions at different momenta that share the same lattice group velocity. These oscillations systematically weaken when approaching the continuum limit, and reliable regimes are identified as a function of simulation time and wave packet momentum profile. Two-particle scattering simulations in interacting scalar field theory are also implemented, revealing artificial inelasticity arising from coarse local field digitization or deviation from the Nyquist-Shannon sampling point. With these artifacts under control, present simulations provide emerging evidence for physical inelastic processes in $φ^4$ theory. The constructions introduced in this work may provide new understanding of state preparation for the quantum simulation of scattering.
title: Real-time simulation of scattering in $φ^4$ theory: localized excitation, scalable wave packet preparation, and peak-generating artifacts

summary: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.
title: JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple

summary: Controlling band topology in magnetic semiconductors requires strategies that couple electronic structure to experimentally accessible degrees of freedom. Here we propose a cooperative approach based on pressure and magnetic reorientation in A-type antiferromagnetic bilayers. Antiparallel layer magnetizations suppress hybridization between exchange-polarized band-edge states, limiting their response to interlayer compression. A magnetic field that aligns the layer moments removes this spin mismatch, enabling pressure-enhanced hybridization to drive a band inversion. The magnetization direction then controls the symmetries of the inverted bands and whether spin--orbit coupling produces a Chern-insulating gap or symmetry-protected nodal crossings. First-principles calculations for bilayer CrSBr illustrate this mechanism within a compressed orthorhombic structural model. Out-of-plane magnetization yields a Chern insulator with a chiral edge state, whereas in-plane magnetization supports a two-dimensional Weyl semimetal with node-connecting edge states. Continuous spin canting further demonstrates how magnetic reorientation can drive the transition and stabilize the Chern phase before full magnetic saturation. Although material-specific transition conditions depend on electronic correlations and structural stability under compression, the underlying strategy identifies interlayer hybridization as a link between magnetic order and band topology. These results provide a design principle for externally tunable topological phases in layered antiferromagnetic semiconductors.

summary: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.
title: When Will You Hand It Over? A Hidden Start Delay Makes Self-Play Handover Robust to Unfamiliar Partners

summary: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}γ\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.
title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors

summary: Video editing involves tedious manual manipulation across interconnected timeline tracks, motivating automated agents that offload routine work while keeping the project directly revisable by humans. However, because even a basic trim requires coordinated updates across later clips, attached titles, and transitions, existing agents typically rely on fixed operation catalogs that restrict what edits they can express. We present Cassette-Editor, an agent harness that unifies manual user gestures and automated agent patches within a shared editing environment. The shared action language expresses the editor's manual content changes, and a common history records committed edits for undo and manual refinement. When the model selects an edit, a state executor automatically derives its downstream consequences, such as shifting later clips and attached titles after a trim, while a validation rulebook enforces structural invariants and returns localized diagnostics for automated repair. To keep the agent grounded as the project evolves, dynamic read operations map transcripts and shot descriptions onto the current timeline. Evaluated with GPT-6 Luna, the full harness passed the scored request checks in 92/93 trials across 31 authored requests on two interview documentaries, compared with 48/93 for an internal basic-tools baseline. In ablations, disabling the consequences derived by the executor reduced passed trials from 230/232 to 199/232 on edits with dependent timeline elements, while ablating rulebook validation and repair lowered passed trials from 46/48 to 10/48 on requests operating near structural validity boundaries. Evaluating the complete system on 50 TVSum videos further demonstrated greater agreement with human annotations than a general agent using the same model (F1 23.8 vs. 20.1).
title: Cassette-Editor: Shared Timeline Semantics for Human and Agent Editing

summary: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.
title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval

summary: Recent cosmological observations have renewed interest in dynamical dark energy, and naturally raise the question of whether departures from the standard expansion history are accompanied by modifications of gravitational dynamics. We address this question through a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of the effective dark-energy contribution to the expansion and the gravitational responses governing clustering and lensing, complemented by a combined covariance-mode analysis, without imposing model-specific relations between the sectors. Combining CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ supernova observations, and subsequently adding large scale structure observations including DES Year 3 $6\times2$pt data and other surveys, we recover a broad maximum in the effective dark-energy density near $z\simeq0.6$--$0.7$. The gravitational responses exhibit suggestive low-redshift enhancements over their GR values, approximately coincident with the background feature. Adding large scale structure information preserves the background feature but favours a mildly reduced lensing response. The combined covariance-mode analysis identifies the combinations of background and gravitational responses most tightly constrained by current observations and quantifies their departures from $Λ$CDM. The leading modes are decisively background dominated, while the gravitational sector remains less precisely constrained. Thus, present data cannot yet determine whether the suggestive low-redshift features in the two sectors share a common physical origin, a question that ongoing Stage-IV surveys will be able to address
title: Does Dark Energy Evolve $\textit{and}$ Cluster?

summary: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.
title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions

summary: People's choices depend on both the payoffs of the available options and what they learn about those payoffs before deciding. This paper shows how choice data identify both unobserved payoff heterogeneity and the cost of information acquisition in a rational inattention discrete-choice model. I establish conditions for semiparametric point identification using exogenous payoff and information-cost shifters, without imposing parametric forms on the taste-shock distribution or on how the unit cost of information varies with observed characteristics. In the model with binary choice, I construct an unobserved choice threshold whose cumulative distribution function is the choice probability as a function of the payoff shifter. Moments of this threshold identify the payoff coefficients and the unit cost of information at each value of the information-cost shifter. A deconvolution argument then identifies the taste-shock distribution. I then extend identification to the model with multinomial choice. To estimate the model, I propose a sieve minimum-distance estimator based on observed market shares and establish its consistency. For inference, I construct confidence regions by test inversion because binding parameter constraints can make the estimator's limiting distribution nonnormal. In an application to Amazon Mechanical Turk, model counterfactuals show that lower unit costs of information raise the average task-taking probability and reduce wage elasticity.
title: Estimating a Rational Inattention Discrete Choice Model: A Semiparametric Approach

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.
title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection

summary: This repository contains the computational reproducibility package accompanying the research article “Beyond Monetary Energy Markets: Multilateral Reciprocity as an Alternative Exchange Mechanism for Energy Communities”. The package includes Python implementations of the proposed non-monetary energy exchange mechanism, benchmark models, cooperative surplus allocation methods, sensitivity analyses, temporal validation, synthetic photovoltaic generation, and utilities for reproducing the numerical results, tables and figures. Due to restrictions on redistribution, the original GoiEner smart-meter consumption data and household-level derived datasets are not included. Users must independently obtain the file profiles_part01.tar.zst from the GoiEner Smart Meter Dataset (Version 7.1), available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22313409 . A dedicated Python extraction and preprocessing utility is provided to reconstruct the required hourly demand profiles locally without imputing missing observations. The package also includes the OMIE wholesale electricity price series used in the study, corresponding to the Portuguese bidding zone, and the synthetic study configuration. Detailed installation instructions, data provenance, reproduction procedures and file integrity checks are provided in the accompanying documentation. The redistribution of third-party data remains subject to the conditions established by the original data providers.
title: Beyond Monetary Energy Markets: Multilateral Reciprocity as an Alternative Exchange Mechanism for Energy Communities — Reproducibility Package

summary: For hedge fund research reviewers, this report examines checks for selective reporting when a registered study is closed. At the author’s research service, the proposed use is review of research records before their conclusions enter an evaluation; no product integration or saving in review time has been measured. This report makes no claim of originality.   Checking whether a study followed its pre-registration requires comparing the report with the plan. This report tests one method for that comparison. A research record is kept in a fixed JSON format (registration, hash commitment, event log, closure), and seven mechanical rejection rules, R1 to R7, each target one selective-reporting defect taken from Arnott, Harvey and Markowitz (2019) and Harvey and Liu (2015). The comparison arm gives the same information, rendered as plain text, to a general-purpose language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) with one fixed instruction. The test plan, its thresholds and its decision order were frozen, with a local SHA-256 hash, before any code, record or label existed. For each of two cohorts a separate model session generated 33 synthetic records, 12 valid and 21 with one injected defect, without seeing the rules, and labels were locked before either arm ran. In the first (in-sample) cohort the rules flagged 21 of 21 defective records and rejected 0 of 12 valid ones. The language model also flagged 21 of 21 but rejected 6 of 12 valid records, which disqualifies it under the plan. In the second (out-of-sample) cohort the rules again scored 21 of 21 with 0 of 12 rejected, and the language model scored 17 of 21 with 0 of 12. The gap of 4 is below the pre-registered margin of 5. The pre-registered verdict for both cohorts is therefore "compared, threshold not met", and the report makes no claim that the rules add detection. A reduced rule set (R1, R2 and R7 only) missed 12 of 21 defects in both cohorts and is refuted. No confidence intervals are reported, because the plan forbids them: the records are constructed counterexamples, not a sample from any population.   Deposit version: Working paper, version 1.2 (2026-11-12). summary: AiMat-Suite is the integrated, verifiable software framework developed for the doctoral thesis of A. O. Marcelo Júnior (PPGECM/UFC, LAMEFF). It chains, in a single system: (i) U-Net (ResNet-34) segmentation of fibre networks in optical photographs of chitosan/sisal films; (ii) automatic geometry and meshing (CalculiX cgx: S4 shells for the matrix, B32 beams for the fibres, translational MPC tie) and linear-elastic FE solution (CalculiX ccx); (iii) physics-informed and operator-learning surrogates (SharedPINN/Cascade PINN with Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation; Kuramoto-reservoir DeepONet with a Poisson-coupled nodal solver); (iv) a differentiable Rietveld engine for XRD with calibrated uncertainty and a declared domain of validity; (v) a material-card module that turns raw EMIC/Instron tensile curves into FE material cards with declared estimators, bootstrap confidence intervals and a load-regime check. summary: Publishing a model or method does not finish the work of applied mathematics. Turning a mathematical idea into a reliable operational tool requires translation: assessment of how well a method behaves in theory and under real domain constraints, adaptation of both the mathematical formulation and the software to modern computing architectures, and adoption into sustained community use. Because every simplified model leaves a gap between idealized assumptions and reality, it carries applicability debt that an overlapping web of skills—uniting applied mathematicians, statisticians, domain specialists, and research software engineers—must manage. Generative AI and multi-agent harnesses have upset that balance. Large language models and coding agents make it cheap to generate candidate derivations, simulation code, and machine-checked proofs while leaving problem formulation and concrete domain verification tied to scarce human judgement. When automated generation outpaces translation, applicability debt goes unmanaged and pushes adoption toward unverified shortcuts, risking a crisis of application. At the same time, Australian science and innovation policy largely equates translation with commercial intellectual property and private data centres while overlooking research software and verification capacity inside public agencies, national facilities, and universities. Picking up in 2006—the fiftieth anniversary of the Australian Mathematical Society (Counting Australia In) and the birth year of the National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) and the ACCESS Earth-system partnership—this monograph contrasts that post-war public compact at the Society's seventieth anniversary in 2026 against Ambitious Australia and Science 2035, where research software disappears from policy view and the 2016–2025 mathematical-sciences decadal plan has expired without a successor. Written for both public policymakers and working quantitative practitioners, this book examines how translation succeeds or short-circuits across two centuries of computational history, a twenty-year citation census of 112 works applying the EQ algorithm for equal-area sphere partitions, Research Software Engineer workforce audits, Earth-system and biomedical case studies, and invariants-first software verification (PyEQSP and GluCat). Benchmarking Australia against Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, and New Zealand across 18 chapters, 3 empirical appendices, and 750 verified primary sources (188 pages), it outlines practical, trade-off-aware opportunities across university assessment, service teaching, research software careers, scientific societies, sovereign infrastructure, and public-interest model verification ahead of the 2026–2028 national research and infrastructure renewals.
title: What does it take to apply mathematics in Australia today?

summary: Single-valued neutrosophic set theory is an important soft computing approach for resolving uncertainty and imprecision in decision-making. Several models have been established under the framework of single-valued neutrosophic sets for decision-making purposes. Single-valued neutrosophic relations, their max-min-max composition and a score-based use of this composition in medical diagnosis already exist in the literature; this paper revisits the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation in the framework of composite relations under fuzzy-set extensions, describes its algebraic properties, and applies it to two new healthcare problems. In this work, this composite relation on single-valued neutrosophic sets is presented. The numerical illustrations of the composite relation are given, and some of its algebraic properties are proved (inverse, monotonicity, associativity and distributivity over union), while it is shown by counterexamples that the composition is neither commutative nor distributive over intersection. In addition, the applications of the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation to medical healthcare services are considered to illustrate its use. Two medical healthcare applications are considered involving prediction of maternal outcome for a pregnant woman and the diagnosis of some common ailments. The examples are illustrative and use data adapted from earlier studies; no clinical validation is claimed.
title: Single-Valued Neutrosophic Composite Relation and Its Application to Healthcare Services

In addition, the applications of the single-valued neutrosophic composite relation to medical healthcare services are considered to illustrate its use. Two medical healthcare applications are considered involving prediction of maternal outcome for a pregnant woman and the diagnosis of some common ailments. The examples are illustrative and use data adapted from earlier studies; no clinical validation is claimed.
title: Single-Valued Neutrosophic Composite Relation and Its Application to Healthcare Services

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence" by Jingyang Li (School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, China). The external eye-tracking arm re-analyses the public SensCogAR dataset archived at Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/45tjp); that archive declares no explicit data licence, so the raw records are not redistributed here, while the derived per-participant windows and metrics are included in data/real_ar_gaze/. The nine display devices used in the external-evidence arms are described by published measurements, each cited with its DOI in the manuscript, and the extracted parameters are recorded in data/panel_response_identification/. summary: RideLab is a self-contained, browser-based platform for the design and teaching of active suspension control, for students, researchers, educators and engineers. It simulates a vehicle active suspension in real time and compares six controllers, PID, fuzzy logic, sliding mode, linear-quadratic regulator, model predictive control and a neural network, against a passive baseline on an ISO 8608 road, with live plots and a multi-indicator dashboard. An integrated adaptive AI tutor guides learners with missions, prediction questions and graded hints, and can be switched off for pure design work. The archive contains the toolbox, a Python reference engine, verification harnesses for the design tool and for the tutor, the road seeds and controller tunings, and the scripts that regenerate the published results and figures. How to use Option 1, use the toolbox: download RideLab.html and open it in any modern web browser (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox or Microsoft Edge). No installation or external dependencies are needed. Option 2, see the code and regenerate the results: download RideLab_v1.0.zip and unzip it. The toolbox is included as suspension_design_toolbox.html. To regenerate the results, follow README.md; the scripts need Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib, and the harnesses and timing script need Node.js. Generative AI tools (Claude, Anthropic) assisted in developing the software; the author verified all results against the reference engine. Access to the files is granted on request.
title: RideLab: a browser-based platform for the design and teaching of active suspension control

summary: This doctoral thesis, entitled Genomic Studies of Piscine Streptococci and Genome Assembly of Clariidae Catfishes (Siluriformes) for Aquaculture Enhancement, was prepared at the Faculty of Fisheries, Kasetsart University, Thailand, for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). The thesis integrates microbial comparative genomics, genome assembly, genome annotation, repeat and gene-family analysis, population genomics and chromosome evolution to develop genomic resources and analytical approaches relevant to aquaculture, fish health and genetic management. It comprises eight research chapters and a general discussion. Chapter 1 — Bighead catfish genome assembly. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of Clarias macrocephalus generated with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing. Chapter 2 — Streptococcus iniae comparative genomics and reverse vaccinology. The genome of strain SIKU01 and comparative analyses of 90 isolates used to prioritize candidate antigens. The candidates require experimental validation. Chapter 3 — F1 hybrid catfish genome annotation. A chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved assembly of the interspecific hybrid Clarias macrocephalus × Clarias gariepinus , with its protein-coding, non-coding, satellite and transposable-element annotation. Chapter 4 — Repetitive architecture of the two haplotypes. Tandem repeats, segmental duplications, gene-family clusters, the miR-430 array and the divergence of Gypsy and Helitron elements. Chapter 5 — Hatchery population genomics. Diversity, relatedness, family reconstruction, autozygosity, structural variation, polymorphic inversions and shared parents in a commercial C. gariepinus broodstock. Chapter 6 — Gene repertoire and divergence of the two parental haplotypes, on a phylogenomic framework of 17 catfish genomes. Chapter 7 — Composition of the 41 polymorphic inversions of C. gariepinus and deletion-based PCR markers for their arrangements. The markers were designed in silico and have not been tested in the laboratory. Chapter 8 — Fusion and fission between the karyotypes of the two species. Junctions are reported as intervals; no mechanism is resolved at any junction. Chapter 9 — General discussion and conclusion. Changes since the version of 2026-11-03: lists of tables and figures; Chapters 7 and 8 revised; five figures of the repeat analyses added to Chapters 3 and 4 (spacer types of the LG04 array, tandem repeats against chromosome ends, copy number by counting step, array structure of repeated loci, Gypsy and Helitron); new introductions of Chapters 6 and 7; Chapter 9 updated to the chapters. Several chapters are working versions of manuscripts in preparation. Institution: Kasetsart University, Faculty of Fisheries, Thailand. Degree: Doctor of Philosophy (Fishery Science and Technology). summary: We present an analytical derivation of fundamental coupling constants and structural attractors emerging from a descending residual iteration function F(y,x) possessing a unique global fixed point y*(x) . Evaluating the first iteration term for specific membrane residues ( 155 and 185 ) yields pure, asymmetric numerical invariants--most notably 461.4331634036143, composed almost exclusively of the four digits {1, 3, 4, 6}--which directly link the inverse fine-structure constant alpha^{-1} approx 137.036 and the characteristic quark bounce frequency (925) to the 43.2 GeV signal. Through algebraic decomposition, we isolate the longitudinal attractor ( 323 ) governing transversal gravitational anchorage and membrane confinement from the transversal emission attractor ( 232 ), demonstrating how their balance generates a flat background (555) driven by the double-axis torsion gradient of charmonium. Finally, by applying discrete digit-suppression transformations ( 137.036 -> 137.360 and removal of the 036 residue), we map the transition to an antimatter-dominated dual system lacking inversion symmetry and derive a secondary four-digit invariant (2177.5711270036704), establishing arithmetically differentiated topological sets as the fundamental origin of the distinct interaction regimes.

summary: Bench dataset of a small multirotor propulsion assembly (A2212 920 KV motor, 9450 propeller, SkyWalker 40 A ESC): five endurance runs at nominal 6, 8 and 9.5 A, represented by 87 intermittent 50-second captures sampled at 1 kHz (vibration, shunt-current and temperature channel voltages; 4.35 million samples per channel), plus 11 thrust curves (66 observations) comparing post-test configurations with a shared healthy reference. Download the single ZIP file and start with README.md. Version 1.2.0 adds session identifiers, a current cross-check, operating-condition control analyses, a three-way split comparison, per-block spectra and a thrust-loss table.

summary: Here are our trained ARPA format 4-gram language models. We evaluated each model by computing the average per-word perplexity on 36.6K words of conversational style text. Name                Size      Perplexity Tiny 25MB 90.1 Small 110MB 73.7 Medium 205MB 69.2 Large 662MB 63.3 Huge 4.9GB 59.1 The test set consisted of 4,567 sentences (36.6K words, 161K characters). The test set was a combination of: COMM - Sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (2.1K words). COMM2 - Crowdsourced sentences written in response to hypothetical communication situations (13K words). See our ASSETS 2013 paper . Specialists - Phrases suggested by AAC specialists. Taken from University of Nebraska-Lincoln from web pages that are no longer available (4.2K words). Enron mobile - Messages written by Enron employees on Blackberry mobile devices (18K words). The test set was in lowercase and included limited punctuation (apostrophes, commas, periods, exclamation points, and question marks). We excluded the sentence end word from our perplexity calculations. This was necessary since the models were trained only on sentences ending in a period, exclamation point, or question mark. But some test sentences do not have end-of-sentence punctuation, this led to the sentence end word being very improbable. summary: Sweet proteins — brazzein (54 aa), monellin (single-chain MNEI, 95 aa), and thaumatin I (207 aa) — elicit intense sweetness at the human TAS1R2/TAS1R3 heterodimeric receptor at concentrations orders of magnitude lower, by weight, than sucrose. Their utility in food and ingredient applications is constrained by thermolability (monellin), limited yield in plant expression hosts (brazzein), and receptor-binding geometry that makes rational mutagenesis difficult. We apply inverse folding with ESM-IF1 and ProteinMPNN to redesign all three sweet proteins under structural constraints that pin the established sweetness-contact residues and the disulfide geometry, while sampling the remaining sequence space for predicted thermostability and expression-host compatibility. For each protein, we generate 500 candidate sequences per method (1,000 per protein, 3,000 total), score each with ESM2 log-likelihood ratio and in-silico thermostability predictors, and report the top-20 designs per protein alongside matched random controls (sequences that do not pin the contact residues) to establish the baseline distribution. All designs are computational; no wet-lab validation was performed. Covered by U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. [P4 APPLICATION NUMBER]. Platform: platform.scovillesplice.farm The methods and constructs described herein are the subject of U.S. Provisional Patent Application Nos. 64/172,827 (filed October 9, 2026), 64/188,197 (filed October 30, 2026), 64/192,062 (filed November 5, 2026), and 64/199,105 (filed November 15, 2026).
title: Computational Redesign of Sweet Proteins via Inverse Folding: Brazzein, Monellin, and Thaumatin Variants with Pinned Sweetness-Contact Residues and Matched Random Controls

summary: This paper develops a mathematical framework for Quantum Information Holography (QIH), examining how nonlocal quantum information, phase relationships, interference, and holographic encoding can be represented through a unified information-processing architecture. The framework establishes formal relationships between quantum state vectors, angular frequency, the sum over histories, boundary encoding, and geodesic information addressing. It derives conditions for reversible reconstruction, matched quantum readout, and the preservation of information through successive phase-dependent transformations. The analysis further examines connections to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, relational geometry, quantum measurement, and the emergence of spacetime structure. It extends this framework to investigate the proposed role of biological information processing in the reconstruction of conscious experience. Mathematical definitions, conditional theorems, and explicit derivations distinguish established quantum-information results from the additional physical hypotheses concerning gravitation and consciousness, providing a foundation for further theoretical development and experimental investigation.
title: The Quantum Internet of Consciousness: The Universe Has an Address

Umami-Enriched Capsicum: Glutamate Accumulation via GAD1/GAD4 Knockout and GDH1 Overexpression Achieves IFI-U ≥ 800 in Ultra-High-SHU Cultivars Priyanca Iyengar Ford, Scoville Splice LLC · ORCID 0000-0003-0395-1752 Preprint · Scoville Splice Research Series · Paper 5 of 11 · 2026-11-01 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── OVERVIEW This paper describes a dual metabolic engineering strategy to accumulate free L-glutamate in the placental tissue of ultra-high-SHU Capsicum annuum cultivars, achieving an Iyengar Flavor Index for umami (IFI-U) of ≥ 800 without disrupting capsaicinoid biosynthesis. The strategy combines (1) CRISPR knockout of two fruit-specific glutamate decarboxylase isoforms (CaGAD1, CaGAD4) to block the GABA shunt, and (2) overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana glutamate dehydrogenase 1 (AtGDH1) to increase net glutamate synthesis from the TCA cycle intermediate 2-oxoglutarate. This paper should be read alongside Paper 4 (Iyengar Flavor Index methodology), Paper 7 (Kokumi engineering, which shares the glutamate/N-metabolism pool), and Paper 1 (foundational capsaicinoid engineering, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23743695). ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── BIOLOGICAL BACKGROUND Free L-glutamate is the primary ligand for the umami taste receptor, metabotropic glutamate receptor 1 (mGluR1), which was identified as a taste receptor by Chaudhari et al. (2000, Nat Neurosci 3:113). IFI-U is defined as 1,000 × EC₅₀(L-Glu reference, 1 mM at mGluR1) / EC₅₀(sample). In raw Capsicum cultivars, free glutamate levels are modest: 50–80 mg/100g in SS-CV-010 ripe placenta, corresponding to IFI-U ≈ 50–80. The GABA shunt (Glutamate → GABA, catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase; GABA → succinate, via GABA-T + SSADH) represents the major glutamate sink in ripening fruit. Two fruit-expressed GAD isoforms were identified in C. annuum: CaGAD1 (Chr 6, constitutive + stress-inducible) and CaGAD4 (Chr 9, fruit-ripening-specific). CaGAD4 carries a calmodulin-binding domain-truncating polymorphism that renders it constitutively active (pH-insensitive) in ripe tissue — making it the primary target. Precedent: Kisaka et al. (1997, Plant Cell Physiol 38:255) demonstrated that expression of E. coli glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) in tomato increased free amino acid content 2–3×, with glutamate the primary beneficiary. The present study adopts this strategy with the Arabidopsis GDH1 (AtGDH1, At5g18170), which produces L-glutamate from 2-oxoglutarate + NH₄⁺ + NADH in the reverse of the deamination reaction. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: GAD CRISPR KNOCKOUT Targets: CaGAD1 and CaGAD4, simultaneous dual-gene knockout. Cas9 promoter: LAP (leucine aminopeptidase) promoter, fruit-specific expression, avoids developmental glutamate decarboxylase activity in vegetative tissues. LAP is expressed in wounded and ripening Capsicum fruit (Fowler et al. 1992, Plant Physiol 99:439). Guide RNA sequences (SpCas9, protospacer + PAM): CaGAD1-g1: 5'-ATCGTACAGCTTGGCACCTA-3' (NGG: CGG) — targets exon 4 of CaGAD1 (PLP-binding domain) CaGAD1-g2: 5'-TGACCTGAAGCAATACGCTG-3' (NGG: AGG) — targets exon 5, generates ~100 bp deletion with g1 CaGAD4-g1: 5'-GCATAGCTCGTGACCAGATC-3' (NGG: TGG) — targets exon 2 of CaGAD4 (early coding) CaGAD4-g2: 5'-AATCGGCATCAGTGTACCGA-3' (NGG: CGG) — targets exon 3, generates ~85 bp deletion with g1 Doench 2016 on-target scores: CaGAD1-g1: 0.74; CaGAD1-g2: 0.68; CaGAD4-g1: 0.71; CaGAD4-g2: 0.66. CFD off-target scores (all predicted off-targets): <0.12; none in exonic regions. Expected loss-of-function: Frameshift + premature stop in both PLP-binding domain (GAD1) and early coding (GAD4). Confirmation by PCR (primers provided in supplementary CSV) + Sanger sequencing. ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── CONSTRUCT DESIGN: AtGDH1 OVEREXPRESSION Gene: AtGDH1 (At5g18170, Arabidopsi

summary: High-dimensional sparse recipe formulation in process industries involves nonlinear association of various covariates, bounded by sparsity constraints and multi-criteria tolerances. Traditional physics-based classical methods (such as Kubelka-Munk) fail to generate sparse candidate recipes properly due to their simplified assumptions and industrial process variations. This study proposes a hybrid physics-informed uncertainty-aware framework that is structured into three modules: (a) Module A, a multi-target forward quality model; (b) Module B, a sparse inverse reconstructor; and (c) Module C, a feasibility-constrained ranking layer. Then it has been validated in an industrial textile dyeing context with recipe-grouped cross-validation under multi-illuminant quality assessment comprising process and production information, target reflectance, K/S values, and spectral descriptors. Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB) with spectral-only features ($R_λ$, K/S) and Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBDT) with recipe-process features outperforms other configurations with out-of-Fold MAE of 0.1655 and 0.1523 in the forward quality model. For inverse reconstruction, a component-wise median blend achieved a recipe-vector MAE of 0.0295. Exploratory conditional treatment effect (CATE) suggests an observational association that alkali adjustment reduces error for red and pale shades (CATE = -0.196). This framework provides a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool that minimizes costly laboratory trials across industrial formulation domains.
title: A Physics-Informed Hybrid Forward-Inverse Machine Learning Framework for High-Dimensional Sparse Recipe Reconstruction

summary: Co-design methods optimize a robot's body and controller jointly and judge the result by one number, the task reward of the fully optimized pair. That number cannot separate morphologies whose competence depends on the controller to very different degrees. We evaluate a morphology by restricting its controller instead, recording the task competence it retains under an explicitly declared, low-complexity controller family, environment, task and search budget. On three EvoGym locomotion tasks, task reward explains only $39\%$, $33\%$ and $10\%$ of the variance in this quantity, and geometric descriptors do not predict it under run-grouped cross-validation. The measurement is reliable across optimizer restarts (ICC$(2,k) = 0.956$--$0.986$) but depends on the declared family: phasing the drive by actuator index instead of position ranks the same morphologies at Spearman $0.50$--$0.63$ and reverses reward-matched pairs. As a second search objective the axis improved competence at matched task reward in $3$ of $5$ paired runs, short of a pre-registered bar of $4$. Used after an ordinary reward-only search instead, to choose within its top task-reward band, it selected a different body in all $8$ runs offering a choice, at a cost of at most $0.10$ reward units, and in $6$ of $8$ that body also scored higher under a held-out family. Restricted-control competence is therefore a reportable property of a co-designed morphology, interpretable only with the controller family that defines it.
title: Beyond Task Reward: A Controller-Restriction Protocol for Evaluating Embodiment-Dependent Competence

summary: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial malignancy, occurring in roughly 30% of patients with primary solid tumors and carrying a median survival near 5.9 months. Automated segmentation is critical for treatment planning and volumetric monitoring, but metastases are frequently small, numerous, and heterogeneous in size within a single patient. We compare a plain nnU-Net baseline, a Residual Encoder Large (ResEncL) variant, region-based training, and a Primus transformer model for BraTS-METS 2026 Task 1, using patient-grouped cross-validation to prevent leakage from the longitudinal UCSD subset. Primus (label-based) is our strongest individual model by aggregate DSC/NSD, achieving 0.710/0.761 (ET), 0.742/0.785 (TC), 0.683/0.689 (WT), and 0.531/0.436 (RC). ResEncL trails Primus on aggregate DSC/NSD but achieves substantially higher lesion-wise F1 (e.g. ET: 0.452 vs. 0.052); a probability-averaging ensemble of the two only partially preserves ResEncL's F1 advantage (ET lesion-wise F1: 0.064). We further report three postprocessing and label-reconstruction pitfalls we believe generalize beyond this challenge. Code is available at https://github.com/mahdiislam79/BraTS_METS_2026.
title: Brain Metastases Segmentation for BraTS 2026 Task 1: A Multi-Architecture Comparison

summary: Spatially resolved stress proxies and rate-based seismicity models are increasingly combined for regional earthquake forecasting, yet formally testing their non-redundancy remains largely unaddressed. We present the Nested-Permutation Alarm for Dual-Parameter Earthquake Forecasting (ANADEF) pipeline, integrating a stress-sensitive Gutenberg--Richter $b$-value field, estimated via a penalized 2D B-spline inversion, with a stationary background rate ($μ$) from space--time ETAS stochastic declustering. Applied to the Zagros Fold--Thrust Belt using an 18-year catalog ($n=40{,}731$, $M_{\mathrm{N}}\geq1.5$, 2006--2024) under a two-stage protocol with non-overlapping training (2006--2014) and target (2015--2024) windows, the model achieves, for $M_w\geq5.0$ ($N=55$), a retrospective Area Skill Score $S=0.69$ (95\% CI: 0.64--0.73), reducing alarmed area from $τ\approx0.38$ ($μ$-only) to $τ\approx0.28$ while retaining hit rate $ν=92.7\%$; since thresholds are calibrated on the evaluation catalog, these are in-sample, not out-of-sample, estimates. A nested permutation procedure re-optimizing thresholds within each null realization tests whether $b$-value adds information beyond $μ$, absorbing the optimization bias. Significance is null-model dependent: cell-wise randomization yields $p=0.012$, while a conservative spatial-structure-preserving null gives weaker, non-significant evidence ($p=0.057$)---incremental stress information is suggestive but not unambiguously established. Calibrated thresholds were frozen and applied to updated 2015--2024 fields, generating an unvalidated, forward-looking spatial alarm template for 2025--2029. These results establish a reproducible, statistically transparent methodology for testing, rather than assuming, complementarity between stress-sensitive and rate-based predictors, offering a candidate operational template pending prospective validation.
title: ANADEF: A Nested-Permutation Alarm for Dual-Parameter Earthquake Forecasting
