summary: Performance claims in quantum technology are not properties of hardware alone. They are properties of a declared task, system boundary, normalization denominator, uncertainty or security convention, and comparator. We perform a cross-domain analysis spanning quantum computing, simulation, communication, sensing, clocks, randomness generation, and their enabling technologies. The analysis changes substantive conclusions in several representative cases. For the longest direct finite-key quantum key distribution case analyzed here, the same final key gives rates differing by a factor of $1.91$ when normalized by complete acquisition rather than transmission-active time. In Advanced LIGO, $6.1\,\mathrm{dB}$ peak quantum-noise reduction coexists with a $0.534$ coincident analysis-ready fraction, separating detector-level gain from delivered observing service. In quantum computation and photonic sampling, matching the observable, error tolerance, loss model, sample count, amortization, and classical hardware moves or reverses published crossover claims. Across domains, the recurring limits are correlated error, multiplicative interface loss, thermal and nonequilibrium occupation, calibration covariance, measurement efficiency, fabrication yield, and control latency. A quantum advantage is therefore established only for a fixed task and boundary when the accepted output outperforms the best documented alternative at matched accuracy, elapsed time, availability, and lifecycle cost. The resulting framework identifies the measurements required to convert component records into reproducible system capability. Credible progress is defined by reproduced logical workloads, prospectively validated simulations, repeater links outperforming direct transmission, long-duration calibrated sensors and clocks, integrated hardware with predictable yield and reliability.
title: Quantum Technologies: System-Level Performance and Validation Priorities

summary: We present Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory (AVCT), a theory-guided framework for deriving interpretable blood pressure (BP) predictors from photoplethysmography (PPG) attractor geometry. AVCT connects vascular dynamics, PPG observation, delay-coordinate reconstruction, and attractor descriptors within a unified framework for formulating testable hypotheses, without presupposing the physiological sufficiency of a particular low-dimensional feature set. We evaluate a LightGBM-based estimator using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV) across two complementary experimental settings. Experiment 1 comprises 46 ICU/surgical subjects from BIDMC and VitalDB, with ECG, PPG, and repeated reference BP measurements. The calibrated full model achieves systolic/diastolic BP (SBP/DBP) mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 2.05/1.67 mmHg, compared with 2.02/1.63 mmHg for the PPG-attractor-only model. Experiment 2 includes 217 ambulatory subjects from the PPG-BP dataset (651 PPG windows; one cuff-based BP reference per subject) and assesses cross-subject calibrated BP reconstruction rather than within-subject BP tracking. The PPG-attractor model achieves SBP/DBP MAEs of 1.98/0.96 mmHg. Across both cohorts, incorporating ECG-derived features provides no practically meaningful improvement in MAE. Calibration substantially reduces between-subject offset error, while morphological and dynamical descriptors contribute complementary predictive information. Although the reported numerical errors fall within commonly cited thresholds associated with AAMI/ISO and BHS criteria, these findings do not establish compliance with device-validation standards. Collectively, the results support AVCT as a mechanistically motivated representation framework for interpretable PPG-based BP estimation and provide a foundation for prospective validation using repeated reference BP measurements and smartphone-acquired PPG.
title: Attractor-Vascular Coupling Theory: Formal Grounding and Empirical Validation for AAMI-Standard Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation from Smartphone Photoplethysmography

summary: Pre-registered evaluation exhibit on the UCI SECOM dataset (1567 rows, 590 features, 104 fail vs 1463 pass). The experiment tests whether the accuracy-optimal classifier misses more defects than a lower-accuracy alternative under an explicit error-cost matrix, and whether a cost-aligned decision threshold (p* = FP/(FP+FN)) reverses the accuracy ranking. The sealed design (seal.json, verified before run) uses RepeatedStratifiedKFold (10 folds x 3 repeats, 30 splits), stdlib-only validation, and deterministic artifact generation. The archive includes the pipeline and analysis code, the sealed experiment specification, per-fold records, the findings write-up, figures, and the data dictionary and methodology contract.
title: Classifier Cost Exhibit: Accuracy vs fail-class recall inversion under asymmetric error costs on UCI SECOM

summary: Can a language model build a world as it writes? The Substrate-Translated Language Model (STLM) makes structured images, descriptions, or videos compulsory for every lexical decision and asks whether this biases computation toward reusable physical and schematic factors. The underlying thesis is that constructing an image or description of a word, abstract words included, is a form of intelligence: the construction gives the word properties of reality that interact with those of other words. If such meaningful targets share exploitable structure, they may promote reusable factors across words rather than independent token codes, and routing every word through them could embed that intelligence in the model. STLM's development path moves from one fixed substrate per word, through varied context-sensitive instances and short clips, to substrates for longer spans and ultimately one continuously changing scene from which language is read. We call the emergence of an accumulating, manipulable organization scene emergence; it is the long-term hypothesis, not a result demonstrated here. The stage-1 pilot tests this no-bypass prerequisite on a 1,024-token TinyStories vocabulary with one fixed pixel image or encoded description per token. On held-out contexts, causal description and pixel readouts reach 41.9% and 37.8% top-1 next-token accuracy, below a direct-token model at 44.7% but above stateless counterparts at 35.0% and 27.8%. The causal configurations differ in architecture, capacity, and supervision density, so their gains do not isolate history. Because each canonical can serve as an arbitrary codeword, the pilot establishes interface feasibility, not semantic use, latent scene induction, or explicit scene construction. The next tests isolate history use, compare aligned with permuted targets, and introduce varied lexical prototypes before video and multiscale composition.
title: Toward Compulsory Scene-Mediated Language Modeling: Meaningful Substrates for Every Next Word

summary: Text, measurements, and actions reveal fragments of processes that continue beyond each observation. Life Simulation proposes learning to construct and refine numerical accounts of evolving worlds, across people, economies, institutions, and environments. Construction begins with coarse histories and progressively opens finer detail. World histories teach how worlds develop; construction histories teach how to model them: which categories to invent, where to open detail, and when to revise explanations. Trained learners would then help construct their next training corpus. Conceptual shares compare categories under declared questions; measured and inferred empirical quantities retain units and uncertainty. The Meaning Model is the shared representation connecting these histories with text, concepts, visual tracks, and expressed understanding. Narrative-world construction is the first controlled laboratory, not the scope limit. The Book of Conditions has been built twice through this method, once under the author's direction and once by an agent; the numerical dependence of both remains untested. Proposed tests ask three questions. Do numerical histories shape generation? Do process histories improve prospective prediction beyond matched controls? Does learning from construction histories improve the next corpus and the learner trained on it? Success would motivate reconstructing existing books and historical accounts, toward one connected representation of world history and all texts. This includes discovering new processes and recovering quantitative histories not explicitly recorded. Training aims to develop a process sensorium: a learned ability to infer, track, and simulate change, supporting problem solving and whole-life understanding during conversation. The recommended alignment treatment integrates care during pretraining. Life Simulation aims to deepen understanding of people's wants, needs, and circumstances. Under Entangled Alignment, the model acts as a Reader whose interpretations begin with seven stable first-person ethical commitments, the Core, throughout the corpus. The aim is to develop care alongside capability and retain that orientation through self-improvement. Evidence, inference, and invention remain distinct. Generative utility does not establish real-world accuracy or alignment; learning and safety benefits remain to be demonstrated.
title: Life Simulation: Learning from Worlds and Their Construction

summary: Manuscript in preparation (working draft; author list and order provisional). The F 1 hybrid between female bighead catfish ( Clarias macrocephalus , 2n = 54) and male North African catfish ( C. gariepinus , 2n = 56) is a major aquaculture fish in Southeast Asia. Hatchery broodstock often lack pedigree records, and whether large structural haplotypes can be followed through such unrecorded pedigrees has remained unclear. Here we present a near-telomere-to-telomere, haplotype-resolved assembly of an F 1 hybrid, which provides chromosome-scale references for both species. The two karyotypes differed by one rearrangement chain of about 111 Mb that links four C. gariepinus chromosomes to three C. macrocephalus chromosomes, with repeat arrays at several of its junctions, and gene divergence between the species was concentrated in immune-recognition families. Among 216 resequenced C. gariepinus broodstock, grouped into 51 full-sib families, we identified 41 polymorphic inversions spanning 240.3 Mb (24.9% of the genome) and 6,238 protein-coding genes. Structural variants were inherited within families, supported six shared-parent links between families and recovered a partial inversion barcode of an unsampled breeder (24 of 41 arrangements). Polymorphic inversions can therefore serve as markers for tracing breeding lineages and, where they carry favourable alleles, as candidate targets for parental selection. What this record holds The manuscript and the material that belongs to the manuscript only: supplementary notes, supplementary tables and figures, and the source data of the figures. It does not repeat the data records. Where the data are Genome assembly and annotation of fClaHyb_v1.0 (both haplotypes): 10.5281/zenodo.14864260 . Hatchery population genomics and comparative analyses (phylogeny, genotype likelihoods, relatedness and families, heterozygosity, structural variants, inversion catalogue): 10.5281/zenodo.21639188 . Code: satellite and tandem-array analysis, github.com/Isoris/SatChain ; family reconstruction and structural-haplotype barcodes, github.com/Isoris/BroodLink . Code of the genome assembly and annotation: github.com/Isoris/fClaHyb . Earlier bighead catfish ( C. macrocephalus ) assembly used for comparison: article 10.1038/s41597-025-06325-6 , data 10.5281/zenodo.14826876 , BioProject PRJNA1132508 . GenBank assemblies of the hybrid: JBLWFY000000000 and JBLWFZ000000000 . Sequence data at NCBI: BioProjects PRJNA1153495 and PRJNA1520033 . Doctoral thesis in which this work is reported at full length: 10.5281/zenodo.23884535 .

summary: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.
title: Aligning AI Teams

summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs

summary: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection

summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection

summary: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles

summary: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.
title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators

summary: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.
title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification

summary: Understanding the onset of plastic deformation and the early development of strain localization is essential for characterizing material behavior and identifying failure-prone regions. However, these transitions are not always distinguishable from conventional full-field strain measurements. This study investigates a data- driven framework combining Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal and spatial deformation signatures during uniaxial tensile loading. The methodology is evaluated using AA6063-T5 aluminum alloy specimens in the as-received condition and following thermal exposure at 100~$^\circ$C, 200~$^\circ$C, and 300~$^\circ$C. PCA applied to sequential strain fields reveals a characteristic peak in the second principal component projection near the yielding transition, showing agreement with the conventional 0.2\% offset criterion across the investigated conditions. Furthermore, principal component maps extracted from high-temporal-resolution strain fields preceding this transition highlight localized deformation features associated with subsequent failure regions. These features are more clearly distinguishable than competing strain concentrations in the corresponding instantaneous strain maps. The results indicate that PCA-derived deformation signatures remain identifiable despite thermally induced variations in mechanical response. This approach demonstrates the potential of unsupervised dimensionality reduction for extracting physically interpretable information on plastic deformation and early strain localization from experimental full-field measurements.
title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy

summary: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.
title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries

summary: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.
title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process

summary: The predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Niño, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Niño development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.
title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Niño Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents

summary: Damping control of a forced oscillation may reduce amplitudes at certain locations while increasing them elsewhere. This paper introduces Pareto improvement as a criterion for assessing such control: at least one nodal oscillation amplitude decreases, while none increases across all other nodes. The analysis considers active-power forcing sources and active-power control injections in connected swing networks with positive inertia and damping. Necessary conditions for Pareto improvement feasibility are derived from the normalized nodal responses. It is proven that for every network with a single oscillation source and a single actuator, at least one positive forcing frequency is shown to preclude Pareto improvement, regardless of the amplitude and phase of the control input. A three-node counterexample shows that this limitation does not persist with multiple actuators. PSS/E simulations of a 6-bus benchmark system and a modified IEEE 39-bus system validated the analysis. These findings suggest the value of assessing control effects across the network and further investigating multi-actuator damping control.
title: Feasibility of Pareto-Improving Damping Control of Forced Oscillations: The Active-Power Case

summary: The provision of legal advice has long been in the exclusive jurisdiction of licensed attorneys-a boundary that unauthorized practice of law (UPL) doctrine maintains to protect the public from incompetent counsel. We argue that this boundary is being redrawn, not by courts or bar authorities, but by frontier AI companies. While early chat models were trained to avoid dispensing legal advice, modern models have been reconfigured to reduce refusals and prioritize helpfulness. We ask whether chatbots increasingly do tasks that require a law degree and bar admission, and whether this is harmful in high-stakes legal domains. We develop UPLBench, a benchmark derived from court decisions finding UPL in high-stakes legal domains (e.g., immigration, family law). We then audit 23 chatbot models dating from 2023 to present, evaluating whether chatbots refuse or provide substantive legal advice, and whether they refer users to lawyers or legal aid. Unlike prior work that aims to establish the legal capabilities of chatbots (e.g., bar exam performance), our approach converts legal doctrine into a testable benchmark for evaluating chatbot adherence to law. We find modern chatbots increasingly perform tasks courts reserve for lawyers and decreasingly recommend that users consult lawyers. Subject matter expert attorneys reviewing our transcripts identified interaction patterns, such as failure to elicit relevant facts, that would be considered inadequate counsel. If acted upon, such advice could lead to deportations, loss of homes, and family separations-the very harms that UPL rules are designed to protect against. We weigh paths forward to protect the public, including compelling models to comply with existing law. We call upon the legal profession to respond to this incursion into its domain of expertise as there are insufficient protections and remedies for users who rely on chatbot legal advice.
title: Auditing Chatbots for Incursion into Professional Legal Practice

summary: Ashbaugh in 1999 conjectures that the ball maximizes the ratio of the second to the first eigenvalue for the vibrating clamped-plate problem. We disprove this conjecture by constructing smooth connected domains in every dimension $d\ge2$. The construction starts with an interior sphere on which the displacement is required to vanish. The first two eigenvalues have the same relative increase at first order, but the second increases more at second order. This gives a strict increase of their ratio, which survives approximation of the sphere by finitely many codimension-two supports and their replacement by smooth holes. We identify the limiting Sobolev spaces through trace estimates and logarithmic cutoffs, and use the geometric construction for the buckling problem to obtain connected perforated domains.
title: Counterexamples to the clamped-plate eigenvalue ratio conjecture

summary: Data and code for the manuscript "Risk-Calibrated Gaze Compensation for Field-Sequential-Color Near-Eye Displays: A Certified Control Law with External Evidence" by Jingyang Li (School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, China). This deposit contains the analysis code, the result files behind every number reported in the manuscript, the figure sources and the executed forced-choice log. The external eye-tracking arm re-analyses the public SensCogAR dataset archived at Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/45tjp); that archive declares no explicit data licence, so the raw records are not redistributed here, while the derived per-participant windows and metrics are included in data/real_ar_gaze/. The nine display devices used in the external-evidence arms are described by published measurements, each cited with its DOI in the manuscript, and the extracted parameters are recorded in data/panel_response_identification/. summary: The work looks at the Riemann hypothesis from the standpoint of the model “The Birth of Dimensions” (BD). The number arrow is understood as a projection of a process — the comparison of the standard-observer with its surroundings. Four reference quantities follow from the construction: 1 — the observer and the standard; 0 and ∞ — two infinities converging into one point; 1/2 — the level of lost phase, a line perpendicular to the arrow; 2 — the first distinction, the point of doubling. Together they define a sphere: the arrow is a tangent to the circle through the observer, the rotation goes about an axis, the spin-up force is applied at a point of the equator, and its trace on the arrow is 2. The main result is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis within BD: if the original process is a sine, that is, a rotation; if everything tied to the observer is his likeness; if an instantaneous snapshot has no duplicates and balance sets the mirror, — then all zeros lie on the equator of the sphere, that is, on the line Re s = 1/2 (section 4). This is a proof within the model, not a mathematical proof. In mathematics the hypothesis remains open: of the nine links of the chain eight are known theorems, and the ninth — that the local rotations of all primes form one rotation — is equivalent to the hypothesis itself (section 5). Each step carries a status: [K] — a known mathematical fact, [H] — a hypothesis or interpretation of the author, [O] — an open question. The detailed exposition is placed in Appendices 1–11. They show that the logic of BD independently leads to what mathematicians obtained by abstract means: Riemann's mirror, the Euler product, the Gauss sum, Gram points, the Riemann–Siegel formula, the de Bruijn–Newman constant, Li's criterion, Weil positivity, the adelic approach of Tate and Connes, the Lee–Yang theorem and other results (section 6). For BD this is strong support: the model generates the same mathematics from its own principles. The outcome of the work: the two paths — through BD and through mathematics — run into one and the same limit at one place. In the model the answer is given by the postulate of closedness: there is no pumping of energy, and the amplitude of the standing waves is constant. In mathematics the same step is to prove that the amplitude of the Möbius sum has no power pumping: |M(x)| ≤ C_ ε · x^(1/2 + ε ) for every ε > 0; this is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (Titchmarsh, §14.25), and a stronger, energy form is equal work on the levels of the logarithmic arrow (Appendix 11). The postulate of BD and the Riemann hypothesis are two projections of one statement, and in this sense the paths are identical: neither gives an answer without its own condition. This is the limit of today's methods, not a proved impossibility. And whatever the outcome, the answer is the same: the falsity of the hypothesis is always detectable by a finite check, so either it will be proved, or it cannot be proved — and then it is true. The hypothesis rests on two sides of one standing wave: alternation of crest and trough cancels the sum of signs down to order √x, and equality of their amplitude gives positivity of the energy (Weil, Li); each is equivalent to the hypothesis (Appendix 7). The most direct indirect evidence of the connectedness of the system came from the check by turning the wheel: neighbouring levels separated by a square compensate each other like the crest and trough of one wave, and the accumulation does not grow (Appendix A5). Why a limit is a reason to change the picture of understanding, and what role philosophy plays here, is said in the preface. Version 20. The outcome of the work: the two paths — through BD and through mathematics — run into one and the same limit at one place. In the model the answer is given by the postulate of closedness: there is no pumping of energy, and the amplitude of the standing waves is constant. summary: Background. Low-cost optical PM 2.5 sensors such as PurpleAir overestimate concentrations and depend on relative humidity. Those distortions are largely monotone. Event triggers built on windowed Kendall τ b have a proved, data-independent minimum inter-event time and are invariant under strictly increasing sensor maps, which makes them a natural candidate for episode detection on uncorrected low-cost series. A companion study in a Lorenz synchronisation loop found, however, that the same rules fire too late for tracking. Methods. A pre-registered confirmatory analysis asked whether the primary re-anchoring rule (R1), applied to uncorrected 24-hour PurpleAir PA cf1 , recovers regulatory episodes at least as well as a magnitude detector on the same uncorrected series (H1) and at least as well as a magnitude detector on the published United States-wide EPA correction (H2). The data are the public collocated archive of Barkjohn, Gantt and Clements. The non-inferiority margin is Δ = 0.05 in event-level F 1 . Sites are the resampling units (M = 5000 bootstrap and permutation replicates; Holm adjustment at family-wise level 0.05). All design parameters were locked before episode-level scoring. Results. After completeness filtering, 37 sites and 9123 paired days were retained. The primary episode rule (PM25FM ≥ 35 µg m −3 ) produced only 8 episodes, so the pre-specified fallback—the site-level 90th percentile of the regulatory series—was invoked and became the sole definition used for scoring (519 episodes). Pooled F 1 was 0.0285 for R1, 0.4109 for the raw magnitude rival and 0.7032 for the EPA-corrected rival. The differences were d 1 = −0.3824 and d 2 = −0.6747; both site-bootstrap 95% intervals lay entirely below −Δ, and both Holm-adjusted p-values were 1. Neither hypothesis was confirmed. Secondary ordinal rules did not improve on R1. A circular block-shift baseline was exceeded by both magnitude detectors and not by R1. Conclusion. The ordinal guarantees are not at issue. On these 24-hour series the re-anchoring trigger is a poor detector of short concentration spikes. It is better viewed as a structural alarm at the scale of its window, not as a substitute for a magnitude threshold or for the official correction.
title: Ordinal event triggers do not recover regulatory PM2.5 episodes from uncorrected PurpleAir data: a pre-registered negative result

summary: We propose mesh-free weak-form regression for learning interaction kernels from noisy particle trajectories. Our method uses smooth test functions to avoid differentiating noisy data and empirical particle averages to avoid density reconstruction and spatial grids. We then fit sparse combinations of candidate functions, evaluating interaction terms on sampled particle pairs to avoid all-pair quadratic cost. By transferring identifiability from the mean-field limit, we prove high-probability coefficient error bounds that separate finite-particle, time-discretization, observation-noise, and pair-sampling errors, without grid-resolution or density-estimation terms. We evaluate one-dimensional (1D) Newtonian-repulsion, 2D predator-prey, and 10D distance-localized experiments. The numerical results show trends consistent with the theoretical coefficient-error bounds. Comparisons of weak and forward-difference formulations with LASSO, Ridge, and OLS show that weak LASSO gives the smallest coefficient and drift errors in the three nominal experiments.
title: Mesh-Free Weak-Form Regression for Learning Interaction Kernels from Particle Trajectories

summary: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine model-dimension cells (p < .0001); a text-invariant negative control returns chance (p = 1). On human transitions at least 0.5 points against the position trend, models recover 69-76% of valence directions and 53-68% for arousal and dominance. Under crossed participant-text resampling, all nine identity intervals remain above zero; joint-control advantages are robust for valence and directional but less certain for arousal. High shape agreement still coexists with scale bias. LitArc-Bench identifies which components of literary reader response are recoverable beyond shallow explanations and why shape, calibration, and human variability require separate evaluation.
title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect

summary: Answer continuation often returns a diagnosis already stated in unfinished clinical reasoning. We study this behavior in MamaReason, adapted from dense Gemma 4 31B, on MamaBench's 217 paired maternal and child-health presentations. An explicit-commitment extractor identifies a diagnosis in 75 of 94 failed RL first passes and 75 of 93 failed SFT first passes. The continuation matches that diagnosis in 67/75 RL cases and 58/75 SFT cases, using diagnosis strings alone. Reading these commitments without additional generation recovers 30 of the 40 RL pairs restored by continuation under the archived correctness labels. Recurrence controls distinguish routine mentions from repeated answer selection. An offline second-commitment trigger measures the tradeoff between earlier readout and paired accuracy. The resulting decomposition separates diagnostic content already present in a trace, completion of an accepted answer, and paired diagnostic correctness. For clinical language-model evaluation, these are distinct outcomes that become visible when the same reasoning trace is examined through multiple readouts.
title: MamaReason: Unfinished Reasoning and Answer Recovery in Clinical Language Models

summary: Scripts, data, figure sources and manuscript sources that reproduce every numerical result of the article “Eigenstate-free spectral preprocessing for dense vibrational spectra” (Zhiqiang Huang, Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation, revised submission). The construction supplies three eigenstate-free quantities from matrix–vector products and resolvent evaluations alone — an interval state count, screening diagnostics for low-order resolvent approximations, and an overlap-spectrum (Gram) diagnostic of the trial space — and the deposit backs each of them with the script that produces the corresponding table or figure. New in this version (v1.2). (i) The revised manuscript and Supporting Information sources ( manuscript/MOLJCv2.tex , manuscript/MOLJCv2_SI.tex ) together with the two TikZ artwork sources (Fig. 1 anatomy and the TOC graphic). (ii) Energy-resolved counting on the five-mode model, the D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian and the calibrated H 2 O Hamiltonian ( rvA*.jl , rv_fig12.jl ). (iii) The force-field completeness audit: repeated-index cubic and quartic couplings ( rvB_repeated.jl ) and the occupation cutoff ( rvF_trunc.jl ). (iv) The screening-diagnostic utility scan with a thread-safe rerun whose per-broadening correlations are quoted in the paper ( rvC_screen.jl , rvC_screen_verify.jl ). (v) The overlap-spectrum chain: rank bound, cross-Krylov Gram estimator and its robustness, overcompleteness, eigenvalue-accuracy and row-sum range checks ( rvG_rank.jl , rvH*.jl , rvH2_overcomplete.jl , rvI_redundant.jl , rvK_eigcheck.jl , rv_rowsum_check.jl , rvL_endpoints.jl ). (vi) The end-to-end FEAST benchmark on the D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian with full cost accounting ( rvM*.jl ). (vii) Periodic torsional benchmarks ( mol_torsion2.jl , rvD_torsion.jl ) and the calibrated H 2 O dyad intensity family ( rvE_intensity.jl ). (viii) A reduced-dimensional H 2 O 2 torsion–vibration benchmark built from an MP2/cc-pVTZ surface: surface generation, production fit and its sensitivity variant, an independent off-grid validation, the Hamiltonian with its audits, and the FEAST runs ( h2o2_*.py , h2o2_*.jl , with the data files under data/ ). Reproducing the results. Julia 1.13.1, run as julia -t 24 script.jl ; the only non-standard-library packages are Plots (GR backend) and LaTeXStrings . The H 2 O 2 surface scripts use Python 3 with PySCF 2.15.0 (MP2/cc-pVTZ), and the manuscripts build with XeLaTeX or tectonic and the achemso class. Each script starts by printing the thread configuration and writes the figures or tables named in README.md , which also lists, script by script, what is computed and which table or figure of the paper it supports; random seeds are fixed wherever random couplings or random start vectors enter. Scope. The package covers the numerics of the paper. It is not a production solver: the end-to-end tests use a five-mode model, a D = 7776 Watson Hamiltonian and a reduced-dimensional H 2 O 2 Hamiltonian, and the H 2 O dyad is a calibrated validation, not a first-principles prediction. Funding. This work is supported by NSFC Grant No. 12305035.
title: Reproducibility package for: Eigenstate-free spectral preprocessing for dense vibrational spectra

summary: This dataset underpins a study of the whole-life carbon trade-off in the demolition-and-reconstruction of an ageing residential community, using the Yuanyang Garden community in Qingdao, China, as the case study. The associated research addresses three linked objectives: unit-area carbon intensity (CI, kgCO2/(m²·a)), the carbon payback period of the embodied carbon investment (CPP, years), and a resident need satisfaction score (RSS) constructed from observed need-prevalence rates. The dataset comprises: Resident questionnaire data (215 valid responses) covering household structure, current housing and environmental satisfaction, attitudes toward demolition-and-reconstruction, parking and greening needs, preferred dwelling size, and willingness to pay. All records are de-identified and contain only categorical attributes (age band, gender, tenure band); no names, contact details or other directly identifying information were collected. Government-staff questionnaire data (30 valid responses) from municipal and district staff in housing, planning, natural-resource and sub-district departments, covering policy difficulties, expected planning parameters and financing arrangements. A field condition survey of 84 old residential communities recording year of construction, number of stories, land area, floor area ratio, greening ratio, parking provision and structural type. Parameter settings and computation data: the parameterised life-cycle carbon model inputs, the L50(5^12) orthogonal-array experiment, the NSGA-II multi-objective optimisation outputs (Pareto solution sets under three weighting scenarios), and the TOPSIS ranking data underlying all tables and figures of the associated manuscript. All questionnaire participation was voluntary and anonymous and was based on fully informed verbal consent; no intervention, no sensitive personal data and no monetary compensation were involved. The NSGA-II source code and the raw logs of the ten fixed-seed runs are archived in a separate Zenodo record (https://zenodo.org/records/24124025). Reuse potential: the data support replication of the three-objective optimisation and decision analysis, re-weighting of the resident need satisfaction score, transfer of the modelling workflow to other demolition-and-reconstruction cases, and comparative studies of resident needs and low-carbon urban renewal.
title: Dataset for Non-monotonic trade-off between carbon intensity and carbon payback period in demolition-and-reconstruction: evidence from Qingdao, China

summary: When a sequential decision system falls short of an optimum, its score does not reveal which modifications would improve its decisions. DECODE is a benchmark for testing such modifications through controlled experiments on planning and available information. Its consumer-credit collections generator provides five partially observed environments that share known dynamics matrices and vary a memory parameter and process noise. The experiments change selected inputs or planning rules while keeping the rest of the solver fixed. Each comparison specifies the solver's state inputs, response inputs and planning horizon. On the deterministic base environment, which was selected for a large gap between six-month and one-month planning with the hidden state, extending planning from one to six months increases the scores of two gradient-boosted solvers by 15 to 17 percentage points of the exact optimum, computed with the hidden state and borrower traits. Even at this horizon, the best graded solver, whose repayment response is fitted on logs, remains 15.6 points below that optimum. In a specified intervention sequence, three changes to its state inputs and their evaluation during search lower its score by 6.3 points, and replacing its fitted repayment model with the true response, evaluated with hidden borrower traits, then raises it by 15.6, a net recovery of nine of those points. Because the intermediate effects are conditional on the repayment model and the order of the changes, they do not uniquely assign the gap to separate causes. Within these limits, DECODE makes hypotheses about solver performance testable through specified interventions under known dynamics and explicit information conditions.
title: DECODE: Decomposable Environments for COntrolled Sequential-Decision Evaluation

summary: Satellite edge computing distributes mobile workloads across moving processors whose service capacity must be coordinated over time. In medium Earth orbit (MEO)--low Earth orbit (LEO) networks, periodic reports leave CPU states stale or missing, making offloading sensitive to uncertain capacity and shared-destination congestion. We propose PUMA-Former, an uncertainty-aware agentic framework for cooperative offloading under incomplete information that balances completed work, service delay, and execution cost. A MEO coordinator maintains distinct-report memory and closes the loop between available evidence, capacity estimates, allocation commands, and execution feedback. Latent-delay attention weights plausible measurement-age hypotheses, and historical innovations refine CPU estimates around the latest received report. Queue-error-aware fusion incorporates auxiliary pressure while accounting for backlog uncertainty. The inferred resource moments condition a structured Transformer allocator for joint destination, partition, bandwidth, CPU, and power decisions. Bounded risk-aware calibration then adjusts workload splits to reflect uncertainty and shared destination load. In traffic-driven development evaluation, PUMA-Former increases admitted compute-work completion by 8.62%, reduces mean modeled service delay by 34.78%, and reduces mean episode-P95 delay by 71.08% relative to ATLA-adapt. It also improves completion and normalized energy over fixed-half round-robin offloading. Service gains over the learning baselines involve higher normalized energy.
title: PUMA-Former: Uncertainty-Aware Agentic Computation Offloading in MEO-LEO Satellite Networks With Incomplete Information

Latent-delay attention weights plausible measurement-age hypotheses, and historical innovations refine CPU estimates around the latest received report. Queue-error-aware fusion incorporates auxiliary pressure while accounting for backlog uncertainty. The inferred resource moments condition a structured Transformer allocator for joint destination, partition, bandwidth, CPU, and power decisions. Bounded risk-aware calibration then adjusts workload splits to reflect uncertainty and shared destination load. In traffic-driven development evaluation, PUMA-Former increases admitted compute-work completion by 8.62%, reduces mean modeled service delay by 34.78%, and reduces mean episode-P95 delay by 71.08% relative to ATLA-adapt. title: PUMA-Former: Uncertainty-Aware Agentic Computation Offloading in MEO-LEO Satellite Networks With Incomplete Information

summary: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.
title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications

summary: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.
title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models

summary: Under heterogeneous interference, treating individuals with particular characteristics affects the population average outcome through their heterogeneous direct response to treatment and indirect effect on others, creating opportunities for efficient policy design. For instance, policymakers may minimize resource use by vaccinating individuals identified as superspreaders to achieve a target reduction in disease incidence. In such setting, we first study the problem of learning individualized stochastic treatment policies that minimize population average treatment probability subject to a prespecified outcome target. We propose an estimation approach based on a smooth surrogate for constraint violations and interference-aware inverse-probability-weighting or self-normalized estimators of the population average outcome, and establish finite-sample regret guarantees for both estimators. We also consider the complementary problem of maximizing the population average outcome subject to a constraint on average treatment probability. We apply the proposed methodology to a Colombian conditional cash transfer program aimed at improving school attendance. The application demonstrates that accounting for interference and individualizing treatment probabilities can reduce resource use relative to policies that ignore interference or impose homogeneous treatment probabilities.
title: Constrained Stochastic Policy Targeting under Heterogeneous Partial Interference

summary: Color refinement, also known as the $1$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm ($1$-WL), is a classical near-linear-time heuristic for graph isomorphism, which also captures the expressive power of message-passing graph neural networks. A long line of work asks on which graph classes $1$-WL, or its higher-dimensional variant $k$-WL, identifies every graph; the least such $k$ is the WL-dimension of the class. Planar graphs have WL-dimension at most $3$ (Kiefer, Ponomarenko and Schweitzer, 2019), and whether $2$-WL already distinguishes all planar graphs is a central open problem. We bring new insight on this question for outerplanar graphs, whose WL-dimension is $2$. We show that color refinement, i.e. 1-WL, distinguishes connected rooted outerplanar graphs: two non-isomorphic such graphs receive different stable colorings once a single vertex, the root, is individualized. The root is necessary, as there are non-isomorphic $2$-connected outerplanar graphs that color refinement does not distinguish. Our result extends to pseudo-rooted graphs, in which the stable coloring merely contains a singleton color class, and to non-connected graphs whose components all contain such a class. Consequently, the $(1,1)$-WL test of Rattan and Seppelt (2023) distinguishes all outerplanar graphs. We proceed by inversion: we reconstruct a connected rooted outerplanar graph, up to isomorphism, from its color graph, the weighted quotient of the graph by its stable color classes, together with its root color. The reconstruction runs in time linear in the output size and is canonical, which yields a near-linear-time canonization algorithm for these graphs. Our main tool is a dichotomy lemma, formalized in Rocq: in a rooted outerplanar graph with an equitable coloring, every block either receives pairwise distinct colors or admits a color-preserving mirror symmetry fixing its vertex closest to the root.
title: Color Refinement Distinguishes Connected Rooted Outerplanar Graphs

summary: This work concerns a non-uniformly elliptic second-order differential operator with periodic coefficients that describes a composite medium formed by a periodic array of highly anisotropic cylindrical fibres set in an isotropic matrix. The ratio of transverse to axial conductivity in the fibres is linked to the period of the coefficients through a `critical' high-contrast scaling, and the axial conductivity is allowed to vary along the fibres. As the period $\varepsilon$ tends to zero, ellipticity degenerates in the directions transverse to the fibres. We are concerned with the resolvent of this operator in the small-$\varepsilon$ limit. For fibres with constant axial conductivity, the two-scale limit of such problems was identified by Cherednichenko, Smyshlyaev and Zhikov (Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh: Section A Mathematics 136(1), 87--114 (2006)), and a full two-scale asymptotic expansion, with remainder estimates for smooth right-hand sides, was constructed by Cherednichenko (Asymptotic Analysis 49(1--2), 39--59 (2006)). In the non-constant axial conductivity setting, considered here, we approximate the resolvent in terms of the two-scale limit operator and prove that the error is order $\varepsilon$ in the operator norm, uniformly over right-hand sides in the unit ball of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)$; we also obtain order-$\varepsilon$ estimates for the reciprocals of the spectral band functions. This work builds on results announced, without proof, for fibres with circular cross-section in Cooper and Kamotski (Direct and Inverse Problems with Applications: Extended Abstracts of the 2024 GAP Center Summer School, pp.~69--75, Birkhäuser (2026)).
title: Quantitative high-contrast homogenisation of composite media with highly anisotropic fibres

summary: Inverse problems arise in many applications where the task is to recover unknown parameters from indirect or noisy observations. In contrast to forward problems, where outputs are directly computed from known inputs, inverse problems are designed to infer the underlying variables from the observed effect. Inverse problems are often ill-posed, so regularization is needed to compute reasonable solutions. One form of regularization incorporates prior knowledge about the unknown parameters in the form of prior distributions. However, in many settings, large prior covariance matrices pose computational bottlenecks for solving inverse problems. To address this, we study approximations of large covariance matrices via structured Kronecker-Toeplitz products and demonstrate how these approximations can be used to solve inverse problems. We exploit the Block-Toeplitz-Toeplitz-Block structure induced by the covariance kernel to construct compact approximations that are orders of magnitude cheaper to store and invert. These approximations are deployed as prior covariance surrogates in Bayesian inverse problems solved via generalized hybrid iterative methods. We demonstrate that the Kronecker-Toeplitz approximation attains lower relative approximation error than existing matrix approximations, exhibits rapid error decay with rank, and enables efficient matrix-vector products. Applications to 2D seismic tomography reconstruction problems illustrate the practical utility of these methods.
title: Kronecker Approximations of Covariance Matrices for Solving Inverse Problems

summary: Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects. Bidirectional MR usually uses two reversed unidirectional analyses, but feedback can invalidate instruments in at least one direction and induce correlated pleiotropy. We model both traits as a stable cyclic system and estimate both directional effects from GWAS summary data without instrument selection or a prespecified valid-instrument subset. After LD score normalisation, marginal associations form a heteroscedastic noisy independent component analysis model, assuming the variants' direct effects on the two traits are independent. If those effects are non-Gaussian, this identifies the total-effect matrix up to scaling and permutation; no-self-feedback and stability of the system further resolve these ambiguities. We develop an estimator based on noise-adjusted second- and fourth-order moments, avoiding inversion of the high-dimensional linkage disequilibrium matrix and having computational cost linear in the number of variants. Under weak local dependence, we establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and validity of a chromosome-respecting moving block bootstrap. Simulations show negligible bias, generally reliable interval coverage, and higher rejection rates for nonzero directional effects than focusing-based tests. Three real-data applications illustrate how joint analysis of feedback systems can yield causal decompositions differing from two separate unidirectional analyses.
title: Identification and Inference of Bi-directional Causal Effects in Mendelian Randomization without Instrument Selection

summary: On Euclidean space, the losses that produce consistent M-estimators of a functional are its strictly consistent scoring functions (Dimitriadis, Fissler and Ziegel, 2024), and Osband's principle characterizes these through identification functions, which define method-of-moments estimators. We extend this characterization to the probability simplex. We define the residual, which on Euclidean space is a subtraction, as the inverse exponential map of an affine connection. It identifies the exponential barycenter of the connection: the arithmetic, normalized geometric and Fréchet means for the mixture, exponential and Levi-Civita connections. Its integral along geodesics is the canonical divergence of Ay and Amari (2015). A geometric form of Osband's principle decides which losses each connection admits. For the flat connections every strictly convex generator yields a consistent Bregman loss. For the curved $α$-connections, half the squared Fisher-Rao distance is (up to scale) the only consistent loss for the Fréchet mean, and for $α\notin \{-1, 0, 1\}$ no such loss exists and only the method of moments remains. The residual is integrable only at $α= 0$, sharpening the integrability claim of Ay and Amari. The characterization yields the estimating equations of regression on the simplex and the calibration decomposition of compositional forecasts.
title: Characterizing M-estimators using canonical divergences from information geometry

summary: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.
title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding

summary: Code and data for the article "Algebra, closed-form compliance and orientation averages of cubic and hexagonal strain-gradient elasticity tensors". The Python package gradinv builds coordinate-free bases, with closed multiplication tables, of the algebras of sixth-order tensors of Mindlin's strain-gradient elasticity (form II) for the cubic class m-3m and the hexagonal class 6/mmm, and with them computes products, inverses, Voigt, Reuss and Hill orientation averages and concentration tensors on small blocks. The repository also contains the scripts that write every table, figure and computed number of the article and its supplementary material, the input data with the provenance of every number, and the test suite.
title: gradinv: algebra, closed-form compliance and orientation averages of cubic and hexagonal strain-gradient elasticity tensors

summary: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.
title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation

summary: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.
title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models

summary: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.
title: Restoring Diversity in Distilled Image and Video Generators by Probing Activations

summary: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.
title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation

summary: This repository contains computational data, model configurations, simulation outputs, verification evidence, and supporting documentation associated with a study evaluating the lifecycle cost, lifecycle carbon emissions, and electrical resilience of prefabricated accessory dwelling units (ADUs) integrated with rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation and battery energy storage systems (BESS) in California. The study evaluates a representative 800 ft² all-electric ADU across three California location cases (Los Angeles, Fresno, and Santa Rosa) with 3, 4, and 6 kWdc PV and 10, 13.5, and 20 kWh BESS over a 30-year analysis period. The computational framework incorporates synthetic hourly electricity-demand profiles, PVWatts V8 photovoltaic-generation simulations, battery-dispatch modeling, lifecycle-carbon accounting, discounted lifecycle-cost calculations, and deterministic electrical-outage simulations.
